Enable JavaScript for the animation. The worked example below gives the same documented procedure.

#### Why This Matters

Decryption must reconstruct cell lengths before filling columns. Following a complete original example makes conventions observable: a changed boundary, pairing rule or final cell changes the ciphertext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

AMSCO belongs to the American Cryptogram Association’s repertoire of hand-solvable transposition puzzles. This exhibit uses the [ACA specification and complete worked example](<https://www.cryptogram.org/downloads/aca.info/ciphers/Amsco.pdf>), printed p. 32 of its Cipher Exchange Guidelines. The sheet permits either a single letter or a digraph in the first cell.

The specification is not a dated military operating manual. It does not establish a particular invention date or operational deployment, so this page does not invent one. Its educational value lies in a small change to [columnar transposition](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html>) that makes decryption geometry less obvious.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Exact ACA Procedure

- Choose a permutation of the column ranks. This demo uses 41325: physical columns are read in order 2, 4, 3, 1, 5 (ranks 1–5).

- Choose the starting cell length: two letters by default here, as in the worked example. Fill left to right, alternating digraph and single-letter cells. Alternate the starting length on each new row as well. Thus the first column also alternates.

- If text ends inside a digraph cell, leave that final cell with one letter. Do not append null letters or fill later cells.

- Read each column from top to bottom, in ascending rank order.

- To decrypt, use the ciphertext length, column count and first-cell convention to reconstruct the cell geometry and actual final-cell length. Calculate each column’s capacity, fill columns in rank order, then read cells by rows.

For an even number of columns, alternating the first cell on the next row matters: a continuous alternation through a flattened list of cells implements a different cipher.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

ACA Worked Example

Key `41325`, digraph first. The first row is `IN | C | OM | P | LE`; the second is `T | EC | O | LU | M`. The final row is incomplete: `A | PH | S`. The prepared message has 57 letters.

```text
Plaintext:
INCOMPLETECOLUMNARWITHALTERNATINGSINGLELETTERSANDDIGRAPHS

Ciphertext:
CECRTEGLENPHPLUTNANTEIOMOWIRSITDDSINTNALINESAALEMHATGLRGR
```

This complete answer is transcribed from the ACA sheet. An additional hand-derived even-width check uses key `12`, digraph first: `ABCDEF` makes rows `AB | C` and `D | EF`, yielding `ABDCEF`.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Cryptanalysis and Limits

AMSCO preserves letters and their frequencies. A solver has to discover the width, column order and initial cell length, then judge reconstructed neighbouring letters. Probable words, anagramming and scored permutation search are applicable transposition attacks. There is no claim here of a named wartime break: the cited ACA sheet specifies a puzzle, not an operational cryptanalytic history.

For a fixed width n, the rank order has n! possibilities and there are two starting-cell conventions. This is a settings count, not a security estimate; language structure provides information that exhaustive counting ignores.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Reconstruction and Teaching Limits

The engine implements the ACA’s cell-length convention and exact incomplete-row reconstruction. Both first-cell conventions are selectable. It needs a genuine permutation, with no repeated or missing ranks: use 2–25 columns in this interface. Ranks greater than nine must be space-separated.

Case folding, accent stripping and nonletter removal are stated input conveniences. No escape sequence or padding is introduced, and decryption returns the normalized letters rather than the original punctuation. Animated cell boundaries show why the receiver must reconstruct geometry before inserting ciphertext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

| Family | Variable-cell columnar transposition |
| Key | Permutation of column ranks; first cell length |


Sources and Further Reading

[American Cryptogram Association, *AMSCO*](<https://www.cryptogram.org/downloads/aca.info/ciphers/Amsco.pdf>), Cipher Exchange Guidelines, printed p. 32: normative cell convention, 41325 key and complete worked example. The sheet is undated.

The diagrams are this site’s original rendering. Factual example strings are credited to ACA; no PDF scan, source artwork or extended source quotation is reproduced.

### Arabic Nomenclators

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Arabic scholarship preserves an early systematic account of frequency-based cryptanalysis.

Broken (by its own inventors)

RegionAbbasid Caliphate (Baghdad, House of Wisdom)

Era~750-1350 CE

Key Figureal-Kindi (~801-873 CE)

Landmark Text*Risalah fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma* (Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages)

Modern LessonCryptanalysis is the indispensable counterweight to cryptography

#### Why This Matters

Al-Kindi’s ninth-century treatise is the earliest surviving systematic account of frequency-based cryptanalysis commonly identified in histories of the subject. It is important evidence of Arabic cryptanalytic scholarship. It does not establish a 500-year monopoly, nor prove that every later cryptanalytic method descended directly from one text.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Administrative and diplomatic communication supplied settings for secret writing in the medieval Islamic world. Surviving Arabic works discuss ciphers and methods of solving them. The generic nomenclator below is a modern teaching model; without an identified historical key, it must not be treated as a reconstruction of a particular Abbasid chancery system.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How a Nomenclator Worked

A nomenclator combines a letter substitution with entries for names or words. Some systems also include nulls and homophones. These features vary by key: neither their presence nor their strength should be assumed for every Arabic chancery. A larger table can complicate analysis without making it immune to language patterns.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

Al-Kindi's Frequency Analysis

Statistical cryptanalysis

Method: language statistics and contextual hypotheses

Al-Kindi describes comparing symbol frequencies with those of the message’s language, alongside linguistic reasoning. A frequency ranking is a starting hypothesis, not a rule that the most common symbol must always be the same letter. This is an early documented method, not a polynomial-time solution to every cipher in every human language.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Why Baghdad?

Arabic scholarship combined mathematical and linguistic traditions. Its development spanned different places and centuries: al-Khwarizmi’s ninth-century algebra and Ibn al-Haytham’s later optics should not be compressed into one simultaneous House of Wisdom invention of “the experimental method.”

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Hall | I · World Origins |
| --- | --- |
| Region | Abbasid Baghdad |
| Era | ~750-1350 CE |
| Key Figure | al-Kindi |
| Innovation | Frequency analysis |
| Treatise | *Risalah* (~850 CE) |
| Comparison | Later European nomenclators; direct transmission is not established here |
| Lasting impact | Early documented statistical cryptanalysis |

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapters 2–3, on Arabic cryptanalytic scholarship and the uncertainty of its transmission to Europe. Al-Kindi’s surviving treatise supports a history of frequency analysis, not a claim to solve all ciphers efficiently.

Hall II · Substitution Renaissance Italy · 1500s–1600s

### Argenti Family Cipher Vatican papal nomenclators · 1500s–1600s

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Papal cipher specialists whose surviving manuscripts document the craft of Renaissance nomenclators.

DesignersGiovanni Battista Argenti & his nephew Matteo Argenti

EmployerPapal cipher office, late 1500s–early 1600s

TreatiseSurviving cipher manuscripts and compilations

MechanismHomophonic substitution + nomenclator + nulls

StatusStandard Vatican system into the 17th century

#### Why This Matters

Giovanni Battista Argenti and Matteo Argenti served the papal cipher office in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Surviving keys and manuscripts document their work on diplomatic ciphers. Matteo succeeded his uncle Giovanni Battista in 1591; Marcello was Matteo’s younger brother, not his nephew.

Matteo’s manuscripts discuss homophones, nulls, codewords, and cryptanalysis. Aloys Meister published papal cryptographic material in 1906. [Satoshi Tomokiyo’s source-based analysis](<https://cryptiana.web.fc2.com/code/polyalphabetic.htm>) distinguishes Matteo’s service in 1591–1605 from his later compilation of material. These techniques were not all invented at once in a 1591 handbook.

Nomenclators remained important in European diplomacy for centuries, with substantial variation among keys and administrations. The Argenti documents are valuable examples, not evidence that every later chancery or the earlier Babington correspondence copied a single Argenti pattern.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

An Argenti cipher has three layers stacked on top of one another:

- **Homophonic alphabet.** Each plaintext letter is assigned several cipher symbols (typically 2–4 for common letters, 1–2 for rare). The choice among those symbols depends on the key and procedure; rotation in the widget below is a teaching convention.

- **Nomenclator.** A short list of named persons, places, offices, and frequent words gets dedicated codes that bypass the alphabet entirely — “the Pope”, “the Emperor”, “Paris”, etc.

- **Nulls.** Meaningless symbols sprinkled at agreed positions to confuse a cryptanalyst counting frequencies.

The demo alternates between two numeric homophones per letter. This is a deliberately simple model of multiple representations, **not an exact Argenti key or selection procedure**. Giving every letter equally many homophones does not flatten its combined language frequency. Try `AAAAAA` with the demo seed `ARGENTI`: it produces `66 40 66 40 66 40`. These numbers belong to this invented teaching key.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Single-letter frequency attack (limited)

Complexity: Very high against a properly-designed nomenclator

When each letter has two homophones, their combined counts retain the letter’s frequency. Analysts can test groupings using context and probable words. Length influences the available evidence, but there is no blanket rule that every long note falls and every short diplomatic note is safe.

Compromise of the codebook itself

Complexity: Espionage problem, not cryptanalytic

A stolen keylist can expose messages independently of cryptanalysis. The sources identified here do not establish that capture was the most frequent cause of compromise for every nomenclator or that the Vatican followed a uniform annual replacement cycle.

Eventually obsolete

Later cryptanalysis and changing practice

Wallis and other professional analysts attacked diplomatic nomenclators, but their use did not end around 1700. Codebooks and related mixed systems continued alongside other methods well beyond that date.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Argenti lesson | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| Homophones split letter counts; higher-order patterns can remain | Compare statistical leakage with ECB’s repeated-block leakage; homophones provide no authentication |
| Layered defences (alphabet + nomenclator + nulls) | Defence in depth: cipher + MAC + nonces + key rotation |
| Regular replacement of compromised or overused keys | Modern key-management policies set lifetimes appropriate to the system and threat |
| Best-in-class systems still need cryptanalysts to validate them | Independent academic review; NIST competitions; open-source scrutiny |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

Research Trail

For the Vatican cryptographic tradition, David Kahn's chapter on papal ciphers remains the standard narrative entry point, but the best specialist trail runs through Satoshi Tomokiyo's *Cryptiana* essays and archival notes on early-modern nomenclators. Use this exhibit alongside [Wallis Ciphers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/wallis-ciphers.html>) and [Mary Stuart's Castelnau letters](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/mary-stuart-castelnau-letters.html>) to follow the same diplomatic cipher family across three centuries.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Designers | Giovanni Battista Argenti & his nephew Matteo Argenti |
| --- | --- |
| Employer | Papal cipher office, late 1500s–early 1600s |
| Treatise | Surviving cipher manuscripts and compilations |
| Mechanism | Homophonic substitution + nomenclator + nulls |
| Status | Standard Vatican system into the 17th century |

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 3, “The Rise of the West,” on Giovanni Battista, Matteo and Marcello Argenti. The interactive codebook is a teaching model, not a transcription of a papal key.

Hall V · American Field American Revolution · 1779–1780

### Arnold–André Book Cipher Book codes · 1779–1780

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Book codes concealed parts of the correspondence; André’s capture exposed documents about West Point.

Compromised by capture (1780)

OperatorsMajor General Benedict Arnold & Major John André (British Army)

Year1779–1780 (coded correspondence survives from June 1779)

BookBlackstone’s *Commentaries on the Laws of England* (also Bailey’s *Dictionary*)

FormatTriple page.line.word, e.g. `27.4.6` = page 27, line 4, word 6

CompromiseAndré captured 23 Sept 1780 with incriminating West Point documents

#### Why This Matters

Arnold negotiated with the British through John André, offering to deliver West Point. Their secret correspondence is an important example of the relationship between book codes and operational concealment. A cover name or cipher convention should be tied to a particular surviving letter rather than invented to make the story vivid.

The correspondence used several book codes. Kahn describes an initial scheme based on volume I of the fifth Oxford edition of William Blackstone’s *Commentaries on the Laws of England*, followed by Nathan Bailey’s dictionary and then a smaller, unidentified dictionary. The codes changed; they should not be presented as one fixed reference book throughout the affair.

André was captured near Tarrytown on September 23, 1780, carrying documents concerning West Point. He was executed on October 2; Arnold escaped. The [New York State Archives’ documentary exhibition](<https://www.nysarchivestrust.org/exhibits/treason-during-american-revolution/capture>) supports the capture account. It does not establish the additional claim that the cipher’s reference book or key was found in his boot.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Both correspondents own identical copies of an agreed reference book. To encrypt a word, the sender finds it in the book and writes down a triple `page.line.word`. To decrypt, the receiver looks up that triple in their own copy and recovers the plaintext.

The reference book may be public, but its identity, edition, and indexing convention can be secrets shared by the correspondents. A published book is still key material in that role, and both search and capture may compromise it. Merely searching a courier does not automatically reveal every missing parameter.

In the Blackstone scheme, words absent from the book could be spelled using letter positions, marked by a stroke through the final number. Later dictionary arrangements used different conventions. The particular book, edition and procedure must therefore be identified before a numeric group can be interpreted.

The demo above uses a deterministic 240-word “book” organised as 12 pages × 5 lines × 4 words. Words not in the book fall through to per-letter triples on “page 14”, bracketed by sentinel triples `13.1.1` and `15.1.1` — invented software conventions, not historical Arnold–André procedures.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Compromised

Capture of the courier (23 September 1780)

Complexity: Three militiamen, an unscheduled patrol

André was returning from West Point in civilian clothes; the circumstances of his mission and capture led to his trial as a spy. John Paulding, David Williams, and Isaac Van Wart stopped him near Tarrytown, found the documents in his boot, and turned him over to the Continental Army. He was tried, convicted, and hanged within ten days.

Document capture exposed the plot

Evidence: captured West Point documents; no key capture established here

The documented capture exposed incriminating documents. That is different from proving that all earlier cipher correspondence was deciphered using a captured key. Book-code security depends on the chosen text, conventions, traffic, and attacker knowledge; it cannot be certified from this operational episode.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Arnold–André lesson | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| Public reference as the key | A public text can be selected through a secret agreement; a public root certificate has a different role |
| Single point of failure (the courier) | A compromised delivery path can expose metadata and physical documents |
| Document capture versus cryptanalysis | Operational failure and mathematical cryptanalysis are different attack routes |
| Compromise of documents in transit | A physical search can expose documents even without recovering a cipher key |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

Research Trail

Satoshi Tomokiyo's *Cryptiana* notes on the Arnold-André correspondence are among the clearest specialist introductions to how Revolutionary-era book ciphers were actually organised on the page. They pair well with this exhibit because they show the operational side of book codes rather than only the treason narrative.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Exhibit 41 of 174 Ancient · ~500 BC

### Atbash

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Hebrew alphabet reversal, demonstrated with a modern A↔Z, B↔Y adaptation

Inspection (it is its own inverse)

OriginHebrew scribes (Book of Jeremiah)

Year~500 BC

Key TypeNone (fixed reflection)

Broken ByInspection (it is its own inverse)

Modern LessonCiphers without keys offer no security

#### Why This Matters

Atbash reverses an alphabet. In the modern Latin adaptation shown here, A maps to Z, B to Y, on through M↔N. It appears inside the Hebrew Bible — the prophet Jeremiah uses Atbash to disguise the names BABEL and KASDIM as SHESHACH (Jeremiah 25:26 and 51:41) and LEB-KAMAI (Jeremiah 51:1). Its self-inverse mapping offers a mathematical comparison with later reciprocal systems; a direct historical lineage is not established.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Atbash reverses a fixed alphabet and is its own inverse: applying the same mapping twice restores the input. Enigma and XOR-based systems also have reciprocal properties, but this shared mathematics does not show that their designers inherited the mechanism from Atbash. Biblical uses need not have served the same purpose as a modern secret-key cipher.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Replace each letter with its mirror across the alphabet:

```text
A B C D E F G H I J K L M
| | | | | | | | | | | | |
Z Y X W V U T S R Q P O N
```

So HELLO → SVOOL. Encrypt twice and you are back where you started.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Recognition

Complexity: Trivial

There is no key. Anyone who recognizes the system can decrypt instantly. Frequency analysis is not even needed — the unique letter pattern of A↔Z reflection is visible at a glance once a reader knows the trick.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Atbash | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Self-inverse operation | XOR in modern stream ciphers — same operation encrypts and decrypts |
| Reflector concept | Enigma's Umkehrwalze (reflector) made the machine reciprocal |
| Security through obscurity fails | Kerckhoffs' principle: only the key should be secret |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 41 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Era | Ancient · ~500 BC |
| Trust | Broken |
| Origin | Hebrew scribes (Book of Jeremiah) |
| Year | ~500 BC |
| Key Type | None (fixed reflection) |
| Broken By | Inspection (it is its own inverse) |
| Modern Lesson | Ciphers without keys offer no security |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

Culture Link: Atbash in Modern Fiction

Atbash appears repeatedly in puzzle fiction because it is both discoverable and dramatic. See Hall XIII's [Da Vinci Code exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/da-vinci-code.html>) for how simple substitution layers are staged as "ancient mysteries" in modern thriller narratives.

*The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, David Kahn (revised edition, 1996), “The First 3,000 Years”: Hebrew alphabet reversal and the Jeremiah examples. The A–Z mapping shown here is a modern adaptation.

Renaissance · 1586

### Autokey

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Vigenère's self-extending key — the message becomes its own key.

Crib propagation and language-scored searches; ordinary repeating-key Kasiski analysis does not apply directly.

OriginBlaise de Vigenère (1586), refining Bellaso/Cardano

Year1586

Key TypeShort keyword, then plaintext itself extends the key

Broken ByCrib propagation and statistical analysis

Modern LessonSelf-keyed schemes still leak: the key is no longer random once it carries plaintext statistics

#### Why This Matters

Plaintext autokey extends a primer with the message itself. It avoids cycling a short keyword at a fixed period, but letters and passages can still repeat. This changes the attack surface rather than proving 350 years of field security. Joshua Holden’s [*The Mathematics of Secrets: Cryptography from Caesar Ciphers to Digital Encryption*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#holden>) (2017), §5.3, distinguishes several historical self-keying constructions.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Cardano, Bellaso, and Vigenère discussed different self-keying and polyalphabetic ideas. The familiar repeating-key “Vigenère” cipher is associated with Bellaso’s 1553 work; Vigenère’s 1586 book included autokey constructions. The widget teaches the specified keyword-plus-plaintext model, rather than reproducing every feature of those historical systems.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Pick a short keyword K. Encrypt the first |K| plaintext letters with K under a Vigenère shift. Then take the plaintext itself, prepend K, and use that string as the running key for the rest of the message. Decryption recovers K-many letters first, then uses those recovered plaintext letters as the key for the next stretch — and so on. There is no fixed cycled keyword after the primer. The appended message still contains language structure and may repeat.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Crib Propagation

Crib propagation is straightforward; finding a correct crib or primer can require substantial search

The extended key is related to the plaintext and is not independent random material. A guessed plaintext letter reveals a later key letter, allowing the guess to propagate at a distance equal to the primer length. Crib testing and language scoring can exploit this structure; there is no universal guarantee of recovery within a specified number of trials.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Autokey | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Self-extending key | CFB feeds ciphertext back through a keyed block cipher; that is distinct from appending bare plaintext as a keystream |
| Plaintext feedback | Language structure in the appended plaintext supplies statistical clues; a repeating-key period test is not a general autokey solver |
| ‘Don't reuse keys’ isn't enough | Natural-language key material can expose exploitable statistical structure |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Break This Cipher

Ciphertext: `QOXSXPWRYOSKP`

Hint: the primer is a single Renaissance-style keyword, but the rest of the key comes from the plaintext itself.

 Reveal Answer

**Plaintext:** AUTOKEY REVEAL
 **Primer:** QUEENLY

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| --- | --- |
| Trust | Broken |
| Origin | Blaise de Vigenère (1586), refining Bellaso/Cardano |
| Year | 1586 |
| Key Type | Short keyword, then plaintext itself extends the key |
| Broken By | Crib propagation and statistical analysis |
| Modern Lesson | Self-keyed schemes still leak: the key is no longer random once it carries plaintext statistics |

Exhibit 39 of 174 Elizabethan · 1586

### The Babington Plot Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

*An intercepted correspondence that became evidence against Mary, Queen of Scots.*

Thomas Phelippes, working for Sir Francis Walsingham · within days of interception

Used ByMary, Queen of Scots & Anthony Babington

Year1586 (correspondence May–August)

Key TypeTeaching model: 23 letter symbols + 36 codewords + 4 nulls + 1 "doubleth"

KeyspaceTeaching model: 64! token assignments, not a historical security estimate

Broken ByThomas Phelippes, working for Sir Francis Walsingham · within days of interception

Modern LessonCryptography is an operational system, not just an algorithm — channel security and forgery resistance matter

#### The delivery route and the second reader

For an outgoing letter, follow the household’s message into the brewer’s cask and the channel operated through Gilbert Gifford. That covert delivery channel was controlled by Walsingham’s network. Thomas Phelippes could copy and decipher intercepted correspondence; intelligence reached Walsingham while the delivery channel continued to operate.

- **Delivery:** Mary’s household; the brewer’s cask; Gifford’s channel; onward delivery to the correspondent.

- **Access to the contents:** interception within that channel; Phelippes’s copying and decipherment; a reading for Walsingham.

These are connected routes, not a claim that Walsingham personally carried each original to its destination. Ask where a copy could leave the delivery chain without stopping the letter.

Sources: Simon Singh, *The Code Book*, chapter 1, cited in the book’s chapter 1 notes; Alan Bryson, [“The Gallows Letter,” British Library](<https://www.bl.uk/stories/blogs/posts/the-gallows-letter>), on interception and Phelippes’s decipherment of Mary’s 17 July 1586 letter.

#### Why This Matters

In 1586 Mary, Queen of Scots, was held at Chartley. Walsingham’s agents intercepted her encrypted correspondence with Anthony Babington. The letters became evidence at her trial, followed by her execution on February 8, 1587. Cryptanalysis mattered, alongside interception, secretarial testimony, and the political and judicial process; it was not the sole cause of the outcome.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

By 1586, Mary had been held in England for about eighteen years. Walsingham sought evidence of her involvement in plots against Elizabeth. The correspondence passed through secretaries and couriers; it should not be described as necessarily written in Mary’s own hand.

Gilbert Gifford helped establish a channel that Mary’s correspondents believed private, but Walsingham’s agents could intercept and decipher its letters. The historical system combined letter symbols, codewords, and special signs. The exact 64-token inventory used below belongs to the museum’s model, not a verified transcription of the original key.

Phelippes deciphered Mary’s July 17 letter and added a postscript requesting the conspirators’ names. **No reply supplying those names is established by this account.** Walsingham’s August 3 letter worried that the postscript had made Babington suspicious. See the [British Library’s discussion of the surviving documents](<https://www.bl.uk/stories/blogs/posts/the-gallows-letter>).

💡

The deciphered correspondence was used against Mary, who disputed the accusations. A dramatic statement about her reaction is not a substitute for the surviving trial and correspondence records.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The cipher was a **nomenclator**, combining substitution with a codebook. The following inventory describes the **museum’s teaching model**; its token counts and assignments are not an archival facsimile:

```text
23 letter symbols   (no J, V, W — folded onto I, U, UU)
36 codewords        (THE, AND, OF, MARY, QUEEN, ELIZABETH, POISON, …)
 4 null symbols     (decoys — drop on decode)
 1 "doubleth"       (means: double the previous letter)
─────────
64 total glyphs
```

Museum teaching inventory: letter signs, codewords, nulls and a doubling instruction. These drawn glyphs and assignments are illustrative, not a transcription of the 1586 key.

This software uses a greedy-longest-match scan: it selects a codeword where possible, otherwise a letter token. It can insert nulls and abbreviate doubled letters. These are the model’s deterministic rules, not a documented reconstruction of a clerk’s exact working procedure.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Frequency Analysis on the Letter Glyphs

Complexity: Moderate · Took Phelippes days, not weeks

Letter substitution leaks repeated patterns and language statistics; codewords and nulls complicate analysis. Frequency counts supply hypotheses, not a guaranteed E–T mapping or a complete reconstruction of Phelippes’s method. The surviving evidence establishes his successful decipherment, not the precise workflow previously asserted here.

Ciphertext Forgery (Active Attack)

A documented forged-postscript episode

Knowledge of an enciphering key lets an attacker create plausible new ciphertext. Phelippes’s forged postscript illustrates impersonation after key compromise. It is not a formal chosen-ciphertext attack: no decryption-oracle experiment is established, and the requested reply is not known to have arrived.

Operational Compromise (Channel Capture)

Complexity: Trivial once the courier turned

Control of the delivery channel enabled interception and alteration. Modern end-to-end encryption can protect messages over an adversary-controlled transport when endpoint keys and authentication remain secure. Compromising an endpoint or its secret key is a different and more powerful attack.

⚠️

**Two distinct failures:** the historical cipher was deciphered, and possession of its enciphering knowledge enabled a forged message. Adding codewords does not erase language structure. Authentication can resist outsider forgery only while the relevant authentication key remains secret.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Babington-Era Concept | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Nomenclator: codewords for whole tokens | Compression dictionaries (Huffman, LZ77) and tokenizers — same idea, modern math |
| Double-letter abbreviation | Format conventions can compress text; they are not authentication |
| Forged ciphertext to extract information | Impersonation after key compromise; distinct from a formal chosen-ciphertext attack |
| Trusted channel that is actually compromised | End-to-end encryption with verified identity (Signal Protocol's safety numbers, key transparency logs) |

🎓

**Modern comparison, not a claimed direct lineage:** authenticated encryption checks message integrity as well as confidentiality. It does not prevent an attacker who has stolen the shared authentication key from generating valid messages. Nor can a modern primitive settle the historical counterfactual about Mary’s trial.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 39 of 174 |
| --- | --- |


About this Demo

The original cipher chart survives in The National Archives (SP 12/193). This demo uses ASCII tokens drawn from a 64-symbol pool — `⟨a01⟩…⟨a23⟩`, `⟨w01⟩…⟨w36⟩`, `⟨n01⟩…⟨n04⟩`, and `⟨x2⟩` — but the seed shuffles which symbol stands for which letter, codeword, null, or the doubleth, so a symbol's prefix says nothing about its role. Under the default seed `BABINGTON`, for example, the doubleth is `⟨w18⟩` and `⟨x2⟩` is the codeword DEATH.

Try encoding "*POISON THE QUEEN AT THE TOWER*" and notice how POISON, THE, QUEEN, and TOWER each get their own codeword (one glyph for the whole word). Then encode "ATTACK" and watch the double-letter abbreviation apply on the doubled T.

When spelling with letter symbols, the demonstration folds J to I, V to U, and W to UU. The recovered text keeps those folds: WORK returns as UUORK, and V as U. Whole-word code entries retain their complete spelling; for example, the codeword TOWER decodes as TOWER. Labels such as a01 are shuffled token names, not fixed alphabet positions. These are explicit model conventions, not proof that all Elizabethan cipher alphabets used the same inventory.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Break This Cipher

Decode this synthetic teaching dispatch (seed: `BABINGTON`):

```text
⟨w25⟩ ⟨a14⟩ ⟨w32⟩ ⟨a20⟩ ⟨w33⟩ ⟨a17⟩ ⟨x2⟩
```

Reveal solution

The dispatch reads **DAGGER ELIZABETH AT THE TOWER DEATH** — paste the ciphertext into the demo and switch to *Decrypt* to verify. The seed shuffles the symbol-to-token assignment, so each glyph stands for whichever word the shuffle deals it.

Hall XIII · Culture Baroque Germany · 1750

### Bach's B-A-C-H Motif

The four notes B♭ – A – C – B♮ spell 'BACH' in German musical notation — a self-signature Bach embedded in his final unfinished fugue.

Musical cryptogram

RegionLeipzig, Saxony

YearComposed ~1742–1750

ComposerJohann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750)

TrackB (note-spelling demo)

#### Interactive Exhibit

Type any word using only the letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H. The widget will spell it out as German note names and an English-equivalent pitch sequence. Track B — illustrative encoder, not security.

 Word (letters A–H only)  [Input input: type=text; initial value=BACH]  Spell as notes

##### Why This Matters

In German musical notation, B♭ is written 'B' and B♮ is written 'H'. The four-note sequence B♭–A–C–B♮ therefore literally *spells* the surname BACH. Johann Sebastian Bach used this motif as an embedded signature in several works, most famously as the third subject of the unfinished final fugue (Contrapunctus XIV) of *The Art of Fugue*, BWV 1080. The surviving fugue breaks off unfinished. That physical ending does not establish that Bach died while writing it, and the BACH subject appears before the break.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The German naming convention treats H as the 'natural' B and B as the 'flat' B, a leftover of medieval mode notation. This idiosyncrasy gave German composers a unique alphabet of pitches: every musical note name from A through H is also a letter. Later composers including Schumann, Liszt, Brahms, Reger, Schoenberg, Webern, and Shostakovich used or paid tribute to the BACH motif. Shostakovich extended the idea to spell his own initials: D-S-C-H = D – E♭ – C – B♮ (since 'Es' = E♭ and 'H' = B♮ in German), the four notes that open his Eighth String Quartet and haunt the Tenth Symphony.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

As a cipher this is a one-to-one substitution between the eight German letter names A–H and their pitch classes (B and H distinguish B-flat and B-natural). Its 'plaintext space' is therefore tiny — only words spelled with A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H can be encoded. It is closer to a *signature* than to encryption. But it demonstrates a principle that recurs across cipher culture: a structured medium can carry an encoding. A public mapping alone does not provide confidentiality.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

Modern composers continue the tradition: Alban Berg's *Lyric Suite* embeds the initials of his secret love Hanna Fuchs-Robettin; Olivier Messiaen developed a 'communicable language' that spelled prayers in French phonetic note-equivalents; computer-music practitioners encode entire ASCII strings into MIDI. The BACH motif illustrates a musical signature. Calling it a cryptogram does not make it secret-key encryption or establish it as the first musical use of encoded meaning.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    (function () {
      var GERMAN = { A:'A natural', B:'B-flat', C:'C natural', D:'D natural',
                      E:'E natural', F:'F natural', G:'G natural', H:'B natural' };
      var ENGLISH = { A:'A', B:'B\u266d', C:'C', D:'D', E:'E', F:'F', G:'G', H:'B\u266e' };
      window.encode = function () {
        var raw = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').toUpperCase();
        var out = document.getElementById('output');
        var lines = [];
        var notes = [];
        for (var i = 0; i < raw.length; i++) {
          var c = raw[i];
          if (!GERMAN[c]) {
            lines.push('  ' + c + ' \u2192 (not a German note name)');
          } else {
            lines.push('  ' + c + ' \u2192 ' + GERMAN[c]);
            notes.push(ENGLISH[c]);
          }
        }
        if (notes.length === 0) { out.textContent = 'Use letters A B C D E F G H only.'; return; }
        out.textContent = lines.join('\n') + '\n\nPlayed as: ' + notes.join('  \u2013  ');
      };
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode(); });
    })();
```

### Bacon's Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

Binary encoding in 1605 — Francis Bacon hid messages in the typeface itself

Pattern recognition · Statistical analysis of A/B distribution

InventorSir Francis Bacon

Year1605

Key Type5-bit binary (A/B patterns)

Broken ByPattern recognition · Statistical analysis of A/B distribution

Modern LessonTwo-symbol representation and steganography

#### Why This Matters

Francis Bacon’s cipher — devised by 1605 and fully described in his 1623 *De Augmentis* — was one of the earliest documented uses of binary encoding — representing each letter as a 5-bit sequence over two centuries before Boolean algebra and three centuries before digital computing.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Sir Francis Bacon described his cipher in *De Augmentis Scientiarum* (1623). Each letter of the alphabet is represented by a 5-bit binary sequence using only two symbols (A and B). Bacon's original application was steganography: hide a secret message within an innocuous text by printing the covering text’s letters in two distinguishable typefaces — for example, roman and italic in a teaching illustration. Bacon’s proposal used two alphabets with subtler differences.

Bacon’s two-symbol alphabet is an early documented example of binary representation. Its historical interest does not establish a direct line of invention to Boolean algebra or electronic computing.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

```text
Bacon's binary alphabet:
A = AAAAA    N = ABBAA
B = AAAAB    O = ABBAB
C = AAABA    P = ABBBA
D = AAABB    Q = ABBBB
E = AABAA    R = BAAAA
...
Z = BBAAA

Example: HI = AABBB ABAAA
(each letter = 5 A/B symbols)

Following the common modern convention (Bacon's own alphabet had 24 letters, merging U/V as well), I and J share
the same code ABAAA (a 25-letter alphabet).

Steganographic use:
Normal text: AABBB ABAAA
Hidden in cover text by using two fonts:
normal=A, italic=B across 10 characters
```

```html
    <text x="0" y="16" font-size="14"><tspan fill="#5AC8A0">T</tspan><tspan fill="#5AC8A0">h</tspan><tspan fill="#E8C97A" font-style="italic">i</tspan><tspan fill="#E8C97A" font-style="italic">s</tspan><tspan fill="#E8C97A" font-style="italic"> </tspan><tspan fill="#5AC8A0">i</tspan><tspan fill="#E8C97A" font-style="italic">s</tspan><tspan fill="#5AC8A0"> </tspan><tspan fill="#5AC8A0">a</tspan><tspan fill="#5AC8A0">n</tspan></text>
    <text x="0" y="36" font-size="9" fill="#706878">A  A  B  B  B  A  B  A  A  A</text>
    <text x="0" y="52" font-size="9" fill="#C9A84C">→ H=AABBB + I=ABAAA</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

Each letter = 5 binary symbols. Normal typeface = A, italic = B — hiding messages in plain sight

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

A/B Distribution Analysis

Complexity: Trivial (as cipher) · Moderate (as steganography)

As a pure cipher, Bacon is trivially broken — it's a fixed binary encoding of the alphabet. As steganography in printed text, detection requires identifying two typefaces, which is usually obvious with magnification. Modern steganography detection uses statistical analysis of pixel distributions or bit-level patterns.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Bacon's Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| 5-bit binary alphabet (A/B) | ASCII: 7-bit binary encoding of 128 characters; UTF-8: variable-width binary |
| Two-symbol encoding | Binary notation also uses two symbols; this similarity does not establish direct historical descent |
| Steganographic application | Modern steganography: hiding data in image LSBs, audio files, network timing |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 33 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Era | 1605 |
| Trust | Broken |
| Inventor | Sir Francis Bacon |
| Year | 1605 |
| Key Type | 5-bit binary (A/B patterns) |
| Broken By | Pattern recognition · Statistical analysis of A/B distribution |

#### Sources and Reading

*The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, David Kahn (revised edition, 1996), “The Pathology of Cryptology”: Bacon’s 1605 allusion,1623 description,24-letter alphabet and two typefaces. The museum’s 25-letter mapping is a stated modern variant.

### Bazeries Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A historical hand-cipher procedure and an explicitly simplified browser model

Layered frequency analysis

InventorÉtienne Bazeries

Year~1890s

Key TypeNumeric key; substitution plus group reversal

Broken ByLayered frequency analysis

Modern LessonKey-controlled multi-layer operations

#### Why This Matters

Étienne Bazeries reconstructed historic French nomenclators and proposed cipher devices of his own. His mechanical cylinder, the hand cipher bearing his name, and this browser’s simplified model are distinct constructions.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Étienne Bazeries was one of the most famous cryptanalysts of his era — he reconstructed a Rossignol-era nomenclator in correspondence from about two centuries earlier. Ironically, he also designed his own cipher and spent years trying to convince the French military to adopt it, without success.

Bazeries proposed a 20-disk cylinder independently of Jefferson’s earlier 36-disk description. The later U.S. M-94 belongs to a related but separately developed cylinder tradition; none of these devices is the two-square hand procedure described below.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

**ACA hand-cipher convention:** choose a number and spell it out to key a 5×5 ciphertext square, merging I/J. The plaintext square has its alphabet written down columns. Reverse groups of plaintext according to successive key digits, then substitute between corresponding square cells.

For example, key 3752 uses successive group lengths 3, 7, 5 and 2. This is group reversal, not columnar transposition.

**Browser model boundary:** the widget above instead accepts 2–99, builds a 26-letter keyword substitution from the English number name, and reverses fixed-size groups. The size is min(6, max(2, (key mod 7)+2)); key 42 therefore uses pairs. It does not implement the ACA two-square rule or the mechanical cylinder. Its outputs are model exercises, not historical test vectors.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Multi-Layer Frequency Analysis

Complexity: Hard

Both layers depend on the key, so their search spaces should not be multiplied as though they were independent. This widget has only 98 selectable numbers, making exhaustive comparison straightforward. That bound applies to this model, not to every historical Bazeries procedure.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Bazeries Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Single key controls multiple operations | AES key schedule: one master key generates all round keys |
| Inventor = famous codebreaker | Security through obscurity fails: cipher design must be public and peer-reviewed |
| Mechanical cylinder version | Compare the separate cylinder tradition with moving wired-rotor machines |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 22 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Era | 1890s · France |
| Trust | Broken |
| Inventor | Étienne Bazeries |
| Year | ~1890s |
| Key Type | Numeric key; substitution plus group reversal |
| Broken By | Layered frequency analysis |

#### Sources and Reading

American Cryptogram Association, [“Bazeries” specification and worked example](<https://www.cryptogram.org/downloads/aca.info/ciphers/Bazeries.pdf>); David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 8, for Bazeries and his separate cylinder. The numerical widget’s rule is documented above so it can be distinguished from the source procedure.

Hall XII · Unsolved · Virginia Treasure Legend 19th Century · published 1885

### Beale Ciphers

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Three ciphers published in 1885, claiming to describe an 1820s buried treasure — two of them still unsolved

Unsolved (Beale 1 & 3)

OriginJames B. Ward pamphlet, Lynchburg, Virginia (1885)

Author of plaintextsClaimed by the pamphlet to be Thomas J. Beale, 1820s — unverified

Cipher typeBook cipher (number = Nth word, take first letter)

SolvedBeale 2 only (key: Declaration of Independence)

UnsolvedBeale 1 (treasure location) and Beale 3 (heirs)

Treasure value (claimed)Unverified treasure claim; no valuation established

#### Why This Matters

Two dates run through this exhibit and they are not interchangeable. **1885** is when the ciphers demonstrably enter the record: James B. Ward published a pamphlet in Lynchburg, Virginia, titled *The Beale Papers*, containing three numerical ciphertexts. **The 1820s are only what that pamphlet claims** — that a man named Thomas Jefferson Beale buried a fortune in gold, silver and jewels near Buford's Tavern in Bedford County in 1819 and 1821, and left the box of papers with innkeeper Robert Morriss in 1822. No ciphertext, letter or document from the Beale story is attested anywhere before 1885.

The pamphlet's story assigns each cipher a job: cipher 1 names the location, cipher 2 itemises the contents, cipher 3 names the heirs. Its anonymous narrator, who says he received the papers from Morriss and worked on them for some twenty years, solved cipher 2 by trying the Declaration of Independence as the key text and read out a precise inventory of buried treasure. Ciphers 1 and 3 have no generally accepted decipherment.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The treasure story’s authenticity is disputed. The surviving 1885 publication is evidence that the story and numerical texts were circulated then; it does not independently authenticate the claimed earlier events. A readable construction for cipher 2 can be created deliberately, so its decoding does not settle whether treasure existed or whether ciphers 1 and 3 encode meaningful messages. Statistical arguments about those sequences have also produced conflicting interpretations, as the sources below explain.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

A book cipher converts each plaintext letter to the position of a word in a reference text whose first letter matches.

```text
Plaintext: G O L D
           ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓
Declaration words: 48=god, 12=one, 42=laws, 15=dissolve
Ciphertext: 48 12 42 15
```

To decrypt, you need the exact same edition of the reference text the encoder used. An insertion or omission can shift later word numbers; a wrong lookup can also corrupt only the affected letter.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Beale 2: Right Book Found

Complexity: Lucky guess

The anonymous narrator of the 1885 pamphlet supplies a Declaration-of-Independence decoding of the second sequence. That demonstrates a readable construction for B2, not the historical truth of the treasure claim or that B1 and B3 must have meaningful plaintexts and missing books.

Beale 1 & 3: Still Open

Status: No generally accepted decipherment

B1 and B3 have no generally accepted decipherment. Hammer and Gillogly should not be presented as reaching the same conclusion: Kahn reports that Hammer regarded his tests as support for a genuine cipher, whereas Gillogly’s 1980 paper argues for a hoax interpretation. Alphabetical runs produced by applying the Declaration key to B1 are evidence to examine under an explicit model, not proof of either a treasure or a hoax.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Beale Ciphers | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Book cipher principle | A shared text supplies a lookup reference; ordinary prose is not a uniformly random cryptographic key |
| Edition specificity | Exact format agreement: edition changes can alter coordinate lookups |
| Hoax-resistance of evidence | Provenance and reproducibility matter as much as the math |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

Sources

- [James B. Ward, publisher]. *The Beale Papers, Containing Authentic Statements Regarding the Treasure Buried in 1819 and 1821, Near Bufords, in Bedford County, Virginia, and Which Has Never Been Recovered.* Lynchburg, Va., 1885. The primary document — and the earliest attestation of any part of the story.

- Gillogly, James J. “[The Beale Cipher: A Dissenting Opinion](<https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0161-118091854979>).” *Cryptologia* 4, no. 2 (1980): 116–119. Source for the alphabetical-run anomaly in B1.

- Hammer, Carl. “Signature Simulation and Certain Cryptographic Codes.” *Communications of the ACM* 14, no. 1 (January 1971): 3–14; and “[Higher-Order Homophonic Ciphers](<https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0161-118191856075>),” *Cryptologia* 5, no. 4 (1981): 231–242, replying to Gillogly.

- [Wikipedia, *Beale ciphers* ↗](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beale_ciphers>) — used here for the pamphlet chronology (burial in 1819 and 1821 per the pamphlet's own title, box left with innkeeper Robert Morriss in 1822, box opened 1845, pamphlet published by James B. Ward in 1885) and for the point that nothing in the story is attested before 1885.

Exhibit 09 of 174 Victorian · 1857

### Beaufort Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

The cipher that encrypts and decrypts with the same operation

Kasiski Examination · Index of Coincidence

InventorAdmiral Sir Francis Beaufort

Year1857

Key TypeRepeating keyword

Broken ByKasiski Examination · Index of Coincidence

Modern LessonSymmetric operations in stream ciphers

#### Why This Matters

The Beaufort cipher is a Vigenère variant with an elegant reciprocal property: the same operation both encrypts and decrypts. Its reciprocal mapping simplifies the operator’s procedure while retaining the vulnerabilities of a repeating key.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Sir Francis Beaufort — famous for the Beaufort wind scale — devised a variant of the Vigenère cipher with an elegant property: the same operation encrypts and decrypts. Where Vigenère adds key to plaintext modulo 26, Beaufort subtracts plaintext from key. Because of this reciprocal property, you never need to switch between an encryption and decryption mode.

David Kahn describes a cipher card published under Beaufort’s name in 1857, after his death. His naval rank does not by itself establish Royal Navy operational adoption. Its weakness is identical to Vigenère's: the repeating key creates detectable periodicity.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The Beaufort cipher uses a tabula recta like Vigenère but with a different lookup direction:

```text
Vigenère: C = (P + K) mod 26
Beaufort: C = (K - P + 26) mod 26

Key:    S  E  C  R  E  T
Plain:  H  E  L  L  O  W
Cipher: L  A  R  G  Q  X
```

Because K − (K − P) = P modulo 26: Decrypt(C, K) = Encrypt(C, K). This simplifies the operation; it does not remove the need to distribute and protect the key.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 380 130" style="width:100%;max-width:380px;height:auto" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Beaufort vs Vigenere formula comparison">
  <style>text{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace;fill:#EDE5D4}</style>
  <!-- Vigenere -->
  <rect x="5" y="5" width="175" height="50" fill="rgba(90,144,200,.08)" stroke="rgba(90,144,200,.2)" stroke-width="1" rx="6"></rect>
  <text x="15" y="25" font-size="9" fill="#5A90C8">VIGENÈRE</text>
  <text x="15" y="42" font-size="11" fill="#B8B0A0">C = (P + K) mod 26</text>
  <!-- Beaufort -->
  <rect x="200" y="5" width="175" height="50" fill="rgba(201,168,76,.08)" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.2)" stroke-width="1" rx="6"></rect>
  <text x="210" y="25" font-size="9" fill="#C9A84C">BEAUFORT</text>
  <text x="210" y="42" font-size="11" fill="#C9A84C">C = (K − P) mod 26</text>
  <!-- Key difference -->
  <text x="5" y="82" font-size="10" fill="#5AC8A0">★ Beaufort is reciprocal: Enc(P) = Dec(C) with same key</text>
  <rect x="5" y="92" width="370" height="30" fill="rgba(90,200,160,.06)" stroke="rgba(90,200,160,.15)" stroke-width=".5" rx="4"></rect>
  <text x="15" y="112" font-size="9" fill="#706878">Key=S Plain=H → C = (S−H) = (18−7) = 11 = L   |   C=L → P = (S−L) = (18−11) = 7 = H ✓</text>
</svg>
```

Subtraction instead of addition makes Beaufort self-inverse — encryption and decryption are the same operation

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Kasiski Examination

Complexity: Moderate

The Beaufort cipher shares Vigenère's fatal flaw: the repeating key. Identical plaintext segments that align with identical key segments produce identical ciphertext. Repetition distances and index-of-coincidence tests can suggest a period. Language scoring can then rank key-letter candidates; short texts and accidental repetitions can mislead.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Beaufort Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Reciprocal operation (encrypt = decrypt) | Many binary stream ciphers use reciprocal XOR: A XOR B XOR B = A |
| Key-driven alphabet selection | A cryptographic stream generator derives a pseudorandom keystream from a secret key and its nonce/counter state |
| Repeating key weakness | Correct nonce/counter management prevents reusing the same keystream positions under a key; individual values can still recur |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall X: Hall of Codebreakers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/codebreakers.html>)› Arne Beurling

Hall X · Codebreakers WWII · Sweden

### Arne Beurling

His two-week breakthrough revealed the T52’s structure; assistants and a continuing team effort turned it into intelligence.

Codebreaker Biography

BornFebruary 3, 1905, Gothenburg, Sweden

DiedNovember 20, 1986, Princeton, New Jersey

EducationUppsala University — PhD 1933

ProfessionMathematician (complex analysis, harmonic analysis)

Key BreakSiemens T52 Geheimschreiber — June 1940 (two weeks)

SourceSwedish Defence Staff cryptographic service; FRA from 1942

LegacyMathematical analysis; IAS member 1952–1954; faculty from 1954

✏️

#### Arne Beurling

1905 – 1986

Arne Beurling was a Swedish mathematician. In 1940 he reconstructed essential features of the Siemens T52 from intercepted traffic. The [FRA’s historical account](<https://fra.se/omfra/frashistoria/gskrivarenocharnebeurling.4.55af049f184e92956c42a59.html>) credits his principal breakthrough to about two weeks, with assistance from Hans Rudberg and Bertil Nyman.

##### Why This Person Matters

Reconstructing an unknown cipher machine from its traffic is an exceptional analytic achievement. It is different from recovering every later message key. Daily-key work and practical decryption required other analysts and equipment; treating the whole operation as a solitary, permanent solution hides those contributions.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

The Geheimschreiber Problem

The T52 enciphered five-bit teleprinter signals using ten pinwheels to control bit mixing and permutation. These were not Enigma-style wired alphabet rotors. Traffic sent through Sweden provided intercepted material for the attack; the wheel mechanism and operating procedure both mattered.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

The Two Weeks

The interception operation belonged to the Swedish Defence Staff’s cryptographic service; FRA became an independent agency in 1942. After the structural breakthrough, teams still had to solve daily settings. Beurling and engineer Vigo Lindstein developed equipment for decryption. The initial success did not guarantee uninterrupted access to every later variant or all wartime traffic.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-columns"></use></svg>
```

After the War

Beurling joined the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton as a member in 1952 and became a faculty member in 1954. The Institute records his faculty appointment through 1973, followed by emeritus status until 1986.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Born | February 3, 1905, Gothenburg, Sweden |
| --- | --- |
| Died | November 20, 1986, Princeton, New Jersey |
| Education | Uppsala University — PhD 1933 |
| Profession | Mathematician (complex analysis, harmonic analysis) |
| Key Break | Siemens T52 Geheimschreiber — June 1940 (two weeks) |
| Source | Swedish Defence Staff cryptographic service; FRA from 1942 |
| Legacy | Mathematical analysis; IAS member 1952–1954; faculty from 1954 |

Exhibit 140 of 174 1994 · Refuted 1999

### Bible Code — Equidistant Letter Sequences

A lesson in probability: ELS counterexamples and experimental flexibility challenge claims of hidden prophecies.

Statistical claims challenged by controlled counterexamples and analysis of selection flexibility.

Claimed byWitztum, Rips & Rosenberg (1994); Michael Drosnin (1997)

MethodEquidistant Letter Sequences (ELS) in Hebrew Torah text

Refuted byMcKay, Bar-Natan, Bar-Hillel & Kalai — *Statistical Science* 14:150 (1999)

Modern LessonSearching many alternatives creates opportunities for chance matches; significance depends on the test and selection process

#### Why This Exhibit Exists

This exhibit concerns a disputed claim of hidden messages, not a demonstrated encryption system. It separates the 1994 statistical experiment on Genesis from later popular predictions, and uses ELS searches to explain why a pattern’s existence alone does not establish intent or statistical significance.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

In 1994 Israeli mathematicians Doron Witztum, Eliyahu Rips, and Yoav Rosenberg published a paper in *Statistical Science* claiming to find statistically significant equidistant letter sequences (ELS) in the Hebrew text of Genesis. They claimed that names of famous rabbis and associated dates occurred unusually close together under their chosen ELS proximity measure.

The paper caused a sensation. In 1997 journalist Michael Drosnin published *The Bible Code*, extending the method to predict modern events — the assassination of Yitzhak Rabin (cited after the fact), the Gulf War, and others. Drosnin's challenge: "When my critics find a message about the assassination of a prime minister encrypted in *Moby-Dick*, I'll believe them."

Brendan McKay published *Moby-Dick* assassination-name examples in response to Drosnin’s popular challenge. This was distinct from the 1999 statistical paper by McKay, Bar-Natan, Bar-Hillel and Kalai, which examined the Genesis experiment’s data and design choices and reported unsuccessful new tests. Neither finding means that every text has the same matches.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How ELS Works

Take any text. Remove all spaces, punctuation, and numbers, keeping only letters. This gives you a letter string. Now pick a target word and a **skip value** *d*. Starting at position *p*, read every *d*-th letter: positions *p*, *p+d*, *p+2d*, and so on. If the result spells your target word, you have found an ELS at (start=*p*, skip=*d*).

```text
Text = ABCDEFGHI, target = ADG
Zero-based start 0, positive skip 3: positions 0, 3, 6.

For length N, target length m, and positive skips 1…D:
valid start/skip pairs = Σ max(N − (m−1)d, 0).

N = 100,000, m = 4, D = 1,000:
98,498,500 valid pairs (not 100,000,000).
Under independent uniformly distributed A–Z letters,
expected hits = 98,498,500 / 26⁴ ≈ 215.54.
```

The expectation above uses an **independent uniform-letter model**, not real prose. With independently sampled nonuniform letters, multiply the number of valid pairs by the product of the target letters’ probabilities. Overlapping searches need not be independent for this expectation, but a significance test needs an appropriate distribution and must account for other searched words and settings.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Explore ELS Matches and a Shuffled Control

The boxes compare a prose passage with a shuffled control containing the same letters. Their hit counts may differ. **This comparison is an illustration, not a significance test or proof that the texts are statistically indistinguishable.** A sound test needs a specified hypothesis, null model, search procedure, and accounting for all comparisons.

📊

**Analytic expectation:** searching for **** in a text of **** letters at skips 2–**** predicts approximately **** hits. This expectation uses an idealized model; it is not a significance test.

Try target words: `EDEN`, `DEATH`, `WAR`, `KING`, `ASSASSIN`. Hit counts depend on the text, target and allowed skips. Longer words can occur, and prose can differ from its shuffled control. These observations require a specified statistical test; this widget does not supply one.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How the Claim Was Refuted

Statistical Replication Test (McKay et al., 1999)

Method: Examine experimental flexibility and attempt independent tests

The 1999 paper examines choices in the Genesis experiment. Its §6 demonstrates how changing permissible rabbinical names and spellings can produce a strong-looking result in a Hebrew *War and Peace* passage while weakening the Genesis result. It is a demonstration of selection flexibility, not an identical search using an unchanged list in both books. The separate *Moby-Dick* examples address Drosnin’s popular interpretation.

The Multiplicity Problem (searching for significance)

Method: Combinatorial argument

Trying more names, spellings, skips, directions, and texts creates more opportunities for matches. Hits are not certain for every target, and no single search-space count applies without specifying those choices. Exploratory discoveries need independent confirmation or a statistical method that accounts for the selection process.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What This Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Mistake in the Bible Code claim | Modern cryptographic parallel |
| --- | --- |
|  Searching billions of (start, skip) pairs post-hoc and reporting only the hits |  **Statistical significance in security audits:** under valid null hypotheses, 1,000 tests at a 0.05 threshold have an expected 50 false positives; the observed count need not be exactly 50 |
|  Treating a pattern found in scripture as non-accidental without comparing to a random baseline |  **Distinguisher attacks:** a valid linear or differential distinguisher requires showing the bias in the cipher is *greater than expected from a random permutation*, not merely that a bias exists |
|  Unaccounted flexibility in selecting names, spellings and tests can change reported significance |  **Chosen-input bias:** choosing a dataset after inspecting results can invalidate a test’s stated significance |
|  Short texts and flexible interpretation can permit competing readings |  State the cipher model and constraints before judging a proposed decipherment; a plausible phrase alone does not identify the original message |
|  Publication and independent examination can reach different conclusions |  **Security proofs require adversarial review:** a published claim still needs independent examination of its assumptions, evidence, and reproducibility; publication alone does not settle it |

⚠

**On the original 1994 paper.** The criticism concerns the experimental choices and the interpretation of the evidence. It does not establish the authors’ motives. Multiple-comparison problems were known before 1994; the important question is whether the reported procedure accounted adequately for its choices and search flexibility.

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

The Numbers

For an illustrative text of 78,000 letters, a five-letter target, and positive skips 1–1,000, there are 75,998,000 valid start/skip pairs. Compare two explicitly idealized alphabets:

75,998,000 start × skip pairs searched

1 in 26⁵ = 1 in 11.9M chance per pair

~6.40 expected hits: independent uniform A–Z model

~14.75 expected hits: independent uniform 22-letter model (N / 22⁵)

These expectations are for artificial independent-letter models. Hebrew has 22 base letters, not 26; its real letter frequencies and textual structure are not uniform. A number of hits alone cannot establish significance, and a 78,000-letter example should not be mislabeled as the complete Torah.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

Primary Sources

- **The claim:** Witztum, Rips & Rosenberg — "Equidistant Letter Sequences in the Book of Genesis." *Statistical Science* 9:3 (1994), pp. 429–438.

- **The popular version:** Michael Drosnin — *The Bible Code*. Simon & Schuster, 1997. (*This exhibit is a direct response to this book's methodology and conclusions.*)

- **The refutation:** McKay, Bar-Natan, Bar-Hillel & Kalai — "Solving the Bible Code Puzzle." *Statistical Science* 14:2 (1999), pp. 150–173. [Author’s research page and paper](<https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~bdm/dilugim/StatSci/>).

- **Moby-Dick experiment:** Brendan McKay's personal site preserves the analysis: [users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~bdm/dilugim/moby.html](<https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~bdm/dilugim/moby.html>)
