#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function () {
  'use strict';
  if (typeof window.ELS === 'undefined') return;
  const { normalise, findELS, expectedHits } = window.ELS;

  // A passage from Moby-Dick (opening + early chapters) — public domain.
  // ~1 400 letters after normalisation; enough for a live demo without
  // making the page slow on mobile.
  const MOBY_SOURCE = `
  Call me Ishmael. Some years ago never mind how long precisely having
  little money in my purse and nothing particular to interest me on shore
  I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.
  It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and regulating the circulation.
  Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth whenever it is a damp
  drizzly November in my soul whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing
  before coffin warehouses and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet
  and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me that it
  requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping
  into the street and methodically knocking peoples hats off then I account
  it high time to get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for
  pistol and ball. With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself upon
  his sword I quietly take to the ship. There is nothing surprising in this.
  If they only knew it almost all men in their degree some time or other
  cherish very nearly the same feelings towards the ocean with me.
  There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes belted round by wharves
  as Indian isles by coral reefs commerce surrounds it with her surf.
  Right and left the streets take you waterward. Its extreme downtown is
  the battery where that noble mole is washed by waves and cooled by breezes
  which a few hours previous were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds
  of water gazers there. Circumambulate the city of a dreamy Sabbath afternoon.
  Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip and from thence by Whitehall
  northward. What do you see. Posted like silent sentinels all around the
  town stand thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries.
  Some leaning against the spiles some seated upon the pier heads some
  looking over the bulwarks of ships from China some high aloft in the
  rigging as if striving to get a still better seaward peep. But these are
  all landsmen of week days pent up in lath and plaster tied to counters
  nailed to benches clinched to desks. How then is this. Are the green
  fields gone. What do they here. But look. Here come more crowds pacing
  straight for the water and seemingly bound for a dive. Strange. Nothing
  will content them but the extremest limit of the land.`;

  const PROSE_LETTERS = normalise(MOBY_SOURCE);

  // Build a letter frequency table from the prose
  function buildFreq(s) {
    const f = {};
    for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
      const c = s[i];
      f[c] = (f[c] || 0) + 1;
    }
    return f;
  }

  // Generate a random text of the same length with the same letter distribution
  function makeRandom(len, freq) {
    const pool = [];
    for (const [ch, cnt] of Object.entries(freq)) {
      for (let i = 0; i < cnt; i++) pool.push(ch);
    }
    let out = '';
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
      out += pool[Math.floor(Math.random() * pool.length)];
    }
    return out;
  }

  const PROSE_FREQ = buildFreq(PROSE_LETTERS);
  let randText = makeRandom(PROSE_LETTERS.length, PROSE_FREQ);

  // --- DOM helpers ---
  function $(id) { return document.getElementById(id); }
  function escHtml(s) {
    return s.replace(/[&<>"]/g, c => ({'&':'&amp;','<':'&lt;','>':'&gt;','"':'&quot;'}[c]));
  }

  function renderHits(hits, containerId) {
    const el = $(containerId);
    if (!hits.length) {
      el.innerHTML = '<span style="color:var(--tx3);font-size:.8rem;">No hits at these parameters.</span>';
      return;
    }
    const show = hits.slice(0, 12);
    el.innerHTML = show.map(h =>
      `<div class="els-hit-item">start=<span>${h.start}</span>  skip=<span>${h.skip}</span>  &hellip;<span>${h.skip > 0 ? '' : '(rev)'}</span></div>`
    ).join('') + (hits.length > 12
      ? `<div style="color:var(--tx3);font-size:.75rem;margin-top:.4rem;">&hellip; and ${hits.length - 12} more</div>`
      : '');
  }

  function runSearch() {
    const word = ($('els-word').value || '').toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
    if (!word.length) return;
    const maxSkip = Math.min(5000, Math.max(10, parseInt($('els-maxskip').value, 10) || 500));

    const opts = { minSkip: 2, maxSkip: maxSkip, maxResults: 500 };
    const proseHits = findELS(PROSE_LETTERS, word, opts);
    const randHits = findELS(randText, word, opts);
    const expected = expectedHits(PROSE_LETTERS.length, word, { minSkip: 2, maxSkip: maxSkip });

    $('els-prose-count').textContent = proseHits.length >= 500 ? '500+ ' : proseHits.length;
    $('els-rand-count').textContent = randHits.length >= 500 ? '500+' : randHits.length;
    renderHits(proseHits, 'els-prose-hits');
    renderHits(randHits, 'els-rand-hits');

    $('els-compare').style.display = '';
    $('els-expected-row').style.display = '';
    $('els-word-display').textContent = word;
    $('els-n-display').textContent = PROSE_LETTERS.length.toLocaleString();
    $('els-maxskip-display').textContent = maxSkip;
    $('els-expected-display').textContent = Math.round(expected).toLocaleString();
  }

  $('els-search').addEventListener('click', runSearch);
  $('els-word').addEventListener('keydown', e => { if (e.key === 'Enter') runSearch(); });
  $('els-word').addEventListener('input', e => {
    e.target.value = e.target.value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g, '');
  });
  $('els-random').addEventListener('click', function () {
    randText = makeRandom(PROSE_LETTERS.length, PROSE_FREQ);
    runSearch();
  });
})();
```

### Bifid Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Felix Delastelle's masterwork: fractionation meets transposition

Statistical analysis · Hill climbing

InventorFelix Delastelle

Year1902

Key Type5×5 keyword square

Broken ByStatistical analysis · Hill climbing

Modern LessonConfusion + diffusion combined

#### Why This Matters

Delastelle’s Bifid combines coordinate substitution with transposition, spreading each letter’s coordinate information across positions. This is a useful early illustration of diffusion; it is not established here as the first system ever to combine substitution and transposition.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Felix Delastelle was a French amateur cryptographer who invented several remarkable ciphers in the late 19th century. The Bifid (from Latin *bifidus*, “split in two,” from *findere*, “to split”) is widely considered his masterpiece. It combines a Polybius square with a transposition technique in a way that creates genuine interdependence between letter positions — a property Shannon would later call diffusion.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Using a 5×5 Polybius square with a keyword:

- Convert each plaintext letter to its (row, col) coordinates

- Write all row numbers in a row, then all column numbers beneath

- Read pairs from the combined sequence

- Convert each pair back to a letter using the square

```text
Key square (keyword SECRET):
  S E C R T
  A B D F G
  H I K L M
  N O P Q U
  V W X Y Z

HELLO → H(2,0) E(0,1) L(2,3) L(2,3) O(3,1)
Rows:    2  0  2  2  3
Cols:    0  1  3  3  1
Combined: 2 0 2 2 3 | 0 1 3 3 1
Pairs: (2,0)(2,2)(3,0)(1,3)(3,1)
Cipher: HKNFO
```

Bifid fractionation: coordinates are split, concatenated, and re-paired — mixing row and column information across positions

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Statistical Cryptanalysis + Hill Climbing

Complexity: Moderate-Hard

Bifid mixes coordinate information within a chosen period. Some variants use fixed-size groups; this demo uses its documented grouping rule. Computer attacks can search candidate squares using language scores, but success depends on period, text length, key conventions, and search effort. No fixed few-hundred-character guarantee applies universally.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Bifid Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Fractionation (split letter into coordinates) | Bit diffusion: every bit of plaintext influences multiple ciphertext bits |
| Row/column interleaving | AES MixColumns: mixes 4 bytes of each column together |
| Polybius square lookup | AES uses a fixed public nonlinear S-box, combined with separate key addition and diffusion |

Hall X · Codebreakers WWII · Britain

### Bill Tutte

From keystream first recovered by John Tiltman, Tutte and his colleagues inferred the structure of an unseen Lorenz machine.

Codebreaker Biography

BornMay 14, 1917, Newmarket, Suffolk

DiedMay 2, 2002, Kitchener, Ontario, Canada

EducationTrinity College, Cambridge — BA Natural Sciences (Chemistry) 1938; PhD Mathematics 1948

RecruitedBletchley Park, 1941

Key AchievementInferred Lorenz structure from recovered key material, 1941–early 1942

ImpactEnabled Heath Robinson and Colossus — an early programmable electronic digital computer

Post-warMajor contributions to graph theory; University of Waterloo; Fellow of the Royal Society

🧮

#### Bill Tutte

1917 – 2002

William Thomas Tutte was a Cambridge chemistry graduate and research student when he was recruited to Bletchley Park in 1941. Assigned to the Research Section working on "Fish" — the German teleprinter cipher systems — he was given a 4,000-character depth: two messages that an operator had transmitted in the same Lorenz SZ40 settings, with changes to the wording and abbreviations. John Tiltman first read the depth by hand: the XOR of the two ciphertexts is the XOR of the two plaintexts, which let him separate both messages and so recover the raw keystream. Tutte was then given that key to analyse. By analysing patterns in this recovered keystream, Tutte and colleagues in the Research Section inferred the machine’s structure by early 1942: the wheel groups, their lengths and their interaction. He did this entirely on paper, never having seen a Lorenz machine. His analysis was the foundation for the Tunny-breaking algorithms developed at Bletchley, which in turn drove the construction of the Robinson machines and ultimately Colossus. His work has been described by post-war analysts as "one of the greatest intellectual feats of World War II."

##### Why This Person Matters

Bill Tutte's Lorenz analysis is the purest example of what cryptanalysis at its highest level actually is: the reconstruction of an unknown physical system from its outputs alone. Unlike Enigma, where the machine's general design was known, the Lorenz SZ40 was entirely unknown to British intelligence when Tutte was given the key material Tiltman had recovered. The structure emerged through mathematical analysis. The practical consequence was Colossus — the machine designed by Tommy Flowers and programmed by a team to automate Tutte's statistical attacks — which became the world's first operational programmable digital electronic computer. The work connected cryptanalysis with an important early application of programmable electronics. Wartime secrecy long kept this contribution from wider public recognition. His postwar mathematical career was equally distinguished: he made major contributions to graph theory, matroid theory, and combinatorics. He holds the rare distinction of being a world-historical figure in two separate fields.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

The Lorenz SZ40

The Lorenz SZ40 (Schlüsselzusatz — "cipher attachment") was a teleprinter cipher machine used for Hitler's highest-level communications — the "Führer's telegraph." Unlike Enigma (a letter substitution device), Lorenz worked on the 5-bit Baudot teleprinter code and combined the plaintext with a pseudorandom keystream generated by twelve rotating pin wheels. The keystream was the XOR of contributions from two groups of wheels (the Chi wheels and the Psi wheels), with two motor wheels controlling the irregular stepping of the Psi group. The complexity was far greater than Enigma: the number of possible wheel positions exceeded 10 to the 19th power. The cipher was used by German High Command, Army Group commanders, and directly by Hitler for strategic communications throughout the war.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

The Depth and the Reconstruction

On August 30, 1941, a German operator sent a 4,000-character message to another station. The receiving station asked for a repeat. The operator retransmitted — using the same Lorenz wheel settings, but with wording and abbreviations changed. This pair of ciphertexts produced with a reused keystream was intercepted by the British "Y stations." Tutte examined repetitions and periodic structure in Tiltman’s recovered key. Working with the Research Section through early 1942, he inferred the machine’s wheel groups, sizes (41, 31, 29, 26, 23 in the Chi set; 43, 47, 51, 53, 59 for Psi; and 61, 37 for motor wheels) and their interaction. This was a tour de force of reverse engineering conducted entirely through mathematical inference.

#### Three Different Unknowns

Diagnosing an unseen machine, recovering wheel pin patterns and finding a message’s starting positions were separate tasks. Success at one supplied information for the next.

Swipe or scroll the table horizontally to see every column. Keyboard: focus the table area and use the arrow keys.

Inputs, unknowns and methods in Tunny cryptanalysis

| Task and period | Input and unknown | Method and contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Infer structure 1941–early 1942 | Recovered key from Tiltman’s depth; unknown wheel groups, lengths and interaction. | Tutte and the Research Section analysed repetitions and periodic structure. |
| Break wheel patterns Turingery, 1942 | Recovered key and a known machine structure; unknown pin patterns. | Turing’s method used XOR differences between adjacent key symbols to recover wheel patterns. |
| Find message settings Later statistical work; Colossus operational in 1944 | Ciphertext and known wheel patterns; unknown starting positions for a message. | Tutte’s statistical methods used differencing; Flowers’s team built [Colossus](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/colossus.html>) to accelerate counting for setting searches. |

These tasks formed part of a larger process: a promising setting was not yet a complete plaintext, and manual work remained essential.

Sources: I. J. Good, Donald Michie and Geoffrey Timms, *General Report on Tunny: With Emphasis on Statistical Methods* (1945), §43B, printed p. 313 / collected PDF p. 307, for Turingery; Paul Gannon, *Colossus: Bletchley Park’s Greatest Secret* (Atlantic Books, 2014 edition), chapter 10, “Fishing the Depths,” converted PDF pp. 94–97, and chapter 13, “Making the Difference,” converted PDF pp. 132–135, especially p. 133. Gannon’s converted PDF numbering is not verified print pagination.

Source: NSA Center for Cryptologic History, [*Brigadier John Tiltman: A Giant Among Cryptanalysts* (2007), pp. 25–26](<https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/misc/tiltman.pdf>), distinguishes Tiltman’s manual message/key recovery from the subsequent structural analysis.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

From Lorenz to Colossus

Tutte’s reconstruction and subsequent statistical methods supported both manual and machine-assisted Tunny cryptanalysis. The Newmanry’s Heath Robinson used two paper tapes and electronic counting; synchronising the tapes was difficult. Tommy Flowers and his team replaced the second tape’s wheel-pattern role with electronic generation in Colossus. Mark 1 entered operational use in February 1944. Colossus was a specialised programmable electronic digital machine, not a general-purpose stored-program computer. Manual analysis in the Testery remained essential alongside the machines.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall X: Hall of Codebreakers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/codebreakers.html>)› Bletchley Park

Hall X · Codebreakers WWII · 1939–1945

### Bletchley Park

A wartime codebreaking centre linking cryptanalysis, interception, engineering and intelligence reporting.

LocationBletchley, Buckinghamshire, England

OperationAugust 1939 – 1945 (wartime operation)

PersonnelAbout 10,000 at Bletchley and associated outstations at peak

Key BreaksEnigma and Tunny (Lorenz): teams built on distinct mathematical and operational breakthroughs

HardwareBombe search machines; Colossus operational at Bletchley in 1944

Estimated impactMajor Allied intelligence contribution; estimates of time saved are counterfactual

#### Why This Matters

Thousands of people worked at Bletchley Park and its outstations, many of them women. Enigma and German teleprinter systems required different attack organizations. For Tunny, John Tiltman first recovered messages and keystream from a reused-setting transmission; Tutte and colleagues then analyzed the machine’s structure. The later Colossus effort combined mathematical work, engineering, and sustained operation.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-columns"></use></svg>
```

The Organization

Bletchley Park housed several operational sections. Hut 6 attacked Army and Air Force Enigma; Hut 3 interpreted and reported the resulting intelligence. Hut 8 attacked Naval Enigma, with intelligence work in Hut 4. The Testery and Newmanry worked on Tunny, the British name for Lorenz traffic. Intercepts arrived through a wider network of listening stations. British Enigma work built on the Polish breakthroughs shared with British and French colleagues in July 1939.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

The Bombe

The British Bombe was a specialized **electromechanical search machine**, designed by Alan Turing and improved through Gordon Welchman’s diagonal board and engineering work. It tested constraints derived from a crib and produced candidate settings for checking. Production totals and daily output changed over the war; a fixed claim of three to five keys every day is not supported here.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Colossus and the Lorenz Break

Lorenz enciphered strategic teleprinter traffic. Tiltman’s recovered keystream made Tutte’s structural analysis possible. Tommy Flowers and his team built Colossus to accelerate statistical tests developed by the cryptanalytic organization; it did not simply decrypt arbitrary traffic automatically. Colossus Mark 1 worked at Dollis Hill in late 1943 and entered operational use at Bletchley in early 1944. See [The National Museum of Computing](<https://www.tnmoc.org/colossus>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

Secrecy and After

Staff were bound by official secrecy, and many accounts became public only decades later. F. W. Winterbotham’s *The Ultra Secret* (1974) brought the wartime intelligence story to a much wider readership, but was not a complete official history of every operation. Dilly Knox died during the war in 1943; others lived to see later recognition. The story involves analysts, engineers, intercept operators, translators and administrative staff, not only its best-known mathematicians.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Location | Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, England |
| --- | --- |
| Operation | August 1939 – 1945 (wartime operation) |
| Personnel | About 10,000 at Bletchley and associated outstations at peak |
| Key Breaks | Enigma and Tunny (Lorenz): teams built on distinct mathematical and operational breakthroughs |
| Hardware | Bombe search machines; Colossus operational at Bletchley in 1944 |
| Estimated impact | Major Allied intelligence contribution; estimates of time saved are counterfactual |

#### Sources and Reading

Bletchley Park, [“Home of the Codebreakers”](<https://artsandculture.google.com/story/bletchley-park-home-of-the-codebreakers-bletchley-park/7gUxRIPFAxsA8A>), for the combined site-and-outstation count; its [“Early Days” episode description](<https://audioboom.com/posts/7391959-e97-early-days>) identifies the August 1939 move records. GCHQ, [“The Pyry Forest Meeting”](<https://www.gchq.gov.uk/information/the-pyry-forest-meeting>), documents the Polish contribution. The National Museum of Computing’s Tunny account distinguishes the Testery and Newmanry.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>) › [Hall VII: Mechanical Cipher Machines](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/machines.html>) › Turing–Welchman Bombe

Exhibit 168 of 1741940 · Britain

### Turing–Welchman Bombe

A crib becomes a network of constraints; machinery searches for settings that survive.

Codebreaking machine; not an encryption system.

#### Why This Matters

The Bombe mechanised part of the attack on Enigma. Alan Turing developed the crib-based approach; Gordon Welchman’s diagonal board improved the search. British Tabulating Machine Company engineers built the machines. Operators and analysts remained essential.

#### How the Search Worked

A guessed plaintext passage, called a crib, was aligned with intercepted ciphertext. Its letter relationships formed a menu. The Bombe tested rotor arrangements against these constraints; contradictions eliminated candidates. A stop indicated a candidate to check, not a finished plaintext. Welchman’s diagonal board exploited the reciprocal connections of Enigma’s plugboard.

#### Read a Constraint

Suppose a proposed crib places A against ciphertext A. Enigma cannot encipher a letter as itself, so that alignment is impossible before a machine search begins. A different alignment may survive this first check and still fail the connected menu constraints. Surviving a filter is evidence to investigate, not proof of a correct key.

#### Historical Context and Limits

The first British Bombe, Victory, entered service in March 1940; the Turing–Welchman version followed in August. The earlier Polish bomba was an important predecessor with a different attack. This was an electromechanical codebreaking machine, not an encryption system or a general-purpose computer. It attacked Enigma, not Lorenz.

#### Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 168 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Type | Codebreaking machine |
| In service | 1940 |

#### Sources and Further Reading

[The National Museum of Computing: Turing–Welchman Bombe](<https://www.tnmoc.org/bombe>) — reconstruction and historical account.

This is a static historical exhibit. No cipher engine or machine simulator is claimed.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall V: Military & Field](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/military.html>)› Book Cipher

18th–20th c.

### Book Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

If both correspondents have the same book, the book itself is the key.

Security depends on the book, edition and indexing rule; identifying the source or exploiting context can expose messages.

OriginPre-revolutionary French military couriers; American Revolutionary War

Year1700s onward

Key TypeAn agreed-upon book; ciphertext is a list of (page, line, word) or (page, word) coordinates

Broken ByIdentifying the book — the Beale Cipher 2 was solved when the anonymous pamphleteer (published by James Ward, 1885) tried the Declaration of Independence

Modern LessonKey distribution is the hard part; the underlying primitive can be trivial

#### Why This Matters

A book cipher uses an agreed reference text and indexing convention. For a page–line–word system, both parties need matching pagination. The unknown reference gives an attacker a search problem, but its size is not unbounded and a famous or predictable book may be easy to guess. Different historical “book ciphers” used different indexing rules.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The Arnold–André correspondence is one historical book-code example. The Beale pamphlet is different evidence: its anonymous narrator claims to have decoded the second sequence using the Declaration of Independence, and James B. Ward published the pamphlet in 1885. Publication does not establish Ward as the solver or verify the earlier narrative. The evidence for one book-code episode does not establish the procedures of unrelated intelligence services.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Pick a book and an edition. To encode the word *RIVER*, scan the book until you find that word; record its location as `(page, line, word)` — say `(127, 14, 6)`. Send the triplet. Variants: **letter-level** book ciphers (every plaintext letter is encoded as the position of any matching letter in the book), **word-only** ciphers (faster but less flexible — rare words must be spelled out), and **number-only** ciphers (the running Beale-style format that is just lists of integers).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Identify the Book

Complexity: Depends on candidate books and indexing rules

If the reference text and indexing rules are recovered, the corresponding lookups are mechanical. Repeated coordinates and contextual knowledge may help identify them. The unsolved Beale sequences do not prove that a key book exists: a different construction or a hoax remains possible.

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Book Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| The hard part is key distribution | Same insight drives modern PKI |
| Out-of-band key sharing | Couriered books prefigure Diffie-Hellman: get a shared secret without revealing it on the wire |
| Unguessable secrets | If the adversary knows your book is one of 50 popular novels, you have at most ~6 bits of key |

Hall X · Codebreakers Europe · 1550–1850

### Cabinet Noir — Black Chambers of Europe

European state interception offices opened, copied and sometimes deciphered selected diplomatic mail before resealing it.

Period~1550–1848 CE

GeographyFrance, Austria, Britain, Papal States, Prussia, Venice

French Cabinet NoirFrench royal postal interception and cryptanalysis, including the Rossignols

Austrian Geheime KabinettskanzleiPeak 1750–1848; intercepted letters across Europe

British Secret OfficeGPO interception unit, operating 1660s–1844

Modern LessonPostal interception provides an earlier comparison for communications intelligence

#### 🔓 Interactive Explorer

Try encoding a message as this cipher does.

 Simulate a Cabinet Noir intercept  [Input input: type=text; initial value=THE AMBASSADOR REQUESTS SAFE PASSAGE]  Encode

##### Why This Matters

European governments developed postal interception and cryptanalytic offices whose practices offer comparisons with later communications intelligence. Staff could open, copy, analyse and reseal selected letters. Practices and institutions differed by country and period; this was not one continuous organisation ancestral to every modern agency.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-columns"></use></svg>
```

The French Cabinet Noir

Antoine Rossignol and his son Bonaventure served the French monarchy in cryptographic and cryptanalytic roles. Kahn dates Antoine’s celebrated Réalmont decipherment to 1628. Earlier European state cryptologists already existed, so the Rossignols should not be called the first professional cryptanalysts in Europe. Royal nomenclators also changed over time.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-columns"></use></svg>
```

The Austrian Geheime Kabinettskanzlei

Vienna’s Geheime Kabinettskanzlei exploited access to postal routes and diplomatic correspondence. Its work combined physical interception, copying and decipherment. Reading selected dispatches could reveal negotiating positions, but does not establish access to every communication of every other power. Kahn describes the office’s closure in 1848.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-columns"></use></svg>
```

Britain's Secret Office

British postal interception and the Decyphering Branch became subjects of controversy in 1844, notably after the opening of Giuseppe Mazzini’s letters. Kahn distinguishes the end of diplomatic interception in June from dissolution of the Decyphering Branch in October. That episode should not be described as the permanent end of all British state mail interception.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Comparing Postal and Electronic Interception

Postal opening and modern electronic interception share questions about access, secrecy, technical capability and oversight. Their institutions and legal settings differ. A comparison with Room 40, Bletchley Park or later agencies is useful, but a direct organisational chain from every black chamber to both GCHQ and NSA is not established.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| --- | --- |

| Austrian Geheime Kabinettskanzlei | Peak 1750–1848; intercepted letters across Europe |
| British Secret Office | GPO interception unit, operating 1660s–1844 |
| Modern Lesson | Postal interception provides an earlier comparison for communications intelligence |

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 5, “The Era of the Black Chambers,” on Rossignol, European postal offices and the institutional changes of 1844–1848.

```javascript
    // Simulate wax-seal removal and resealing (humorous demo — just shows the "intercepted" message)
    function cnEncode(t) {
      const ts = new Date().toISOString().replace('T',' ').slice(0,16);
      return '[INTERCEPTED ' + ts + ' | Cabinet Noir Vienna] ' +
             t.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z ]/g,'') +
             ' | [RESEALED — ORIGINAL WAX IMPRESSION PRESERVED]';
    }
```

### Caesar Cipher

#### Why This Matters

Suetonius records Caesar’s use of a letter shift. The modern A–Z demonstration makes modular substitution easy to inspect; it does not establish the invention date of substitution encryption.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg id="cipherWheel" viewBox="0 0 300 300" style="width:100%;max-width:300px;height:auto;display:block;margin:0 auto" aria-label="Caesar cipher wheel showing outer plaintext ring and inner shifted ciphertext ring">
```

Caesar cipher wheel — outer ring: plaintext, inner ring: ciphertext. Drag the slider to change the shift.

[Image: Caesar cipher disc (Chiffrierscheibe) by Linge, Pleidelsheim, Germany; source: https://ciphermuseum.com/images/artifacts/mechanical-cipher-disk.png]

Caesar Cipher Disc (Chiffrierscheibe) — Linge, Pleidelsheim, Germany. Modern reproduction of the classical rotary disc design. Image: Hubert Berberich (HubiB) · Public Domain

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Julius Caesar used this cipher to communicate with his generals during the Gallic Wars. Suetonius records it in *The Twelve Caesars* (c. 121 AD): *"If he had anything confidential to say, he wrote it in cipher, that is, by so changing the order of the letters of the alphabet, that not a word could be made out."*

Suetonius describes Caesar’s shift of three. His account of Augustus describes a different convention, including AA for Z rather than a modern wraparound alphabet. This exhibit’s fixed 26-letter model should not be mistaken for a facsimile of Roman correspondence.

💡

**ROT13** — the modern variant — applies a shift of 13. Because 13+13=26, ROT13 is its own inverse: applying it twice returns the original text. It's still used in online forums to hide spoilers.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Each letter is replaced by the letter a fixed number of positions down the alphabet. The shift wraps around using modular arithmetic:

```text
Encrypt: C = (P + shift) mod 26
Decrypt: P = (C − shift + 26) mod 26

Example (shift = 3):
  A → D    N → Q
  B → E    O → R
  Z → C    (wrap-around)
```

**Encryption steps:**

- Convert each plaintext letter to a number (A=0, B=1 … Z=25)

- Add the shift value and take modulo 26

- Convert the result back to a letter

- Non-alphabetic characters (spaces, punctuation) pass through unchanged

Shift Diagram (shift = 3)

Plain

Cipher

Each plain letter maps to the cipher letter directly below it.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Frequency Analysis

Al-Kindi described frequency analysis in the ninth century; no first break of Caesar’s messages is established here

Long English samples often have E among their most frequent letters, but individual messages may differ greatly. A Caesar shift preserves the observed letter counts. Treating the most common ciphertext letter as E proposes a key; other shifts and the resulting language must still be checked.

Brute Force

Complexity: Trivial · Keyspace: 25

The entire keyspace is just 25 shifts. There are only 25 nonidentity shifts to test. Recognizing the intended plaintext can still require context. This is the simplest form of exhaustive key search — a technique that scales to modern ciphers but requires vastly more computation.

⚠️

**Why it fails fundamentally:** there are only 25 nonidentity shifts on A–Z (26 including leaving the text unchanged). AES-256 has 2²⁵⁶ possible keys. The difference illustrates why a tiny keyspace is vulnerable, but keyspace size alone never proves a cipher secure.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Caesar Concept | Evolved Into |
| --- | --- |
| Letter substitution | AES combines nonlinear byte substitution with key addition and diffusion; a substitution table alone preserves frequencies |
| Shift = key | Symmetric key concept — both parties share a secret parameter |
| 25-key space | Generic search of a uniform AES-256 key takes about 2²⁵⁵ trials on average |
| Frequency leak | Diffusion in block-cipher design spreads input changes; this is not a property of every cryptographic construction |

🎓

**Shannon's confusion:** Claude Shannon (1949) defined "confusion" as making the relationship between key and ciphertext as complex as possible. Caesar’s relation `C = P + k (mod 26)` is easy to invert for each candidate key. “Zero confusion” is not a numerical security measurement. AES combines nonlinear substitution with other round operations; its strength cannot be attributed to an S-box alone.

It is a modern example of why classical ciphers remain pedagogically powerful: fast to learn, satisfying to break, and instantly reusable in storytelling.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

const ALPHABET = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
let mode = 'enc';

// ── Build shift diagram ──────────────────────────────
function buildDiagram(shift) {
  const pr = document.getElementById('plainRow');
  const cr = document.getElementById('cipherRow');
  if (!pr) return;
  pr.innerHTML = ''; cr.innerHTML = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < 26; i++) {
    const pc = document.createElement('div');
    pc.className = 'a-cell a-plain';
    pc.textContent = ALPHABET[i];
    pr.appendChild(pc);
    const cc = document.createElement('div');
    cc.className = 'a-cell a-cipher';
    cc.textContent = ALPHABET[(i + shift) % 26];
    cr.appendChild(cc);
  }
}
buildDiagram(3);

// ── Build cipher wheel ───────────────────────────────
function buildWheel(shift) {
  var svg = document.getElementById('cipherWheel');
  if (!svg) return;
  svg.querySelectorAll('text').forEach(function(t){ t.remove(); });
  var A = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
  for (var i = 0; i < 26; i++) {
    var angle = (i * 360 / 26 - 90) * Math.PI / 180;
    var ox = 150 + 122 * Math.cos(angle), oy = 150 + 122 * Math.sin(angle);
    var t = document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'text');
    t.setAttribute('x', ox); t.setAttribute('y', oy);
    t.setAttribute('text-anchor', 'middle'); t.setAttribute('dominant-baseline', 'central');
    t.setAttribute('fill', '#EDE5D4'); t.setAttribute('font-family', 'var(--fm,monospace)');
    t.setAttribute('font-size', '11'); t.textContent = A[i]; svg.appendChild(t);
    var ci = (i + shift) % 26;
    var ix = 150 + 82 * Math.cos(angle), iy = 150 + 82 * Math.sin(angle);
    var t2 = document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'text');
    t2.setAttribute('x', ix); t2.setAttribute('y', iy);
    t2.setAttribute('text-anchor', 'middle'); t2.setAttribute('dominant-baseline', 'central');
    t2.setAttribute('fill', '#C9A84C'); t2.setAttribute('font-family', 'var(--fm,monospace)');
    t2.setAttribute('font-size', '11'); t2.setAttribute('font-weight', '700');
    t2.textContent = A[ci]; svg.appendChild(t2);
  }
  var label = document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'text');
  label.setAttribute('x', '150'); label.setAttribute('y', '150');
  label.setAttribute('text-anchor', 'middle'); label.setAttribute('dominant-baseline', 'central');
  label.setAttribute('fill', 'var(--gold-dim)'); label.setAttribute('font-family', 'var(--fm)');
  label.setAttribute('font-size', '7'); label.setAttribute('letter-spacing', '.1em');
  label.textContent = 'SHIFT ' + shift; svg.appendChild(label);
}
buildWheel(3);

// ── Mode ─────────────────────────────────────────────
function setMode(m) {
  mode = m;
  document.getElementById('btnEnc').classList.toggle('active', m === 'enc');
  document.getElementById('btnDec').classList.toggle('active', m === 'dec');
}

function onShiftChange(v) {
  document.getElementById('shiftLabel').textContent = v;
  document.getElementById('shiftVal').textContent = v;
  buildDiagram(parseInt(v));
  buildWheel(parseInt(v));
}

// ── Cipher ───────────────────────────────────────────
function caesar(text, shift, enc) {
  shift = ((shift % 26) + 26) % 26;
  if (!enc) shift = (26 - shift) % 26;
  return text.toUpperCase().split('').map(ch => {
    const c = ch.charCodeAt(0);
    if (c >= 65 && c <= 90) return String.fromCharCode(((c - 65 + shift) % 26) + 65);
    return ch;
  }).join('');
}

function runCipher() {
  const msg   = document.getElementById('msgInput').value;
  const shift = parseInt(document.getElementById('shiftSlider').value);
  const result = caesar(msg, shift, mode === 'enc');
  document.getElementById('outputBox').textContent = result;
}

function clearDemo() {
  document.getElementById('msgInput').value = '';
  document.getElementById('outputBox').innerHTML = '<span class="output-empty">Result appears here…</span>';
}

// ── Frequency analyzer ───────────────────────────────
const EN_FREQ = {E:12.7,T:9.1,A:8.2,O:7.5,I:7.0,N:6.7,S:6.3,H:6.1,R:6.0,D:4.3,L:4.0,C:2.8,U:2.8,M:2.4,W:2.4,F:2.2,G:2.0,Y:2.0,P:1.9,B:1.5,V:0.98,K:0.77,J:0.15,X:0.15,Q:0.10,Z:0.07};
const MAX_EN = Math.max(...Object.values(EN_FREQ));

function buildFreqGrid() {
  const g = document.getElementById('freqGrid');
  if (!g) return;
  g.innerHTML = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < 26; i++) {
    const ch = ALPHABET[i];
    const cell = document.createElement('div');
    cell.className = 'freq-cell';
    cell.id = 'fc_' + ch;
    cell.innerHTML = `<div class="f-bar"><div class="f-fill" id="fb_${ch}" style="height:0px"></div></div><div>${ch}</div>`;
    g.appendChild(cell);
  }
}
buildFreqGrid();

function updateFreq() {
  const txt = document.getElementById('freqInput').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
  if (!txt.length) { buildFreqGrid(); document.getElementById('freqHint').textContent = ''; return; }
  const counts = {};
  for (const ch of txt) counts[ch] = (counts[ch]||0)+1;
  let maxCh = 'E', maxCount = 0;
  for (const ch in counts) if (counts[ch] > maxCount) { maxCount = counts[ch]; maxCh = ch; }
  const guessedShift = (maxCh.charCodeAt(0) - 69 + 26) % 26;

  for (let i = 0; i < 26; i++) {
    const ch = ALPHABET[i];
    const pct = ((counts[ch]||0)/txt.length)*100;
    const h = Math.round((pct / 15) * 32);
    const el = document.getElementById('fb_'+ch);
    const cell = document.getElementById('fc_'+ch);
    if (el) el.style.height = Math.max(h,2)+'px';
    if (cell) cell.classList.toggle('hi', ch === maxCh);
  }
  document.getElementById('freqHint').textContent =
    `Most common: ${maxCh} → Guessed shift: ${guessedShift}`;
}

// ── Auto-break (chi-squared cryptanalysis) ───────────
function escapeHtml(s) {
  return String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g, c => ({
    '&':'&amp;','<':'&lt;','>':'&gt;','"':'&quot;',"'":'&#39;'
  }[c]));
}

function renderBreakResults(candidates) {
  const box = document.getElementById('breakResults');
  if (!box) return;
  if (!candidates.length) { box.innerHTML = ''; return; }
  let html = '<div class="break-rank-tag">Most likely → least likely (chi-squared distance, lower = better)</div>';
  candidates.forEach((c, i) => {
    const truncated = c.plaintext.length > 80 ? c.plaintext.slice(0, 80) + '…' : c.plaintext;
    const cls = i === 0 ? 'break-row best' : 'break-row';
    html += `<div class="${cls}">
      <span class="break-shift" aria-label="Shift ${c.shift}">+${c.shift}</span>
      <span class="break-text" title="${escapeHtml(c.plaintext)}">${escapeHtml(truncated)}</span>
      <span class="break-score" aria-label="Chi-squared score">${c.score.toFixed(1)}</span>
    </div>`;
  });
  box.innerHTML = html;
}

function runAutoBreak() {
  const txt = document.getElementById('breakInput').value.trim();
  const box = document.getElementById('breakResults');
  if (!txt) {
    box.innerHTML = '<p class="break-empty">Paste a Caesar ciphertext above and press Break Cipher.</p>';
    return;
  }
  if (!window.CaesarBreak) {
    box.innerHTML = '<p class="break-empty">Auto-break engine failed to load.</p>';
    return;
  }
  const ranked = window.CaesarBreak.breakCaesar(txt);
  renderBreakResults(ranked);
}

function clearAutoBreak() {
  document.getElementById('breakInput').value = '';
  document.getElementById('breakResults').innerHTML = '';
}

document.getElementById('breakRunBtn').addEventListener('click', runAutoBreak);
document.getElementById('breakClearBtn').addEventListener('click', clearAutoBreak);
// Allow Ctrl/Cmd+Enter inside the textarea to run the break.
document.getElementById('breakInput').addEventListener('keydown', e => {
  if ((e.ctrlKey || e.metaKey) && e.key === 'Enter') { e.preventDefault(); runAutoBreak(); }
});

function revealAnswer() {
  document.getElementById('answerReveal').style.display = 'block';
}

// Auto-run on load
runCipher();
```

### Cardano Autokey 1550 historical idea · modern comparison model

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Cardano’s self-keying idea, compared with a modern one-letter-primer plaintext-autokey model.

The one-letter-primer widget is a modern comparison with Vigenère-style plaintext autokey, not Cardano’s exact procedure.

OriginGirolamo Cardano, Italy

Year1550 (*De Subtilitate*)

Key TypeSingle priming letter

Secret choice in this modelOne of 26 primer letters

Modern LessonKey reuse from the plaintext is not the same as key freshness

#### Why This Matters

Cardano described using plaintext as key material, but the one-letter-primer algorithm below should not be attributed to him as an exact reconstruction. Holden’s [*The Mathematics of Secrets: Cryptography from Caesar Ciphers to Digital Encryption*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#holden>) (2017), §5.3, pp. 157–159, distinguishes Cardano’s word-based scheme from Vigenère’s later use of a priming letter. This interactive isolates a simple autokey recurrence for teaching.

In this model, knowing one plaintext letter gives the next key letter and permits forward propagation. A primer of length k changes this to propagation every k positions; it does **not** eliminate the structural weakness. A sufficiently long correct crib can seed several such chains.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Pick a single seed letter `S`. The keystream is

```text
k₀ = S
kᵢ = pᵢ₋₁  for i ≥ 1
```

Encryption uses the standard Vigenère table: cᵢ = (pᵢ + kᵢ) mod 26. Decryption recovers p₀ from c₀ using S, then uses each just-recovered pᵢ as the key for cᵢ₊₁.

**Worked example with S = Q, plaintext MEET ME AT MIDNIGHT:**

```text
Plain : M E E T M E A T M I D N I G H T
Key   : Q M E E T M E A T M I D N I G H
Cipher: C Q I X F Q E T F U L Q V O N A
```

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Probable-word cascade

Complexity: Easy with a crib

With a one-letter primer, a correct plaintext guess propagates one position at a time. Wrong guesses generate alternative chains that need evaluation against language or other evidence. Longer primers change the spacing of propagation rather than making plaintext feedback secure.

26 priming guesses

Complexity: Trivial on short messages

Try every possible seed letter. For each, run the cascade and look for English. The correct plaintext is among the 26 candidates; a short or unusual message may need context to distinguish it.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

The lesson is that reusing message letters as raw key material does not supply independent secrecy. It should not be generalized into a rule that every data-dependent cryptographic construction is insecure: the precise construction and security definition matter.

CTR and ChaCha20 generate keystream from a secret key and nonce/counter state. Their security also depends on correct nonce use. The contrast is with this bare letter recurrence, not a claimed direct historical lineage or a universal ban on processing plaintext in authentication and encryption designs.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Origin | Girolamo Cardano, Italy |
| --- | --- |
| Year | 1550 (*De Subtilitate*) |
| Key Type | Single priming letter |
| Secret choice in this model | One of 26 primer letters |
| Modern Lesson | Key reuse from the plaintext is not the same as key freshness |

Hall IV · Transposition / Steganography Italian Renaissance · 1550

### Cardano Grille 1550 · steganography by template

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A pierced card and an innocuous-looking letter: the recipient overlays an identical grille and reads the secret through the holes.

Weak (steganography, not encryption)

OriginGirolamo Cardano, Italy

Year1550 (*De Subtilitate*)

Key TypeThe grille pattern (positions of the holes)

FamilySteganography / fixed-mask concealment

Modern LessonHiding a message ≠ encrypting a message

#### Why This Matters

Girolamo Cardano described a fixed concealment grille in *De Subtilitate* (1550). Openings in a sheet select parts of a message written underneath; the sender then fills the surrounding space with cover text. Openings can expose letters, syllables or words. The square, one-letter-per-cell layout below is a teaching model, not a requirement of the historical technique.

Variants and descendants of the grille remained in active espionage use into the twentieth century. The [**turning grille**](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/turning-grille.html>) — a square card rotated through four positions to fill an N×N grid completely — was used briefly by the German Army in late 1916–early 1917 for tactical traffic, and broken by French and British analysts within months.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

In this teaching model, the grille is a square card of side *N* with holes punched at agreed-upon positions. Sender and receiver each have an identical card. To encrypt:

- Place the grille over a blank N×N grid.

- Write the secret letter-by-letter through the holes.

- Lift the grille; fill the remaining cells with plausible filler (a poem, a shopping list, a love letter).

To decrypt, the recipient places their grille over the received grid in the same orientation and reads the letters visible through the holes.

The demo on this page uses a key of the form `size:idx,idx,idx,…` — the grid side length followed by the zero-based positions of the holes. The default `5:0,3,7,12,19,21,24` places seven holes in a 5×5 grid.

ℹ️

**About this demo:** To guarantee that Decrypt exactly restores your original message, this demo reversibly escapes the letters X, Q, and Z (as ZA, ZB, ZC) before enciphering, so padding and filler X can never be confused with a real letter. Messages containing X, Q, or Z therefore produce slightly different ciphertext than a strictly classical Cardano grille would. Messages longer than one grille continue into additional grids rather than being truncated.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Capture the grille

Complexity: A search of the office

Copying the grille reveals its selection rule. Messages using that same layout and orientation can then be read if their carriers are available. A different grille, changed convention or separate encryption layer is a separate problem; capturing one card does not automatically expose every past and future message.

Style mismatch

Complexity: Easy with practice

Convincing filler text is hard. A trained censor reading thousands of letters notices stilted phrasing, awkward grammar, and the distinctive cadence of grille-fill — and flags suspicious correspondence for closer inspection.

Brute-force the holes

Complexity: Tractable for small grids

The default demo has seven holes in 25 cells: there are C(25,7) = 480,700 possible masks if only the hole count is known. This counts selections, not a guarantee of a unique readable extraction. Natural-language scoring can rank candidates; several short extractions may look plausible. A turning grille has different rotational constraints and needs its own count.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

The fixed grille illustrates **steganography**: concealing the existence or location of a message within a carrier. Modern image embedding and covert channels offer useful comparisons, but a direct historical line of descent is not established by the similarity.

Concealment and confidentiality are different goals. A plausible cover may escape notice, but this grille provides no encryption or authentication once the selected text is exposed. Separate encryption can protect content even if the hiding method is discovered; it does not by itself make the carrier undetectable.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Origin | Girolamo Cardano, Italy |
| --- | --- |
| Year | 1550 (*De Subtilitate*) |
| Key Type | The grille pattern (positions of the holes) |
| Family | Steganography / fixed-mask concealment |
| Modern Lesson | Hiding a message ≠ encrypting a message |

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 4, on Cardano’s fixed grille, and discussion of German turning grilles in 1916–1917. Fixed concealment and turning-grille transposition are distinct procedures.

Exhibit 46 of 174 Modern · 1918

### Chaocipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

John Byrne's 1918 disk cipher — disclosed after 92 years, then cryptanalyzed

Published key-recovery attacks by Lasry, Rubin, Kopal and Wacker (2016).

InventorJohn F. Byrne

Year1918 (disclosed 2010)

Key TypeTwo scrambled 26-letter alphabets

Famous factHeld secret for 92 years; public cryptanalysis followed the 2010 disclosure

Modern LessonState evolution needs analysis under explicit attack conditions

#### Why This Matters

John Byrne — Irish-American writer and friend of James Joyce — invented the Chaocipher in 1918 and spent four decades trying to convince the US government and AT&T to adopt it. Its design was not publicly available during those proposals. His 1953 autobiography *Silent Years* included challenge ciphertexts; the algorithm became public 57 years later. In 2010, his family donated his papers to the National Cryptologic Museum and the algorithm was finally published. It turned out to be elegantly simple: two rotating disks that permute themselves after each letter.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Byrne promoted Chaocipher for decades after devising it in 1918. His death in 1960 preceded the family’s 2010 donation of the papers to the National Cryptologic Museum. Public disclosure enabled researchers to distinguish the algorithm from its secret initial alphabets and to study specific key-recovery attacks. Earlier secrecy and unaccepted proposals are not evidence of a general security proof.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Two 26-letter alphabets, called the "left" (ciphertext) and "right" (plaintext) wheels, are independently scrambled. To encrypt one letter:

```text
1. Find the plaintext letter on the right wheel.
2. The ciphertext letter is at the same position on the left wheel.
3. Rotate both wheels so the touched letters are at the "zenith" (position 0).
4. Permute the LEFT wheel: take the letter at position 1, slide it into position 13.
5. Permute the RIGHT wheel: rotate it one position, then take the letter at
   position 2 and slide it into position 13.
6. Repeat for the next plaintext letter.
```

The evolving wheels change the substitution after each letter. The widget derives its left alphabet by deduplicating the seed and appending unused A–Z letters; its right alphabet is that sequence rotated by 13. This restricted key setup is a teaching choice, not support for entering two independently chosen historical wheel alphabets.

```text
Widget seed: CHAOCIPHER
Left:  CHAOIPERBDFGJKLMNQSTUVWXYZ
Right: KLMNQSTUVWXYZCHAOIPERBDFGJ
Plaintext:  WELLDONEISBETTERTHANWELLSAID
Ciphertext: DSZYOZXXGRZVVUSRQUBYXYJBMZIE
```

The wheel operations follow Moshe Rubin’s *Chaocipher Revealed: The Algorithm* (2010), pp. 1–5. The example above uses the museum’s seed-derived wheels, so its ciphertext differs from Byrne’s published example with two separately chosen wheels.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Disclosure (2010)

Algorithm disclosure enabled public analysis

The Byrne family donated the Chaocipher papers to the National Cryptologic Museum in 2010, making the algorithm public after 92 years. Disclosure itself was not a cryptanalytic break; it allowed researchers to study the keyed construction.

Known-Plaintext and In-Depth Attacks

Published key-recovery attacks

A known-plaintext key-recovery method was published in 2010. In 2016, George Lasry, Moshe Rubin, Nils Kopal, and Arno Wacker published a hill-climbing attack against multiple messages encrypted with the same initial settings, plus a known-plaintext attack on short in-depth messages. Their [Cryptologia paper](<https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2015.1091797>) establishes weaknesses in the classic cipher; it does not claim a general ciphertext-only break of every isolated message.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Chaocipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Self-modifying state | RC4 updates byte-oriented state; ChaCha20 generates 64-byte blocks from a key, nonce and counter |
| Algorithm secrecy is not security | Kerckhoffs’ principle: evaluate security with the algorithm public |
| Simple components, complex evolution | Simple components can produce evolving mappings; that alone does not establish security |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| Inventor | John F. Byrne |

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall V: Military & Spy Ciphers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/military.html>)› Che Guevara’s Checkerboard and Pad

Hall V · Military Ciphers Cold War · 1956–1967

### Che Guevara’s Checkerboard and Pad

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A checkerboard converts letters into digits; a secret digit pad supplies a separate encryption layer. This is not the full VIC construction.

Historical checkerboard-plus-pad system; the widget compares a condensed VIC model, not Guevara’s historical pad system.

UserErnesto "Che" Guevara

Era1956–1967

FamilyStraddling checkerboard + digit pad

Key TypeCheckerboard and secret pad digits

Compromise routeBolivian Army capture (1967)

Modern LessonKey handling is part of communications security

#### Why This Matters

Accounts of Guevara’s communications describe a **straddling checkerboard with a digit one-time pad**. The [CrypTool researcher’s reconstruction](<https://www.kopaldev.de/2022/04/27/cryptography-for-everybody-the-straddling-checkerboard-cipher-and-che-guevara/>) illustrates that combination. Sharing a checkerboard component with VIC does not make the two complete systems equivalent.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

VIC derives key material and applies transpositions. A one-time-pad system instead requires independent, uniformly random secret digits, never reused, as long as the digit message. These are materially different security assumptions. The museum has not established the former claim that Guevara received a particular KGB cipher course in Moscow.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How the Straddling Checkerboard Works

A straddling checkerboard gives some letters one-digit codes and others two-digit codes. This is a reversible encoding, not a guarantee against frequency analysis. Adding fresh secret pad digits modulo 10 can provide one-time-pad secrecy if the pad conditions are actually met.

ℹ️

**About this demo:** The widget uses the museum’s condensed VIC engine, including chain addition and two transpositions. It is a **comparison exercise, not a reconstruction of Guevara’s pad system**. Its keyword-generated digits are not a one-time pad.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Exposed

Physical capture

Complexity: Trivial with materials in hand

Captured documents can compromise a communications system without breaking its mathematics. [A U.S. memorandum dated July 15, 1967](<https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v31/d168>) already discusses captured guerrilla documents; exposure cannot all be assigned to Guevara’s October capture. This exhibit makes no claim of ciphertext-only key recovery or of a verified 24-hour transfer of cipher materials to Langley.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| --- | --- |

| Family | Straddling checkerboard + digit pad |
| Key Type | Checkerboard and secret pad digits |

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall VI: Civil War Gallery](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/civil-war.html>)› Chinese Telegraph Code

Hall VI · Telegraph Era Late Qing → PRC · 1881–1980s

### Chinese Telegraph Code Standard Telegraph Codebook · 1881

Four-digit character codes connected Chinese writing to telegraph networks; confidentiality required an additional protection layer.

Public codebook (super-enciphered when secret)

OriginEarly European contributors; later Chinese revisions

Year1870s development; Zheng Guanying revision 1881

MappingFour-digit groups for characters included in the applicable edition

UseCivil telegraphy publicly; diplomatic / military traffic super-enciphered

StatusDocumented administrative use: Hong Kong identity-card particulars

#### Why This Matters

The Sheridan Libraries’ account of *Dian bao xin bian* (1909) describes an earlier Danish contribution, refinement in Shanghai in 1872, and Zheng Guanying’s revision in 1881. Chinese telegraph codebooks assign four-digit numbers to the characters included in their tables, allowing messages in Chinese to travel through telegraph networks. These are character encodings, not secret encryption by themselves. Successive editions and regional variants do not necessarily give every character the same number; the sender and receiver must use compatible tables. Chinese Commercial Code numbers also have administrative uses. Hong Kong’s Immigration Department lists a name in Chinese commercial code, where applicable, among identity-card particulars. This is a specific documented use, not evidence that every mainland passport or Taiwanese registration carries the same code field.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The codebook is a giant lookup table. Each included character maps to a four-digit number in the selected table; the operator transmits the digits as Morse code. The receiver looks up each 4-digit group in their copy of the same codebook and recovers the character.

For confidentiality, some systems superenciphered the numeric codegroups. NSA’s account of Viguier’s 1873 proposal describes adding a key number digit by digit modulo 10, without carries. A codebook plus an additive is a broad design pattern also found in other systems; it does not mean all such systems used identical arithmetic, group sizes or key procedures.

The demo uses an invented A–Z table and adds the same numeric input to each four-digit group modulo 10,000, with carries. This is a deliberately small teaching model. It differs from the digitwise historical example and is neither a transcription of a Chinese codebook nor a one-time-pad system.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was (and Was Not) Broken

Public codebook → trivial without superencipherment

Complexity: Lookup only

Civil traffic used the published codebook with no additive. Anyone with a copy could read the messages — the codebook was a transmission convenience, not a cipher.

With additive: depth attack

Condition: shared additive and compatible arithmetic

Reusing an additive exposes relations between codegroups. For this demo, subtracting ciphertext groups modulo 10,000 cancels the shared additive. In a digitwise system, cancellation must instead be performed digit by digit modulo 10. Recovering the actual text still requires codebook information or other constraints; reuse does not automatically solve every message.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| CTC lesson | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| Codebook plus separate encipherment | Compare layers of representation and protection; a block cipher is not a public codebook |
| Codebook ID numbers persist in identity systems | Unicode also assigns numeric identifiers; neither system supplies secrecy by itself |
| Adapting a script to a hostile transport | Punycode / IDN encoding for non-ASCII domain names |
| Reused additive material exposes relations | AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 require nonce uniqueness under a key |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| --- | --- |
| Year | 1870s development; Zheng Guanying revision 1881 |
| Mapping | Four-digit groups for characters included in the applicable edition |
| Use | Civil telegraphy publicly; diplomatic / military traffic super-enciphered |

#### Sources and Reading

NSA, [“The Chinese Telegraph Code”](<https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/news-features/declassified-documents/history-today-articles/02%202018/15FEB2018%20The%20Chinese%20Telegraph%20Code.pdf>) (15 February 2018), for Viguier’s digitwise additive example; Hong Kong Immigration Department, [identity-card particulars](<https://www.immd.gov.hk/eng/faq/faq_hkic.html>), for the contemporary administrative use.

These support edition-specific character encoding, not the museum’s invented Latin lookup table.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall XIII: Cipher Culture](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/culture.html>)› Cicada 3301

Hall XIII · Culture Internet era · 2012–2014

### Cicada 3301

An anonymous 2012–2014 internet recruitment puzzle that combined steganography, classical ciphers, GPS coordinates on physical posters, and a copy of the *Liber Primus* hand-illustrated in glyphic runes.

Multi-stage ARG / recruitment puzzle

RegionGlobal (online + physical posters in 14 cities)

YearThree releases: Jan 2012, Jan 2013, Jan 2014

Issued byAnonymous group signing as '3301'

TrackB (puzzle-stage walkthrough)

#### Interactive Exhibit

Step through the four major puzzle layers used in Cicada's 2012 release: Caesar decode, URL extraction, image steg hint, and book-cipher index. Each button reveals the kind of move solvers had to make. Track B — narrative walkthrough.

 Pick a Cicada 2012 puzzle stage (1\u20134)  [Input input: type=number; initial value=1]  Walk this stage

##### Why This Matters

On 4 January 2012 a plain image appeared on 4chan reading 'Hello. We are looking for highly intelligent individuals.' Solving it required Caesar-shift decoding, OutGuess image steganography, a book code on the Mabinogion, a call to a Dallas telephone number, a prime-number step, GPS coordinates that pointed to QR-coded posters in cities on several continents, a second book code on William Gibson's *Agrippa (A Book of the Dead)*, and ultimately a Tor hidden service. Two further puzzles ran in 2013 and 2014. The third released digital page images of *Liber Primus* in a runic alphabet. CicadaSolvers’ status account, checked on 26 October 2026, distinguishes a solved 17-page first set from a 58-page second set with two solved pages (56 and 57). “The first 19 pages” is not the correct description. The identity of '3301' has never been confirmed.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The 2012 puzzle alone employed: a Caesar shift, digital steganography (the OutGuess tool), URL discovery, a book code on the Mabinogion — the "Lady of the Fountain" text as printed in Bulfinch's *Mythology* — a telephone recording that set a prime-number task, a second book code on Gibson's *Agrippa (A Book of the Dead)*, and finally an invitation by private email. Solvers who finished within the deadline reported being asked to write essays on cryptography and privacy; some never heard back. Theories about who '3301' was range from a private intelligence-recruitment outfit to a libertarian cryptography collective.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

Cicada combined classical ciphers with steganography, cryptographic signatures, internet services and collaborative puzzle solving. These are distinct tools: a PGP signature can authenticate a message’s key origin without revealing who controls that key. The difficulty of the overall hunt is not a ranking of cryptographic security.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

Cicada illustrates how communities combine several kinds of evidence in a puzzle hunt. Similarities to institutional recruitment challenges do not establish that GCHQ or NSA copied its design. Reports of new solutions or messages require reproducible methods and careful provenance checks.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```
