### Colossus

Electronic counting accelerated the statistical search behind the Tunny breakthrough.

Codebreaking machine; synthetic two-wheel setting experiment, not full decryption.

#### Why This Matters

Colossus helped attack Lorenz teleprinter traffic, known at Bletchley Park as Tunny. Tommy Flowers and his team built it at the Post Office Research Station. The first machine was working at Bletchley Park in February 1944.

#### How the Search Worked

Punched paper tape supplied ciphertext. Electronic logic evaluated combinations of tape data and generated wheel patterns, while counters accumulated statistical scores. This accelerated the search for Lorenz chi-wheel settings. Colossus supported a larger cryptanalytic process; it did not automatically turn arbitrary intercepted traffic into readable messages.

#### Tape Clock → Condition → Count

Colossus read intercepted ciphertext from a continuous paper-tape loop. Sprocket holes supplied the timing signals for counting and electronic wheel movement. The wheel patterns were generated electronically, replacing the second synchronized tape used by Heath Robinson. At about 5,000 tape characters per second, the reader supplied many observations for each statistical trial; that figure is not 5,000 keys or completed trials per second.

- **Clock:** a tape timing pulse presents the next character and coordinates the electronic pattern.

- **Condition:** configured logic combines selected tape and wheel signals.

- **Count:** a counter increments when that condition is satisfied.

- **Select:** at the end of the count, a configured “set total” can select scores for printing.

The original worked example below isolates one counter. Let A and B be two selected binary inputs to the logic, and count positions where `A XOR B = 0`. The six positions and their values are invented teaching data, not historical traffic or a full Colossus simulation.

Swipe or scroll the table horizontally to see every column. Keyboard: focus the table area and use the arrow keys.

One fixed setting: count equal input bits

| Position | A | B | A XOR B | Running count |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 |
| 4 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| 5 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 3 |
| 6 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 4 |

**Final score: 4.** In “exceeds set total” mode, a set total of 3 selects this score for printing; a set total of 4 does not. Other selection modes were available. A slower reading of the same positions at the same setting would still count 4: speed changes elapsed time, not the logical result. A selected score is evidence to investigate, not a recovered plaintext.

The machine had five separate counters, allowing several conditions to be counted together subject to shared stepping and spanning controls. This example shows only one condition. The [existing two-wheel experiment below](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/colossus.html#chi-setting-search>) illustrates statistical comparison across candidate settings; the [three-task history](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bill-tutte.html#tunny-three-tasks>) separates setting from structural inference and wheel-pattern recovery.

Sources: I. J. Good, Donald Michie and Geoffrey Timms, *General Report on Tunny: With Emphasis on Statistical Methods* (1945), §53B, printed pp. 333–334 / collected PDF pp. 327–328, and §53F–G, printed pp. 337–338 / collected PDF pp. 331–332; Paul Gannon, *Colossus: Bletchley Park’s Greatest Secret* (Atlantic Books, 2014 edition), chapter 15, “Inventing the Electronic Computing Machine,” converted PDF pp. 153–156, especially pp. 154, 156. Gannon’s converted PDF numbering is not verified print pagination. The six-position table is an original teaching example based on these mechanisms.

#### Try a Two-Wheel Chi-Setting Search

Given known chi-wheel patterns, search their initial settings. Here D = Z XOR chi, and delta means XOR of adjacent symbols. Count dots (zeroes) in delta D1 XOR delta D2, equivalently delta Z1 XOR delta Z2 XOR delta chi1 XOR delta chi2. Impulses 1 and 2 are the two low bits in this five-bit representation. All 41 × 31 = 1,271 candidate settings are counted.

This is synthetic five-bit traffic with an explicitly planted residual statistic: the parity of D1 XOR D2 changes with probability 0.30 before added noise. The known wheel patterns are synthetic. It illustrates the historical two-impulse counting condition; it does not emulate German language, psi/motor wheels, Colossus hardware or full Tunny decryption.

Tape length
- 64

- 256

- 1024 [selected]

- 4096
 Additional parity noise
- None

- 25%

- 50% — no planted bias
 Search settings

Run the search, then compare a short tape or the no-bias control. A high score alone does not identify a plaintext.

The displayed sigma is a single-setting score. Selecting the best of 1,271 settings changes its interpretation; the experiment compares that maximum against maxima from 39 seeded independent uniform-symbol null tapes. The null assumes independent five-bit symbols and is not a historical traffic model. Short or noisy traffic can be inconclusive. Finding wheel settings, recovering unknown wheel patterns, and recovering plaintext are separate problems.

Source: I. J. Good, Donald Michie and Geoffrey Timms, *General Report on Tunny: With Emphasis on Statistical Methods* (1945), §§23A–C, printed pp. 78–80 / collected PDF pp. 81–83; Colossus machinery in §§53A–D, printed pp. 333–335 / collected PDF pp. 327–329. Formula and notation checked against the page images.

#### Historical Context and Limits

Bill Tutte reconstructed the cipher’s logical structure, enabling later machine-assisted methods. Colossus was programmable through controls and connections, but was neither a stored-program computer nor a general-purpose machine. Its role concerned Lorenz, not Enigma. The National Museum of Computing houses a working reconstruction.

#### Advanced Bounded Columnar Search

Supply a known width first. The staged option estimates column adjacency, and for incomplete rectangles retains the best relative-offset alignment. Segment slides and segment swaps preserve some neighboring columns while moving larger blocks. The second phase scores the full candidate text using the museum language model.

 Ciphertext (letters only; up to 2,000)

TIIEATFSHSSROMTEETX

Known width (0 searches 2–12) [Input columnar-search-width: type=number; initial value=8]  Seed [Input columnar-search-seed: type=number; initial value=2018]  Total score evaluations [Input columnar-search-budget: type=number; initial value=6000]  Restarts [Input columnar-search-restarts: type=number; initial value=4]   [Input columnar-search-staged: type=checkbox; initial value=; checked]  Adjacency initialization [Input columnar-search-align: type=checkbox; initial value=; checked]  Incomplete-column alignment [Input columnar-search-segments: type=checkbox; initial value=; checked]  Segment slides and swapsSearch candidates

```text
Change one option at a time to compare searches with the same seed and budget.
```

Limits: widths 2–12, at most 20,000 score evaluations, including adjacency preprocessing, phase-transition scoring and every restart. Unknown-width mode divides one total budget across widths 2–12; preprocessing may exhaust a width's allocation. This bounded adaptation samples moves and combines normalized adjacency/alignment scores; it does not reproduce Lasry's alternating thresholds, exhaustive neighborhoods, optimized triplet scores or large-key performance. Language-model fitness uses the museum's bigram/trigram model. A candidate remains unverified even if it looks readable.

Classroom experiment: [run the fixed 24-trial comparison and keep its receipt](<https://ciphermuseum.com/teaching.html#columnar-classroom>). It reuses this solver with four supplied-answer messages, three seeds and two variants. The worksheet separates exact plaintext from exact key recovery and retains failed or preprocessing-exhausted runs. A shared seed alone does not make changed algorithms follow matching random paths.

Source: George Lasry, *A Methodology for the Cryptanalysis of Classical Ciphers with Search Metaheuristics* (2018), §§5.3.2–5.3.4, printed pp. 69–78 / supplied PDF pp. 90–99. Evaluation principles: §§4.5–4.7, printed pp. 57–60 / PDF pp. 78–81.

#### Why This Matters

Columnar transposition rearranges positions while preserving letter counts. It is a useful way to study the difference between a large number of possible keys and the statistical structure an attacker can exploit.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Columnar systems appear in historical military and recreational cryptography, sometimes combined with other operations. “Columnar transposition” describes a family of writing and reading conventions, not one securely dated nineteenth-century invention. Complete rectangles, incomplete final rows and padding rules produce different attack problems.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Write the message in rows across a grid whose width is the keyword length. Number the columns by alphabetical order of the keyword letters. Read off columns in that numbered order. [Myszkowski transposition](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/myszkowski.html>) changes how repeated keyword letters are handled: tied columns are read together across each row.

```text
Keyword: ZEBRA → Z=5, E=3, B=2, R=4, A=1
Columns:  5  3  2  4  1
          W  E  A  T  H
          E  R  F  O  R
          E  C  A  S  T
          I  N  G  X  X

Read col 1(A): HRTX
Read col 2(B): AFAG
Read col 3(E): ERCN
Read col 4(R): TOSX
Read col 5(Z): WEEI
```

How It Was Broken

Frequency Analysis + Anagramming

Complexity: Moderate

Transposition preserves the plaintext's letter counts. A distribution resembling English can suggest transposition, but does not identify it with certainty. Analysts try plausible widths and rearrange columns, looking for useful letter contacts and readable text. Several messages with the same width and column order let them test one arrangement against more evidence.

#### Try it: rearrange several intercepts

One promising pair of letters can be a coincidence. Can you find an order that makes **three messages** readable at once? Each synthetic message fills four rows of five letters. The sender read the five columns in the same secret order; we have already split each received message into five equal strips.

Select a strip and move it left or right. The corresponding column moves in every message. Read each reconstructed message across its rows. Spaces were removed; no letters were added as padding.

Selected strip
- Strip A

- Strip B

- Strip C

- Strip D

- Strip E
  Move left Move right

  [Input ma-control: type=checkbox; initial value=; checked]  Include a different-key control

Current order: **A → B → C → D → E**

**** across the three same-key messages. This counts adjacent letter pairs from a small English list, only within rows. It is a clue, **not a probability or confirmation**; a wrong order can also score well.

Check arrangement Reveal shared order Reset strips

Try an arrangement, then check it against the prepared messages.

What this exercise assumes

The width, equal column lengths and shared key are supplied to isolate the rearrangement problem. Real analysis may need to establish those facts first and handle incomplete rectangles, padding or multiple transpositions. The fourth intercept deliberately uses a different column order: a key recovered for one group need not solve other traffic. “Check” compares with the known answer to these invented examples; a contact score alone cannot validate a real intercept.

Our small contact list is: TH, HE, IN, ER, AN, RE, ON, AT, EN, ND, TI, ES, OR, TE, OF, ED, IS, IT, AL, AR, ST, TO, NT, NG, SE, HA, AS, OU, IO, LE, VE, CO, BE, RT, WA, SC, RO and UR. It is a teaching heuristic, not a fitted language model.

Reading companions: Helen Fouché Gaines, [*Cryptanalysis: A Study of Ciphers and Their Solution*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#gaines>) (1939; Dover edition 1956), Chapter VII, “General Methods — Multiple Anagramming, Etc.”; Joshua Holden, [*The Mathematics of Secrets: Cryptography from Caesar Ciphers to Digital Encryption*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#holden>) (2017), §3.7. These motivate the method; the messages and simplified score here were created for this exercise.

This exercise needs JavaScript to rearrange the strips. The worked columnar example above remains readable without it.


What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Columnar Transposition | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Column reordering | AES ShiftRows: cyclic shifts within the rows of the byte state |
| Grid-based permutation | Permutation layers rearrange positions; a Feistel round also combines values |
| Keyword-controlled order | A key can select a permutation; AES key expansion is a different operation |

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

Transposition Variants

Classical transposition practice includes route systems, regular columnar, Myszkowski ordering, and compound forms such as double transposition. Each variant preserves letter frequencies while changing positional structure.

The Nihilist transposition family extends these ideas into numbered-grid operations, showing how small procedural tweaks can significantly change attack difficulty.

### Commercial Telegraph Codebooks ABC, Bentley’s, Lieber’s · 1870s–1930s

Five letters of nonsense that meant “ship the cargo via Suez and reply with prices in pounds sterling”. The compression layer of the Victorian internet.

Public commercial codebooks reduce telegraph length and ambiguity; they do not inherently provide confidentiality.

Notable codebooksABC Code (1873), Bentley’s (1906), Lieber’s, Western Union

Codeword formatVaried; five-letter groups became important in the 20th century

Charged asDependent on tariff, date and codeword length

UseCivilian commerce, shipping, banking, and insurance

StatusMostly public; private codebooks added a confidentiality layer

#### Why This Matters

Commercial codebooks replaced frequently used business expressions with compact codewords to reduce telegraph charges. Formats and billing rules changed over time. A phrase could become a single code group, but a public book did not thereby provide secrecy.

Commercial codes included ABC, Lieber’s and Bentley’s. Kahn describes the 1903 international rules permitting pronounceable artificial words up to ten letters, and the subsequent combination of two five-letter groups within that allowance. Bentley’s *Complete Phrase Code* followed in 1906. A universal five-letter CVCVC tariff rule is therefore misleading.

Private codebooks and additional encipherment could obscure the codeword meanings. Their protection depended on access to the book, traffic patterns and the added cipher, not simply on whether a printed volume was labelled private.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

A two-part codebook can provide two lookup directions; historical layouts varied:

- A **plain index** listing every English word or phrase the codebook covers, in alphabetical order, each beside its codeword.

- A **code index** listing every codeword in alphabetical order, each beside its plaintext.

The museum’s CVCVC pattern uses 20 consonants (excluding Y) and five vowels, allowing 20³ × 5² = 200,000 combinations. If all 21 consonants were allowed, the count would be 231,525. Neither count is the number of entries in a particular historical book. Error-detecting designs restrict the vocabulary so that likely transmission errors are less likely to produce another valid codeword.

The demo above operates on a small fixed wordlist using exactly the CVCVC encoding scheme. Words not in the wordlist fall through to a per-letter codebook so the round-trip stays clean for arbitrary input.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

Where the Confidentiality Came From (and Where It Failed)

Public codebooks: no confidentiality at all

Complexity: Lookup

Anyone with a copy of ABC or Bentley’s could read public-codebook traffic. Their job was compression and error-checking, not secrecy.

Private codebooks: tractable for state actors

Complexity: Within reach of professional cryptanalytic bureaus

A fixed one-to-one phrase code preserves repeated groups and can expose relationships between messages. Known business context can help infer entries. The volume and type of traffic, use of alternatives and any super-encipherment affect how much can be recovered; no universal recovery time follows.

Codebook + super-encipherment

Security depends on the added cipher and key handling

An additional cipher can protect codegroups, but it must be analysed on its own terms. Additive reuse can expose relationships, as in some military code systems. That analogy does not show that every private commercial code used the same construction or had the same weakness.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Codebook lesson | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| Compression and encryption are separate functions | HPACK (HTTP/2) and QPACK (HTTP/3) compress fields. Shared compression state can create length-based leakage; compression is not encryption |
| Pronounceable codewords for telegram tariffs | BIP-39 mnemonic seed words for Bitcoin wallets |
| Checking distance between codewords | Hamming distance in modern error-correcting codes |
| Private codebook = monoalphabetic on the phrase alphabet | Repeated phrase groups can reveal structure; a large codebook alone does not prove security |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Notable codebooks | ABC Code (1873), Bentley’s (1906), Lieber’s, Western Union |
| --- | --- |
| Codeword format | Varied; five-letter groups became important in the 20th century |
| Charged as | Dependent on tariff, date and codeword length |
| Use | Civilian commerce, shipping, banking, and insurance |
| Status | Mostly public; private codebooks added a confidentiality layer |

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 22, “Rumrunners, Businessmen, and Makers of Non-secret Codes,” on commercial code formats, tariffs and Bentley. For the modern comparison: [RFC 7541, §7.1](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7541.html>), on length-based leakage and shared HPACK compression state.

### Confederate Vigenère

Confederate repeating-key ciphers and the Union analysts who read some of their dispatches

Union analysts exploited repeated keywords and language patterns.

InventorConfederate Signal Corps · E.P. Alexander

Year1862

Key TypeVigenère keyword (15 letters typical)

Broken ByUnion cryptanalysts; Kasiski published a general method in 1863

Modern LessonOperational security failures

#### Why This Matters

Confederate forces used repeating-key Vigenère systems during the Civil War. Union analysts solved a number of dispatches by exploiting predictable text and reused keys. Kasiski’s 1863 publication is part of the broader history of the cipher, not evidence that Union analysts used his method.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Confederate cipher disks and tables implemented repeating-key substitution. Kahn describes Union solutions, including a message sent during the Vicksburg siege on May 25, 1863, with the key MANCHESTER BLUFF. He also records transmission errors and occasions when delayed solutions were no longer operationally useful.

Reusing a key across messages can extend the value of a recovered key, but does not mean that every Confederate message used the same system or was read. The historical examples establish particular successes, not universal access to Confederate communications.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

```text
Confederate keywords documented in historical record:

1863: 'Manchester Bluff' (15 letters) — documented Vicksburg dispatch
      Used by Pemberton and J.E. Johnston
      during the Vicksburg campaign

1863: 'My Old Kentucky Home' (17 letters)
      Used by General Buckner

1864: 'Complete Victory' (15 letters)
      Shared by Jefferson Davis, R.E. Lee,
      Kirby Smith, S.D. Lee, J.G. Walker

1865: 'Come Retribution' (15 letters)
      Used by Davis, Lee, Johnston,
      and Breckenridge in final months

All Vigenère: C = (P + K) mod 26
```

Cipher disks and tables implemented repeating-key Vigenère; Union analysts solved particular intercepted dispatches

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Key Length Detection + Frequency Analysis

Historical attacks and later statistical methods

A modern analyst can use repeated sequences and the index of coincidence to test candidate periods, then analyse each position class. The index of coincidence was developed after the Civil War; it should not be attributed to Union operators. Their documented solutions also exploited likely words, message context and recovered keys.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Confederate Vigenère | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Known keywords used for months | Key rotation: modern protocols change session keys frequently |
| Sharing a key among multiple correspondents | Key compartmentalization: different systems use different keys |
| Repeating natural-language keyword | Modern algorithms do not cycle a raw keyword through the plaintext |

### Copiale Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A 105-page eighteenth-century manuscript — deciphered through computational and linguistic analysis in 2011

Knight, Megyesi, Schaefer (USC/Uppsala, 2011)

OriginPrivately owned German manuscript; earlier examined in East Berlin

Date of creation~1760–1780

Length105 pages, ~75,000 characters

Symbol set~90 unique handwritten symbols

Broken ByKnight, Megyesi, Schaefer (USC/Uppsala, 2011)

Plaintext languageGerman

ContentInitiation rituals of the "Oculist Order"

#### Why This Matters

The Copiale manuscript contains about 75,000 handwritten characters across 105 pages. In 2011 Kevin Knight, Beáta Megyesi, and Christiane Schaefer reported its decipherment using computational analysis and human linguistic reasoning. It contains German text about a secret society’s rituals. Their [original paper](<https://aclanthology.org/W11-1202/>) documents the sequence of hypotheses, including unsuccessful ones.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

A crucial discovery was that unaccented Roman letters represented **word spaces**, while other signs encoded the text. They were not arbitrary meaningless filler. Grouping symbols by their contexts, testing likely words, and examining German spelling helped the researchers work out the system.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The manuscript uses homophones, word separators, and signs for some letter groups and concepts. Its roughly 90 cipher signs do not divide uniformly among 26 letters. The common letter E has several representations; unaccented Roman letters mark spaces. The model should not equate every extra symbol with a random null.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Computational and Linguistic Analysis (2011)

Complexity: Computational

The initial automated attack on the wrong subset of symbols failed. The published solution combined statistical tools with changes of hypothesis and linguistic interpretation; switching a language setting did not instantly produce the full plaintext.

Hypothesis-Driven Symbol Classification

Complexity: Insight

Recognizing the space symbols and language-dependent groups was essential. A good statistical tool cannot compensate for an incorrect assumption about which symbols carry letters, separators, or other information.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Copiale Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| NLP for cryptanalysis | Modern statistical models attack historical ciphers |
| Homophonic substitution at scale | More symbols alone do not establish security; language structure and symbol roles matter |
| Documents survive their secrets | A late decipherment does not establish continuous secrecy or resistance to every earlier reader |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

#### Sources and Reading

Kevin Knight, Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer, [“The Copiale Cipher”](<https://aclanthology.org/W11-1202/>) (2011), §§1–5; and *“The Secrets of the Copiale Cipher”*, *Journal for Research into Freemasonry and Fraternalism* 2(2), pp. 314–324 (issue dated 2011; copyright 2012), especially p. 315 for private ownership and the physical manuscript’s estimated 1760–1780 date. An owner’s 1866 inscription is not its creation date.

Hall V · American Field American Revolution · 1778–1783

### Culper Ring / Tallmadge Code Washington’s spy ring codebook · 1779

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Tallmadge’s numerical vocabulary helped protect intelligence sent from British-held New York. The surviving record and the invented browser codebook are distinguished below.

Historical numerical codebook; captured documents and contextual evidence are distinct from cryptanalytic breaks.

DesignerMajor Benjamin Tallmadge, US Army (Washington’s intelligence chief)

YearIn active use 1779 – 1783

MechanismCodebook of ~760 numbered entries (people, places, words)

OperatorsAbraham Woodhull (Samuel Culper Sr) and Robert Townsend (Samuel Culper Jr)

StatusNo British break of the cipher itself recorded

#### Why This Matters

By 1778 George Washington’s army had been forced out of New York City and the British held the harbour, Manhattan, and most of Long Island. Washington needed reliable, sustained intelligence from inside that perimeter — ship arrivals, troop movements, the names of ranking British officers in the city. He turned to a 24-year-old Continental Army officer, Major Benjamin Tallmadge, who in late 1778 organised what is now called the Culper Spy Ring.

Tallmadge’s solution to the secrecy problem was a numerical codebook with roughly 760 numbered entries. Each entry was a person, place, military term, or common word. “Gen. Washington” became `711` and “New York” became `727`. Tallmadge, Washington, Woodhull and Townsend were among its users; this page does not establish an exhaustive distribution list. It was used continuously from 1779 until the end of the war — and no British break of the cipher itself is recorded. Surviving copies of Tallmadge’s codebook are in the Library of Congress.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The codebook is a parallel-list nomenclator. The plaintext list runs alphabetically through the words and proper names of interest; each entry has a number from 1 to roughly 760. The cipher list runs in numeric order, each number against its plaintext, so the recipient can decode.

Operators wrote messages using ordinary English for low-value content and substituted code numbers for sensitive words — names of officers, ship counts, place names. Numbers were embedded in otherwise innocuous letters (“I saw 711 yesterday and he asked after the 178 in 727” — “I saw Washington yesterday and he asked after the enemy in New York”).

Because the word list is alphabetical, an entry's number tells you roughly where its word falls in the alphabet. Entries 1–710 are common words; 711–763 are the proper nouns. Read straight from the codebook:

| Code | Meaning |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 178 | enemy | sits in the alphabetical run 175 *embark* · 176 *employ* · 179 *example* |
| 355 | lady | the entry behind the "Agent 355" legend — a word, not a person |
| 596 | secret |  |
| 711 | Gen. Washington | first of the proper nouns |
| 727 | New York |  |

In the consulted edited transcription, 178 is *enemy*, not *spy*. The list contains many s-words after 606 *speaker*; 756 *Spain* belongs to the separate proper-name section. Transcription gaps and printing errors make the original manuscript important for claims about the complete vocabulary.

For deeper concealment, Culper messages were written in James Jay’s invisible ink (“sympathetic stain”) between the lines of cover letters. Invisible ink concealed the presence of writing, a different purpose from replacing words with numbers.

The demo above uses a stable 215-entry codebook indexed from 100. Words not in the codebook fall through to per-letter codes in the 800s, bracketed by sentinels 998 and 999 — conventions invented for this widget. Tallmadge’s supplementary substitution alphabet was different; the 800-series and 998/999 markers are not transcribed from his key.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was (Not) Broken

No British cryptanalytic break

Complexity: Hard without a captured codebook

Repeated numerical entries can reveal word patterns, and uncoded surrounding text can supply clues. The sources cited here do not establish a successful British cryptanalytic reading of the codebook. That historical record is not a quantitative security estimate.

Operational risks

Operational risk: capture of the shared codebook

Possession of the relevant codebook would let an adversary interpret its numerical entries without solving a substitution problem. Courier security, secrecy of agent identities and invisible ink served different operational purposes. None makes a reused codebook mathematically unbreakable.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Culper lesson | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| Codebook + invisible ink = layered defence | Defence in depth — multiple independent security layers |
| Distribution of shared code material | Modern key management: split knowledge, dual control, HSMs |
| Embedding ciphertext in plausible cover traffic | Steganography and traffic-analysis-resistant protocols |
| Both operational procedures and cipher design matter | Key theft can bypass the need to solve the underlying mathematical problem |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Designer | Major Benjamin Tallmadge, US Army (Washington’s intelligence chief) |
| --- | --- |
| Year | In active use 1779 – 1783 |
| Mechanism | Codebook of ~760 numbered entries (people, places, words) |
| Operators | Abraham Woodhull (Samuel Culper Sr) and Robert Townsend (Samuel Culper Jr) |
| Status | No British break of the cipher itself recorded |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

Benjamin Tallmadge, 1779 — Raynham Hall Museum edited transcription ↗](<https://raynhamhallmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/Culper-Code-Book.pdf>) A modern typeset adaptation, edited by Michael Goudket, with spelling changes and missing or uncertain entries; it is not a manuscript facsimile.

Hall XIII · Cipher Culture Fiction · 2003

### The Da Vinci Code

Dan Brown’s 2003 thriller uses Atbash, anagrams and numerical clues as plot devices.

Pop Culture

AuthorDan Brown

Published2003 (Doubleday)

Copies soldWidely sold internationally; copies are not a count of individual readers

Ciphers featuredAtbash, anagram, Fibonacci sequence, mirror writing

ImpactPopular cipher fiction; documented tourism effects at some featured sites

Historical accuracyContested — numerous anachronisms, see panels below

#### 🔓 Interactive Explorer

Try encoding a message as this cipher does.

 Message (Atbash encodes it)  [Input input: type=text; initial value=SOPHIA]  Encode

##### Why This Matters

*The Da Vinci Code* brought cipher-themed puzzles to a large fiction audience. Reports of increased tourism at featured sites are a different claim from increased cryptography education. The sources below do not establish that National Cryptologic Museum visits doubled or that the novel caused a measurable rise in cryptography-course enrolment.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

Ciphers in the Book

The novel features: (1) an Atbash-encoded message (used famously in the Book of Jeremiah 25:26 — SHESHACH = BABEL via Atbash), reinforcing Hebrew scripture connections; (2) anagram-based clue-solving, an analogy to transposition ciphers; (3) the Fibonacci sequence as a numerical clue, not an anticipation of modern cryptography; (4) mirror writing attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, who genuinely used right-to-left script in his notebooks — though not as a serious cipher.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What the Book Gets Right

Atbash is a real Hebrew cipher used in the Old Testament. Leonardo da Vinci genuinely wrote in mirror script, though scholars believe this reflected left-handedness and personal habit rather than cryptographic intent. The Priory of Sion was a real (minor) French organization, though not of medieval origin. The novel offers fictional examples of pattern recognition and contextual guessing, both useful in some forms of historical cryptanalysis.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

What the Book Gets Wrong

The Priory of Sion conspiracy is largely a 20th-century hoax; the “historical” documents Brown cites were forged in the 1960s by Pierre Plantard. The Fibonacci key usage described in the novel conflates several distinct cipher systems. Numerous art-historical details (Mona Lisa dimensions, Last Supper iconography) are anachronistic or fabricated. Brown's bibliography mixes serious scholarship with debunked conspiracy literature without distinguishing between them.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Cultural Impact

The Da Vinci Code sparked: record tourism to the Louvre, Rosslyn Chapel, and Rennes-le-Château; a 2006 film adaptation; a bestseller in 44 languages; and widespread popular interest in "hidden messages" in Renaissance art that persists across social media to this day. For cryptography educators, the book is both a gateway and a source of misconceptions to correct.

📚Exhibit Sources

- [CBC News — “Da Vinci Code cited in Louvre attendance record”: the Louvre drew a record 7.3 million visitors in 2005, and museum officials named Dan Brown’s novel among the causes ↗](<https://www.cbc.ca/news/entertainment/da-vinci-code-cited-in-louvre-attendance-record-1.625684>)

- [CBC News — “Louvre sets another attendance record in 2006” (roughly 8.3 million visitors) ↗](<https://www.cbc.ca/news/entertainment/louvre-sets-another-attendance-record-in-2006-1.646006>)

- [Rosslyn Chapel Trust — “Research reveals Da Vinci Code impact”: the chapel’s own visitor figures, 38,141 before publication rising to more than 176,000 in the year of the film ↗](<https://www.rosslynchapel.com/news/research-reveals-da-vinci-code-impact-21-years-after-publication/>)

- [Wikipedia — *The Da Vinci Code* (publication history and reception) ↗](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Da_Vinci_Code>)

Removed as unsourced: a "verified spike in enrollment in cryptography and medieval history courses". The word *verified* claimed evidence that could not be located — no institutional or peer-reviewed data for it was found. The tourism figures below it are cited and stay.

#### Embedded script 2 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    // Atbash demo inlined for Da Vinci Code page
    function daVinciEncode(t) {
      const A='ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
      return t.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'').split('').map(c=>{
        const i=A.indexOf(c); return i>=0?A[25-i]:c;
      }).join('') + ' (Atbash)';
    }
```

### D'Agapeyeff Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A 1939 numeric challenge with no generally accepted reconstruction of its method.

Unsolved challenge cipher

RegionLondon, England

Year1939, in *Codes and Ciphers*, OUP

AuthorAlexander d'Agapeyeff

TrackB (frequency analyzer)

#### Interactive Exhibit

The widget loads a 130-digit excerpt of the 395-digit ciphertext (or paste the full cryptogram yourself) and will tally adjacent digit pairs. It counts overlapping pairs after removing spaces. Uneven counts can suggest hypotheses but do not establish a cipher family. This is an analytic helper, not a solver.

 Numeric ciphertext

75628 28591 62916 48164 91748 58464 74748 28483 81638 18174 74826 26475 83828 49175 74658 37575 75936 36565 81638 17585 75756 46282 92857 46382 75748 38165

 Tally digit pairs

##### Why This Matters

Alexander d’Agapeyeff published a 395-digit challenge in *Codes and Ciphers* (Oxford University Press, 1939). Its method has no generally accepted reconstruction. Researchers report that he later could not recall how he had enciphered it; that report does not identify a lost key or establish that the printed text is error-free.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The digits are printed in five-digit groups. The widget’s default is the first 26 groups (130 digits), checked against the reproduced challenge page. Fractionation followed by transposition is one line of investigation, not a recovered description of the author’s method.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

Nonuniform frequencies do not prove that a sequence encodes a meaningful message. A Polybius-style hypothesis must specify its coordinate alphabet, grouping, transposition and any treatment of the odd final digit. Dividing 395 by two does not establish a plaintext length, and no justified unicity-distance calculation is supplied here.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

Gordon Rugg and collaborators investigated possible human error as well as computational attacks. Their report identifies a mistake in another worked example in the book; that is a reason to investigate transcription or enciphering errors, not proof that this challenge contains one. A convincing candidate needs explicit rules that reproduce the printed digits and explain any proposed correction.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    (function () {
      window.encode = function () {
        var raw = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').replace(/[^0-9]/g, '');
        var out = document.getElementById('output');
        if (raw.length < 4) { out.textContent = 'Need at least 4 digits.'; return; }
        var counts = {};
        for (var i = 0; i < raw.length - 1; i++) {
          var pair = raw[i] + raw[i+1];
          counts[pair] = (counts[pair] || 0) + 1;
        }
        var entries = Object.keys(counts).map(function (k) { return [k, counts[k]]; });
        entries.sort(function (a, b) { return b[1] - a[1]; });
        var lines = ['Digits analysed: ' + raw.length, 'Overlapping pairs analysed: ' + (raw.length - 1), 'Distinct adjacent pairs: ' + entries.length, '', 'Top 12 pairs by frequency:'];
        for (var j = 0; j < Math.min(12, entries.length); j++) {
          lines.push('  ' + entries[j][0] + '  \u00d7 ' + entries[j][1]);
        }
        lines.push('');
        lines.push('For independent uniform decimal digits, each pair has expected count ' + ((raw.length - 1)/100).toFixed(2) + '. Overlapping pairs are not independent observations.');
        out.textContent = lines.join('\n');
      };
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode(); });
    })();
```

Hall XIII · Culture Edwardian Britain · 1903

### Conan Doyle's Dancing Men

The fictional stick-figure cipher Sherlock Holmes solves in *The Adventure of the Dancing Men* (1903) — a frequency-analysis primer disguised as a Strand magazine story.

Fictional substitution cipher

RegionNorfolk, England (in-fiction); London (publication)

YearPublished *Strand Magazine*, December 1903

AuthorSir Arthur Conan Doyle

TrackB (alphabet mapper)

#### Interactive Exhibit

Type a short message and the widget will display each letter as a labelled 'dancing man' tag. The story below explains how Holmes used counts and context. Track B — illustrative.

 Plaintext message  [Input input: type=text; initial value=ELSIE PREPARE TO MEET THY GOD]  Encode

##### Why This Matters

Arthur Conan Doyle’s *The Adventure of the Dancing Men* (1903) uses a pictographic substitution cipher as a central plot device. Holmes combines symbol counts, likely letters and contextual guesses to interpret messages threatening Elsie Cubitt. It is a fictional demonstration of cryptanalytic reasoning, not the first popular account: Poe’s *The Gold-Bug* appeared in 1843.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Doyle’s story shows stick-figure glyphs for only part of the alphabet, with little flags marking word breaks. Later complete alphabets are reconstructions. The cipher in the story is broken in the classic way: count letter occurrences in the longest message, identify the most frequent symbol as E, then use word patterns (single-letter words = A or I, three-letter common words = THE) to back-solve the rest. Holmes solves the system in a few hours — the same way William Friedman would later teach US Army Signal Intelligence Service trainees to attack monoalphabetic ciphers in the 1930s.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

A monoalphabetic substitution preserves letter counts and repeated patterns. These clues often help with language text, but no fixed fifty-letter threshold or minutes-long solution guarantee follows. Short messages and unusual vocabulary can remain ambiguous, and published glyph transcriptions need to be checked against the relevant edition.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

The story illustrates how patterns and context can expose a substitution. Publicly known glyphs provide encoding rather than secrecy; a hidden monoalphabetic key has weaknesses even with a large permutation space. This does not imply that every short substitution cryptogram has a uniquely recoverable plaintext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    (function () {
      // Stylised "dancing-man" placeholders \u2014 each letter shown as [LET], spaces preserved.
      window.encode = function () {
        var raw = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').toUpperCase();
        var out = document.getElementById('output');
        var enc = raw.split('').map(function (c) {
          if (c === ' ') return '   ';
          if (!/[A-Z]/.test(c)) return c;
          return '[\u015b' + c + '\u015b]';
        }).join('');
        var freq = {};
        raw.split('').forEach(function (c) { if (/[A-Z]/.test(c)) freq[c] = (freq[c] || 0) + 1; });
        var entries = Object.keys(freq).sort(function (a, b) { return freq[b] - freq[a]; });
        var freqLines = entries.slice(0, 6).map(function (k) { return '  ' + k + ' \u00d7 ' + freq[k]; });
        out.textContent = 'Cipher (each tag = one dancing figure):\n\n' + enc +
          '\n\nFrequency (top 6) \u2014 Holmes\u2019s attack starts here:\n' + freqLines.join('\n') +
          '\n\n(In English, E should dominate. If your message is long enough, it does.)';
      };
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode(); });
    })();
```

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall XI: Modern Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/modern-crypto.html>)› DES (Data Encryption Standard)

Modern · 1977

### DES (Data Encryption Standard)

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A landmark public, government-standardised block cipher — and the cipher that started a generation of academic cryptanalysis.

Broken (brute force, 1998)

OriginIBM (Lucifer, 1971), modified by NSA, standardised by NBS as FIPS 46

Year1977

TypeSymmetric block cipher (Feistel network, 64-bit block, 56-bit key)

StatusDES withdrawn in 2005; NIST disallowed new TDEA protection after 2023

Modern RoleHistorical foundation; legacy TDEA data may still require processing during migration

#### Why This Matters

DES made a complete modern block-cipher specification widely available as a US federal standard. Its public scrutiny helped establish academic cryptanalysis. Differential and linear cryptanalysis used DES as a major test case and influenced the design of later ciphers.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

IBM developed DES from its earlier cipher research, with technical advice from NSA, and NBS standardised it in 1977. Biham and Shamir’s public differential cryptanalysis prompted renewed examination of its design. In 1994, IBM designer Don Coppersmith published S-box and permutation criteria that had been chosen to resist such attacks. His account establishes IBM’s earlier knowledge and design role; the S-boxes should not be attributed simply to NSA.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

DES is a 16-round Feistel network. The 64-bit plaintext is split into two 32-bit halves L and R. Each round computes `L<sub>i+1</sub> = R<sub>i</sub>` and `R<sub>i+1</sub> = L<sub>i</sub> ⊕ F(R<sub>i</sub>, K<sub>i</sub>)`. The round function F expands R to 48 bits, XORs the round subkey, passes the result through eight 6-to-4-bit S-boxes (the heart of DES's non-linearity), and applies a final permutation. Sixteen rounds of this with sixteen subkeys derived from the 56-bit master key produce a reversible block cipher. Its 56-bit key is too small to withstand modern exhaustive search.

#### A differential through one S-box

XORing the same subkey into two inputs leaves their difference unchanged: `(x XOR k) XOR (x′ XOR k) = x XOR x′`. The nonlinear S-box then produces some output differences more often than others. For DES S1 and input difference `34`, enumerate all 64 possible six-bit inputs:

Selected S1 difference-distribution entries; differences are hexadecimal

| Output difference | Count out of 64 | Probability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 02 | 16 | 1/4 |
| 04 | 2 | 1/32 |
| 00 | 0 | 0 |
| 09 | 0 | 0 |

Now suppose a teaching example exposes the inputs *before* the subkey XOR and the S1 output difference. Keep each six-bit candidate k for which `S1(x XOR k) XOR S1(x′ XOR k)` matches that observation. All values below are hexadecimal:

Filtering the 64 possible S1 subkeys

| Inputs | Output XOR | Surviving subkeys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01, 35 | 0D | 07, 11, 17, 1D, 23, 25, 29, 33 |
| 21, 15 | 03 | 00, 14, 17, 20, 23, 34 |

The intersection is **`{17, 23}`**, so these observations do not identify a unique subkey. Both pairs use input difference `34`; a suitable observation with a different difference is needed to distinguish these survivors. This component example assumes exposed intermediate information, not ordinary intercepted DES ciphertexts or full-DES key recovery.

[Explore difference tables and bounded attacks in Biham Lens](<https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-biham-lens/>). Its exercises are separate from the [historic full-DES differential attack and its resource requirements](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/modern-attack-evidence.html#des-differential>).

Eli Biham and Adi Shamir, *Differential Cryptanalysis of the Data Encryption Standard* (1993), §3.2, Examples 3.4–3.7. Numbered pp. 15–22, especially pp. 18–20, refer to the authors’ repaginated 7 December 2009 recompilation.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-shield"></use></svg>
```

Security & Cryptanalysis

In 1998 the EFF's Deep Crack machine recovered a DES key in about 56 hours. Differential and linear cryptanalysis also showed important theoretical weaknesses, although their data requirements limit their practical use. Triple-DES extended DES's useful life, but retained its small 64-bit block size. NIST withdrew SP 800-67 Rev. 2 on 1 January 2024: TDEA is disallowed for applying new protection, while processing already protected data remains permitted. This is a NIST transition rule, not a claim that every banking deployment ended on that date.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Where You Use It Today

| Where | How DES is Used |
| --- | --- |
| Banking (1980s–2010s) | ATM PIN encryption, EMV chip cards (3DES); legacy systems still in slow migration |
| Unix passwd (until 1990s) | `crypt(3)` used DES iterated 25 times to hash passwords |
| Kerberos v4 | DES was the original Kerberos cipher; v5 added AES support |
| Cryptanalysis education | DES remains a useful teaching example because Feistel, S-boxes, and the avalanche effect are easiest to demonstrate on it |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Era | Modern · 1977 |
| --- | --- |
| Status | DES withdrawn in 2005; NIST disallowed new TDEA protection after 2023 |
| Origin | IBM (Lucifer, 1971), modified by NSA, standardised by NBS as FIPS 46 |
| Year | 1977 |
| Type | Symmetric block cipher (Feistel network, 64-bit block, 56-bit key) |
| Modern Role | Historical foundation; legacy TDEA data may still require processing during migration |

#### Primary Sources

[NIST withdrawal notice for TDEA (2023; effective 1 January 2024)](<https://csrc.nist.gov/News/2023/nist-to-withdraw-sp-800-67-rev-2>).

#### Conditional-linear analysis: a dated research result

Biham and Perle’s 2018 study selects data to increase linear bias. One reported operating point uses about 2<sup>41.9</sup> known plaintexts and analysis work at 85% success. This is conditional-linear analysis, distinct from differential–linear composition. [Read the experimental scope, work accounting and primary source](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/modern-attack-evidence.html#des>).

#### Sources and Reading

Don Coppersmith, [“The Data Encryption Standard (DES) and its strength against attacks”](<https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.383.0243>), *IBM Journal of Research and Development* 38(3), May 1994, pp. 243–250, especially the introductory account of the IBM team and previously unpublished design criteria.

Hall V · Military Ciphers Historical letter-pad system

### Diana Cryptosystem

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A reciprocal trigraph table for letter pads; the public lookup card and secret key material serve different roles.

MethodReciprocal letter-pad conversion

EraExact service dates not established here

FamilyOne-Time Pad (trigraphic variant)

Key MaterialSecret random-letter pad plus a public trigraph lookup card

TrustHistorical Only

Modern LessonCorrect OTP use is unbreakable; logistics often fail before the math

#### Why This Matters

DIANA illustrates the separation between a public conversion rule and a secret one-time pad. A trigraph table combines a message letter with a pad letter to obtain the ciphertext letter. Its reciprocal rule lets the same table recover the message. The table can be public; confidentiality depends on independent, uniformly random secret key material used only once.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

**Historical evidence scope:** the source verified for this exhibit explains the DIANA table and its operation. It does not establish precise introduction or retirement dates, a continuous Vietnam-to-Gulf-War service history, or particular theater deployments. Those historical claims are not asserted here.

Source for the conversion method: Dirk Rijmenants, [“DIANA — A Fast Reciprocal One Time Pad Table”](<https://rijmenants.blogspot.com/2017/10/a-fast-reciprocal-one-time-pad-table.html>) (12 October 2017).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Each pad page carries lines of random key letters, used once and destroyed. The DIANA rule is that plaintext, key, and cipher letters of every position sum to 25 modulo 26 (with A=0 … Z=25): **C = 25 − P − K (mod 26)**. That makes the system doubly reciprocal — the same Tri-Graph table both encrypts and decrypts, and any two letters of the trigram give the third — so an operator who memorized the 126 trigram combinations could work without the card at all.

```text
Worked arithmetic example (not evidence of a particular deployment):

Pad key:    GORWY WETFR COYET
Plaintext:  ATTAC KATDA WNXYZ
Ciphertext: TSPDZ TVNRI BYEXH

First letter: A(0) with key G(6) → 25−0−6 = 19 = T
Decryption is the same lookup: T with key G → 25−19−6 = 0 = A
```

ℹ️

**About this demo:** The demo implements the authentic DIANA rule (C = 25 − P − K mod 26) but repeats your short keyword as the key so you can experiment — a real DIANA pad used truly random, never-repeated key letters, which is what made it unbreakable.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

Why Pads Fail in Practice

Pad reuse / loss / capture

Risk depends on which key material is compromised

The trigraph lookup card is public conversion information, not the secret pad. Capturing that card alone does not decrypt messages. Capturing the corresponding pad exposes the text it protects; reusing pad letters reveals relations between messages, but does not guarantee an immediate complete decipherment. Key generation, distribution, protection and destruction all matter. Perfect secrecy also supplies no message authentication.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Relationship to Modern Crypto

For a fixed-length message, independently uniform secret pad letters make each ciphertext equally likely regardless of that message. Reusing the pad invalidates this one-time guarantee. Modern symmetric encryption instead aims at computational security under stated assumptions and usage limits. TLS is a protocol, not a single symmetric cipher, and neither approach hides all metadata automatically.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Method | Reciprocal letter-pad conversion |
| --- | --- |
| Era | Exact service dates not established here |
| Family | One-Time Pad (trigraphic variant) |
| Key Material | Secret random-letter pad plus a public trigraph lookup card |
| Trust | Historical Only |
| Modern Lesson | Correct OTP use is unbreakable; logistics often fail before the math |

Exhibit 26 of 174 Confederate · 1862

### Confederate Dictionary Code

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Confederate dictionary codes: secrecy and interoperability depend on the shared reference

Known dictionary + position lookup

InventorJefferson Davis · Confederate War Department

YearSpring 1862

Key TypePage and word number from shared dictionary

Broken ByKnown dictionary + position lookup

Modern LessonShared key material management

#### Why This Matters

Dictionary codes require both parties to agree on the exact reference and indexing rules. A page, column and word address is meaningful only within that shared edition. This is a practical interoperability lesson as well as a secrecy problem: a public dictionary is not a high-entropy secret key.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Kahn records Jefferson Davis sending Albert S. Johnston a dictionary in March 1862 and explaining the address 146.L.20 as page 146, left column, word 20, for “junction.” He also describes Confederate naval officers obtaining paired dictionaries. The evidence supports the need for matching references; it does not establish the particular Webster edition or the Lee–Johnston edition-mismatch anecdote previously associated with this example.

The matching reference and indexing rules must be shared with the intended recipient. Edition mismatch is a possible interoperability failure, not an episode established by the example above.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

```text
Illustrative dictionary coordinates, not a transcription of a historical edition

Encoding:
  Find the word in the dictionary
  Record: (page number)(position on page)

  'ship' = page 674, word 26 → (674)26
  'attack' = page 51, word 8  → (51)8
  'tomorrow' = page 312, word 3 → (312)3

Security depends on the reference, indexing rules,
message patterns and attacker knowledge
```

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]


Invented page/position examples showing a dictionary lookup; these are not verified entries in Webster’s 1857 edition

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Dictionary Acquisition

Complexity: Easy if dictionary identified

Once the source dictionary is identified (which edition, which publisher), the code breaks completely — every page and position can be looked up directly. That is a conditional attack: this exhibit does not document a particular Union recovery of the dictionary used in the example.

⚠️

**The operational failure:** An edition mismatch can make a dictionary-coded message unreadable to its intended recipient. Operational cryptography must ensure that all parties can actually communicate.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Confederate Dictionary Code | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Shared reference = shared key | Public-key methods help establish keys, but authenticating identities and managing credentials remain necessary |
| Dictionary lookup = decryption | Hash tables: O(1) lookup structures in computer science |
| Edition mismatch = communication failure | Protocol versioning: cryptographic standards must specify exact parameters |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 7, “Crises of the Union,” for Davis’s 146.L.20 example and Confederate naval dictionary arrangements. The diagram uses invented entries.

Modern · 1976

### Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 2 4 5v6c0 5 3.5 9 8 11 4.5-2 8-6 8-11V5z"></path><path d="m9 12 2 2 4-4"></path></svg>
```

Secure (Modern)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Key agreement over a public channel: computational assumptions protect against passive eavesdropping; authentication addresses active impersonation.

OriginWhitfield Diffie & Martin Hellman, ‘New Directions in Cryptography' (1976); Ralph Merkle’s related public-key research

Year1976

TypePublic-key key-agreement protocol — **not a cipher** (does not encrypt data)

StatusWidely used; finite-field DH and elliptic-curve variants such as X25519 have different parameter choices

Modern RoleContributes shared secrets to TLS, SSH, Signal and WireGuard; some protocols also combine post-quantum mechanisms

#### Exchange a value, then ask who sent it

**Toy teaching model — no real security.** We fix public parameters p = 23 and g = 5. Choose each participant’s private exponent and watch what they publish and calculate. All values are displayed for learning; these tiny numbers protect nothing.

Alice’s private exponent a [Input dh-a: type=number; initial value=6] Bob’s private exponent b [Input dh-b: type=number; initial value=15]

Exchange and compare

Run the example, then change one private exponent.

Source for the construction: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, [“New Directions in Cryptography” (1976), §III](<https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1976.1055638>). This invented small-number exercise adds no identity verification or key derivation.

JavaScript is needed for the exercise; a worked example follows below.

#### Why This Matters

Diffie–Hellman showed how two parties can agree on a secret over a public channel without first transporting that secret. The unauthenticated exchange protects against a passive eavesdropper under its computational assumptions. A secure protocol must also authenticate the participants or their exchanged values to resist an active intermediary.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Diffie and Hellman published ‘New Directions in Cryptography' in *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory*, November 1976. The paper proposed both public-key encryption (as a goal) and the key-exchange protocol (as a working example). Three British researchers at GCHQ — James Ellis, Clifford Cocks, and Malcolm Williamson — developed classified public-key ideas during 1970–1974 but classification kept their work secret until 1997. The 1976 paper directly inspired Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman to find RSA the following year.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Both parties agree on a large prime *p* and a generator *g*. Alice picks a secret integer *a* and sends *g<sup>a</sup> mod p*. Bob picks a secret integer *b* and sends *g<sup>b</sup> mod p*. Each computes the shared value *K = g<sup>ab</sup> mod p* — Alice raises Bob's value to her secret, Bob raises Alice's value to his. An eavesdropper sees *p*, *g*, *A = g<sup>a</sup>* and *B = g<sup>b</sup>*. Recovering an exponent *a* or *b* is a **discrete logarithm problem (DLP)**. Computing only the shared value *K* is the **computational Diffie–Hellman problem (CDH)**. A DLP solver gives a CDH solver: recover *a*, then compute *B<sup>a</sup>*. The converse is not established for arbitrary groups. See [Reduction & Proof](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/reduction.html>) for why the direction of an implication matters.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

One direction, with toy numbers

With *p* = 23, *g* = 5, *A* = 8 and *B* = 19, a discrete-log solver finds *a* = 6 because 5<sup>6</sup> mod 23 = 8. It can then compute the shared value 19<sup>6</sup> mod 23 = 2. These tiny parameters are for arithmetic only.

Source: Dan Boneh and Victor Shoup, *A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography*, version 0.6 (January 2023), §10.4.2. Learning whether the value looks random is a further security question, distinct from merely computing it.

#### Which oracle makes the reverse reduction possible?

A DLP solver gives a CDH solver. The reverse direction needs additional, group-specific conditions. A **full two-input DH oracle** accepts two freely chosen points `[a]G, [b]G` and returns `[ab]G`, multiplying hidden scalars. Ordinary point addition gives `[a+b]G`. A fixed-secret service that only returns `[s]P` is a different capability and does not supply the paper's efficient method.

Reported P256 experiment with a simulated full DH oracle

| Offline work | Online work | Required access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| About 3.0 TB auxiliary codebook; about one week on a dual AMD EPYC 7742 | 23,656 simulated full-oracle calls in 32 seconds | The experiment knew discrete logs to simulate the full oracle; the authors report no real-world instantiation |

These results do not establish that P256 was broken in 32 seconds. Other curves' figures are partly estimates, and the largest codebooks are unrealizable. The oracle, simulation status, offline cost and online time are inseparable parts of the result. Source: [Dlog is Practically as Hard (or Easy) as DH](<https://tches.iacr.org/index.php/TCHES/article/view/11161>), pp. 2–3, 7, 12–16.

#### From a shared value to keys for different purposes

HKDF-SHA-256 first **Extracts** a pseudorandom key (PRK) from input key material (IKM): `PRK = HMAC-SHA-256(salt, IKM)`. It then **Expands** that PRK with an `info` byte string and requested output length. A protocol can use different labels for its two traffic directions.

Reproducible fixture: IKM is the 32 bytes `00 01 … 1f` (hexadecimal), salt is 32 zero bytes, and labels below are UTF-8. These published bytes have no secrecy; they are separate from the tiny DH arithmetic above. Extract gives:

`46bd320605c5a6b6163ab70bc6345b92a5f908e79fe58979c23ebb47d1a5e307`

HKDF-SHA-256 outputs for the fixed input above (hexadecimal)

| Info label | Bytes | Output key material |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `museum-demo/client-to-server` | 16 | `a6d093bc8d19224f252d50a07c32bd77` |
| `museum-demo/client-to-server` | 32 | `a6d093bc8d19224f252d50a07c32bd778b08327a06548f672adda01ae4a9d1f2` |
| `museum-demo/server-to-client` | 32 | `cefaddbcf88b04083d511449e158fc5cfc33dcf08759adda9bb09759e02ff728` |

Identical inputs reproduce identical outputs. Changing only the requested length keeps a common prefix; use purpose labels rather than length alone to separate uses. Changing the direction label changes this example's output. Salt and info need not be secret. HKDF does not create new input entropy or make a guessable password or tiny DH group secure; it is not a password-stretching function. Authentication and group validation remain necessary.

Change these inputs in the existing [Crypto Lab: KDF Chain](<https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-kdf-chain/>), under **HKDF: Extract and Expand**, to inspect PRK, output key material and expansion blocks.

Source: David Wong, *Real-World Cryptography* (2021 edition), §8.6, “Key derivation with HKDF,” PDF pp. 349–356 in the reflowed edition, which has no printed pagination. The fixed fixture is a museum example, not a protocol key schedule.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-shield"></use></svg>
```

Security & Cryptanalysis

Resistance to recovering the shared value rests on the computational Diffie–Hellman assumption in the selected group; discrete-log hardness alone does not establish that assumption. Parameter size, subgroup choice and public-key validation all matter; a bit length alone does not establish security. The 2015 Logjam work demonstrated a downgrade to export-grade 512-bit finite-field DH and studied the benefits of precomputation for widely shared groups. Suitable group sizes and validation matter; moving to an elliptic curve also requires a specified secure construction. DH is vulnerable to *active* man-in-the-middle attacks because the exchanged values are unauthenticated — protocols that need protection from active attackers must combine DH with authentication (for example signatures, certificates or a suitable pre-shared-key protocol). A human password requires a properly designed password-authenticated key exchange, not an improvised password check.

Two input-validation failures are often merged and should not be. Forcing a peer’s shared secret into a small subgroup compromises that session and can leak a few bits; recovering a server’s *static* private exponent additionally requires that one exponent be reused across many such queries. A 2016 measurement study found that none of more than twenty surveyed libraries validated subgroup orders by default before January 2016, yet feasible full key recovery was confined to particular applications. The elliptic-curve counterpart — altering only the *y* coordinate of a peer’s public point — broke Bluetooth pairing in 2018. Both are laid out with their access and assumptions in [what an attack result actually shows](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/modern-attack-evidence.html#small-subgroup>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Where You Use It Today

| Where | How Diffie-Hellman is Used |
| --- | --- |
| TLS 1.3 (HTTPS) | TLS 1.3 supports ephemeral finite-field DH, ECDH and pre-shared-key modes; PSK-only exchange does not provide the same forward-secrecy guarantee |
| Signal | X3DH and the classical Double Ratchet are historical foundations. Signal later introduced PQXDH and the Triple Ratchet with a continuing post-quantum ratchet |
| SSH | DH and ECDH are among SSH key-exchange families; negotiated choices vary |
| WireGuard / Tor | WireGuard uses Curve25519; Tor’s ntor handshake also uses Curve25519. Their complete protocols differ. |
| IPsec / IKEv2 | IKEv2 negotiates key-exchange groups; no single group set applies to every VPN |

📜

#### Dilly Knox

1884 – 1943

Alfred Dillwyn Knox — universally 'Dilly' — was a classical scholar who became a leading British cryptanalyst. He deciphered German naval codes in WWI from Room 40, solved the commercial Enigma in the 1930s, and at Bletchley Park broke the Abwehr (German intelligence) Enigma variant — the system that protected Germany's spy networks across occupied Europe. A notoriously eccentric figure who often worked from his bathtub, Knox died of cancer in February 1943, before the end of the war.

##### Why This Person Matters

Knox worked on German naval systems in Room 40 during the First World War and later on commercial and military Enigma variants. His team, including Mavis Batey and Margaret Rock, achieved important Abwehr Enigma breaks. Those contributions should be distinguished from Marian Rejewski’s reconstruction of German Army Enigma wiring in Poland in 1932.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Room 40 and the Zimmermann Telegram

Knox’s Room 40 service connected his First and Second World War careers. The Zimmermann Telegram was deciphered by a different Room 40 team; working in that organization does not establish that Knox personally supplied the methods for that particular solution.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Attacking Enigma Variants

Commercial Enigma machines could be purchased and examined. Knox developed attacks on related systems, including a method known as rodding. This must not be conflated with reconstructing the unavailable German military wiring from traffic. British, Polish, and French work supplied different parts of the later Allied effort; no single prewar researcher was the predecessor of every success.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-person"></use></svg>
```

Mavis Batey and the Female Codebreakers

Mavis Lever (later Batey) and Margaret Rock worked in Knox’s team and contributed to its Enigma successes. GCHQ’s account describes his mentoring of women cryptanalysts and dates the first issued Abwehr decrypt to 25 December 1941. Reading Abwehr communications helped British intelligence assess German agent networks and deception; this was a team achievement involving cryptanalysis and wider intelligence work.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

