##### Why This Matters

Elgar sent the cryptogram to Dora Penny on 14 July 1897. Its three lines are commonly transcribed as 87 symbols. The arc counts and orientations permit 24 symbol classes, but handwritten marks can be ambiguous. A proposed reading must explain the transcription and the decoding rules, not merely produce a plausible sentence.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

David Kahn discusses the note in *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), chapter 21. Later proposed readings disagree about its rules and content. Both English text and music have been investigated; neither hypothesis should be treated as established merely because Elgar was a composer.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

This inspector draws stylized semicircular arcs in eight orientations. It does not transcribe the complete manuscript or recover a key. In *Dorabella Cipher as Musical Inspiration* (2021; arXiv version deposited 2025), Bradley Hauer and colleagues compare transcriptions and use a combined 87-symbol reading. Their musical output is presented as a creative composition process, not an authenticated solution.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

Why It Has Resisted

Why It Resists

Evidence: 87 commonly transcribed symbols

Frequency statistics depend on how the handwritten symbols are transcribed. An 87-symbol sample gives limited evidence, but its length alone neither rules out monoalphabetic substitution nor proves that a unique reading is impossible. A language-model score ranks candidates under a chosen model; it does not authenticate Elgar’s intended message.


What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Dorabella Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Sample size matters | The amount of evidence matters, alongside the cipher assumptions and available context |
| Local maxima are seductive | A high language-model score needs independent confirmation |
| Context can constrain a reading | Transcription, language, authorial context and reproducible rules can help discriminate among candidates |

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    (function () {
      var SAMPLES = ['\u25dc', '\u25dd', '\u25de', '\u25df'];
      function draw() {
        var arcs = parseInt(document.getElementById('dora-arcs').value, 10);
        var angle = parseInt(document.getElementById('dora-angle').value, 10);
        var svg = document.getElementById('dora-symbol');
        var rings = '';
        for (var i = 0; i < arcs; i++) {
          var r = 18 + (i * 10);
          rings += '<path d="M 70 ' + (70 - r) + ' A ' + r + ' ' + r + ' 0 0 1 70 ' + (70 + r) + '" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" fill="none" />';
        }
        svg.innerHTML = '<g transform="rotate(' + angle + ' 70 70)">' + rings + '</g>';
        document.getElementById('dora-output').textContent =
          'Selected symbol class\n' +
          '- Arc count: ' + arcs + '\n' +
          '- Orientation: ' + angle + '°\n\n' +
          'There are 3 arc classes × 8 orientations = 24 possible symbols.\n' +
          'With only 87 characters of ciphertext, many substitution mappings can score as plausible language by chance.';
      }
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
        document.getElementById('dora-render').addEventListener('click', draw);
        draw();
      });
    })();
```

#### Why This Matters

Pair formation is part of the cipher, not mere presentation. Following a complete original example makes conventions observable: a changed boundary, pairing rule or final cell changes the ciphertext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

This page reconstructs one edition: [*Vorläufige Schlüsselanleitung zum Doppelkastenschlüssel*, Ausgabe Dezember 1941](<https://cryptocellar.org/wmc/schluesselanleitung-dk-1941.pdf>). The German armed forces used a two-box digraph cipher in WWII; its arrangement and repeated substitution distinguish it from the generic [Two-Square exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/two-square.html>).

Related procedures changed over time. The 1940 instructions, the later *Truppenschlüssel* and *Nachrichtenschlüssel* are not interchangeable names for this implementation. In particular, the Truppenschlüssel’s single-stage substitution must not be substituted for this edition’s two stages. RS44 began replacing Double Playfair during 1944.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Exact December 1941 Procedure

- Prepare letters; J is represented by II (two letters), as §4 requires. If the length is odd, append an operator-selected letter other than X. This demo chooses Z by default and never removes it automatically.

- Write each full 34-letter block as two rows of 17. Divide a final shorter, even block equally between two shorter rows; do not pad it to 17 columns.

- Form pairs vertically: top-row letter first, bottom-row letter second. Locate the first in square A and the second in square B.

- If the positions share a row, replace each by its right neighbour, wrapping at the edge, and output the B replacement first. Otherwise take the rectangle corners: first output from B at A’s row and B’s column, second from A at B’s row and A’s column.

- Apply that same rule again to the intermediate pair, still locating its first letter in A and its second in B. The second result is ciphertext.

For decryption, locate the ciphertext pair’s first letter in B and second in A. Apply the inverse rule twice: same-row moves are leftward, and rectangle corners cross back. Rebuild the two plaintext rows and read the top row before the bottom. Adjacent repeated letters are not split by a Playfair-style X.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Original Manual Example

The squares and 54-letter message come from printed pp. 4–6, §§9–23. Two short examples pin both branches: `AA → VR → FY` and `FA → TR → VD`. The full message uses a 34-letter block followed by a 20-letter block.

```text
Square A: HILQETUARSBKXFGPWCOZDVYMN
Square B: ZNOCHBXAVIUDTGWMYELSKPQRF

Prepared plaintext:
FEINDLIQERANGRIFFAUFSTRASZEADORFSTRIQBEHAUSENABGEWEHRT

Ciphertext body:
VDLGCTUQZREOMFCIFEALFYLBAPKWCTEIWBTYMFLNMVMQZTVLHUPILF
```

The engine is checked against these printed answers in both directions. No output from this engine was used to invent the expected values.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Cryptanalysis and Limits

Ostwald and Weierud describe Allied work on Double Playfair by John Tiltman’s British team and U.S. cryptanalysts, including Joseph S. Schick’s account of the 849th Signal Intelligence Service, using known or probable plaintext and digraph statistics. The cipher’s plaintext arrangement changes which letters are paired; it does not remove statistical structure.

Their modern hill-climbing results concern the related *Truppenschlüssel*. Those results must not be described as a test of this December 1941 two-stage engine. The daily key consists of two ordered 25-letter squares; a nominal settings count does not establish resistance to crib-based cryptanalysis.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Reconstruction and Teaching Limits

The demo models this edition’s pairing, same-row rule, two substitution stages and inverse reconstruction. The museum applies accent stripping and discards punctuation and digits. German field-message abbreviations, umlaut expansion, spelled-out numbers, operational headers, identification groups, daily-key distribution and emergency square construction are left to the operator and are not simulated.

The real operator chose an odd-length filler from the allowed letters. A selectable, repeatable filler makes testing understandable; it is not an undocumented escape protocol. A genuine trailing Z remains indistinguishable from a filler Z. The UI enforces the 500-letter transmitted-body limit. The pure engine can process longer blocks for complexity testing when that operational check is explicitly disabled.


Sources and Further Reading

[Original December 1941 manual](<https://cryptocellar.org/wmc/schluesselanleitung-dk-1941.pdf>): printed pp. 3–6, §§4, 9–23; NARA RG 457, Box 7, Nr. 57; facsimile curated by Frode Weierud at [CryptoCellar](<https://cryptocellar.org/wmc/index.html>).

[Olaf Ostwald and Frode Weierud, *Modern Cryptanalysis of the Truppenschlüssel*](<https://cryptocellar.org/pubs/mcts.pdf>) (2021 author manuscript; published in *Cryptologia* 47(3), 2023, pp. 261–281): historical comparison and procedure distinctions. Its attack results target Truppenschlüssel.

Square diagrams are rendered from factual key letters; no source scans or third-party images are reproduced.

### Double Transposition

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Two columnar transpositions compose two position permutations

Anagramming · Hill climbing (difficult)

InventorNo single inventor established here

YearDocumented military use in the First World War

Key TypeTwo columnar keywords

Broken ByAnagramming · Hill climbing (difficult)

Modern LessonMultiple cipher rounds

#### Why This Matters

Double transposition can make reconstruction substantially harder than one pass. Its security still depends on message length, column widths, key selection, padding and available related traffic. A count of key pairs is not a measured security level.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

German forces used double transposition during the First World War, and related systems appeared in later military and agent communications. This operational history does not establish the German military as the original inventor. Applying two transpositions creates another permutation of the same letters; their frequencies remain unchanged.

Computer attacks can exploit language scores and structural constraints. Short ciphertexts or unknown dimensions may make a particular attack difficult or ambiguous, while other instances are recoverable. Comparisons should state the keys, text length, search budget and success criterion.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Apply columnar transposition twice using two different keywords:

```text
Step 1: Apply columnar transposition with key MARK
Step 2: Apply columnar transposition with key LION

There are k1! × k2! pairs of column-order settings
when each key can be any permutation of its columns.
Different pairs may induce the same permutation;
this is not a proof of k1! × k2! distinct ciphertexts.
```

Double transposition: two successive column reorderings with different keys — the result depends on both keys and the message layout

A 7-letter key gives 5,040 possible column orders. Two such keys give 25,401,600 ordered key pairs. Structured cryptanalysis need not enumerate them all.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Hill Climbing / Simulated Annealing

Complexity: Hard — especially on short ciphertext

Heuristic solvers can search candidate keys using language scores, moves such as swaps, and repeated restarts. Results depend on the implementation and instance. No universal number of iterations or guaranteed recovery time follows from the cipher name alone.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Double Transposition | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Two-pass permutation | AES applies 10–14 rounds of operations — multiple passes through cipher structure |
| Large combined keyspace | AES 128-bit key: 2¹²⁸ possible keys — exponentially larger |
| No substitution, only permutation | AES combines nonlinear SubBytes, byte-reordering ShiftRows, and linear MixColumns (omitted in the final round) |


#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), discussion of First World War transposition practice. George Lasry, *A Methodology for the Cryptanalysis of Classical Ciphers with Search Metaheuristics* (2018), treats attacks as experiments with defined instances and evaluation criteria.

#### Elonka Dunin

b. 1958

Elonka Dunin is a game developer, cryptography researcher and author. Her websites collect information about Kryptos and other unresolved cryptograms, and her books introduce classical cryptanalysis to general readers. Her work includes documentary research and public explanation as well as attempts at decipherment.

##### Why This Person Matters

Dunin’s work illustrates the importance of documenting evidence and making it accessible. Her Freedom of Information Act request helped bring NSA records about early Kryptos solutions into public view in 2013. A researcher’s archive can be useful without being an official certification of a cipher’s status; dates, sources and the meaning of “solved” still need checking.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lock"></use></svg>
```

Kryptos Research

Jim Sanborn’s *Kryptos* was installed at CIA headquarters in 1990. K1 and K2 use Vigenère-family substitutions; K3 uses transposition. Jim Gillogly publicly announced solutions in 1999, following earlier work at the NSA and David Stein’s independent CIA solution in 1998. Dunin’s documentation distinguishes these histories. The 2025 discovery of K4 plaintext material in Sanborn’s archive is a different achievement from reconstructing its encryption method; see the [Kryptos exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kryptos.html>) for that distinction.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-quill"></use></svg>
```

The Famous Unsolved Codes List

Her *Famous Unsolved Codes and Ciphers* list brings together puzzles with different kinds of uncertainty. An undeciphered language, an uncertain inscription and a known encryption system with a missing key are not the same problem. Such lists are starting points for research, and their historical entries must be checked against later discoveries.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

Game Design and Cipher Narrative

Dunin worked in online game development at Simutronics. Her publications include *The Mammoth Book of Secret Codes and Cryptograms* (2006) and, with Klaus Schmeh, *Codebreaking: A Practical Guide* (2020). The latter presents techniques, worked cases and challenges, including both Gillogly’s IRA work and Bean’s later solution.

Evidence and Reading

Elonka Dunin and Klaus Schmeh, *Codebreaking: A Practical Guide* (Robinson, 2020), author biographies and IRA case studies. Dunin’s [Kryptos archive](<https://elonka.com/kryptos/>) and [FAQ](<https://elonka.com/kryptos/faq.html>) document her research and the K1–K3 solution history; older status statements in the FAQ need to be read in their original context.

### ECDSA

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 2 4 5v6c0 5 3.5 9 8 11 4.5-2 8-6 8-11V5z"></path><path d="m9 12 2 2 4-4"></path></svg>
```

Secure (Modern)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A signature scheme built on elliptic curves, with nonce handling essential to protecting the signing key.

OriginScott Vanstone, 1992; standardised as ANSI X9.62 (1999) and FIPS 186

Year1992

TypeDigital signature algorithm — **not a cipher** (verifies a signature against a key, encrypts nothing)

Rests onScheme-specific assumptions; solving ECDLP breaks key secrecy

StatusSigns TLS certificates, Bitcoin and Ethereum transactions, and software updates

#### Why This Matters

Encryption protects confidentiality. A digital signature lets a verifier check a message against a public key. Certificates, authorization rules and context connect that key to a domain, person or permitted action. ECDSA is used for many certificates, software signatures and cryptocurrency transactions, although those ecosystems also use other signature schemes.

It is also the museum's clearest case of the difference between a mathematical signature construction and implementation failures. Nonce mistakes are a particularly revealing example; secure implementation also requires careful arithmetic, validation and side-channel protection.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Elliptic curves entered cryptography in 1985, proposed independently by Neal Koblitz and Victor Miller. The appeal was efficiency: the discrete logarithm problem seemed much harder on a curve than in the integers modulo a prime, so a 256-bit curve key offered roughly the security of a 3072-bit RSA key. Scott Vanstone adapted the existing Digital Signature Algorithm to curves in 1992, and ECDSA was standardised as ANSI X9.62 in 1999. Bitcoin adopted it in 2009, which put the algorithm in front of a far larger and more adversarial audience than the standards bodies had imagined.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Fix a curve, a base point *G* on it, and the number *n* of points *G* generates. A private key is a number *d*; the matching public key is the point *Q* = *dG*. Recovering *d* from *Q* means solving the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, for which no practical classical attack is known on properly chosen large groups.

To sign a message hash *h*, pick a one-time random number *k* — the **nonce** — and compute:

R = kG · r = R<sub>x</sub> mod n · s = k<sup>−1</sup>(h + rd) mod n

The signature is the pair (*r*, *s*). A verifier who has only *Q*, *h* and the signature recomputes a point from them and reduces its x-coordinate modulo *n* and compares the result with *r*. The private key never appears in the check — that asymmetry is the whole point.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-flask"></use></svg>
```

Sign and verify, live

This runs a genuine curve, small enough to read: *y*² = *x*³ + 3*x* + 2 over the integers mod 97. It has 102 points plus the point at infinity, so *n* = 103 — a prime, which means every point except the identity generates the whole group. Real ECDSA uses much larger approved parameters and specified hash-to-integer processing. This browser toy exposes its keys and uses small integers; it is not a secure signing tool.

The nonce that sank the PlayStation 3

The nonce *k* must be secret. Reusing it with **distinct message-hash values modulo *n*** is dangerous: the two signature equations then share an unknown. Subtract them and *k* falls out; substitute back and the private key follows. No lattice, no supercomputer — secondary-school algebra:

k = (h₁ − h₂) / (s₁ − s₂) then d = (s₁k − h₁) / r

All arithmetic in these recovery formulas is modulo *n*; division means multiplication by a modular inverse.

In December 2010 fail0verflow demonstrated that reused ECDSA nonces exposed PlayStation 3 signing keys. The example shows why secrecy of the long-term key is not enough: the per-signature nonce must be generated and handled correctly. Deterministic nonce generation, as specified by RFC 6979, is one established way to avoid relying on fresh randomness for each signature; it does not remove other implementation risks.

first message h₁  [Input h1: type=number; initial value=11]   second message h₂  [Input h2: type=number; initial value=29]   Sign both with the same nonce Recover the private key

Sign two messages with one nonce, then attack.


Security & Cryptanalysis

No practical classical attack is known against properly parameterised ECDSA with suitable curves and hashes. Implementations can fail through nonce reuse, weak randomness, faults, or side-channel leakage. **Partial nonce leakage can enable key recovery**, but success depends on the amount and structure of leakage, measurement noise and the number of signatures available; it is not an unconditional result for any leaked bit.

**Deterministic ECDSA** derives the nonce from the private key and message hash, removing dependence on fresh signing randomness. With the same inputs it produces the same signature. It does **not guarantee collision-free nonces** for different messages, and it does not remove side-channel or fault risks. Correct randomised ECDSA is also possible; secure key generation still needs suitable randomness.

Source: [RFC 6979 (August 2013), §§1, 3.2 and 4](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6979.html#section-4>), an Informational RFC. Its deterministic nonce procedure retains implementation-security requirements. This exhibit uses visitor-selected toy nonces and does not implement RFC 6979.

Like all discrete-logarithm cryptography, ECDSA falls to a sufficiently large quantum computer running Shor's algorithm. [Resource estimates distinguish logical/physical qubits and modeled runtime](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/modern-attack-evidence.html#quantum-resources>); RSA figures do not automatically transfer to elliptic-curve targets. ML-DSA is one standardized post-quantum signature option and uses module-lattice assumptions — the [Learning With Errors](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/learning-with-errors.html>) exhibit introduces one relevant family of assumptions, not a proof of the complete signature scheme.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Where You Use It Today

ECDSA is one signature option in TLS, cryptocurrency protocols and software verification. TLS also supports other signature schemes, and a resumed or PSK handshake need not send a fresh certificate signature. Bitcoin uses both ECDSA and, for Taproot, BIP 340 Schnorr signatures. A browser’s connection indicator does not identify the signature algorithm.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-key"></use></svg>
```

At a glance

**Private key:** a number *d*.

**Public key:** the point *Q* = *dG*.

**Signature:** a pair (*r*, *s*).

**Hard problem:** find *d* given *Q* — the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm.

**Fatal mistake:** reusing the nonce *k* for distinct message-hash values modulo *n*. Two valid signatures then expose the private key.

The mathematics is in the [Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/elliptic-curves-real.html>): the group law that makes *dG* meaningful, and the finite field it runs in.

#### Primary Sources

[FIPS 186-5 (2023)](<https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/186-5/final>); [RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3, 2018), §§2 and 4.2.3](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446.html>); [RFC 6979 (deterministic DSA/ECDSA, 2013)](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6979.html>); [BIP 340 (Schnorr signatures used with Bitcoin Taproot)](<https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0340.mediawiki>). Bitcoin therefore does not use ECDSA for every transaction.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  var PM = window.ProtocolMath, C = PM.CURVE;
  var NS = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  function mk(t,a){var e=document.createElementNS(NS,t);for(var k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;}
  function el(id){return document.getElementById(id);}

  // every affine point, for the scatter
  var PTS=[];
  for(var x=0;x<C.p;x++){
    var rhs=PM.mod(x*x%C.p*x + C.a*x + C.b, C.p);
    for(var y=0;y<C.p;y++) if(y*y%C.p===rhs) PTS.push({x:x,y:y});
  }

  var svg=el("curve");
  function draw(Q){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    var W=700,H=360,pad=34;
    var sx=function(v){return pad + v*(W-2*pad)/(C.p-1);};
    var sy=function(v){return H-pad - v*(H-2*pad)/(C.p-1);};
    PTS.forEach(function(pt){
      svg.appendChild(mk("circle",{cx:sx(pt.x),cy:sy(pt.y),r:2.4,fill:"var(--tx3,#8a8a94)","fill-opacity":".55"}));
    });
    function mark(pt,color,label){
      if(!pt) return;
      svg.appendChild(mk("circle",{cx:sx(pt.x),cy:sy(pt.y),r:7,fill:"none",stroke:color,"stroke-width":"2.5"}));
      var t=mk("text",{x:sx(pt.x)+11,y:sy(pt.y)-9,fill:color,"font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"14","font-weight":"700"});
      t.textContent=label; svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    mark(C.G,"var(--gold,#d4a24c)","G");
    mark(Q,"var(--red,#c94f3d)","Q = dG");
  }

  function clampInt(id,lo,hi){
    var v=parseInt(el(id).value,10);
    if(isNaN(v)) v=lo;
    v=Math.max(lo,Math.min(hi,v));
    el(id).value=v; return v;
  }

  function sign(){
    window.__lastSig=null;
    var d=clampInt("d",1,C.n-1), h=clampInt("h",0,C.n-1), k=clampInt("k",1,C.n-1);
    var Q=PM.ecMul(d,C.G,C.a,C.p);
    draw(Q);
    var sig=PM.ecdsaSign(h,d,k,C);
    if(!sig){ el("sigOut").innerHTML="Nonce k = "+k+" is degenerate for this message &mdash; real ECDSA resamples and tries again."; return; }
    var ok=PM.ecdsaVerify(h,sig,Q,C);
    el("sigOut").innerHTML =
      "Q = dG = ("+Q.x+", "+Q.y+")<br>"+
      "signature (r, s) = (<b>"+sig.r+"</b>, <b>"+sig.s+"</b>)<br>"+
      "verify with public key only: <b style=\"color:"+(ok?"var(--green,#5AC8A0)":"var(--red,#c94f3d)")+"\">"+
      (ok?"valid":"REJECTED")+"</b>";
    window.__lastSig={sig:sig,h:h,Q:Q,d:d};
  }

  function verifyOther(){
    if(!window.__lastSig){ sign(); }
    var L=window.__lastSig;
    if(!L) return;
    var h2=(L.h+1)%C.n;
    var ok=PM.ecdsaVerify(h2,L.sig,L.Q,C);
    el("sigOut").innerHTML =
      "Same signature (r, s) = ("+L.sig.r+", "+L.sig.s+"), but message hash changed "+L.h+" &rarr; "+h2+"<br>"+
      "verify: <b style=\"color:"+(ok?"var(--red,#c94f3d)":"var(--green,#5AC8A0)")+"\">"+
      (ok?"accepted &mdash; a collision on this tiny toy curve":"REJECTED for these inputs")+
      "</b><br><span style=\"opacity:.75\">Real parameter sizes make such accidental acceptance negligibly likely under the usual security assumptions, not mathematically impossible.</span>";
  }

  function reuse(){
    window.__reuse=null;
    var d=clampInt("d",1,C.n-1), k=clampInt("k",1,C.n-1);
    var h1=clampInt("h1",0,C.n-1), h2=clampInt("h2",0,C.n-1);
    if(h1===h2){ el("atkOut").textContent="Use two different messages — identical messages give identical signatures, which is not a leak."; return; }
    var s1=PM.ecdsaSign(h1,d,k,C), s2=PM.ecdsaSign(h2,d,k,C);
    if(!s1||!s2){ el("atkOut").textContent="Degenerate nonce for this pair; nudge k and retry."; return; }
    window.__reuse={h1:h1,h2:h2,s1:s1,s2:s2,d:d,k:k};
    el("atkOut").innerHTML =
      "Signed both with the same nonce k = "+k+":<br>"+
      "&nbsp;&nbsp;h&#8321;="+h1+" &rarr; (r, s) = ("+s1.r+", "+s1.s+")<br>"+
      "&nbsp;&nbsp;h&#8322;="+h2+" &rarr; (r, s) = ("+s2.r+", "+s2.s+")<br>"+
      "<b>Notice r is identical in both.</b> That is the tell — r depends only on k. Now press <em>Recover the private key</em>.";
  }

  function attack(){
    var R=window.__reuse;
    if(!R){ el("atkOut").textContent="Sign two messages with one nonce first."; return; }
    var out=PM.recoverFromReusedNonce(R.h1,R.s1.s,R.h2,R.s2.s,R.s1.r,C.n);
    if(!out){ el("atkOut").textContent="Could not solve — try a different message pair."; return; }
    var hit=(out.d===R.d);
    el("atkOut").innerHTML =
      "k = (h&#8321; &minus; h&#8322;) / (s&#8321; &minus; s&#8322;) = <b>"+out.k+"</b>"+(out.k===R.k?" &check;":"")+"<br>"+
      "d = (s&#8321;k &minus; h&#8321;) / r = <b style=\"color:var(--red,#c94f3d)\">"+out.d+"</b>"+
      (hit?" &mdash; that is the private key, recovered from two signatures and nothing else.":"")+
      "<br><span style=\"opacity:.75\">No search, no guessing. This is the arithmetic that cost Sony its console.</span>";
  }

  el("sign").addEventListener("click",sign);
  el("verifyOther").addEventListener("click",verifyOther);
  el("reuse").addEventListener("click",reuse);
  el("attack").addEventListener("click",attack);
  sign();
})();
```

### Egyptian Substitution Hieroglyphs

The Khnumhotep II tomb inscription: unusual signs at the boundary of ornament and concealment.

Decorative concealment

SiteTomb of Khnumhotep II, Beni Hasan, Egypt

Year~1900 BCE (12th Dynasty)

MethodReplacement of standard hieroglyphs with unusual variants

PurposeDisputed — likely scribal display or sacred concealment

Modern LessonUnusual writing does not by itself establish secret-key encryption

#### Hieroglyph Substitution Demo

This widget maps modern A–Z letters to selected hieroglyphic-looking signs. The assignments are invented for display: they are neither Egyptian transliteration nor a reconstruction of the Khnumhotep inscription. Track B — illustration, not historical encryption.

 Input  [Input input: type=text; initial value=KHNUMHOTEP]  Render Hieroglyphs

##### Why This Matters

Khnumhotep II’s tomb at Beni Hasan contains unusual hieroglyphic writing, often cited in histories of cryptography. Whether such choices primarily conveyed secrecy, learned display, or religious meaning must be distinguished from the observable use of unusual signs. They do not establish the origin of every later substitution cipher.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Egyptian scribes had two parallel writing systems by 1900 BCE: monumental hieroglyphs for inscriptions and the cursive hieratic for everyday documents. The Khnumhotep tomb belongs to the monumental tradition, where elaboration was prized. Egyptologists debate whether the unusual variants were meant to obscure meaning from casual readers, to flatter the gods through visual richness, or to display the scribe's erudition. All three motives — secrecy, sanctity, and craft — recur throughout cipher history.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Worked

Egyptian writing combined phonetic and other sign functions. Its alternate spellings cannot simply be equated with a one-to-one A–Z substitution. The modern widget demonstrates the visual effect of an unfamiliar symbol set, not the ancient inscription’s exact linguistic mechanism.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Cipher, Code, or Ornament?

Encoding represents information, encryption uses a security construction to protect it, and steganography attempts to conceal its presence. Unusual writing alone does not prove that a secret-key cipher was intended. This is a useful boundary case, provided that its uncertainty remains visible.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Hall | I · World Origins |
| --- | --- |
| Region | Middle Kingdom Egypt |
| Era | ~1900 BCE |
| Site | Beni Hasan, tomb of Khnumhotep II |
| Method | Symbol substitution |
| Track | B (visualization) |
| Compare | Atbash and Caesar; no direct line of descent established |

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 2, “The First 3,000 Years.” Kahn distinguishes this inscription’s unusual writing from secret writing in the modern sense; the museum does not treat it as a reconstructed A–Z cipher.

```javascript
        var src = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').toUpperCase();
```

🦅

#### Elizebeth Smith Friedman

1892 – 1980

Elizebeth Smith worked at Riverbank Laboratories and married William Friedman. She later led U.S. Coast Guard cryptanalytic work against smugglers and wartime spy communications. Her achievements included training analysts and supplying expert evidence in prosecutions. The wartime work was a **team effort**, not a single-handed dismantling of every South American spy network.

#### From a ship’s radio to the witness stand

##### The Bear Cat, September 1930

As David Kahn recounts in *The Codebreakers*, chapter 22, the rumrunner *Bear Cat* drew a pursuing Coast Guard cutter farther out to sea. On 22 September its shore contact advised it to keep going. After the cutter abandoned the pursuit the next day, the smuggler returned to its rendezvous. Reading that exchange afterwards exposed the tactic; reading it in time could have supported a different decision. This episode is a failed opportunity to intervene, not a claim that decipherment sank the ship.

##### New Orleans, May 1933

Coast Guard listeners at Mobile intercepted Consolidated Exporters Corporation’s radio traffic and sent it to Friedman’s unit in Washington. In the trial beginning 1 May 1933, Friedman explained her decipherments under challenge from the defence. Readable traffic had become evidence that needed to withstand examination.

Source: Patrick D. Weadon, [“A New Kind of Detective Work, 1920–1933,” p. 2, “The Trial”](<https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/pre-wwii/new_detective_work.pdf>); Kahn, chapter 22, as cited in the book’s chapter 8 notes. For a claimed message-to-person link, ask what a vessel log, interception record or independent witness would establish. The reading alone cannot answer every question about who acted.

#### Riverbank: a reading must survive a test

Elizebeth Smith arrived at George Fabyan’s Riverbank Laboratories in 1916, where a project sought Baconian messages in Shakespeare. She and William Friedman developed practical cryptanalytic work there; their later *The Shakespearean Ciphers Examined* (1957) challenged claimed decipherments. Finding a possible pattern and establishing an intended message are different tasks. Sources: the [Marshall Foundation’s account of Riverbank](<https://www.marshallfoundation.org/articles-and-features/elizebeth-who/>) and the Friedmans’ 1957 book, also discussed in chapter 7’s notes.

[Open the evidence workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html>). Record a proposed reading, its rule and an observation that could disprove it. Could someone apply the same rule without being told the answer?

##### Why This Person Matters

Friedman worked within government institutions, including the Coast Guard and Treasury. Secrecy and uneven attribution obscured parts of her contribution, but it was documented before the 2017 biography. For example, the NSA recognized her in its Cryptologic Hall of Honor and named a building for both Friedmans in 2002. See the [NSA biography](<https://www.nsa.gov/Press-Room/Digital-Media-Center/Biographies/Biography-View-Page/Article/1623028/elizebeth-s-friedman/>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

Rum-Running and the Coast Guard

The Coast Guard credits its cryptanalytic operation with deciphering approximately 12,000 smuggling messages. Friedman also testified in criminal cases. Messages, distinct cipher systems, codebooks and prosecutions are different counts. See the [Coast Guard’s historical account](<https://www.history.uscg.mil/Research/THE-LONG-BLUE-LINE/Article/2925266/the-long-blue-line-mrs-friedmanthe-coast-guards-cryptologist-in-charge-and-nsc/>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Nazi Spy Networks

Friedman’s wartime unit analyzed clandestine Axis communications, including systems used in South America. This work combined analysts, interception, and interagency cooperation. Cryptanalytic intelligence supported counterintelligence investigations; recovering messages and arresting agents were distinct contributions.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

William and Elizebeth

William Friedman led the Army’s Signal Intelligence Service; PURPLE was solved by its team, including Frank Rowlett and Genevieve Grotjan, not by William alone. Elizebeth had a distinct career with her own collaborators. Their contributions can be recognized without inferring medical causes, private motives, or a deliberate design of every official record.

Encrypt Reset to defaults

🔐

**Symmetric by design.** Enigma encrypts and decrypts with the same machine state. To decrypt, set the same rotors, rings, positions, and plugboard, then type the ciphertext. The original plaintext appears.

#### A procedure gives the machine a pattern

Under the earlier German Army procedure, an operator selected a three-letter message key and enciphered it twice at the daily ground setting. Six indicator letters were sent. The first and fourth positions therefore concealed the same plaintext letter, as did the second and fifth, and third and sixth; the changing rotor positions meant their ciphertext letters need not match.

Marian Rejewski and his Polish colleagues used relationships across such indicators to study permutations and constrain settings. This was an attack on a machine used under a particular procedure. In September 1938 the ground-setting procedure changed, so the earlier daily-setting analysis must not be confused with every later Polish method. The repeated-key practice itself continued beyond that change.

Source: Marian Rejewski, [“An Application of the Theory of Permutations in Breaking the Enigma Cipher” (1980)](<https://doi.org/10.4064/am-16-4-543-559>). In the simulator, repeat a letter and reset the same settings: that demonstrates reproducible rotor behaviour, not a replay of Rejewski’s attack.

#### Why This Matters

Breaking Enigma contributed important intelligence during World War II. Estimates of how much Allied signals intelligence shortened the war concern the wider ULTRA effort and are historical counterfactuals, not measurements attributable to this cipher alone.

Historical Context

Arthur Scherbius patented the Enigma machine in 1918 as a commercial product. The German military adopted it in 1926 and progressively enhanced it throughout WWII. At its peak, the three-rotor Enigma I had 158,962,555,217,826,360,000 combinations of rotor order, starting positions, and ten plugboard pairs with ring settings fixed — and the naval M4 more still.

**The Polish breakthrough.** The story properly begins not at Bletchley but in Warsaw. In 1932 the young Polish mathematician **Marian Rejewski**, working for the Biuro Szyfrów with colleagues **Jerzy Różycki** and **Henryk Zygalski**, reconstructed the wiring of the German Army Enigma's rotors using intercepted traffic and compromised documents obtained through French intelligence. Rejewski did this by formulating message-key permutations as group-theoretic equations and solving them. By 1938 the Poles were reading roughly three-quarters of intercepted German Enigma traffic, using their own electromechanical machines (the *bomba kryptologiczna*, a predecessor using a different attack) and Zygalski's perforated sheets.

**The handover.** When Germany added two new rotors and changed procedures in late 1938, the Polish bureau's lead shrank. On **25 July 1939**, five weeks before the German invasion, Rejewski and his colleagues met British and French cryptanalysts in a forest near Pyry, south of Warsaw, and presented them with everything: the rotor wirings, the bomby, the Zygalski sheets, working Enigma replicas. The handover supplied crucial knowledge and equipment, building on earlier work in several countries.

**Hut 6 and Hut 8.** At Bletchley Park, **Hut 6** (under Gordon Welchman, then Stuart Milner-Barry) attacked German Army and Luftwaffe Enigma; **Hut 8** (under Alan Turing, then Hugh Alexander) attacked Naval Enigma — a far harder problem due to rigorous procedures and, from February 1942, the four-rotor M4 used by the U-boat fleet. Naval decrypts helped convoy routing and anti-submarine operations, alongside other intelligence and operational measures.

**Turing's bombe and Welchman's diagonal board.** Turing's bombe mechanised crib-based attacks: given a guessed plaintext fragment, it tested rotor settings electrically at the rate of thousands per minute, exploiting the loops in the implied permutation graph. Welchman’s diagonal board strengthened the constraint checking by exploiting reciprocal plugboard connections. Over 200 bombes were built, operated by Wrens working in shifts day and night.

**Strategic impact.** Sir Harry Hinsley, the official historian of British intelligence in WWII, estimated that ULTRA — the codename covering decrypts from Enigma and other systems — shortened the war in Europe by *at least* two years and "possibly four." This is a historical estimate rather than a measurable counterfactual. The value of particular decrypts varied by campaign and period.

*Sources: Hinsley, “British Intelligence in the Second World War,” HMSO 1979–1990; Kozaczuk, “Enigma,” 1984; Welchman, “The Hut Six Story,” 1982; Hodges, “Alan Turing: The Enigma,” 1983.*

How It Works

```text
Three-rotor Enigma (basic model):

1. Plugboard: swap 10 pairs of letters
   (150 trillion possible settings)

2. Three rotors: the rightmost advances
   before each letter; notches govern the others
   (17,576 rotor position combinations)

3. Reflector: sends signal back through
   rotors in reverse
   (this is Enigma's fatal flaw: a letter
   can never encrypt to itself)

4. Rotor selection: 3 from 5 rotors
   (60 rotor order combinations)

Total: ~158 quintillion settings
But: same letter never encrypts to itself → cribs work
```

How It Was Broken

Crib-Based Cryptanalysis (Turing's Bombe)

Complexity: Computationally intensive · Required dedicated machines

Enigma's fatal flaw: a letter can never encrypt to itself (the reflector guarantees this). If you know (or guess) a plaintext word — called a crib — you can eliminate all configurations where any crib letter would encrypt to itself. Weather vocabulary could supply useful guessed plaintext, though message formats varied. A correct crib supplies constraints for key search, while an incorrect guess can fail to produce a valid candidate. The Bombe machine tested the remaining configurations electromechanically at thousands per minute.

Operator Errors

Human factors

Predictable plaintext, repeated settings, captured material, and operating procedures gave attackers useful information. Machine structure mattered too: the reflector’s no-self-encipherment property helped reject impossible cribs. It is misleading to attribute the breaks exclusively to human error rather than mathematics.

##### 1 · Self-encryption rejection

Enigma's reflector means no letter can ever encrypt to itself. This fact lets you reject impossible candidate alignments of a crib without testing rotor settings: if any letter of the crib lines up with the same letter in the ciphertext, that placement is impossible.

BDZGOWCXLTKSBTMCDLPBMUQOFXYHCX

Suspected crib (e.g. WETTER, KEINE, OBERKOMMANDODERWEHRMACHT)  [Input eg-crib-text: type=text; initial value=WETTER]

Click "Check all placements" to see which positions survive the self-encryption rule.

Each row is a candidate placement of the crib over the ciphertext. Rows in red are impossible (a crib letter would have to encrypt to itself). Rows in green survive and would be passed to the bombe for full testing.

##### 2 · Brute-force rotor & position search

With the plugboard and ring settings fixed, the rotor order and starting positions form a search space of **60 × 17 576 ≈ 1 054 560** configurations. The bombe was needed because the plugboard explodes this by a further factor of ~1.5 × 10<sup>14</sup>. Without the plugboard, the search is small enough to run in your browser. Below: enter a ciphertext encrypted with rings AAA and no plugboard, give it a known crib, and watch the search recover the rotor settings.

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Enigma Machine | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Rotor substitution per keypress | AES: round keys change each round, creating a different transformation per step |
| Reflector creates a no-self-encipherment constraint | Reciprocity alone is not a weakness; XOR-based stream encryption also uses a self-inverse operation |
| Physical key distribution (codebooks) | Diffie–Hellman enables public-channel key agreement; authentication and key management still matter |
| Structure and operational procedures both mattered | Modern systems also need side-channel defenses and sound key-handling procedures |

Worked Example

```text
Plaintext:  A T T A C K
Settings:   Rotors I-II-III, Reflector B
            Ring setting: 01-01-01 (AAA)
            Plugboard: (A↔M) (T↔G)
            Start position: A-A-Z

Encrypting the first letter "A":
(Rotor III steps first: positions A-A-Z → A-A-A)
1. Plugboard: A → M  (A is swapped with M)
2. Rotor III:  M → maps to Z
3. Rotor II:   Z → maps to E
4. Rotor I:    E → maps to L
5. Reflector B: L → maps to G
6. Rotor I  ←  G → maps to F
7. Rotor II ←  F → maps to W
8. Rotor III←  W → maps to R
9. Plugboard:  R → R  (no swap for R)
Lamp "R" lights up.

Full message: ATTACK → RXWKBV

Stepping occurs before encipherment. The rightmost rotor advances each time.
Notch positions trigger the other rotors, including the middle double-step.
Changing rotor state changes the substitution, but an individual
plaintext letter can still produce the same output at different positions.
```

Further Reading & Other Enigma Resources

The encryption side of Enigma is well-covered on the open web. Several excellent simulators and explainers already exist; the rotor-search and crib-rejection demos above are this museum's contribution. The resources below offer further explanations, simulators and historical accounts.

##### Video explainers

- [Mike Pound & Computerphile — *Enigma & the Bombe* playlist ↗](<https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLzH6n4zXuckqmf_x8yLfTd2KrBgaQQwZl>)
 Dr Pound's University of Nottingham series is the gold-standard general-audience explanation. The videos explain the machine and crib-based attacks.

- [Bletchley Park Trust ↗](<https://www.bletchleypark.org.uk/>)
 The site itself, in Buckinghamshire — Hut 6, Hut 8, the rebuilt Bombe in Block H. If you can visit, do.

##### Other interactive Enigma simulators

- [Louise Dade — Enigma Simulator ↗](<https://enigma.louisedade.co.uk/>)
 Long-running, accurate, and visually beautiful — a skeuomorphic interface that mimics the look and feel of a real Enigma I machine. Best for the tactile experience.

- [Cryptii — Enigma pipe ↗](<https://cryptii.com/pipes/enigma-machine>)
 An in-browser cryptography toolkit. Clean UI, real Enigma logic, and uniquely lets you chain Enigma with other ciphers in a visual pipeline.

- [101computing.net — Enigma Machine Emulator ↗](<https://www.101computing.net/enigma-machine-emulator/>)
 A polished, classroom-friendly simulator with configurable rotors, plugboard, and ring settings. Widely used in UK GCSE and A-level computer-science teaching.

##### Cryptanalysis & the Bombe

- [Tony Sale — Virtual Bombe ↗](<http://www.codesandciphers.org.uk/virtualbp/tbombe/tbombe.htm>)
 The late Tony Sale led the rebuilding of Colossus at Bletchley. His menus-and-diagonal-board walkthrough of the bombe is the most authoritative source on the open web. Dense but accurate.

- [Crypto Museum — Enigma index ↗](<https://www.cryptomuseum.com/crypto/enigma/>)
 The reference for rotor wirings, machine variants, and operating procedures. The wirings used in this exhibit's engine were verified against this site.

##### Books

- Hodges, Andrew. *Alan Turing: The Enigma.* Princeton University Press, 1983 (rev. 2014). The definitive biography; chapters 4–6 cover Hut 8.

- Welchman, Gordon. *The Hut Six Story.* McGraw-Hill, 1982. First-person account by the architect of the diagonal board.

- Kozaczuk, Władysław. *Enigma: How the German Machine Cipher Was Broken.* University Publications of America, 1984. The Polish side of the story, in detail.

- Hinsley, F. H. *British Intelligence in the Second World War.* HMSO, 1979–1990 (5 vols). The official history; source for the "two-to-four-year" shortening estimate.

The Erskine Messages — All Three Now Broken

Three naval M4 signals intercepted by HMS *Hurricane* in the North Atlantic in 1942 went unread at the time. Ralph Erskine reprinted them in a 1995 letter to *Cryptologia* as an open challenge, and for a decade they were the best-known still-unsolved Enigma traffic.

In January 2006 Stefan Krah launched the **M4 Message Breaking Project**, a distributed-computing effort combining brute-force rotor search with hill-climbing on the plugboard. The first signal fell on **20 February 2006** — Kptlt. Hartwig Looks of *U-264*, forced under by depth charges. The second fell on **7 March 2006** — a routine sighting-and-weather report signed Schroeder, matching the war diary of *U-623*.

The third resisted for another seven years. It was broken in **January 2013** by Dan Girard, with Michael Hörenberg, and proved to be a fuel-and-provisions report from Kptlt. Hermann Rasch of *U-106*. **None of the three remains unsolved.**

These later solutions combined historical knowledge, cryptanalytic search and substantial computation. They do not establish that every surviving Enigma message is solvable under the same conditions.

*Sources: Stefan Krah, [M4 Message Breaking Project ↗](<https://www.bytereef.org/m4_project.html>); Michael Hörenberg, [Breaking German Navy Ciphers ↗](<https://enigma.hoerenberg.com/index.php?cat=M4+Project+2006>); John Leyden, “Codebreakers unravel second Enigma intercept,” *The Register*, 15 March 2006; Ralph Erskine, letter to *Cryptologia*, 1995.*

Operation Boniface

British planners concealed ULTRA's true source by attributing critical insights to a fictional high-level human spy codenamed **Boniface**. This deception protected the Enigma break by explaining "impossibly accurate" intelligence without revealing cryptanalytic capability.

#### Rejewski: What the Plugboard Cannot Hide

Under the earlier repeated-indicator procedure described above, positions 1 and 4 concealed the same letter. Across enough indicators, an analyst could connect each first-position ciphertext letter to its fourth-position partner. These links form a permutation.

A plugboard change relabels the cycles of that permutation without changing their lengths. Rejewski used these characteristics to constrain machine settings. The characteristic was not a unique fingerprint of the entire key, and the procedure changes of 1938 altered the attack conditions.

**Eight-letter teaching model:** six fixed, reciprocal substitutions stand in for six successive machine states. Each invented three-letter key is encrypted twice. This model has no Enigma rotor wiring or stepping. Change the plugboard and predict whether the cycle lengths will change.

Plugboard relabeling
- No swaps

- A ↔ H, B ↔ E

- A ↔ C, D ↔ F

Invented six-letter indicators, all at one common starting state

| Message | Indicator | Position 1 → 4 |
| --- | --- | --- |

Without swaps:

Selected plugboard:

Enable JavaScript to derive the cycles.

Why the cycle lengths survive

If R is the first-to-fourth permutation and S relabels the alphabet, the new permutation is S ∘ R ∘ S<sup>−1</sup>. Following a cycle still takes the same number of steps; only its labels change. This is conjugation. In a reciprocal plugboard S<sup>−1</sup> = S.

There are analogous relations for positions 2→5 and 3→6. The exercise displays just 1→4. It assumes complete coverage of the toy alphabet; real intercept collections could be incomplete. See [Group Theory](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/group-theory.html>) for the broader mathematical vocabulary.

**Sources:** Bauer, *Decrypted Secrets*, 4th ed. (2007), pp. 431–437, especially §19.6.2.5; Marian Rejewski, [“An Application of the Theory of Permutations in Breaking the Enigma Cipher”](<https://doi.org/10.4064/am-16-4-543-559>), *Applicationes Mathematicae* 16(4), 1980, pp. 543–559.

#### When a Key Rule Narrows the Search

“Never use yesterday’s rotor in the same position” sounds like a way to avoid a pattern. Once an attacker knows yesterday’s order and the rule, it removes possibilities. The 1944 US 6812 Division Bombe Report explicitly describes this practice and the resulting 32 orders to test.

Choose three distinct rotors from five: there are 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 orders before restrictions. Predict the remaining count, then switch on a rule. The exact-order restriction below is included for comparison; it is weaker than prohibiting every repeated position.

Yesterday’s known order (left to right)
- I – II – III

- V – II – III

- II – IV – V
  [Input rules-exact: type=checkbox; initial value=]  Forbid yesterday’s exact order  [Input rules-position: type=checkbox; initial value=]  Forbid any rotor in yesterday’s position

Enable JavaScript to enumerate the permitted orders.

**State the limit:** this is an exact count of one part of the configuration, not Enigma’s total security or the time required for a break. The bit count assumes uniform selection among permitted orders and conditions on the known previous order. Policies can serve other purposes; a smaller allowed set alone does not decide whether a modern key-management policy is sound.

**Sources:** Bauer, *Decrypted Secrets*, 4th ed. (2007), pp. 481–482; [US 6812 Division Bombe Report (Eastcote, 1944), printed p. 12](<https://codesandciphers.org.uk/documents/bmbrpt/bmbpg017.htm>), reproduced as web page 17.

Compare this deterministic pruning with [Banburismus evidence scores](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/joan-clarke.html#banburismus-experiment>) and [cribs obtained from another cipher system](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/kisses.html>).

Hall VII · Machines Cold War · 1956

### Fialka M-125 Soviet 10-rotor machine · 1956

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Ten rotors, irregular stepping, and a punched-card substitution: a distinct Cold War machine with important differences from Enigma.

Never publicly broken by cryptanalysis in operational service; obsolete today.

OriginSoviet Union (Warsaw Pact issue)

YearIn service 1956 – ~1990

Rotors10 (alternating forward/reverse stepping)

ReflectorYes; the complete circuit permits self-encipherment

StatusNo public break of operational traffic; museum documentation covers surviving machines

The interactive is a Fialka-inspired, seeded 26-letter rotor model. It does not reproduce the M-125's 30-contact alphabet, authentic rotor wiring, key-card configuration, or stepping system.

#### Why This Matters

Fialka M-125 entered service in 1956 and was used by the Soviet Union and allied countries. Variants had different keyboards and country-specific rotor wiring. It was one of several communications-security systems, not the device through which every Warsaw Pact signal passed.

The machine changed several features familiar from Enigma, including the wheel count, stepping, and input substitution. Improvements to particular weaknesses do not prove that a design has no others.

This exhibit establishes no public cryptanalytic break of operational traffic. That historical record does not establish security today; this obsolete system is presented for historical study.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Adjacent rotors move in opposite directions. Mechanical pin patterns control irregular stepping; not every wheel necessarily advances on each keypress. The punched card supplies a substitution rather than setting the rotor order, ring positions, or stepping pins. See the [Crypto Museum’s documented machines and technical reference](<https://www.cryptomuseum.com/crypto/fialka/>).

Three further design choices matter:

- **Self-encipherment is possible.** Fialka’s electrical arrangement permits a letter to encipher to itself, unlike military Enigma.

- **Punched-card substitution.** A daily card replaces the plugboard’s role; the other machine settings remain separate.

- **Thirty-contact alphabet.** The later M-125-3M supports mixed letters, numbers, and punctuation through operating modes; 30 contacts do not individually represent all those symbols at once.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was (Not) Broken

No public cryptanalytic break

Complexity: no verified public estimate supplied here

This exhibit cites no public reconstruction of a successful cryptanalytic attack on operational traffic. Absence of a public account is a limitation of the record, not a measured work factor or proof of mathematical security.

Compromise via key material and HUMINT

Complexity: N/A — traffic decrypted using stolen settings, not cryptanalysis

Captured settings or compromised personnel can bypass the need for a cryptanalytic attack. This is a general threat model, not evidence that all Western access to Fialka traffic followed a particular documented route.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Fialka design choice | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| Bidirectional rotor stepping | State-update rules matter; these rotor rules do not describe Trivium or A5/1 |
| Removing “no letter encrypts to itself” | Bias removal in modern S-box design |
| Daily punched-card substitution | Scheduled replacement of key material; not a key-derivation protocol |
| Key compromise is a separate threat | Protecting keys remains necessary even when an algorithm resists known attacks |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Hall XIII · Cipher Culture African American oral traditions

### Field Hollers and Coding Songs

Songs can carry meanings understood differently by different listeners; each claimed historical code still needs evidence.

Oral expression and context can conceal meaning; this widget is not an authenticated historical code.

ContextAntebellum America, Underground Railroad

EraAntebellum traditions and later documentation

MethodContext-dependent meaning; no fixed cipher reconstructed

KeyShared community knowledge (out-of-band)

Notable Example“Follow the Drinking Gourd”: first published in 1928

Modern LessonConcealing a message and encrypting its content are different aims

#### 🎧 Modern Vowel/Consonant Annotation

This modern illustration marks vowels with ● and consonants with ◦ while leaving every letter visible. It is neither encryption nor a reconstruction of a historical field-holler code. It does not encode rhythm or stress.

Plain message  [Input hollerInput: type=text; initial value=MEET AT THE OLD OAK]

 Encode

##### Why This Matters

Field hollers and spirituals are related but distinct vocal traditions. Songs could communicate shared meanings, but that does not establish a universal musical code. In particular, **“Follow the Drinking Gourd” is not a securely documented antebellum route cipher**: its first publication was in 1928, long after emancipation.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Enslaved people faced restrictions on movement, assembly, and literacy. Oral communication mattered in those conditions. Specific accounts of signaling should be evaluated individually; neither every field holler nor every spiritual should be interpreted as an escape instruction.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

Communication Through Song Structure

Shared context can give words or musical choices a private meaning. A specific claim that a melody or rhythm conveyed an escape instruction needs evidence from its historical setting. Shared meaning should not be converted into a fixed codebook without that evidence.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

The Drinking Gourd as Navigation

The Big Dipper can help locate the North Star. That navigational fact is distinct from the song’s historical use. The [National Park Service’s account](<https://www.nps.gov/articles/drinkinggourd.htm>) identifies the song as a postwar composition and reproduces its 1928 publication. Later interpretations of its river imagery do not prove that escapees followed it as a contemporary map.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Relationship to Modern Steganography

Steganography aims to conceal a message’s presence; encryption aims to conceal its content. Neither goal is guaranteed merely by using music, image pixels, or network timing. An observer may recognize, intercept, or disrupt a covert channel, and shared meanings may be disclosed.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| Context | Antebellum America, Underground Railroad |
| --- | --- |
| Era | Antebellum traditions and later documentation |
| Method | Context-dependent meaning; no fixed cipher reconstructed |
| Key | Shared community knowledge (out-of-band) |
| Notable Example | “Follow the Drinking Gourd”: first published in 1928 |
| Modern Lesson | Concealing a message and encrypting its content are different aims |

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    function runHollerCode() {
      const msg = document.getElementById('hollerInput').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z ]/g,'');
      const out = msg.split('').map(c => {
        if (c === ' ') return ' | ';
        const v = 'AEIOU'.includes(c);
        return c + (v ? '●' : '◦');
      }).join(' ');
      document.getElementById('hollerOutput').textContent = out;
    }
```

Exhibit 43 of 174 Early 20th Century · 1902 publication

### Four-Square Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Delastelle's digram cipher: four 5×5 squares, two of them keyed

Digram frequency analysis · simulated annealing

InventorFélix Delastelle (France)

Year~1902

Key TypeTwo keywords (two keyed squares)

Broken ByDigram frequency analysis · simulated annealing

Modern LessonFixed mappings preserve digram statistics

#### Why This Matters

Félix Delastelle developed Bifid and Trifid fractionation and the Four-square digram substitution. The Four-square is his digraphic cousin to Playfair: encrypt letters two at a time, but use two keyed alphabets instead of one. It avoids Playfair's "same row / same column / same letter" edge cases and the needed insertion of X between doubled letters.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Published in his 1902 book Traité Élémentaire de Cryptographie, the Four-square joined the Bifid and Trifid in Delastelle's portfolio of methods built on the Polybius square. The modern procedure is documented by cipher organisations and teaching implementations; this exhibit does not establish a complete military-use history.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Arrange four 5×5 squares (J merged into I) in a 2×2 grid. The top-left and bottom-right are plain alphabets; the top-right and bottom-left are keyed.

```text
┌─────────────┬─────────────┐
│  PLAIN A→Z  │  KEY 1      │
├─────────────┼─────────────┤
│  KEY 2      │  PLAIN A→Z  │
└─────────────┴─────────────┘
```

To encrypt a digram: locate the first letter in the top-left and the second in the bottom-right. Read the cipher digram from the top-right (row of letter 1, column of letter 2) and the bottom-left (row of letter 2, column of letter 1).

ℹ️

**About this demo:** To guarantee that Decrypt exactly restores your original message, this demo reversibly escapes the letters X, Q, and Z (as ZA, ZB, ZC) before enciphering, so padding and filler X can never be confused with a real letter. Messages containing X, Q, or Z therefore produce slightly different ciphertext than a strictly classical four-square cipher would. Odd-length messages are padded with a trailing X.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Digram Frequency Analysis

Complexity: Moderate

A fixed four-square key substitutes digrams. Non-overlapping plaintext-pair counts are therefore relabelled, while individual letter counts need not become uniform. Language scores can guide key searches, but required text length depends on the message and attack.

Simulated Annealing

Complexity: Moderate

Hill climbing and simulated annealing test candidate square pairs using language scores. They can become trapped in poor candidates; runtime and success depend on the search budget, text length and scoring model. This page establishes no universal seconds-long recovery guarantee.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Four-Square Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Digram-level encryption | AES transforms 128-bit blocks through multiple rounds; its security is not a direct scaling of this digram table |
| Multiple keyed tables | AES uses a fixed nonlinear byte substitution as one operation within a larger keyed construction |
| Avoiding edge cases (same-row/col) | Block-cipher designs specify complete round rules; avoiding special cases alone does not establish security |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 43 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Era | Early 20th Century · 1902 publication |
| Trust | Broken |
| Inventor | Félix Delastelle (France) |
| Year | ~1902 |
| Key Type | Two keywords (two keyed squares) |
| Broken By | Digram frequency analysis · simulated annealing |
| Modern Lesson | Fixed mappings preserve digram statistics |

Exhibit 18 of 174 Classical Puzzle Cipher

### Fractionated Morse Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A keyed substitution of Morse triples crosses plaintext-letter boundaries

Structural analysis of Morse patterns

InventorUnknown

YearDate not established here

Key TypeSubstitution alphabet for Morse triples

Broken ByStructural analysis of Morse patterns

Modern LessonEncoding structure remains relevant to cryptanalysis

#### Why This Matters

Fractionated Morse changes the units being substituted: each ciphertext letter represents a triple drawn from dots, dashes and separators. Boundaries need not coincide with plaintext letters, but Morse and language structure still constrain the result.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The American Cryptogram Association specifies one separator between letters and two between words. Three consecutive separators are excluded, leaving 26 of the 27 possible triples for a keyed alphabet. The browser demo simplifies this convention by removing spaces and punctuation; its decoded output is letters only, with trailing separators used for padding.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

- Convert plaintext to Morse code (dots, dashes, letter separators)

- Group the Morse stream into triples (·, -, X where X = separator)

- Replace each triple with a letter using a keyed substitution alphabet

```text
H = · · · ·   E = ·   L = · - · ·
HELLO → ····x·x·-··x·-··x---x  (x = letter separator)
Group triples: ···  ·x·  x·-  ··x  ·-·  ·x-  --x
Each triple → substituted letter
```

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 380 170" style="width:100%;max-width:380px;height:auto" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Fractionated Morse cipher three-step process">
  <style>text{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace;fill:#EDE5D4}rect{rx:4}</style>
  <!-- Step 1 -->
  <rect x="5" y="5" width="370" height="35" fill="rgba(90,144,200,.06)" stroke="rgba(90,144,200,.15)" stroke-width=".5"></rect>
  <text x="15" y="18" font-size="9" fill="#5A90C8">1. TEXT → MORSE</text>
  <text x="15" y="32" font-size="9" fill="#B8B0A0">HELLO → ···· · ·–·· ·–·· –––</text>
  <!-- Step 2 -->
  <rect x="5" y="48" width="370" height="50" fill="rgba(201,168,76,.06)" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.15)" stroke-width=".5"></rect>
  <text x="15" y="62" font-size="9" fill="#C9A84C">2. GROUP INTO TRIPLES</text>
  <g transform="translate(15,70)">
    <rect x="0" y="0" width="28" height="18" fill="rgba(201,168,76,.1)" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.25)" stroke-width=".5" rx="2"></rect><text x="4" y="13" font-size="8" fill="#C9A84C">···</text>
    <rect x="34" y="0" width="28" height="18" fill="rgba(201,168,76,.1)" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.25)" stroke-width=".5" rx="2"></rect><text x="38" y="13" font-size="8" fill="#C9A84C">·x·</text>
    <rect x="68" y="0" width="28" height="18" fill="rgba(201,168,76,.1)" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.25)" stroke-width=".5" rx="2"></rect><text x="72" y="13" font-size="8" fill="#C9A84C">x·–</text>
    <rect x="102" y="0" width="28" height="18" fill="rgba(201,168,76,.1)" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.25)" stroke-width=".5" rx="2"></rect><text x="106" y="13" font-size="8" fill="#C9A84C">··x</text>
    <text x="140" y="13" font-size="9" fill="#706878">... (26 used triples; xxx excluded)</text>
  </g>
  <!-- Step 3 -->
  <rect x="5" y="106" width="370" height="35" fill="rgba(90,200,160,.06)" stroke="rgba(90,200,160,.15)" stroke-width=".5"></rect>
  <text x="15" y="120" font-size="9" fill="#5AC8A0">3. SUBSTITUTE EACH TRIPLE</text>
  <text x="15" y="134" font-size="9" fill="#B8B0A0">···→R  ·x·→A  x·–→Q  ··x→U  ... (keyed mapping)</text>
  <!-- Result -->
  <text x="10" y="162" font-size="9" fill="#C9A84C">★ Variable-length Morse creates irregular groupings → diffusion across letters</text>
</svg>
```

Morse code is split into triples of (·, –, separator) — each triple maps to one ciphertext letter via keyed alphabet

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Morse Structure Analysis

Complexity: Moderate-Hard

Morse and language have predictable structure, including short codes for E and T and constraints on separators. Triple counts and candidate decoded text can guide a search for the keyed alphabet. Success depends on the message, its length and the search procedure; frequency ranking alone does not guarantee recovery.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Fractionated Morse Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Variable-length encoding | Huffman coding: common values get shorter codes — used in data compression |
| Symbol grouping before substitution | Block cipher modes: plaintext is processed in fixed-size chunks |
| Irregular structure as security | Encoding and padding do not themselves supply confidentiality or authentication |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| Inventor | Unknown |
| Year | Date not established here |
| Key Type | Substitution alphabet for Morse triples |
| Broken By | Structural analysis of Morse patterns |

#### Sources and Reading

American Cryptogram Association, [“Fractionated Morse”](<https://www.cryptogram.org/downloads/aca.info/ciphers/FractionatedMorse.pdf>), for the 26-triple convention. This specification does not establish the previously assigned nineteenth-century invention date.

### Freemason Pigpen Tradition

Geometric letter alphabets in Masonic inscriptions and recreational cryptography; conventions vary.

Fraternal symbol-substitution alphabet

RegionEngland, Scotland, France, Germany, USA

YearDocumented example: James Leeson’s gravestone, 1794

Best-known usersMasonic and recreational traditions

TrackB (mason-style decoder)

#### Interactive Exhibit

Type any letter A–Z and the widget will show its pigpen symbol description (which grid, which cell, with-dot or without). Try short messages too. Track B — illustrative; for hands-on encoding see the [Pigpen Cipher exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/pigpen.html>).

 Letter or short word (A–Z)  [Input input: type=text; initial value=MASON]  Describe pigpen symbol

##### Why This Matters

Pigpen represents letters with parts of grids and X-shaped figures, often using dots to distinguish a second set. It appears in fraternal inscriptions and in recreational puzzles. A symbol alphabet can convey affiliation as well as obscure a message; those purposes should be assessed for each object.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Kahn discusses James Leeson’s 1794 gravestone in New York as a documented Masonic example. Claims of a single London standardisation in the 1730s, a medieval Templar origin or specific Hellfire Club use are not established by the evidence cited here. The widget shows a common modern layout, not a transcription of that gravestone.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

With a secret alphabet, pigpen behaves as monoalphabetic substitution and retains letter and word patterns. With a known fixed alphabet, it is immediately reversible by lookup. Recognising the style does not always identify the exact assignment, and short inscriptions need not yield to frequency analysis alone.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

Pigpen-style alphabets are useful recreational exercises because their encoding rule can be drawn and learned quickly. The museum’s [Pigpen Cipher exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/pigpen.html>) uses text stand-ins and a separately labelled drawn variant. Neither widget establishes that a specific film, lodge or historical individual used that exact alphabet.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```
