#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    (function () {
      // Standard mason pigpen: grid1 = ABCDEFGHI, grid2 = JKLMNOPQR (with dot),
      // X1 = STUV, X2 = WXYZ (with dot). Grid cells map to fragment shapes.
      var GRID1 = 'ABCDEFGHI', GRID2 = 'JKLMNOPQR', X1 = 'STUV', X2 = 'WXYZ';
      var SHAPE = ['top-left corner','top edge','top-right corner','left edge','centre square','right edge','bottom-left corner','bottom edge','bottom-right corner'];
      function describe(c) {
        var i;
        if ((i = GRID1.indexOf(c)) >= 0) return 'Grid 1, ' + SHAPE[i] + ' (no dot)';
        if ((i = GRID2.indexOf(c)) >= 0) return 'Grid 2, ' + SHAPE[i] + ' (with dot)';
        if ((i = X1.indexOf(c)) >= 0) return 'X-shape 1, ' + ['upper','left','right','lower'][i] + ' wedge (no dot)';
        if ((i = X2.indexOf(c)) >= 0) return 'X-shape 2, ' + ['upper','left','right','lower'][i] + ' wedge (with dot)';
        return null;
      }
      window.encode = function () {
        var raw = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').toUpperCase();
        var out = document.getElementById('output');
        var lines = [];
        for (var i = 0; i < raw.length; i++) {
          var c = raw[i];
          if (c === ' ') { lines.push(''); continue; }
          var d = describe(c);
          if (!d) { lines.push('  ' + c + ' \u2192 (not in pigpen alphabet)'); }
          else    { lines.push('  ' + c + ' \u2192 ' + d); }
        }
        out.textContent = lines.join('\n') + '\n\n(The full Pigpen exhibit draws a different S–Z variant; its alphabet is not interchangeable with this four-wedge layout.)';
      };
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode(); });
    })();
```

### The GCHQ Trio — Ellis, Cocks, and Williamson

Classified public-key discoveries in 1970–1974, disclosed publicly in 1997.

Invention Biography

James Ellis1924–1997 — proposed non-secret encryption concept, report dated January 1970

Clifford Cocksb. 1950 — proposed an RSA-related construction, 1973

Malcolm Williamsonb. 1950 — developed finite-field key agreement, 1974

OrganizationGCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), Cheltenham

ClassificationTop secret until 1997

Public creditDiffie & Hellman (1976), Rivest, Shamir & Adleman (1977)

RecognitionClifford Cocks: CB 2008

🔑

#### The GCHQ Trio — Ellis, Cocks, and Williamson

1970 – 1974

James Ellis’s classified report on the possibility of non-secret encryption is dated **January 1970**. Clifford Cocks proposed an RSA-related construction in 1973, and Malcolm Williamson developed finite-field key agreement in 1974. Their work remained classified while public academic research independently developed public-key cryptography. Public disclosure of the GCHQ work came in 1997.

##### Why This Person Matters

The episode distinguishes private discovery from publication and public adoption. Public-key methods became central to internet authentication and key establishment, but a mathematical proposal is not the same as a deployed, authenticated, securely encoded protocol. Counterfactual claims that earlier publication would have advanced the entire field by an exact number of years cannot be established.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

James Ellis's Insight

Ellis’s [January 1970 report, *The Possibility of Secure Non-Secret Digital Encryption*](<https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/document/21971-document-02>), argued that the idea was possible without supplying a practical construction. This date is the report’s date, distinct from accounts of his earlier thought process.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Clifford Cocks’s Construction

Cocks’s 1973 work used modular exponentiation with a composite modulus, closely related to the later RSA construction. Knowledge of the factors enables the needed private computation. It is not established that every possible attack on RSA inversion must factor the modulus, nor that Cocks’s formulation and every later RSA protocol were identical in every detail.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Recognition and Impact

The classified discoveries were disclosed in 1997, after independent public research had established public-key cryptography. Ellis died shortly before that disclosure. The IEEE dedicated a milestone to the GCHQ work in 2010. Cocks was appointed Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) in 2008 and elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2015.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| --- | --- |
| Clifford Cocks | b. 1950 — proposed an RSA-related construction, 1973 |
| Malcolm Williamson | b. 1950 — developed finite-field key agreement, 1974 |

| Classification | Top secret until 1997 |
| Public credit | Diffie & Hellman (1976), Rivest, Shamir & Adleman (1977) |
| Recognition | Clifford Cocks: CB 2008 |

Original technical reports are distinct from later historical summaries.

Hall VII · Machines WWII · 1932–1945

### Geheimschreiber T52 (Sturgeon) Siemens & Halske teleprinter cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A ten-wheel teleprinter cipher: Beurling’s 1940 structural breakthrough was followed by continuing team work on daily keys.

Broken (Beurling, 1940)

OriginSiemens & Halske, Germany

YearDeployed ~1932; in heavy WWII use 1940–1945

Wheels10 pinwheels controlling bit addition and permutation; connections vary by model

Plaintext5-bit Baudot teleprinter code

Broken byArne Beurling and the Swedish Defence Staff service, 1940

#### The people behind daily codebreaking

A structural breakthrough still left daily work. Fredrik Wallin’s account, based on FRA archives, describes this operating chain:

- **Intercept:** collect the encrypted traffic.

- **Recover the daily key:** determine the settings needed to read it.

- **Operate App:** enter ciphertext into the decryption apparatus and monitor synchronization. App meant “apparatus,” not a software application.

- **Prepare the report:** assemble the plaintext, clean up its language and type the final report.

Women performed essential operating and interception work; some later led interception shifts. On **1 July 1942**, women were **193 of FRA’s 287 civilian staff**—about 67%. Another 113 seconded military personnel brought the agency total to 400. The 67% figure refers to civilians, not the whole agency.

Source: [Fredrik Wallin, *“We just did it!”* (HistoCrypt 2023), pp. 1–4](<https://ecp.ep.liu.se/index.php/histocrypt/article/view/707>). These staffing totals concern FRA as a whole, not just its T52 team. This panel summarizes Wallin’s archival research; it does not claim an independent archive review.

#### Why This Matters

While Lorenz SZ40/42 (“Tunny”) carried Hitler’s strategic traffic, the Siemens & Halske T52 — codenamed “Sturgeon” at Bletchley Park — carried Luftwaffe and Wehrmacht command traffic over leased Swedish telephone lines from 1940. Swedish access to those circuits supplied material for cryptanalysis.

In 1940 Beurling worked with the Swedish Defence Staff’s cryptographic service, the predecessor of FRA as an independent agency. His approximately two-week breakthrough, assisted by Hans Rudberg and Bertil Nyman, was followed by continuing key-recovery and decryption work. The [FRA account](<https://fra.se/omfra/frashistoria/gskrivarenocharnebeurling.4.55af049f184e92956c42a59.html>) distinguishes these stages.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The T52 family used teleprinter ciphers; later T52d/e models added irregular stepping. Plaintext is encoded in 5-bit Baudot characters and combined with a keystream generated by ten wheels with pairwise-coprime lengths (47, 53, 59, 61, 64, 65, 67, 69, 71, 73). The following two-bank description belongs to this teaching model, not a wiring specification for every T52 variant:

- **Five wheels generate an additive keystream** that shifts each character.

- **Five wheels select, per character, one of several keyed substitution permutations** applied after the additive shift.

In the original T52 the substitution is a bit-permutation on the 5-bit Baudot code. The educational demo above operates on the 26-letter alphabet using mod-26 addition and six keyed permutations of A–Z, which preserves the architectural lesson — additive keystream plus per-character permutation, ten coprime-length wheels — while keeping the round-trip clean for arbitrary text.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Beurling’s reconstruction (1940)

Initial reconstruction in about two weeks; assistants and later key-recovery work also mattered

FRA publishes Carl-Gösta Borelius’s later reconstruction of how Beurling may have proceeded. Borelius describes messages sent with matching settings, frequent letter-shift and space characters, and regularities preserved when bit addition and permutation act on parallel messages. He explicitly presents a hypothesis, not Beurling’s own step-by-step account. See FRA, [“Hur gjorde Arne Beurling för att forcera G-skrivaren?”](<https://www.fra.se/omfra/frashistoria/forceringenavgskrivaren.4.55af049f184e92956c42acb.html>). Letter shift and space were useful statistical clues within this reconstruction; additive masking still had to be accounted for.

App, the decryption apparatus

Purpose: process traffic after suitable keys were recovered

Beurling and engineer Vigo Lindstein developed decryption equipment known as “appar.” It helped process messages once suitable keys had been recovered; it should not be described as automatically finding every daily setting. This exhibit does not establish that all resulting intelligence was shared with the Allies.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Sturgeon lesson | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| Re-using a keystream produces a depth | Nonce uniqueness under a key matters for AES-GCM and ChaCha20 |
| Predictable padding leaks the keystream | Known plaintext can reveal a reused XOR keystream; a padding oracle is a different attack |
| Coprime wheel lengths ≠ cryptographic security | A long period and passing statistical tests do not establish cryptographic unpredictability |
| Reconstruction from intercepted traffic | A design should also be analysed against stronger known- and chosen-plaintext attacks |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Origin | Siemens & Halske, Germany |
| --- | --- |
| Year | Deployed ~1932; in heavy WWII use 1940–1945 |
| Wheels | 10 pinwheels controlling bit addition and permutation; connections vary by model |
| Plaintext | 5-bit Baudot teleprinter code |
| Broken by | Arne Beurling and the Swedish Defence Staff service, 1940 |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

Fish Family Context

**"Fish"** was Bletchley Park's umbrella codename for German teleprinter systems, named after fish species:

- **Tunny** = Lorenz SZ40/42 high-command traffic.

- **Sturgeon** = Siemens T52 Geheimschreiber family.

- **Thrasher** = the Siemens T43 one-time-tape machine, a separate system.

This matters because the British did not face one "German machine cipher" but a layered ecosystem: Enigma for tactical traffic, Lorenz for OKW strategic command, and T52-class Fish circuits for teleprinter channels.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall XIII: Cipher Culture](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/culture.html>)› Poe's Gold-Bug Cipher

Hall XIII · Culture Antebellum America · 1843

### Poe's Gold-Bug Cipher

Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 short story *The Gold-Bug* — a widely read work of fiction presenting cryptanalysis, complete with a worked decipherment of a buried-treasure cryptogram.

Fictional substitution cipher

RegionSullivan's Island, South Carolina (in-fiction); Philadelphia (publication)

YearPublished *Dollar Newspaper*, June 1843

AuthorEdgar Allan Poe (1809–1849)

TrackB (Poe-style frequency tool)

#### Interactive Exhibit

Enter a short English plaintext and the widget will encode it using a symbol set adapted from the cipher in Poe's *The Gold-Bug* (digits and punctuation) — the story's own key covers only the letters that appear in the cryptogram (8=E, ;=T, 5=A…); the rest use invented symbols so every letter can be typed. Click 'analyse' to see the frequency table Poe walked his readers through. Track B — illustrative.

 English plaintext  [Input input: type=text; initial value=A GOOD GLASS IN THE BISHOPS HOSTEL]  Encode + analyse

##### Why This Matters

Poe's *The Gold-Bug* contains one of the most famous worked cryptanalyses in American literature. The narrator's friend William Legrand discovers a parchment bearing 203 numerals and symbols in the 1843 text and breaks it through frequency analysis to recover Captain Kidd's treasure map. Poe explains key decipherment steps and supplies the resulting reading, making cryptanalysis part of the story itself. The story won a $100 newspaper prize and helped popularise cipher solving; a sales figure is not a measured count of readers or cryptanalysts.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Poe invited cipher submissions in *Alexander’s Weekly Messenger* beginning in December 1839 and published solutions during 1840. His 1841 *Graham’s Magazine* essay “A Few Words on Secret Writing” discussed those earlier challenges. The surviving newspaper record does not support treating his boast of universal success as an established cryptanalytic result.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

The story’s substitution relabels letter frequencies and preserves repeated patterns. Legrand combines counts with likely words and context. E’s usual prominence in English is a heuristic, not a guarantee for each message; a frequency ranking by itself does not recover every substitution key. The widget extends the story’s partial alphabet with invented assignments, as its introduction states.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

Poe helped make codebreaking a subject of popular fiction and reader participation. Later stories offer useful comparisons, but similarity alone does not establish a direct chain of influence to every cipher novel, puzzle hunt or wartime recruitment test.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```


Poe's Challenge-Cipher Legacy

Poe’s newspaper challenges show readers taking part in cipher solving before *The Gold-Bug*. They can be compared with later public puzzles without claiming that every modern format descends directly from them.

The surviving publications provide evidence of reader participation, without measuring its reach or proving a direct lineage to later institutions.

#### Sources and Reading

Edgar Allan Poe, *The Gold-Bug* (1843) and “A Few Words on Secret Writing” (1841); Clarence S. Brigham, *Edgar Allan Poe’s Contributions to Alexander’s Weekly Messenger* (1943), introduction, pp. 3–7, for the dated newspaper record and limits of Poe’s claims.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    (function () {
      // Poe\u2019s actual symbol substitutions from the story (selection).
      var MAP = { A:'5', B:'2', C:'\u2014', D:'\u2020', E:'8', F:'1', G:'3', H:'4',
                   I:'6', J:'%', K:'&', L:'0', M:'9', N:'*', O:'\u2021',
                   P:'.', Q:'/', R:'(', S:')', T:';', U:'?', V:'\u00b6', W:'!',
                   X:'@', Y:':', Z:'#' };
      window.encode = function () {
        var raw = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').toUpperCase();
        var out = document.getElementById('output');
        var enc = raw.split('').map(function (c) { return MAP[c] || c; }).join('');
        var freq = {};
        enc.split('').forEach(function (c) { if (c !== ' ') freq[c] = (freq[c] || 0) + 1; });
        var entries = Object.keys(freq).sort(function (a, b) { return freq[b] - freq[a]; });
        var lines = entries.slice(0, 8).map(function (k) {
          var plain = Object.keys(MAP).find(function (p) { return MAP[p] === k; }) || '?';
          return '  ' + k + '  \u00d7 ' + freq[k] + '   (= ' + plain + ')';
        });
        out.textContent = 'Encoded:\n\n' + enc +
          '\n\nFrequency (Poe\u2019s attack route):\n' + lines.join('\n') +
          '\n\nIn the story Poe identifies \u20188\u2019 as E first, exactly this way.';
      };
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode(); });
    })();
```

Hall XIII · Cipher Culture Animation · 2012–2016

### Gravity Falls Cipher System

Alex Hirsch’s animated series invited viewers to look for hidden messages and try classical cipher puzzles.

Pop Culture

CreatorAlex Hirsch

NetworkDisney Channel / Disney XD

RunJune 2012 – February 2016

Cipher familiesExamples include Caesar, Atbash, A1Z26 and Vigenère

CommunityViewers share interpretations and puzzle solutions

Learning opportunityRecognising and trying classical cipher methods

#### 🔓 Interactive Explorer

Try a Caesar shift of three. This exercise demonstrates one cipher family, not the complete series puzzle system.

 Message (Caesar shift 3)  [Input input: type=text; initial value=TRUST NO ONE]  Encode

##### Why This Matters

*Gravity Falls* made hidden messages part of the viewing experience. In interviews, creator Alex Hirsch describes adding codes for fun and expanding those elements in response to fans. The codes invite viewers to recognise patterns, test candidate methods and compare solutions.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

The Cipher Progression

The show’s puzzles include Caesar shifts, reversed alphabets, letter-to-number encodings and keyed Vigenère substitutions. These are different mechanisms, and some puzzles combine steps. The museum’s widget demonstrates only Caesar +3. For an individual screen cryptogram, record its episode, transcription and applicable clue before choosing a method; this page does not certify an exhaustive episode-by-episode key list.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

Community Cryptanalysis

Hirsch’s 2021 interview with Rafael Motamayor for *Inverse* describes unexpectedly enthusiastic responses to the hidden messages and his decision to expand the clues in the second season. Viewers can compare proposed readings and test whether a method consistently fits the supplied text. Public puzzle-solving has a much longer history, including Poe’s nineteenth-century newspaper challenges.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

The Journals as Cipher Texts

The fictional journals also became published books. Disney Publishing describes *Gravity Falls: Journal 3* as combining pages seen in the series with additional material. The book gives readers another way to explore the story’s drawings, clues and hidden messages.

📚Exhibit Sources

- [Disney D23, “Gravity Falls: Solving its Final Mystery” (2016)](<https://d23.com/gravity-falls-solving-its-final-mystery/>): series dates and the creator’s account of hidden codes and audience response.

- [Alex Hirsch interviewed by Rafael Motamayor, *Inverse* (29 March 2021)](<https://www.inverse.com/entertainment/gravity-falls-season-3-video-game-alex-hirsch-interview>): creation of the hidden messages and fan participation.

- *Gravity Falls: Journal 3*, Alex Hirsch and Rob Renzetti (2016); Disney Publishing’s description confirms the published journal format.

#### Embedded script 2 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    // Caesar cipher demo (Gravity Falls S1 cipher type)
    function gfEncode(t) {
      const A='ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
      const shift=3;
      return t.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z ]/g,'').split('').map(c=>{
        if(c===' ') return ' ';
        return A[(A.indexOf(c)+shift)%26];
      }).join('') + ' (Caesar +3)';
    }
```

### The Great Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A Rossignol-era nomenclator used in royal correspondence and reconstructed by Bazeries in the 1890s

Étienne Bazeries (1893): syllabic frequency analysis and contextual cribs.

InventorsAntoine & Bonaventure Rossignol

Year17th century; surviving traffic includes the 1690s

CourtLouis XIII & Louis XIV of France

Key TypeCodebook of ~587 numbered syllables

Broken ByÉtienne Bazeries · 1893 (after ~3 years)

Modern LessonDecoy tokens & variable-length codewords

#### Why This Matters

Bazeries’s reconstruction of a Rossignol-era nomenclator opened historical dispatches to study. The achievement shows how context, repeated groups and syllable hypotheses can recover an old code. Its late decipherment does not establish uninterrupted secrecy against every earlier reader.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Antoine Rossignol became a prominent French royal cryptologist in the seventeenth century. Kahn places the celebrated Réalmont decipherment in 1628, not 1626. Antoine and, later, his son Bonaventure developed and operated royal nomenclators; a single invention date should not be assigned to all of these changing keys.

The Rossignols' code book contained roughly **587 numbers**, each standing for a syllable, a common word, a single letter, or — critically — nothing at all. Some numbers were pure decoys (nulls); Kahn describes one sign that erased the preceding sign. Bonaventure’s son Antoine-Bonaventure also entered the family’s cryptanalytic profession. By 1891, historians studying Catinat’s campaigns had ciphered dispatches they could not read and asked Bazeries for help.

In the 1890s Étienne Bazeries reconstructed a Rossignol-era nomenclator by testing letter and syllable readings against repeated groups and the correspondence’s context. Kahn describes homophones, nulls and an instruction to erase the preceding sign. A deciphered 1691 dispatch led Bazeries to identify General Bulonde with the Man in the Iron Mask, but that historical inference remains disputed.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Unlike a substitution cipher (one symbol per letter), the Great Cipher is a **nomenclator** — a coded vocabulary. The codebook lists numbers paired with syllables:

```text
124 → "le"         301 → "roi"         412 → null (ignore)
 87 → "que"        055 → "Q"           333 → null (ignore)
156 → "men"        702 → "MAJESTÉ"     891 → "DELETE PREVIOUS"
209 → "en"         044 → "X"           ...
```

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

Illustrative code numbers, not a historical key: syllables, nulls and an erasure instruction. This diagram’s erase-one-letter rule is a teaching convention.

In the museum’s model, the encoder works through the message picking the longest matching codeword from the generated book — `RE`, `EN`, `TRE`, etc. — falling back to single letters only when no syllable matched. Occasionally the clerk would sprinkle in null codes as decoys. To decrypt, you needed the codebook in front of you. Without it, the message was just a long list of three-digit numbers.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Frequency Analysis on Syllables

Complexity: Hard · Took Bazeries ~3 years

Bazeries tested syllable interpretations, including groups for *les ennemis*, and used partial readings to extend the reconstruction. Different groups could represent the same syllable or ending; some entries represented individual letters or whole words. A single frequency table was therefore insufficient.

The "Delete" Trap

Complexity: Special codebook instructions

Kahn reports a sign that erased the preceding sign. Such instructions complicate a solver’s model, but the source does not establish that one erasure code alone explains the long delay in decipherment. The browser demo uses its own explicitly defined erase-one-letter convention.

Modern Cryptanalytic Tools

Complexity: Depends on text, model and search budget

Computer search can test candidate codebooks with language scores, but success depends on the corpus, segmentation, nulls and special instructions. No timed recovery of the historical Rossignol codebook is demonstrated here; the small generated example does not establish a minutes-long attack on the original system.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-mask"></use></svg>
```

The Man in the Iron Mask

A dispatch of 8 July 1691 concerned the imprisonment of Vivien Labbé, Seigneur du Bulonde, after his withdrawal from the siege of Cuneo. Two otherwise unattested groups appeared in the passage about his permitted movements at Pignerol. Bazeries interpreted them as referring to a mask. Bazeries believed this was the famous Iron Mask. The identification remains disputed, including the interpretation of the numbers supposedly denoting a mask. David Kahn revisited the evidence in *Cryptologia* 29(1), pp. 43–49 (2005), “The Man in the Iron Mask — Encore et Enfin, Cryptologically.” The letter is evidence of the cipher’s decipherment, not a confirmed solution to the prisoner’s identity.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from the Great Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Variable-length codewords (syllables, not letters) | Compression can remove redundancy; confidentiality still depends on the complete cryptographic construction |
| Null tokens / decoys | Modern padding serves several different goals; nulls alone provide neither confidentiality nor authentication |
| Special codebook instructions (including erasure) | A reminder to model the message format; not evidence of a direct connection to modern honey encryption |
| Lost codebooks complicate later access | Preserving authorized access requires key management; loss of a key does not prove that cryptanalysis is impossible |
| Operator procedure and cipher design both matter | Modern principle (Kerckhoffs): the algorithm should be public; only the key must be secret |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 38 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Era | Baroque · 17th century |
| Security (then) | Historic correspondence deciphered in the 1890s |
| Security (today) | No timed recovery of the historical key demonstrated here |
| Inventors | Antoine & Bonaventure Rossignol |
| Codebook size | ~587 numbered codewords |
| Broken By | Étienne Bazeries · 1893 |
| Famous use | Louis XIV's diplomatic & military mail |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

About this Demo

Bazeries reconstructed 587 equivalents; this widget does not reproduce that historical key. This demo uses a teaching-scale codebook — 50 common digrams + 26 letters + 6 nulls + 1 "delete previous" trap (83 codewords) — deterministically generated from the Codebook Seed.

Try encoding the same message under two different Codebook Seeds: notice how the output changes because common syllables have multiple codes and nulls are sprinkled in at seed-determined positions. Decoding always recovers the original (provided the seed matches).

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 5, “The Era of the Black Chambers,” and Chapter 23, “Ciphers in the Past Tense.” The latter distinguishes the decipherment from Bazeries’ disputed identification of the masked prisoner.

Exhibit 173 of 1741786 · Sweden

### Gripenstierna’s Cipher Machine

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Two people could operate the device while only one saw the plaintext.

Historical device; original lost, later reconstructed from documents. No modern security claim.

OriginFredrik Gripenstierna · Sweden

Year1786 · documented construction

Mechanism57 independently rotated alphabet disks

Key TypeDisk arrangement

Modern LessonSeparate access to plaintext from handling ciphertext

#### Why This Matters

A clerk has to copy a secret dispatch. Must the clerk be allowed to read it? Gripenstierna’s device made that an engineering question: two viewing slits exposed different text to the people on opposite sides.

This Swedish design predates Jefferson’s 1790s wheel proposal. That chronology does not establish a line of descent between them. Its distinctive contribution here is the division of work, as well as its mechanical substitutions.

#### How It Works

The documented design uses 57 disks mounted on an axle. Each disk can turn independently and carries two alphabets. The authorized operator sets a row of plaintext on one side; the assistant copies the corresponding ciphertext from the other. For decryption the assistant sets the ciphertext, and the authorized reader takes off the plaintext.

**Authorized operator’s side**

Encipher: set plaintext.
Decipher: read plaintext.

**Assistant’s side**

Encipher: copy ciphertext.
Decipher: set ciphertext.

Original museum schematic of the roles only. This is not a drawing of the lost machine or a reconstruction of its alphabets.

The arrangement keeps routine copying apart from access to the message. It does not prove that an assistant with unrestricted access to the mechanism could never recover plaintext.

#### What Survives

Boris Hagelin’s account describes an invoice dated 26 August 1786 and written material found in the Swedish National Archives by Sven Wäsström. Hagelin reports that the original machine was lost and that Crypto AG built a replica using the surviving description. A photograph of that replica documents the reconstruction, not the appearance of an authenticated surviving original.

Bauer describes disk permutations as key material. Even 57! possible orders do not establish 254-bit cryptographic security: a count of arrangements is not a bound on the best attack. This exhibit makes no claim of demonstrated operational use or of a documented historical break.

#### Sources and Reading

- Friedrich L. Bauer, *Decrypted Secrets: Methods and Maxims of Cryptology*, 4th ed. (Springer, 2007), §7.5.2, pp. 131–132; see also p. 51 for the separation of operating roles.

- Boris Hagelin, [*The Story of Hagelin Cryptos*](<https://www.cryptomuseum.com/crypto/hagelin/files/hagelin_story_en.pdf>), “The Beginning,” printed pp. 5–7 (PDF pp. 11–13): invoice, disk arrangement, operating roles and reconstruction.

- Further study: Bengt Beckman, [“An Early Cipher Device: Fredrik Gripenstierna’s Machine”](<https://doi.org/10.1080/0161-110291890821>), *Cryptologia* 26(2), 2002, pp. 113–123.

#### Compare the Mechanisms

[Jefferson’s wheel](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/jefferson-disk.html>) uses rows on mixed-alphabet disks. Similar parts need not mean identical operation or shared ancestry.

[Alberti’s disk](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/alberti-disk.html>) provides an earlier way to change substitutions.

[Kryha](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kryha.html>) shows why a large advertised settings space needs cryptanalytic scrutiny.

### Gronsfeld Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A Vigenère-style cipher restricted to numeric shifts from 0 to 9

Kasiski · Only 10 possible shifts per position

InventorTraditionally attributed to Count Gronsfeld

Year17th-century tradition; exact invention date uncertain

Key TypeNumeric keyword (digits 0-9)

Broken ByKasiski · Only 10 possible shifts per position

Modern LessonKey alphabet size matters

#### Why This Matters

The Gronsfeld cipher illustrates a persistent tension in cryptography: usability versus security. For a fixed key length, restricting each shift to 0–9 gives fewer possible keys than permitting 0–25. Whether digits are easier to remember depends on the chosen key and user.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The cipher traditionally attributed to Count Gronsfeld adapts the Vigenère cipher to use numeric keys instead of letter keys. A numeric keyword may be convenient for some users, but greater memorability is not an established property of every numeric key. The tradeoff: digits only give 10 possible shift values (0-9) instead of 26, dramatically weakening the cipher.

The Gronsfeld cipher illustrates a persistent tension in cryptography: usability versus security. A cipher that field operators can't remember correctly is useless — but a cipher that trades security for memorability may be worse than none.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

```text
Key:    3  1  4  1  5  3  1  4
Plain:  A  T  T  A  C  K  A  T
Cipher: D  U  X  B  H  N  B  X

Formula: C = (P + digit) mod 26
Only 10 possible shifts per position (0-9)
```

Digit-only keys (0–9) reduce each position's keyspace from 26 to 10 — leaving ten candidate shifts per column once a period is proposed

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Kasiski + Reduced Keyspace

Complexity: Easy

Gronsfeld shares Vigenère's periodicity weakness, but with only 10 possible shift values per position, each column's key digit can be found by testing just 10 possibilities instead of 26. Period tests supply candidate lengths, and language evidence helps choose among the ten shifts; success and running time depend on the sample.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Gronsfeld Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Digit keys (0-9) | Key entropy matters: AES-256 uses 256-bit keys for 2²⁵⁶ possible values |
| Usability-security tradeoff | Password KDFs raise guessing cost; they do not create entropy absent from the password |
| Small effective alphabet | AES’s bijective 8-bit S-box maps 256 values; output frequencies still depend on its inputs |


Exhibit 162 of 1741930s–1950s · Sweden / Switzerland

### Hagelin C-36 / C-52 Lineage

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Pins and lugs made portable encryption practical — and vendor trust became part of the key

The pin-and-lug family has published cryptanalytic attacks; Greenough’s 1999 C-52 attack uses known plaintext.

DesignerBoris Hagelin

LineageC-36 → C-38 / M-209 → C-52 / CX-52

FamilyMechanical pin-and-lug stream cipher

C-52 eraAround 1952

Published attackH. Paul Greenough · 1999 · known plaintext

#### Why This Matters

Hagelin’s machines made encryption portable without making it electronic. Pins around wheels selected mechanical levers; lugs on a cage converted those binary signals into a changing alphabet shift. The C-series also illustrates a second question: who controls the design, sales, and operating instructions of the equipment you trust?

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Boris Hagelin developed the C-series at AB Cryptoteknik in Sweden during the 1930s. The C-36 belongs to the early pin-and-lug family; the later C-38 became the US Army’s [M-209](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/m209.html>). Around 1952 the C-52 and related CX-52 expanded the design in the era of Hagelin’s Swiss company, Crypto AG.

| Machine | Place in the family |
| --- | --- |
| C-36 | Early portable pin-and-lug design; configurations and lug arrangements varied. |
| C-38 / M-209 | Six pinwheels and a lug cage; the US military’s mass-produced tactical machine. |
| C-52 / CX-52 | Postwar successors with selectable wheels and additional configuration options; some variants used irregular stepping. |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Each wheel carries active and inactive pins. Their positions determine which guide arms engage the lugs attached to cage bars. As the operator turns the handle, displaced bars contribute to a numerical key value. A changing shift combines that value with the input letter.

For a simplified reciprocal letter-subtractor convention, absorb any alphabet offset into K, number A–Z as 0–25 and compute `C = (K − P) mod 26`. Applying the same K sequence to C recovers P. The physical alphabet arrangement and offset must also be specified for a particular machine. The difficult part is generating K, not the subtraction. A long wheel cycle alone does not guarantee that the resulting shifts lack exploitable structure.

[Try the M-209 encrypt/decrypt demo](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/m209.html>) for the museum’s pin-and-lug interactive. It illustrates a related machine, rather than pretending to reproduce every C-36 or C-52 configuration.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

H. Paul Greenough published a **known-plaintext attack in 1999** against the C-52 and similar machines with irregular pinwheel stepping. The paper’s abstract describes recovering the subset of wheels, their order, and active pin positions. This exhibit summarizes that stated scope; it does not reproduce the full attack or establish a universal data requirement. This is a public cryptanalytic result, distinct from a claim that every machine sold under the family name shared one weakness.

The [M-209 exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/m209.html>) covers wartime known-plaintext and statistical attacks on that earlier branch. Public attacks exist against members of the cipher family; those results are not a blanket statement about identical internals or attacks across all variants.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Crypto AG and the Supply Chain

William Friedman’s declassified reports document US intelligence contact with Hagelin, discussions of C-52 variants, and attention to which customers received which machines. Later, Crypto AG was secretly owned by the CIA and West German BND from 1970 as part of the operation known as Rubicon. Selected export designs and procedures were influenced to make foreign traffic readable.

The company history must not be projected backwards onto every C-36. A wartime C-36, a publicly attacked C-52 configuration, and a deliberately weakened later export product are different claims. The lesson is that secret keys cannot repair a supplier’s deliberately constrained design or operating procedure.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

Pin-and-lug machines turn a physical key into a stream of shifts, making key generation, key reuse, and biased output visible. Crypto AG adds the need for independent design review. A trusted brand, an impressive mechanical period, and a confidential sales process are not substitutes for public cryptanalysis.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| Lineage | C-36 → C-38 / M-209 → C-52 / CX-52 |
| Family | Mechanical pin-and-lug stream cipher |
| C-52 era | Around 1952 |
| Published attack | H. Paul Greenough · 1999 · known plaintext |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Sources and Further Reading

### Hill Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Matrix multiplication encrypts blocks — and linear relations enable a known-plaintext attack.

Known plaintext attack (matrix algebra)

InventorLester S. Hill

Year1929

Key TypeInvertible key matrix (n×n)

Broken ByKnown plaintext attack (matrix algebra)

Modern LessonMatrix operations in AES MixColumns

#### Why This Matters

Lester Hill’s cipher illustrates block encryption through matrix multiplication. Its linear structure also gives a particularly clear known-plaintext attack. AES uses linear algebra in MixColumns, but the complete AES cipher includes nonlinear operations and is not simply a larger Hill cipher.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Lester S. Hill published his matrix-based system in the *American Mathematical Monthly* in 1929. It maps groups of letters through an invertible matrix modulo the alphabet size. The system provides a useful introduction to linear algebra in cryptography without establishing a direct historical influence on every later matrix-based design.

Hill also explored mechanical implementation. The cryptanalytic limitation illustrated here follows from the linear equations themselves; no assertion about widespread deployment is needed to demonstrate it.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Convert letters to numbers (A=0, B=1…Z=25). Arrange plaintext in column vectors of length n. Multiply by an invertible n×n key matrix modulo 26.

```text
Key matrix K (2×2):     Plaintext: HI = [7, 8]
| 3  3 |
| 2  5 |    C = K × P mod 26
                        = [3×7+3×8, 2×7+5×8] mod 26
                        = [45, 54] mod 26
                        = [19, 2]
                        = TC
```

Hill cipher: plaintext vector multiplied by key matrix mod 26 — HI becomes TC (this is the demo's default key)

Decryption uses the matrix inverse: P = K⁻¹ × C mod 26. Not all matrices have inverses mod 26 — the key matrix must be chosen carefully.

ℹ️

**About this demo:** To guarantee that Decrypt exactly restores your original message, this demo reversibly escapes the letters X, Q, and Z (as ZA, ZB, ZC) before enciphering, so padding and filler X can never be confused with a real letter. Messages containing X, Q, or Z therefore produce slightly different ciphertext than a strictly classical Hill cipher would. Odd-length messages are padded with a trailing X, and the key matrix must be invertible mod 26 — the demo rejects singular matrices.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Known Plaintext Attack

Complexity: Easy with suitable known blocks

For an n×n Hill key, collect n matched plaintext/ciphertext *blocks* as the columns of matrices P and C. When P is invertible modulo 26 — that is, gcd(det(P), 26) = 1 — the key follows directly: K = C × P⁻¹ mod 26. Merely knowing n blocks does not guarantee this condition. If it fails, more observations or a more general solution of the linear congruences may be needed. The cipher remains vulnerable because the relation is linear.

**Enough information:** the two blocks HI and LL give P = [[7, 11], [8, 11]], whose determinant is −11, coprime to 26. Matched with ciphertext TC and OZ, they recover K = [[3, 3], [2, 5]], the demo’s default key.

**Not enough information:** AA and AB both map to AA and DF under either K = [[3, 3], [2, 5]] or K = [[5, 3], [2, 5]]. Both keys are valid, but these two known blocks do not distinguish them. These examples use classical A = 0 blocks; remember the demo’s X/Q/Z escaping when analyzing other inputs.

Reading: Joshua Holden, [*The Mathematics of Secrets: Cryptography from Caesar Ciphers to Digital Encryption*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#holden>) (2017), §§1.6–1.7. The invertibility check above specifies when the direct matrix-inverse recovery works.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Hill Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Matrix multiplication as cipher operation | AES MixColumns: matrix multiplication over GF(2⁸) for diffusion |
| Multiple letters encrypted together | Block cipher: AES processes 128-bit (16-byte) blocks simultaneously |
| Linear structure = linear algebra attack | AES SubBytes prevents the complete cipher from being one linear matrix transformation |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html

```

Vanstone, *Handbook of Applied Cryptography* (1997), §7.3.2, p. 240; David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), on Hill’s 1929 publication. The worked matrix products and inverse conditions are independently checkable.

Hall I · World Origins · Greece Classical Greece · ~499 BCE

### Histiaeus's Tattooed Messenger

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

An ancient account of steganography: a message concealed beneath regrown hair.

Steganography (concealment)

SourceHerodotus, *Histories* Book V, ch. 35

Year~499 BCE

SenderHistiaeus, tyrant of Miletus, then captive in Susa

MethodTattoo on shaved scalp; sent after hair regrew

Modern LessonConcealment and encryption protect different properties

#### Concealment Visualization

Type a short message. Step through "shave → tattoo → wait for regrowth → send → re-shave" to see how the cover hides the message. Track B exhibit — visualization rather than encryption.

 Secret message  [Input input: type=text; initial value=REVOLT NOW]

1. Shave scalp 2. Tattoo 3. Wait for regrowth 4. Send messenger 5. Recipient re-shaves

##### Why This Matters

Herodotus’s *Histories* 5.35 describes Histiaeus, detained at Susa, urging Aristagoras to revolt. With the roads guarded, he had an enslaved messenger’s head shaved and marked, waited for the hair to grow, then sent him to Miletus with instructions to have his head shaved again. This is an ancient literary account of concealment; the visualization is not independent evidence for every detail of the journey.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The episode appears in Herodotus, *Histories* 5.35. Aeneas Tacticus wrote in the following century; his discussions of concealed messages belong to a separate source, not to Herodotus’s account. The surviving narrative does not establish a universal “first use” of steganography.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Cryptography vs Steganography

Encryption aims to hide a message’s meaning from someone who sees its ciphertext; steganography aims to hide the presence of a message. Herodotus describes concealment without specifying an encryption algorithm. Finding the concealed marks and interpreting them are separate tasks. Modern systems can encrypt a payload before embedding it in cover material.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

The Modern Heir: Steganography Today

Digital steganography can embed information in images or audio, while covert channels can exploit other observable behaviour. Security depends on what an observer can detect, inspect and modify. An overlooked channel is not automatically secure, and finding a hidden payload need not reveal its meaning if it is separately encrypted.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Exhibit 05 of 174 Renaissance · ~1400

### Homophonic Substitution

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Multiple symbols per letter — the Renaissance answer to frequency analysis

Statistical analysis · Structural pattern detection

InventorVarious Renaissance cryptographers

Year~1400 AD

Key TypeSymbol-to-letter mapping table

Broken ByStatistical analysis · Structural pattern detection

Modern LessonNon-uniform output distributions

#### Why This Matters

Homophonic substitution was the Renaissance cryptographers’ answer to frequency analysis: giving common letters multiple cipher symbols can flatten individual-symbol frequencies, although language patterns can still support cryptanalysis.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

European diplomatic ciphers used multiple substitutes for common letters; David Kahn documents a Mantuan example from 1401. This does not establish a direct transmission of al-Kindi’s methods to Renaissance cryptographers. The idea: if common letters betray themselves by appearing too often, give them multiple disguises. The letter E might encrypt as 12, 37, or 44 — chosen at random each time. With a suitable allocation and random selection, the frequency of each common letter is spread across its substitutes.

This system was widely used in European diplomatic correspondence from the 15th through 17th centuries. The Vatican, Italian city-states, and royal courts all employed variations. Some systems used over 100 symbols.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Assign multiple ciphertext symbols to each plaintext letter, weighted by letter frequency. Common letters get more symbols; rare letters get fewer.

```text
E → 12, 37, 44, 71, 83  (5 symbols, ~12.7% freq)
T → 21, 90             (2 symbols, ~9.1% freq)
A → 05, 63             (2 symbols, ~8.2% freq)
Z → 99                 (1 symbol,  ~0.07% freq)
```

Homophonic substitution: E gets 5 symbols, Z gets 1 — more symbols for common letters masks frequency patterns

To encrypt: for each plaintext letter, randomly pick one of its assigned symbols. This illustrative allocation reduces some peaks but does not make frequencies uniform: with equal choice among alternatives, each E symbol has an expected frequency of 12.7% / 5 = 2.54%, each T symbol 9.1% / 2 = 4.55%, and the Z symbol 0.07%. Approximate flattening requires the number of substitutes to track the plaintext distribution; a short message can still vary substantially.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Structural Pattern Analysis

Complexity: Moderate

Even with flattened frequencies, the cipher retains structural patterns. Digraph frequencies (two-symbol sequences) still reflect English digraph statistics — TH, HE, IN, ER appear more often than XX, QQ, ZZ. With suitable ciphertext, statistical scoring and search can recover mappings; success depends on the language, message length, symbol allocation, and search budget.

Poor Symbol Distribution

Complexity: Easy if symbols not perfectly weighted

An uneven allocation or biased choice of substitutes can leave strong frequency peaks. Such a peak suggests hypotheses; it does not by itself identify the underlying plaintext letter.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Homophonic Substitution | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Multiple symbols per letter | Secure encryption aims to conceal plaintext patterns under a specified attack model; uniform symbol counts alone do not establish security |
| Frequency flattening attempt | A one-time pad uses independent uniform pad bits; practical stream ciphers instead generate a pseudorandom keystream |
| Fixed symbol set | AES is deterministic for a fixed key and block. Encryption modes add nonce or IV rules; those rules and authentication matter |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| Exhibit | 5 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Era | Renaissance · ~1400 |
| Trust | Broken |
| Inventor | Various Renaissance cryptographers |
| Year | ~1400 AD |
| Key Type | Symbol-to-letter mapping table |
| Broken By | Statistical analysis · Structural pattern detection |

#### How Many Codes Is the Reader Facing?

A homophonic key is usually described by how many code symbols it holds, and that number does the work. With 26 plaintext letters and at most five homophones each, one fixed key has **at most 130 code types**, so each code symbol carries at most **log<sub>2</sub> 130 ≈ 7.022 bits** — and only if all 130 were equally likely, which proportional allocation does not achieve.

Research collections are built by encrypting many texts, each under its own independently generated key. Pool all that ciphertext and the measured alphabet becomes much larger: eleven thousand codes gives log<sub>2</sub> 11000 ≈ 13.425 bits. **That is a statistic about the collection, not about the letter in front of you.** An attacker who holds one message still faces one key with its own small set of codes. Growing the pool cannot make a single message harder to read, and a cryptanalytic result that improves as the pool grows is measuring the pool.

The worked, fully enumerable version of this — and why a unicity estimate neither certifies a proposed reading nor promises an efficient solver — is in [the entropy exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/entropy.html#pooled-entropy>).

#### Sources and Reading

*Handbook of Applied Cryptography*, Alfred J. Menezes, Paul C. van Oorschot and Scott A. Vanstone (1997), §7.3.2, p.240: proportional homophone sets and residual statistics. *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, David Kahn (revised edition, 1996), “The Rise of the West”: the Mantuan 1401 example and the uncertain transmission of cryptanalytic knowledge.

Cipher traffic can reveal a system while leaving its physical mechanism uncertain.

Historical naval cipher reconstructed from intercepted traffic; the physical IKA mechanism is not established by the cited 2021 study.

UserImperial Japanese Navy · major shore stations

PeriodEarly 1930s · US intercept record

Alphabet49-symbol kana system · 42 + 7

Known FromIntercepted ciphertext and cryptanalytic reports

Modern LessonMatch each claim to its kind of evidence

#### Why This Matters

A working reconstruction can reproduce a cipher’s output without reproducing the original machine. IKA makes that distinction concrete: historical reports describe its cryptographic behavior, while familiar photographs belong to other devices. An artifact’s caption is part of the evidence.

#### What the Traffic Reveals

Chris Christensen’s 2021 study draws primarily on the US Navy’s April 1946 report *RIP 28A*. IKA’s 49-symbol kana system separates a seven-symbol group with fixed substitution from a 42-symbol group with a monthly sequence and staggered movement. Its documented output behavior allows cryptographic reconstruction.

The paper lists US intercepts from late 1931 or early 1932 to July 1933. Those are intercept dates, not a known invention date. It reports that US Navy codebreakers never captured or saw an IKA machine.

#### Four Kinds of Evidence

Evidence distinguished in Christensen’s 2021 study

| Evidence | Supports | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intercepted IKA traffic and reports | Reconstructed substitutions and stepping behavior | Does not identify the physical input, output or stepping mechanism |
| Captured M-1 / ORANGE hardware | The successor machine’s physical design; Figure 2 shows M-1 | A surviving M-1 is not an authenticated IKA |
| Holtwick’s American M-1 analogue | An American implementation; shown in Figure 3 | The study rejects its occasional identification as IKA |
| Proposed IKA mechanisms | Possible realizations of similar cipher behavior | Kryha-like disks or a Damm half-rotor remain hypotheses |

Scroll the table sideways to read all three columns.

No artifact photographs are reproduced here. Consult the paper for the photographs and their attributed captions.

#### What a Replay Would Leave Open

Two mechanisms can implement the same substitutions and stepping sequence. Matching every available ciphertext would test that mathematical behavior; establishing which mechanism the original makers used would require additional physical or documentary evidence. This exhibit offers no machine simulator.

The 2021 study also reports that records of the original cryptanalytic attack were unavailable. A modern reconstruction should therefore identify its own method and assumptions, rather than present them as the historical attack.

[Try the Charles V evidence exercise](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#charles-v>): a partial key can pass a check while still leaving an unknown symbol. [Follow the Portuguese letters of 1649](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/intercept-to-intelligence.html#portuguese-1649>) to see why reading, translation and historical consequences need separate evidence.

#### Sources and Reading

- Chris Christensen, [“The Imperial Japanese Navy IKA Cipher Machine”](<https://ecp.ep.liu.se/index.php/histocrypt/article/view/155>), *HistoCrypt 2021*, DOI 10.3384/ecp183155. See §2–4 for the reconstructed cipher, §5–7 for hardware and analogue attribution, and Appendix A for intercept dates and alphabet splits.

- Underlying reports cited by Christensen: Chief of Naval Operations, *The M-1 Machine System: RIP-28A* (April 1946), NARA RG 38, Box 16; Jack S. Holtwick Jr., *History of the Naval Security Group to World War II: SRH 355* (1971), especially Appendix VIII, 90F–90G. The museum has not independently inspected these archival reports.

The evidence limits above are those of the cited 2021 study. They are not a claim to have checked every surviving collection or later archival discovery.

#### Compare the Evidence

[Kryha](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kryha.html>) provides a comparison for moving alphabets. Similar cipher behavior alone does not establish shared construction.

[PURPLE](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/purple.html>) is a later Japanese diplomatic system with a different alphabet and switching arrangement. “Japanese cipher machine” does not name one interchangeable design.

[The Evidence Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html>) keeps sources, hypotheses and unresolved readings together.

[← CompareKryha](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kryha.html>)[Compare →PURPLE](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/purple.html>)

### IRA Cipher Traffic

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]


The Moss Twomey papers preserve interwar IRA cipher traffic. Jim Gillogly recovered many messages; Richard Bean solved the remaining published challenge in 2019.

Jim Gillogly; Richard Bean solved the final published challenge in 2019

SourceThe Moss Twomey papers, UCD Archives, Dublin

Era1920s; includes a 1923 Vigenère example

FamiliesMainly columnar transposition; also Vigenère

Corpus~300 documents, ~1,300 individual cryptograms

Broken ByJim Gillogly; Richard Bean solved the final published challenge in 2019

Final challenge51 surviving letters; solved by Richard Bean, 2019

#### Why This Matters

This exhibit is about a body of real ciphertext and the man who read it. In 2001 the historian Tom Mahon found roughly three hundred documents containing encrypted messages in a Dublin archive — the papers of Moss Twomey, IRA chief of staff from 1926 to 1936. Between them they held about 1,300 individual cryptograms, mostly dispatches between headquarters and organisers in Britain and the United States, dating from the 1920s. Mahon brought in the American cryptanalyst Jim Gillogly, and together they published *Decoding the IRA* in 2008. Their book left one challenge unresolved; Richard Bean subsequently solved it in 2019.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The collection documents IRA correspondence during the 1920s. Dunin and Schmeh describe both columnar transpositions and a smaller set of Vigenère-encrypted passages embedded in otherwise readable letters, including an example dated 4 May 1923. The collection should not be described as using only one cipher.

For the Vigenère passages, Gillogly combined short samples to search for a reused key. The recovered keyword, GVZKLG, is TEAPOT transformed by a reversed alphabet. Ampersands represented Z in the ciphertext. This case shows why reused keys and operator conventions matter alongside the underlying cipher.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How the Cipher Worked

Most of the cryptograms used [columnar transposition](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html>), the mechanism demonstrated here. The message is written into a grid of fixed line length; the columns are then read out in an order set by a keyword. No letter is ever replaced — every letter of the plaintext survives into the ciphertext, only its position changes. Single-letter frequencies cannot recover the column order, but they can help suggest a transposition and a likely language. Letter-group statistics help score candidate orders.

Operators also padded. In the message Gillogly works through as an example, the encipherer had inserted two columns of meaningless vowels to disguise the shape of the grid.

The demo above uses the museum's columnar engine. It is the right mechanism, but it is a clean-room model: it does not reproduce the padding conventions, the five-letter grouping, or the handwriting of the originals.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Hill climbing over column orders

Method: scored search over candidate column orders

Gillogly wrote hill-climbing software aimed at columnar transposition. In the worked example described by Dunin and Schmeh, he tried line lengths in the range of about eight to fifteen characters, ran the search around a hundred times from different random starting keys, and watched for the point at which recognisable English words began to fall out of a candidate solution. The approach is the same family this museum covers under [hill climbing](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cryptanalysis.html#hill-climbing>), but its success depends on message length, language scoring, transcription and the particular cipher conventions.

The final published challenge — solved in 2019

Richard Bean; damaged or incomplete ciphertext

This surviving 51-letter cryptogram was the unresolved challenge in *Decoding the IRA* (2008):

```text
GTHOO RCSNM EOTDE TAEDI NRAHE
EBFNS INSGD AILLA YTTSE AOITDE
```

Bean’s reconstruction concerns a report about a raid and gelignite in Scotland. *Codebreaking: A Practical Guide*, by Elonka Dunin and Klaus Schmeh (2020), explains a missing L within the ciphertext and an omitted four-letter column, ETDS. A reconstructed 56-letter message, retaining the source’s THLS spelling, can be transposed with the equivalent key BCAFIEHGKDLJ; removing those five letters reproduces the displayed 51 letters. This is a reproducible reconstruction, not recovery of the original keyword.

Evidence and Reading

Elonka Dunin and Klaus Schmeh, *Codebreaking: A Practical Guide* (Robinson, 2020), sections “Jim Gillogly’s solution of IRA Vigenère cryptograms”, “Jim Gillogly’s solution of IRA transposition cryptograms” and “Richard Bean’s solution of the last unsolved IRA cryptogram”. Tom Mahon and James J. Gillogly, *Decoding the IRA* (2008), is the earlier publication discussed there. The University of Queensland’s [23 August 2019 announcement](<https://news.uq.edu.au/2019-08-23-uq-data-scientist-cracks-near-century-old-crypto-code>) independently records Bean’s result and the 51-character ciphertext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

### Jefferson Disk

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

Jefferson’s proposed wheel cipher and independently developed later cylinders

Brute force · Probable word attack

InventorThomas Jefferson (1795) · Independently: Bazeries (1891)

Year1795

Key TypePhysical disk arrangement (36 disks)

Broken ByBrute force · Probable word attack

Modern LessonCompare mechanical implementations of substitution

#### Why This Matters

Jefferson described a wheel cipher in the 1790s. Bazeries later developed a similar cylinder independently, and the American work of Parker Hitt and Joseph Mauborgne led to the M-94, adopted in the early 1920s. Reinvention demonstrates the appeal of the mechanism, not a proof of its security.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Jefferson’s manuscript describes the device but does not establish that he built or deployed it. Bazeries’s later cylinder and the Hitt–Mauborgne development should be identified separately rather than collapsing the whole M-94 invention into its adoption year. The [Signal Corps historical account](<https://www.nsa.gov/Portals/75/documents/news-features/declassified-documents/friedman-documents/publications/FOLDER_205/41762559080174.pdf>) discusses the independent designs.

Jefferson proposed a cylinder with 36 alphabet disks. The later M-94 used 25 disks and enciphered 25-letter blocks; longer messages needed multiple blocks. Its Army and Navy service histories should not be reduced to a claim that one replacement date applied to every U.S. military branch.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

```text
Device: N disks on a spindle, each with
scrambled alphabet around the edge

Encryption:
1. Set disks to spell out message
2. Read off any other row as ciphertext

Decryption:
1. Set disks to ciphertext
2. Look for a row that reads as English

M-94 specifications:
- 25 aluminum disks
- Each disk: alphabet in unique order
- Disk order = key (25! possible orders)
- Block length = 25 characters; longer messages use multiple blocks
```

Jefferson Disk: disks rotated to spell the message; any other row becomes the ciphertext

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Probable Word Attack

Complexity: Moderate

With a fixed disk order and known alphabets, the receiver can inspect the 25 rows other than the ciphertext row. Recovering an unknown disk order is a separate task: probable plaintext, several messages and consistency across disk alphabets can constrain candidates. Language context helps assess a row but does not guarantee a unique answer.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Jefferson Disk | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Physical disk arrangement as key | Key as configuration: RSA uses related public and private parameters; AES accepts 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys |
| Multiple cipher rows per setting | Language context can help select a candidate; this is not the birthday attack on hashes |
| Mechanical implementation | Hardware Security Modules (HSMs): crypto operations in dedicated hardware |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 28 of 174 |

| Era | 1795 (Jefferson) · 1922 (M-94) |
| Trust | Broken |
| Inventor | Thomas Jefferson (1795) · Independently: Bazeries (1891) |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

Wheel-Cipher Lineage

Jefferson’s wheel (1790s), Bazeries’s independent cylinder and the later M-94 and M-138-A illustrate related alphabet-alignment mechanisms. Similarity does not establish direct transmission between every design.

Across these mechanisms, physical alphabet arrangements supply key material. Disk and strip procedures differ, so their exact operating rules must be specified.
