Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Twenty-five disks on a spindle — adopted in 1922 and used for tactical communication.

Tactical only

OriginUnited States Army (Mauborgne, Hitt)

YearIn service 1922 – 1943

Mechanism25 brass disks on a spindle, each a mixed alphabet

LineageIndependent later development resembling Jefferson’s wheel

StatusTactical only; never trusted for strategic traffic

#### Why This Matters

Jefferson described a wheel cipher around 1795, but its operational use is not established here. The US Army adopted the independently developed M-94 in 1922, after World War I. Similarity to the earlier unpublished wheel is not proof of direct descent.

The M-94 served as the standard tactical cipher of the US Army through the 1920s and 1930s and was still in field use in early WWII alongside the M-209 and SIGABA. It was retired in 1943, by which point its tactical-level security was acknowledged as marginal.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Twenty-five aluminum or brass disks slide onto a single spindle. Each disk has the 26 letters of the alphabet engraved around its rim in a different mixed order, and each carries a number (1 through 25) for ordering on the spindle. To encrypt:

- Both sender and recipient agree on the order of the 25 disks for the day.

- The sender turns each disk so that the plaintext message reads horizontally across one row.

- The sender then chooses any *other* row and reads the ciphertext off horizontally.

The recipient stacks the disks in the same agreed order, dials in the ciphertext on the corresponding row, and looks for the row that reads as English. There are 26 aligned rows, of which 25 differ from the ciphertext row. Language and context can suggest the intended plaintext, but uniqueness is not guaranteed.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Multiple-anagram attack on the disk order

Complexity: Tractable for short tactical traffic

The cipher’s key is the daily disk-order permutation (25!) and the chosen offset row. Related intercepts, probable plaintext and the known disk alphabets can constrain candidate orders and offsets. Multiple-anagram analysis is one approach; similar message lengths alone do not guarantee recovery. The Friedman / Kullback team at the SIS demonstrated practical breaks well before WWII.

Captured disk sets

Captured alphabets still leave a key-recovery problem

A captured disk set exposes its alphabets. The analyst may still need the applicable disk order, row choices and message conventions. Capturing hardware is not the same as possessing every traffic key.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| M-94 lesson | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| The hardware key (disk wiring) is the standing key | Modern HSMs hold a master key with a long lifetime |
| The session key is just the disk order | Modern protocols define session-key derivation and separate per-message nonce requirements |
| Tactical vs strategic security tiers | Modern crypto-agility — different protections for different threat models |
| Independent development of similar disk mechanisms | Good cryptographic ideas often arrive decades before the engineering catches up |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Origin | United States Army (Mauborgne, Hitt) |
| --- | --- |
| Year | In service 1922 – 1943 |
| Mechanism | 25 brass disks on a spindle, each a mixed alphabet |
| Lineage | Independent later development resembling Jefferson’s wheel |
| Status | Tactical only; never trusted for strategic traffic |

### M-209 (Hagelin C-38)

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

The US Army's portable WWII pin-and-lug cipher machine

Strong (tactical)

InventorBoris Hagelin (Sweden)

Year1940 US trials; production from 1942

Production~140,000 units (Smith Corona, US)

Key Type6 pinwheels (lengths 26, 25, 23, 21, 19, 17) + 27 lug bars

Period101,405,850 wheel-position cycle; output period may divide it

Modern LessonLong periods alone do not ensure security

The interactive is a deterministic teaching model: a seed generates all six pin patterns and all 27 lug bars. It demonstrates the pin-and-lug mechanism but is not an operational key-sheet simulator.

#### Why This Matters

Boris Hagelin's C-38 design, sold to the US Army as the M-209, became the standard tactical cipher of American forces in WWII. Compact (about the size of a hardcover book), it weighed 2.7 kg and ran without electricity — a clerk operated it by hand, selecting each input letter and turning a crank to print the output on paper tape. The large production contract made the machine a major commercial success.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Hagelin’s cipher-machine business developed the C-series before the war. David Kahn distinguishes the 1940 US trials and negotiations from production beginning in 1942; Kahn and George Lasry report approximately 140,000 machines. The US-produced M-209, associated with the C-38 family, became a widely used portable tactical machine. It offered practical field operation without electricity, but published cryptanalysis shows why its mechanical complexity should not be mistaken for modern security.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Six pinwheels with co-prime lengths (26, 25, 23, 21, 19, 17) advance one position per letter. Each wheel has tiny pins around its edge, set to "active" or "inactive" by the operator. A bank of 27 lug bars reads which wheels are currently active and produces a displacement K from 0 to 27. The indicator alphabet is reversed, so with A=0 encryption uses the reciprocal transformation:

```text
cipher = (25 - plaintext + K) mod 26
```

With no displaced bars A becomes Z; with 20 displaced bars A becomes T. Because the wheel lengths are pairwise co-prime, the joint wheel positions repeat after 26 × 25 × 23 × 21 × 19 × 17 = **101,405,850** steps. The output keystream can have a smaller period, depending on pin and lug settings.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Known-Plaintext Attack

Work depends on message length, pin settings and lug overlap

Known or accurately guessed plaintext exposes the displacement sequence modulo 26 and constrains pin and lug settings. Published attacks exploit this structure, but their cost and success depend on available text and key restrictions. A fixed “hours per message” claim should not be applied to arbitrary historical traffic.

Statistical Lug Recovery

Statistical search under specified key and traffic conditions

Each lug bar contributes one unit if at least one of the pins selected by its lugs is effective. If both selected pins are effective, that bar still contributes only one unit. The total is therefore a sum of bar-level OR results, not simply a separate lug count times each wheel’s pin bit. Lug overlaps affect the distribution and the difficulty of reconstruction; statistics can guide search without guaranteeing unique recovery.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from M-209 (Hagelin C-38) | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Pin-and-lug as keystream generator | Modern LFSR (linear feedback shift register) stream ciphers |
| Co-prime period maximization | Same trick used in pseudo-random number generators today |
| Beaufort involution | Encryption and decryption use the same operation |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 47 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Era | World War II · 1942 production |
| Trust | Broken |
| Inventor | Boris Hagelin (Sweden) |
| Year | 1940 US trials; production from 1942 |
| Production | ~140,000 units (Smith Corona, US) |
| Key Type | 6 pinwheels (lengths 26, 25, 23, 21, 19, 17) + 27 lug bars |
| Period | 101,405,850 wheel-position cycle; output period may divide it |
| Modern Lesson | Long periods alone do not ensure security |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

Hagelin Machine Family

See the [Hagelin C-36 / C-52 lineage exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hagelin-c36.html>) for the family and Crypto AG history. The M-209 belongs to the broader Hagelin line (C-36, C-38/BC-38, and M-209). These pin-and-lug pocket machines traded top-tier security for field practicality and became the standard tactical wheel ciphers for multiple armies.

Later Hagelin successors became part of the Crypto AG ecosystem connected to Operation Rubicon, where intelligence services reportedly leveraged supply-chain influence for cryptanalytic advantage.

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet* (revised edition, 1996), Hagelin discussion; George Lasry, *A Methodology for the Cryptanalysis of Classical Ciphers with Search Metaheuristics* (2018), Chapter 7, especially §7.2.1, “Functional Description,” p. 114, on bar engagement and the Beaufort transformation. The joint wheel-position period is distinct from the period of a particular output sequence.

Track B · Deep Dive 1578–1584

 ⬡ Track B · Annotated Decipherment

### Mary Queen of Scots — The Castelnau Letters

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Fifty-seven letters, containing about 50,000 words, identified and deciphered by George Lasry, Norbert Biermann and Satoshi Tomokiyo; their findings were published in 2023.

57 letters from 1578–1584, approximately 50,000 words; decipherment published 8 February 2023.

Cipher TypeNomenclator; 219 graphical symbol types in the recovered corpus

LanguageFrench

Date1578–1584 (written during the Sheffield captivity)

Archive LocationBibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (several manuscript collections)

Solved ByGeorge Lasry, Norbert Biermann, Satoshi Tomokiyo

Published*Cryptologia*, 2023, vol. 47 no. 2

#### Who made the mistake?

Suppose a clear copy shows the symbols below. Key A gives an odd reading. Did you copy it incorrectly, choose the wrong interpretation, or inherit an error made by the person who enciphered it?

**Invented fixture:** the symbols and keys below are not Mary’s. Slashes mark word boundaries. The copy is assumed accurate for this exercise.

**Recorded symbols (kept unchanged):** `1 5 5 3 / 1 5 / 9`

##### Intended key A

`1 → M; 2 → E; 3 → T; 4 → N; 5 → O; 6 → R`

##### Other key B

`1 → N; 2 → O; 3 → R; 4 → M; 5 → E; 6 → T`

**Literal reading with key A:** `M O O T / M O / ?`

  [Input key-confusion-toggle: type=checkbox; initial value=] Test key B for symbol 5 only; keep key A for the other symbols

**Separate editorial proposal:** `No alternative reading applied.`

Symbol 9 remains unknown under both keys.

How would you distinguish the explanations?

- **Copying error:** return to the source image. Does it actually show 5 or a different symbol?

- **Original key confusion:** check whether repeated exceptions match another key the writer might have used.

- **Our interpretation:** test the proposed rule on a new passage. A more familiar phrase alone does not settle it.

The proposed reading is M E E T / M E / ?. Do not silently replace the original symbols or erase the unexplained 9.

**Historical connection:** Lasry, Biermann and Tomokiyo found recurring enciphering errors in a subset of 17 documents. Several fit symbols from the Mary–Beaton key instead of the Mary–Castelnau key, supporting their hypothesis of cross-cipher contamination. That explanation does not identify a particular secretary or account for every error. [Deciphering Mary Stuart’s lost letters from 1578–1584 (2023), Appendix B, pp. 198–200](<https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2022.2160677>) ([author article PDF](<https://friendsofsheffieldcastle.org/wp-content/uploads/Deciphering-Mary-Stuart-s-lost-letters-from-1578-1584.pdf#page=99>)).

[Keep competing readings in the Evidence Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html#annotations>).

#### Check against another record

Lasry, Biermann and Tomokiyo located plaintext counterparts of **seven** newly deciphered letters in British archives: F42, F46, F58, F69, F78, F96 and F221. They distinguish these from three previously known letters whose ciphertext was not among the recovered BnF material. Compare a decipherment with its counterpart: agreement can test the reading, while omissions require separate examination.

Source: [“Deciphering Mary Stuart’s lost letters from 1578–1584” (2023), §5.1 and the corresponding entries in §5.3](<https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2022.2160677>). [Read the article’s seven-letter inventory (PDF)](<https://friendsofsheffieldcastle.org/wp-content/uploads/Deciphering-Mary-Stuart-s-lost-letters-from-1578-1584.pdf#page=33>). [Continue to the case file](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#mary>).

#### Why This Matters

The researchers initially encountered unidentified ciphertexts among digitised manuscripts at the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Decipherment revealed letters written by Mary Stuart in 1578–1584, mostly to the French ambassador Michel de Castelnau. Their identification was part of the discovery: the documents were not already correctly catalogued as this correspondence.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

The Cipher System: What Mary Used

Mary's Castelnau cipher is a sophisticated Renaissance nomenclator — the same class of system used in the Babington Plot correspondence (1586), which was broken by Thomas Phelippes. The Castelnau cipher is substantially more complex:

- **Symbol alphabet:** 219 distinct graphical symbol types identified across the corpus, including homophones, nomenclature and special signs. Diacritics can change a symbol’s meaning; this is not a 219-letter alphabet.

- **Code groups:** Named persons, places, and frequent political terms replaced by dedicated codewords (e.g., a specific symbol for "Monsieur de Castelnau," another for "Her Majesty the Queen of England").

- **Nulls:** Non-semantic symbols interspersed to inflate symbol frequency counts and frustrate statistical attacks.

- **Special symbols:** The recovered system also includes signs that modify how neighbouring symbols are read. The paper documents their functions; this is not evidence of a separate double-encryption layer.

The plaintext language is French — an additional barrier for analysts who might expect English or Latin in Mary's correspondence.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-person"></use></svg>
```

How the Break Worked: Hill-Climbing at Scale

The attack method, developed by George Lasry, is a variant of the simulated annealing / hill-climbing approach used in modern historical cryptanalysis. The key components:

- **Transcription:** The team converted the handwritten ciphertext symbols into machine-readable identifiers. The approximately 50,000 figure describes plaintext words, not cipher characters.

- **Revised hypotheses:** An initial Italian-language hypothesis gave way to French. Diacritic and symbol assignments were corrected as decipherment progressed.

- **Homophone search:** The first search provisionally treated symbols as letters. Simulated annealing changed mappings and sometimes accepted worse scores to escape local optima, using historical French language statistics.

- **Computer-assisted search:** Candidate substitutions were evaluated using language statistics; human analysis then resolved symbols, words and context that the initial output did not explain.

- **Manual refinement and corroboration:** Lasry, Biermann, and Tomokiyo recovered nomenclature for words, syllables, names and places manually, revised transcription choices, and compared surviving plaintext versions. The search did not automatically recover the complete nomenclator.

Computer-assisted cryptanalysis and archival interpretation complemented one another. Readable fragments helped identify the writer, after which historical context helped refine the decipherment.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-clock"></use></svg>
```

Decipherment Timeline

1578–1584

The studied corpus contains 54 letters from Mary to Castelnau, two from Mary to de la Mothe-Fénelon, and one from Jacques Nau to Jean Arnault.

1586–1587 — a separate episode

The Babington Plot correspondence is intercepted in 1586. Mary is executed on 8 February 1587. Those events should not be confused with the dates of this recovered collection.

Modern archival research

Lasry, Biermann and Tomokiyo transcribe and analyse digitised ciphertexts, identify Mary as their author and reconstruct the cipher.

8 February 2023 — publication

Their article, “Deciphering Mary Stuart’s lost letters from 1578-1584,” publishes the decipherment and historical discussion.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

The following numbers and mappings are invented teaching examples of nomenclator notation. They are not transcriptions of Mary’s manuscripts or entries from the recovered key.

 ·52· ·17· ·38· ·81· ·6· ·73· ·29· ·48· ·92· ·15· ·41·

Each number represents a single item in the nomenclator table. A null symbol (cryptographer's decoy) might appear as · ·98· · or · ·100· · — a high-frequency interspersed symbol that does not contribute to plaintext.

Illustrative entries only; consult the paper for the actual recovered symbols and assignments:

##### One sign changes the reading

Invented fragment: **B A ↻ X Φ**. B and A stand for letters; Φ stands for a person; X is a null. The invented sign ↻ repeats the preceding letter. This fragment is not a quotation from Mary or a French sentence.

 [Input mary-repeat: type=checkbox; initial value=; checked] Apply the repeat modifier ↻

With the modifier: T E E · [Castelnau]. Without it: T E · [Castelnau].

The recovered key includes repeat and delete controls: [Lasry, Biermann & Tomokiyo (2023), §4 and Figure 7](<https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2022.2160677>). Our signs and mappings are invented.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

What the Letters Say

The full content of the deciphered letters is reported in the *Cryptologia* paper and its supplementary materials. Key categories of newly revealed content include:

- **Captivity conditions:** Mary describes her treatment in captivity, her access to correspondence and to her attendants, and her physical health — primary-source details not previously available from the cipher side of the archive.

- **Political strategy:** Mary outlines her diplomatic positioning — appealing to the French crown for intervention, requesting Castelnau relay messages to specific parties at the French court, and describing her view of her prospects in England.

- **Undocumented intermediaries:** The letters name individuals not previously known to have been involved in Mary's communications network, expanding the known cast of her diplomatic circle.

- **Assessment of Walsingham:** Mary's own characterisation of Sir Francis Walsingham and her awareness of surveillance — a rare first-person account of Tudor intelligence from the surveilled rather than the surveiller.

💡

**Historical significance:** The decipherment makes approximately 50,000 words of correspondence available for historical study. Some letters had other surviving versions; the recovery should not be described as an entirely unknown archive in every detail.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-link"></use></svg>
```

Primary Source & Reference

**Lasry, G., Biermann, N., & Tomokiyo, S.** (2023). [“Deciphering Mary Stuart’s lost letters from 1578-1584.”](<https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2022.2160677>) *Cryptologia*, 47(2), 101–202. Published online 8 February 2023; the “2022” in the DOI is not the publication year.

**Original manuscripts:** Several collections at the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The article’s document inventory supplies the individual archival references; this is not a single manuscript volume.

The article documents the cipher, its recovery, letter texts and historical interpretation. See §3.2 for archive shelfmarks, §4.2 for symbol types, §5.1 for the 54+2+1 letter inventory, the author biographies, and Appendix A for the search algorithm. No HistoCrypt 2021 presentation of this result is established here.

**Cryptiana context:** Satoshi Tomokiyo's wider *Cryptiana* work on Renaissance diplomatic ciphers provides the archival and technical backdrop for why the Castelnau nomenclator could be recognised, classified, and finally attacked computationally in the first place.

See also: [George Lasry exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/lasry.html>) · [Babington Plot Cipher](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/babington.html>) · [Further Reading: Cryptologia journal](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html>)

The Solvers

**George Lasry** — Israeli cryptanalyst; built the hill-climbing toolkit used across multiple historical cipher solutions; *Cryptologia* contributor.

**Norbert Biermann** — Pianist, musical coach and arranger; Professor of Repertoire at the Berlin University of Arts in the paper’s 2023 author biography; historical cryptology researcher.

**Satoshi Tomokiyo** — Independent researcher; specialist in Renaissance and early-modern European diplomatic cipher manuscripts; extensive bibliography on Argenti-family systems.

Codebreaker Biography

DiedNovember 12, 2013

🌷

#### Mavis Batey

1921 – 2013

Mavis Lever joined Bletchley Park in 1940 and worked with Dilly Knox. Her work on Italian naval Enigma contributed to decrypts before Cape Matapan in March 1941. Intelligence helped British commanders plan, but the naval victory also depended on reconnaissance, tactical decisions and combat.

##### Why This Person Matters

Batey’s own writings and surviving papers help document women’s cryptanalytic work at Bletchley Park. Churchill Archives Centre preserves her notes and Dilly Knox’s poem acknowledging the team after Matapan. Her biography *Dilly: The Man Who Broke Enigmas* (2009) is a participant’s account of Knox and his colleagues. These sources should not be collapsed into a claim that women’s wartime work was first recognized only in the 2000s.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

The Italian Naval Enigma

Knox’s section analysed Italian naval use of a commercial Enigma variant. Batey’s accounts describe exploiting predictable text and Enigma’s property that a letter could not encrypt to itself. The claim that a message sent twice under different settings is automatically plaintext for the other is incorrect: both are ciphertext unless additional information establishes the underlying message.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

Cape Matapan

Decrypts from Italian naval Enigma helped inform the British response before Cape Matapan in March 1941. Knox’s poem credits Batey and the team. The intelligence contribution belongs alongside naval reconnaissance, decisions and combat; a successful decrypt did not by itself determine every event in the battle.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

After the War

Mavis Batey married her Bletchley colleague Keith Batey in 1942. After the war she researched garden history and campaigned to preserve historic landscapes. Her MBE in the 1987 New Year Honours recognised work on preserving and restoring historic gardens. She also wrote about Bletchley Park, including *Dilly: The Man Who Broke Enigmas* (2009).

Evidence and Reading

Churchill Archives Centre, [“Hidden Voices”](<https://www.chuarchivestories.uk/stories/hidden-voices>), reproduces Batey papers BTEY 3/2 and Knox’s poem BTEY 3/6. UCL, [“Breaking in at Bletchley: Mavis Batey, student codebreaker”](<https://www.ucl.ac.uk/about/search-faces-ucl/breaking-bletchley-mavis-batey-student-codebreaker>), records her interrupted German studies and wartime work. The *London Gazette*, supplement of 31 December 1986, p.12, records her garden-conservation MBE in the 1987 New Year Honours.

### McCormick Notes

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]


Two handwritten notes found with Ricky McCormick in 1999. The FBI released them in 2011 seeking help; “unsolved” is not a declaration of mathematical unbreakability.

The FBI’s 2011 appeal reported the notes unresolved.

RegionSt. Louis, Missouri, USA

YearNotes recovered 30 June 1999

InvestigatorFBI Cryptanalysis & Racketeering Records Unit (CRRU)

TrackB (cluster analyzer)

#### Interactive Exhibit

Paste a transcription, or use the illustrative sample below, to count adjacent letter pairs. The loaded sample is not an authenticated transcription of either note. Spaces, punctuation and numbers are removed before counting, so pairs may cross those boundaries. This is a pattern explorer, not a decoder.

 Illustrative letter sample or your own transcription

RNCBE LRRSE NSE EE NEAR NCBE WLDS NLSE WNSE NCBE NCBSE

 Tally bigrams

##### Why This Matters

Two handwritten notes were found with Ricky McCormick’s body in Missouri on 30 June 1999. The FBI’s appeal of 29 March 2011 reported unsuccessful analysis by its Cryptanalysis and Racketeering Records Unit and the American Cryptogram Association. It asked for new evidence or recognition of the notation. That dated account does not establish the notes’ contents or a cause of death.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

In its 2011 appeal, the FBI attributed to family members the report that McCormick had used coded notes since childhood. The agency sought someone who might recognise the notation or provide context. The marks’ precise rules and meaning remain uncertain, so no invented quotation or particular algorithm is asserted here.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

Repeated clusters and layout offer clues, but they do not establish a unique cipher type or underlying language. Personal shorthand is one possibility. A private notation is not thereby a one-time pad: that term has specific requirements of random, secret, non-reused key material.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

The FBI sought another example of the notation or someone who recognized it. This illustrates the value of contextual evidence: the investigators did not possess a complete account of the writing system. Difficulty interpreting a private note is not proof of strong encryption or of an author’s technical ability.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    (function () {
      window.encode = function () {
        var raw = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g, '');
        var out = document.getElementById('output');
        if (raw.length < 4) { out.textContent = 'Need at least 4 letters.'; return; }
        var counts = {};
        for (var i = 0; i < raw.length - 1; i++) {
          var pair = raw[i] + raw[i+1];
          counts[pair] = (counts[pair] || 0) + 1;
        }
        var entries = Object.keys(counts).map(function (k) { return [k, counts[k]]; });
        entries.sort(function (a, b) { return b[1] - a[1]; });
        var lines = ['Letters analysed: ' + raw.length, 'Distinct bigrams: ' + entries.length, '', 'Top 10 bigrams:'];
        for (var j = 0; j < Math.min(10, entries.length); j++) {
          lines.push('  ' + entries[j][0] + '  \u00d7 ' + entries[j][1]);
        }
        lines.push('');
        lines.push('Pair frequencies depend on the corpus and preprocessing. A frequent pair does not identify its meaning.');
        out.textContent = lines.join('\n');
      };
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode(); });
    })();
```

### Microdot Steganography

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Tiny photographic images concealed in ordinary carriers — a technique used in twentieth-century espionage.

Physical concealment can be discovered by inspection and magnification

InventorDeveloped through multiple stages of microphotography

EraTwentieth century; earlier microphotography

MethodOptical reduction photography; size depends on equipment

Wartime accountFBI detection described by Kahn, August 1941

Broken ByPhysical concealment can be discovered by inspection and magnification

Modern LessonSteganography hides the message; cryptography hides the content

#### 🔓 Interactive Explorer

Explore the difference between an encoding and physical concealment. This illustration does not create a microdot.

 Message to hide in a period  [Input input: type=text; initial value=MEETING LOCATION CONFIRMED]  Encode

##### Why This Matters

Microdots hide a greatly reduced photographic image in an ordinary object or document. Intelligence services used them during the twentieth century, but microphotography predates World War II. Concealing a message and encrypting its contents are separate operations.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

David Kahn’s *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), describes an FBI technician finding a concealed microdot on an envelope in August 1941. Earlier microphotography carried messages during the siege of Paris in 1870, so 1941 is not the origin of photographic message reduction.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Worked

A document can be photographed onto a tiny piece of high-resolution film and concealed in a carrier. Reading it requires suitable magnification. Sizes and equipment vary; this browser does not model optical resolution, manufacture a physical microdot or provide encryption.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

Detection and Countermeasures

Photographic enlargement + mail examination

Detection depends on the carrier, concealment and examination methods

An examiner who suspects a microdot can inspect a carrier using magnification and other forensic techniques. Finding the carrier may defeat concealment, but any independent encryption of its contents must still be addressed separately.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Descendants

Microdots and digital steganography share the goal of concealing the presence of information. Their physical and digital mechanisms differ; twentieth-century microdot development was not the invention of steganography itself.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

#### Embedded script 2 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    function mdEncode(t) {
      // UTF-8 base64 is an encoding only; no optical process occurs here.
      const encoded = btoa(encodeURIComponent(t.trim() || 'MESSAGE').replace(/%([0-9A-F]{2})/g, (_,h) => String.fromCharCode(parseInt(h,16))));
      return 'Base64 illustration: ' + encoded + '\nThis is not a physical microdot and provides no encryption or optical reduction.';
    }
```

Hall XIII · Culture MIT · 1981–present

### MIT Mystery Hunt

An annual puzzle hunt at MIT (since 1981) where teams solve dozens of layered cryptographic, linguistic, and lateral-thinking puzzles to find a hidden coin somewhere on campus.

Annual collaborative puzzle hunt

RegionCambridge, Massachusetts, USA

YearFirst held January 1981

FounderBrad Schaefer, MIT graduate student

TrackB (sample puzzle illustrator)

#### Interactive Exhibit

Try a tiny meta-style puzzle: the widget gives you four short answers, and you must spot which classical cipher links them. Track B — illustrative.

Four puzzle answers were:
**FENCE ENCODE ENIGMA CAESAR**

 What links them? (one word)  [Input input: type=text; initial value=ciphers]  Submit guess

##### Why This Matters

MIT’s Mystery Hunt combines puzzles, team collaboration and a search for a hidden coin. It began in 1981. Team sizes, puzzle counts and finishing times vary by year; the event is not restricted to cryptography, and its puzzle difficulty is not a measure of cryptographic security.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

MIT News attributes the first 1981 hunt to graduate student Brad Schaefer. The winning team earns the opportunity to design the next hunt. Its report on 2015 describes more than 70 registered teams and 2,200 participants, with 158 online puzzles plus events and runarounds. Those are figures for that year, not fixed features of every hunt.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

A meta-puzzle uses answers or other information from earlier puzzles. Cipher recognition may be one step, alongside wordplay, mathematics, images or physical tasks. For example, a designer could use earlier answers to supply a substitution key; this is an illustrative design idea, not an attributed historical Hunt puzzle. The small widget above is an original museum exercise.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

Puzzle hunts encourage collaboration, hypothesis testing and clear records of intermediate results. Those habits can help with historical cipher research. Solving a designed puzzle, however, does not establish that an encryption scheme used in a real protocol is secure or broken.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Exhibit 04 of 174 Ancient roots · medieval cryptanalysis

### Monoalphabetic Substitution

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

26! possible keys, but language patterns survive.

Language statistics and word patterns can expose a fixed substitution.

InventorUnknown (ancient practice)

YearNo single invention date

Key TypeFull alphabet permutation (26! keys)

Broken ByFrequency analysis · al-Kindi’s ninth-century account

Modern LessonS-boxes in AES

#### Why This Matters

A general 26-letter substitution has 26! possible keys, yet it preserves language patterns. Al-Kindi’s ninth-century treatise describes frequency analysis, showing why a large keyspace need not prevent a practical attack.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Monoalphabetic substitution ciphers — where each letter maps permanently to another letter or symbol — are among the oldest cryptographic techniques. They appear in ancient Hebrew texts (the Atbash cipher), Roman inscriptions, and medieval manuscripts. For a modern 26-letter alphabet there are 26! ≈ 4×10²⁶ permutations, but that count does not measure resistance to statistical attacks.

Al-Kindi’s surviving ninth-century treatise explains how letter counts and linguistic knowledge can help solve substitution. It does not prove that every short or unusual message has a unique recoverable plaintext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Replace each plaintext letter with a fixed ciphertext letter according to a secret permutation table. The same letter always maps to the same symbol.

```text
Plain:  ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
Cipher: QWERTYUIOPASDFGHJKLZXCVBNM

HELLO → ITSSG
```

Each plaintext letter maps to exactly one cipher letter — frequencies are perfectly preserved

A brute-force search of all 26! permutations is impractical, but an analyst can exploit repeated letters, word shapes and language statistics instead.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Frequency Analysis (al-Kindi, ninth century)

Difficulty depends on message length, language, and available clues

A substitution preserves the frequency of each plaintext letter under a different label. Common English corpora often have E and T near the top, but a particular message can differ substantially. Frequency guesses are starting hypotheses, tested against word patterns and other evidence, not guaranteed letter assignments.

⚠️

**Why 26! keys doesn't help:** A large keyspace does not remove repeated-letter and language patterns. Those clues often make long messages solvable, while short or unusual messages can remain ambiguous.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Monoalphabetic Substitution | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Letter permutation | AES also uses substitution, but combines it with key addition and diffusion across repeated rounds |
| Fixed substitution leaks frequency | A fixed invertible S-box merely relabels input frequencies; the complete cipher and encryption mode determine what leaks |
| Changes remain local in letter substitution | AES rounds spread changes across a block; approximately half the output bits change on average, not on every input |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| Trust | Broken |
| Inventor | Unknown (ancient practice) |
| Year | No single invention date |
| Key Type | Full alphabet permutation (26! keys) |
| Broken By | Frequency analysis · al-Kindi’s ninth-century account |

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall I: World Origins of Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/ancient.html>)› Morse Code

Hall I · Telegraphy Telegraph age · 1840s →

### Morse Code Telegraphy's universal alphabet · 1840s

Strictly speaking, Morse is not a cipher — it is the encoding that nineteenth and twentieth-century ciphers were carried on top of.

Encoding, not encryption

OriginSamuel F. B. Morse & Alfred Vail, USA

Washington–Baltimore demonstration1844 — "What hath God wrought"

International standard1865 (Paris)

Carrier forVigenère, fractionated Morse, OTP, JN-25, …

Modern roleAviation idents, amateur radio, accessibility

#### Why This Matters

Morse and Vail’s telegraph system helped make rapid long-distance electrical communication practical. International Morse, which differs from early American Morse, was standardised in the nineteenth century. Morse is a public encoding of symbols, not an encryption algorithm.

Encrypted messages travelled over several kinds of communications systems. American Civil War telegraphy used wires, not radio; later military traffic used radio, cables, teleprinters and other media. Morse could carry ciphertext, but was not the transport for almost every important cipher.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Each letter, digit, and punctuation mark is assigned a unique sequence of dots and dashes. Within a character, elements are separated by one short gap; between characters by a longer gap; between words by a still longer gap (this demo uses `/` for the word break).

```text
SOS   = ... --- ...
HELLO = .... . .-.. .-.. ---
73    = --... ...--   (amateur-radio sign-off, "best regards")
```

The code is roughly optimised for English letter frequencies — E is a single dot, T is a single dash, common letters are short, rare letters long. This makes Morse one of the earliest examples of variable-length coding, predating Huffman by a century.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

It was never "broken" — it is a public encoding

Complexity: Trivial (look up the table)

Morse is not, and was never intended to be, a cipher. It is a public encoding designed for transmission efficiency and readability. The cryptographic question is always about the cipher running on top of Morse, not Morse itself.

Operator-fingerprinting

Used for traffic analysis throughout WWII

An operator’s characteristic sending rhythm, or *fist*, can contribute to traffic analysis alongside call signs, schedules and direction finding. Such observations can suggest continuity between transmissions without decrypting their contents; a rhythm alone does not guarantee unique identification.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Morse-era idea | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| Encoding ≠ encryption | Base64, hex, ASCII vs. ChaCha20 — same distinction |
| Variable-length symbols | Huffman coding, gzip, JPEG entropy stages |
| Layered transport | TLS-over-TCP-over-IP — separate concerns at each layer |
| Side-channel: operator fist | Modern timing attacks, keystroke fingerprinting |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Origin | Samuel F. B. Morse & Alfred Vail, USA |
| --- | --- |
| Washington–Baltimore demonstration | 1844 — "What hath God wrought" |
| International standard | 1865 (Paris) |
| Carrier for | Vigenère, fractionated Morse, OTP, JN-25, … |
| Modern role | Aviation idents, amateur radio, accessibility |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

Voyager Golden Record Sidebar

A public encoding specifies how symbols are represented. That role differs from secrecy: knowing Morse, ASCII or a file format should not require a secret key. Encryption may be applied to content before it is encoded for a particular channel.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

Morse + Cipher Combination Pattern

One possible encrypted transmission stack is:

- Encrypt plaintext with a cipher (Vigenere, transposition, OTP, etc.).

- Convert resulting ciphertext to Morse/Baudot for transmission.

- Defender receives symbols, then decrypts upstream.

This layering principle still defines modern protocol stacks: transport encoding and cryptographic secrecy are separate layers.

#### Sources and Reading

U.S. House of Representatives, [“The Capitol’s First Official Telegraph”](<https://history.house.gov/HistoricalHighlight/Detail/35992>), distinguishes Morse’s 1838 demonstration to Congress from the Washington–Baltimore event of 24 May 1844.

Exhibit 164 of 1741902 · France

### Myszkowski Transposition

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Repeated keyword letters change the route: tied columns are read together across rows

Repeated-keyword transposition preserves letter frequencies and is vulnerable to statistical and keyword-search attacks.

OriginÉmile Victor Théodore Myszkowski

Year1902

FamilyKeyword transposition

KeyA word with repeated letters

ExampleTOMATO → 4 3 2 1 4 3

Try It Yourself

Encrypt Decrypt

Message

WEAREDISCOVEREDFLEEATONCE

Keyword (repeated letters share a rank) [Input myszkowski-key: type=text; initial value=TOMATO]

The standard repeated-rank convention, with incomplete final rows and no padding. A keyword without repeats reduces to ordinary columnar transposition. The demo uppercases letters, removes accents, and discards spaces, punctuation, and digits.

Run CipherUse output in opposite mode

Output

Enable JavaScript to use this interactive. The worked example below explains the same steps.

#### Why This Matters

Most [columnar transposition](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html>) implementations break ties between repeated key letters from left to right. Myszkowski assigns those letters the same rank. That one change turns a set of separate columns into a group read across each row, making repeated letters part of the permutation instead of an inconvenience to resolve.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Myszkowski published *Cryptographie indéchiffrable* in Paris in 1902. The title’s claim of indecipherability did not make the system secure. The exhibit follows the repeated-rank convention documented by the American Cryptogram Association: write the message by rows; read single columns downward and tied columns together across rows.

Like other hand transpositions, the method changes positions rather than letter identities. It offers a compact lesson in how a key and an exact tie rule determine a reversible permutation.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Sort the distinct letters of the keyword alphabetically and number them. Every occurrence of the same letter receives the same rank. With `TOMATO`, A = 1, M = 2, O = 3, and T = 4, giving `4 3 2 1 4 3`.

Write the message in rows six letters wide. Read rank 1 down its column, then rank 2. For rank 3, read both O columns from left to right in each row before going to the next row. Do the same for the two T columns at rank 4. Skip missing cells in an incomplete final row.

```text
Key:     T O M A T O
Ranks:   4 3 2 1 4 3
         W E A R E D
         I S C O V E
         R E D F L E
         E A T O N C
         E

Rank 1: ROFO
Rank 2: ACDT
Rank 3: EDSEEEAC
Rank 4: WEIVRLENE
Output: ROFOACDTEDSEEEACWEIVRLENE
```

To decrypt, construct the same occupied cells from the ciphertext length and keyword width. Fill them in rank order using the same tie rule, then read the restored grid by rows. This demo does not add padding, including when the final row is short.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Compare Columnar Transposition

For ordinary columnar transposition, repeated letters usually receive separate positions; TOMATO would have ranks `5 3 2 1 6 4`. Myszkowski’s ranks are `4 3 2 1 4 3`. The difference is visible in the demo’s grid header.

With a keyword containing no repeated letters, the two routes agree under the same no-padding convention. Try ZEBRA here and in [Columnar Transposition](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html>) to study how a tie rule changes the cipher rather than the underlying message.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

How It Can Be Broken

The cipher preserves single-letter frequencies. A suspected keyword width gives a candidate grid shape; probable words and neighbouring-letter scores constrain which positions should become adjacent. Dictionary searches can try likely keywords, while broader searches can score candidate rank patterns directly. A keyword that is easy to remember may also be easy to guess.

This is a broken classical transposition method for study and puzzles. Neither repeated ranks nor the 1902 book’s title provide modern confidentiality. It supplies no integrity check: rearranging the ciphertext can also rearrange the recovered text.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Hall XIII · Cipher Culture Fiction · 2004

### National Treasure

Benjamin Franklin, a hidden Freemason cipher, and the Declaration of Independence — a fictional treasure hunt built around historical documents.

Pop Culture

DirectorJon Turteltaub

StudioWalt Disney / Jerry Bruckheimer Films

Year2004

Ciphers featuredOttendorf / book cipher, spectral lens, Freemason imagery

Real history usedIndependence Hall, the Liberty Bell, Freemason architecture, Franklin

SequelNational Treasure: Book of Secrets (2007)

#### 🔓 Interactive Explorer

Explore a Pigpen alphabet as a companion exercise; the film’s numerical book clue uses a different mechanism.

 Message (illustrative Pigpen exercise, not a reconstruction of the film’s book clue)  [Input input: type=text; initial value=FREEMASON]  Encode

##### Why This Matters

*National Treasure* (2004) turns historical documents and landmarks into a fictional trail of clues. In its plot, marks on the Declaration of Independence lead to a lookup using Benjamin Franklin’s Silence Dogood letters, followed by further clues and a treasure beneath Trinity Church in New York. These are elements of the screenplay, not evidence that the real documents conceal a map.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

Ciphers in the Film

The film calls its numerical lookup an Ottendorf cipher: coordinates select letters from the Silence Dogood texts. The Declaration bears the fictional clue, rather than serving as the reference book. The Pigpen widget above is a separate teaching exercise; it does not demonstrate that specific film mechanism.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What Is Actually True

Real documents and places should be checked independently of the film. The National Archives’ *National Treasure—Fact or Fiction* program examines the distinction. Architectural shapes, Masonic imagery and genuine historical intelligence work do not by themselves authenticate the movie’s treasure narrative.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Cultural Impact

The franchise helped popularise the image of historical documents as puzzle clues. It could not have inspired Byron Preiss’s *The Secret*, which appeared in 1982, more than two decades before the 2004 film. Specific claims about effects on tourism or later puzzle design require their own evidence.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

*National Treasure* (2004), directed by Jon Turteltaub; plot dialogue checked against the film transcript’s Silence Dogood and Trinity Church scenes. For historical context, National Archives, [“Inside the Vault Series Will Debut With a Look at National Treasure”](<https://www.archives.gov/news/articles/inside-the-vault-national-treasure>) (2024). The museum exercise is illustrative.

#### Embedded script 2 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    // Pigpen substitution demo
    function ntEncode(t) {
      // Map A-Z to 26 symbolic names for display
      const names = ['⌐','┴','¬','├','┼','┤','┌','┬','┐',
                     '⌐•','┴•','¬•','├•','┼•','┤•','┌•','┬•','┐•',
                     '╲','╳','╱','╲•','╳•','╱•','▽','△'];
      return t.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'').split('').map(c=>{
        const i=c.charCodeAt(0)-65; return names[i]||c;
      }).join(' ') + ' (Pigpen grid)';
    }
```

A military code built from Navajo vocabulary and a spelling alphabet, developed and used by Navajo Marines.

Never publicly broken in wartime service; a historical military code.

#### Begin with the men’s own accounts

The Smithsonian’s [Native Words, Native Warriors: Code Talking](<https://americanindian.si.edu/nk360/code-talkers/code-talking/>) brings together code talkers’ accounts of training and service. Its [Coming Home section](<https://americanindian.si.edu/nk360/code-talkers/coming-home/>) includes Carl Gorman’s recollection of returning to his community.

After chapter 12, compare what training required with what returning home required. The testimony preserves experiences that a vocabulary table cannot. These are curated historical accounts; the browser demonstration below is a teaching aid.

#### Why This Matters

Navajo Code Talkers combined fluent speech with a memorised military vocabulary and spelling alphabet. Their speed and effectiveness depended on training as well as a language unfamiliar to most enemy listeners.

In the public record, this system was never publicly broken by cryptanalysis in wartime service. That historical record does not establish security today; this obsolete system is presented for historical study.

A second message: code terms and spelling

**Original exercise message: ATTACK GUAM.** Compare the whole-term entry for ATTACK with spelling every letter. GUAM is spelled in both versions. The selected dictionary entries follow the [Navajo Code Talkers’ Dictionary, revised 15 June 1945](<https://www.history.navy.mil/research/library/online-reading-room/title-list-alphabetically/n/navajo-code-talker-dictionary.html>). The dots and slash below are modern display separators, not a transcription of a wartime transmission.

 [Input navajo-whole: type=checkbox; initial value=; checked]  Use the whole-term entry for ATTACK
 [Input navajo-alternate: type=checkbox; initial value=]  Use alternative spelling entries

Changing spelling alternatives preserves the intended letters. Fluent Navajo alone does not supply the specialized military meanings or the spelling convention; both required training. This small selection is not the complete dictionary, a pronunciation guide or a modern encryption recommendation.

Reading connections: Doris A. Paul, *The Navajo Code Talkers* (1973), printed pp. 38–41; Sally McClain, *Navajo Weapon: The Navajo Code Talkers* (2001), printed pp. 50–55.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

 Historical Context

This exhibit honors the Navajo Marines who served as Code Talkers during World War II. The National Archives estimates their number at 375–420. Their work depended on a designed military code, memorisation and communication skills; it remained classified until 1968.

Philip Johnston proposed using Navajo for Marine Corps communications in 1942. The programme developed a specialised code; ordinary fluency in Navajo alone was not equivalent to knowing all its military meanings.

Some of the original 29 code developers served in the later stages of the Guadalcanal campaign in 1942; the original training group should not be equated with a single deployment. The Navajo Nation’s historical account quotes Major Howard Connor, 5th Marine Division signal officer at Iwo Jima: *"Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."*

The programme was declassified in 1968. In 2001 the original 29 recruits were honoured with Congressional Gold Medals; later Navajo Code Talkers received silver medals.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

 How It Works

The code assigned specialised Navajo terms to military concepts. Operators memorised it, but written dictionaries also existed: the Navy preserves a code-talker dictionary revised on 15 June 1945. The alphabet below can also be checked in the [CIA’s reproduction of that dictionary’s alphabet section](<https://www.cia.gov/stories/story/navajo-code-talkers-and-the-unbreakable-code/>).

```text
Military terms → Navajo words by meaning:

Fighter plane   = da-he-tih-hi    "hummingbird"
Bomber          = jay-sho         "buzzard"
Submarine       = besh-lo         "iron fish"
Destroyer       = ca-lo           "shark"
Battleship      = lo-tso          "whale"
General         = bih-keh-he      "war chief"
Colonel         = atsah-besh-le-gai "silver eagle"
America         = ne-he-mah       "our mother"
```

For words or names not assigned a codebook entry — a phonetic alphabet was used, each letter sent as a Navajo word whose English meaning began with that letter:

```text
Phonetic alphabet:
A = WOL-LA-CHEE (ant)
G = KLIZZIE (goat)
I = TKIN (ice)
M = TSIN-TLITI (match)
O = A-KHA (oil)
U = SHI-DA (uncle)
W = GLOE-IH (weasel)

"IWO" = TKIN, GLOE-IH, A-KHA

(Words already in the codebook were sent whole:
"attack" = AL-TAH-JE-JAY)
```

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-shield"></use></svg>
```

 Wartime Performance and Limits

🛡️

No successful Japanese cryptanalytic break is established in the cited wartime record. That is a historical operational result, not proof of mathematical secrecy.

Several practical obstacles confronted an interceptor:

- Navajo was unfamiliar to most Japanese analysts; this does not mean it had no writing, grammar or dictionaries.

- The specialised military meanings and spelling alphabet had to be learned in addition to the language.

- Fluent speakers could transmit and interpret the code quickly in difficult field conditions.

- Training and disciplined use supported the system; unfamiliarity alone is not a modern security guarantee.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

 What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Navajo Code | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Security through linguistic complexity | Security through mathematical complexity — modern encryption must withstand analysis even when its algorithm is known |
| Shared knowledge as the key | Pre-shared keys (PSK): both parties must possess the same secret before communication |
| Memorised code vocabulary | Pre-shared secrets require a protected distribution process; public-key methods offer a different way to establish keys |
| Historical secrecy and later publication | Publication of a historical code does not imply forward secrecy, which is a separate property of modern key establishment |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

 Can You Break This?

A short Navajo Code message. Use what you just learned.

KLIZZIE SHI-DA WOL-LA-CHEE TSIN-TLITI

Hint: Each Navajo word = one letter. A=ant, G=goat, M=match, U=uncle

 Reveal Answer

G U A M

Historical Performance

No measured percentage can express this code’s resistance to attack. The wartime record should be considered alongside training, available personnel, vocabulary consistency and the adversary’s access.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-quill"></use></svg>
```

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

 Beyond Navajo: Other Code Talker Programs

The US military also used other Indigenous-language code systems:

- **Choctaw (WWI):** Choctaw soldiers used their language for US Army communications in France.

- **Comanche (WWII):** The programme initially recruited 17 men. Comanche Code Talkers served with the 4th Infantry Division in Europe; not all 17 recruits served with that division in combat.

- **Hopi (WWII):** Hopi servicemen also worked as code talkers in the Pacific.

🧭

The [Library of Congress Veterans History Project](<https://www.loc.gov/collections/veterans-history-project-collection/serving-our-voices/diverse-experiences-in-service/navajo-code-talkers/>) preserves first-person accounts. The National Archives article [“Semper Fidelis, Code Talkers”](<https://www.archives.gov/publications/prologue/2001/winter/navajo-code-talkers.html>) (2001) documents the code’s development and operational limitations. Historical effectiveness should not be replaced with a numerical security score.

### NEMA — Swiss Rotor Machine

Enable JavaScript to use this interactive. The worked example below explains the same steps.

#### Why This Matters

NEMA shows that a rotor cipher has two designs to understand: the permutations inside its electrical wheels and the mechanism that moves them. Switzerland gave those jobs separate wheels. The resulting machine is more instructive than an Enigma with an extra rotor: its stepping decisions come from two mechanical drive systems.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

NEMA, short for *NEue MAschine* (“new machine”), replaced the Swiss Army’s commercial Enigma K after its traffic had proved vulnerable. Development began during WWII; the Swiss Army issued NEMA operating instructions dated 30 April 1947. Zellweger manufactured the machine in Uster. Training and war-reserve versions used different stepping wheels; diplomatic machines were another variant.

The 1947 date identifies the postwar machine, rather than its wartime design work. The military configuration in this exhibit is deliberately fixed so that visitors can follow every wheel position.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Current enters a static entry wheel, passes through four cipher rotors, reaches a rotating reflector, and returns through the rotors in reverse. There is no plugboard. The reflector makes the operation reciprocal: reset to the same key and run the ciphertext to recover the plaintext.

Each cipher wheel has a separate mechanical stepping wheel. Notches determine which neighbouring wheels can move, and a second track on the red drive wheel gates a slower transmission. Decisions are made from the old positions; eligible wheels then step backwards before the letter is transformed. The reflector can step too.

```text
Fixed wheels (left → right): A/12  B/13  C/14  D/15
Red wheel: 22/1
Start windows: MQQPZQSOEV
Input:  AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
Output: HRSBVOOTZUCRWLMGRMGVWYWOVNF
```

This example is checked against the published rmsk2 NEMA test, whose reference ciphertext came from Geoff Sullivan’s simulator. Decryption must start at `MQQPZQSOEV`, not at the final windows printed by the demo.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Security and Cryptanalytic Limits

The military mechanism has a maximum state period of 17,576 keypresses. A reflector also prevents a letter from encrypting to itself. Those structures constrain a cryptanalyst’s search even though the number of possible initial settings is much larger than the period.

This exhibit does not assert a documented operational break of Swiss NEMA traffic. It presents an obsolete machine and makes no claim of modern security. A message, key schedule, and operating procedure must be evaluated together.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

What This Demo Models

The demo implements the historical A–D wiring, the military 12–15 stepping wheels, red wheel 22/1, moving reflector, and ten lower-row window positions. It omits alternative wheel selections, training and diplomatic variants, number-shift conventions, and message-key procedures. It is a reconstruction for study, not a tool for protecting messages.


## P108 — NFC Authentication: When the Tag Stays Unlocked — The Cipher Museum

- Site path: `ciphers/nfc-deployment.html`
- Public page: https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/nfc-deployment.html
- Snapshot source SHA-256: `c2413d0cfcaa49bd878dd813506707dbbfbd4fc26aa5b888e881bcaed091ec66`

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>) › [Hall XI: Modern Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/modern-crypto.html>) ›NFC Authentication: When the Tag Stays Unlocked

Exhibit 172 of 174 Modern cryptography · research case study

### NFC Authentication: When the Tag Stays Unlocked

A case study of protocol state, key storage, integrity checks and counterfeit hardware.

Protocol and deployment case: results depend on tag model, configuration and attacker access; not a break of AES.

Systems Ultralight C / AES · NTAG 22x DNA

Security question Authentication state and post-authentication commands

Scope Device- and configuration-dependent attacks

Source version Preprint revision 1.1 · 28 August 2026

#### Authentication is only one step

The 2026 “BREAKMEIFYOUCAN!” study examines MIFARE Ultralight C, Ultralight AES, NTAG 223/224 DNA and several compatible or counterfeit products. Its central lesson is that protocol state, writable key storage, integrity checks, key diversification and hardware quality can determine the outcome even when a device uses 3DES or AES.

This is a deployment and protocol case, not a break of the AES primitive. The tag model and configuration matter: results from one counterfeit family do not automatically apply to genuine NXP silicon or every installation.

**Hardware evidence limit:** in §14 the authors report obtaining a few NTAG 223 DNA StatusDetect samples but **no NTAG 224 DNA samples**. Their NTAG 224 DNA interpretations are preliminary, based on documentation and similarities to tested products; they are not measurements on that model.

#### The relay leaves the tag authenticated

In the paper’s relay scenario, the attacker’s goal is to leave the **tag** in an authenticated state. The legitimate reader may time out while the tag accepts the relayed exchange. That is more specific than the usual story of persuading a reader that a distant card is nearby.

Subsequent actions depend on the tag’s access controls and command integrity. Where authenticated key storage remains writable, partial overwrites can reduce the unknown key material. Multiple tags sharing a key can make recovery easier. These conditions belong next to the result; “uses AES” alone does not describe the system.

#### Configuration changes the attack surface

|  Condition to inspect |  Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
|  Locked versus writable key/configuration pages |  Controls whether the relevant post-authentication overwrite path is available. |
|  Command integrity, including enforced CMAC where supported |  Enforced Ultralight AES CMAC protects against unauthorized command injection. The paper separately describes relayed tearing of genuine WRITE commands, conditional on reader timing and the relevant writable storage; CMAC does not make these distinct attack paths equivalent. |
|  Shared versus diversified keys |  Several tags using the same secret can support attacks that are unavailable in that form with per-tag keys. Diversification does not prove every other path safe. |
|  Genuine versus compatible/counterfeit hardware |  Randomness, lock behavior and implementation details differ. Fast results on weak counterfeit generators are separate from genuine-tag results. |
|  Relay timing and authenticated state |  A reader timeout does not by itself demonstrate that the tag returned to an unauthenticated state. |

#### Demonstration, extrapolation and theory

The paper distinguishes implemented attacks from workload estimates and theoretical proposals. In particular, its single-tag Ultralight C proposal in §17 is theoretical. It requires unlocked key pages and access to a legitimate reader. The first 28-bit segment alone is estimated to require about 777 days at two reader-assisted attempts per second; further recovery stages follow. The assumed number of EEPROM writes also exceeds the guaranteed endurance, and the paper’s five-million-write experiment does not demonstrate completion of that first stage. It must not be presented as the fast counterfeit-tag demonstration.

This exhibit follows revision 1.1, dated 28 August 2026. The revision corrects an earlier recovered-bit extrapolation. Numbers copied from an older summary can therefore misrepresent the paper’s current evidence.

A browser demonstration cannot measure physical distance securely. Crypto Lab’s distance-bounding work is a related protocol lesson; this museum exhibit supplies the device history and the distinctions between authentication, proximity, integrity and key storage.

#### Primary source and connections

Nathan Nye and coauthors, [“BREAKMEIFYOUCAN!: Exploiting Keyspace Reduction and Relay Attacks in 3DES and AES-protected NFC Technologies”](<https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/100>), ePrint 2026/100, revision 1.1 (28 August 2026). This is a preprint; ePrint posting does not establish peer review. See §4, §12.1–12.3 for command integrity and tearing, §14 for the NTAG sample limitation, §17 and Appendix A; PDF pp. 3–5, 15–16, 19–22 and 23–30.

### Nihilist Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Russian revolutionaries vs the Tsar's secret police — arithmetic as armor

Frequency analysis of digit pairs · Kasiski-equivalent

InventorTraditionally associated with Russian revolutionaries

Year~1880s

Key TypePolybius square + numeric keyword

Broken ByFrequency analysis of digit pairs · Kasiski-equivalent

Modern LessonLayered cipher operations

#### Why This Matters

Traditionally associated with Russian revolutionaries, this cipher combines Polybius coordinates with Vigenère-style addition — a system designed to be memorized, performed without equipment, and changed instantly when compromised.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The name is traditionally associated with Russian revolutionaries of the late nineteenth century. Kahn qualifies their authorship as possible, not established. The additive system shown here converts plaintext and a repeating keyword to Polybius coordinates and adds the resulting integers.

The cipher combined Polybius square substitution with Vigenère-style numeric addition, producing numerical ciphertext that looked like arbitrary number sequences to an interceptor.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

```text
Polybius square (keyword: NIHILIST, J merged into I):
   1  2  3  4  5
1  N  I  H  L  S
2  T  A  B  C  D
3  E  F  G  K  M
4  O  P  Q  R  U
5  V  W  X  Y  Z

Plaintext:  A   T   T   A   C   K
Polybius:  22  21  21  22  24  34
Key(=NEMO): 11  31  35  41  11  31
Cipher:    33  52  56  63  35  65
```

Letters become two-digit Polybius coordinates, then added to key coordinates — producing numeric ciphertext

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Frequency Analysis on Digit Sums

Complexity: Moderate

The numeric ciphertext has non-uniform digit-sum distribution. Common letters produce common Polybius values; added to a repeating key, the sums cluster around predictable ranges. With enough ciphertext, the key length can be found (Kasiski-equivalent for numbers), and each key digit can be recovered through frequency analysis of the numeric residuals.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Nihilist Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Polybius + addition (two operations) | AES combines several operations; its final round omits MixColumns |
| Numeric output hides letter frequencies | Numeric notation alone hides no statistics; modern security requires a defined construction and attack model |
| Repeating numeric key | Modern designs derive round keys; distinctness alone is not a security guarantee |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

Two Nihilist Ciphers

The name also appears in **Nihilist transposition**, a different construction that reorders rows and columns. It should not be confused with the additive substitution shown here. A source using the name alone needs further procedural detail before its method can be identified.

Operationally, archives and memoirs use the same label for both. Distinguishing which form is present is a key first step in successful cryptanalysis.

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), discussion of Russian cryptography, on the additive cipher and its qualified attribution; Helen Fouché Gaines, *Cryptanalysis: A Study of Ciphers and Their Solution* (1939; Dover reprint 1956), on Nihilist transposition and additive substitution as distinct systems.
