Hall X · Codebreakers WWII · Pacific

### Joseph Rochefort

He led Station HYPO’s team, whose signals intelligence helped US commanders prepare for the Battle of Midway.

Codebreaker Biography

Born1900, Dayton, Ohio

Died1976, Torrance, California

BranchUS Navy

RoleCommander, Station HYPO (Combat Intelligence Unit, Pearl Harbor)

Key BreakJN-25, partially recovered — Imperial Japanese Navy main operational code

Battle supportedMidway, June 4–7, 1942

Posthumous honorDistinguished Service Medal (1986)

⚓

#### Joseph Rochefort

1900 – 1976

Joseph Rochefort was a US Navy codebreaker, linguist, and intelligence officer who commanded Station HYPO — the Combat Intelligence Unit at Pearl Harbor — from early 1941 until his reassignment in 1942. Working in an improvised basement operations center, often sleeping in a bathrobe beside his desk, Rochefort led the team that cracked enough of the Japanese JN-25 additive cipher to name the target of Japan's next major offensive. His intelligence enabled Admiral Nimitz to position three carriers at Midway; the resulting battle sank four Japanese fleet carriers and dealt Japan a major carrier loss in the Pacific.

##### Why This Person Matters

HYPO’s cryptanalysts, linguists and traffic analysts provided intelligence that helped Admiral Nimitz assess Japanese plans. Their work supported fleet decisions; it was not a single person’s victory. The 1986 posthumous Distinguished Service Medal recognized Rochefort’s contribution after earlier efforts to secure that honor had failed.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

The Road to HYPO

Rochefort alternated sea assignments with cryptanalytic, language and intelligence work. Laurance Safford sent him to Hawaii to command Station HYPO in early 1941, before the Pearl Harbor attack. He assembled a team whose analysis of Japanese naval communications became crucial to planning for Midway.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

The Midway Intelligence

In May 1942, analysts believed the Japanese designation AF referred to Midway. A false report of a water shortage, devised through discussion involving Rochefort and Jasper Holmes, helped test that identification. NSA’s account identifies a Japanese message translated by FRUMEL on 22 May. This was corroborating intelligence, not an automatic decryption of all JN-25 traffic. Nimitz’s preparations and the subsequent naval battle also depended on reconnaissance, operational decisions and combat.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

Injustice and Legacy

Rochefort was reassigned after Midway amid disputes over the intelligence work and its recognition. His later service included a floating-drydock command and leadership of the Pacific Strategic Intelligence Group. On 30 May 1986, President Reagan presented the posthumous Distinguished Service Medal to his family; the Reagan Presidential Library preserves the ceremony record. His removal should not be described as the end of all later intelligence work.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Born | 1900, Dayton, Ohio |
| --- | --- |
| Died | 1976, Torrance, California |
| Branch | US Navy |
| Role | Commander, Station HYPO (Combat Intelligence Unit, Pearl Harbor) |
| Key Break | JN-25, partially recovered — Imperial Japanese Navy main operational code |
| Battle supported | Midway, June 4–7, 1942 |
| Posthumous honor | Distinguished Service Medal (1986) |

#### Sources and Reading

National Security Agency, [“CAPT Joseph J. Rochefort, USN”](<https://www.nsa.gov/History/Cryptologic-History/Historical-Figures/Historical-Figures-View/Article/1623007/capt-joseph-j-rochefort-usn/>), on his early-1941 appointment and HYPO’s team; “Water Shortage” (2021), on the AF test; Reagan Presidential Library, photo collection C35259 (01), 30 May 1986, for the medal. The VA’s 2023 biography gives his birth year as 1900 and explains the 1898 date used for enlistment; NSA’s brief biography retains 1898 and misnames the medal, so those two details are not adopted from that page. Intelligence supported the fleet’s decisions; it was not the sole cause of victory.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall I: World Origins of Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/ancient.html>)› The Rosetta Stone

Hall I · World Origins · Egypt → Europe Ptolemaic Egypt · 196 BCE

### The Rosetta Stone

Three scripts, one decree — and the key to fourteen centuries of silenced writing.

Two languages, three scripts; Champollion’s 1822 breakthrough was part of a longer decipherment.

Issued196 BCE, Memphis, Egypt

Discovered1799, Rashid (Rosetta), by French soldiers

ScriptsHieroglyphic, Demotic, Ancient Greek

Deciphered byJean-François Champollion (1822), building on Thomas Young

Modern LessonParallel texts can constrain a proposed decipherment

#### Three-Script Viewer

Compare the roles of the three scripts. These descriptions are teaching summaries, not facsimiles or a reconstruction of Champollion’s working notes. Track B exhibit — visualization rather than encryption.

Hieroglyphic Demotic Greek

 Comparison topic: the royal name Ptolemy  [Input input: type=hidden; initial value=PTOLEMY]

##### Why This Matters

Knowledge of hieroglyphic writing declined in late antiquity. The Rosetta Stone helped its later decipherment because it preserves a decree in two languages, Egyptian and Greek, using three scripts: hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek. It is a multilingual inscription, not an encrypted message.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The stone is a priestly decree affirming the cult of Ptolemy V Epiphanes, issued in 196 BCE. Copies were placed in major temples; the surviving fragment was found in 1799 at Rashid (anglicized "Rosetta") by French soldiers building a fort during Napoleon's Egyptian campaign. After the British defeat of the French, the stone passed to the British Museum, where it has been on near-continuous display since 1802.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Champollion's Breakthrough

Thomas Young identified important phonetic values in royal names. In 1822 Jean-François Champollion showed that phonetic writing was not confined to foreign names: it also helped explain native Egyptian names. His knowledge of Coptic was central to understanding a writing system combining phonetic signs with other kinds of signs.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Cryptography by Analogy

The parallel texts helped scholars relate known content to unfamiliar writing. This resembles the usefulness of a crib in historical cryptanalysis, but translation and script decipherment are not encryption. Modern encryption is designed to resist known-plaintext attacks; publishing some plaintext does not automatically compromise unrelated encrypted messages.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

```javascript
    (function () {

      };
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode('hiero'); });
```

Exhibit 42 of 174 Modern · 1980s

### ROT13

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

The Caesar cipher with shift 13 — its own inverse, ubiquitous on the early internet

Knowing the system

OriginEarly Usenet culture (1980s)

Year1980s popularisation; exact first use not established

Key TypeNone (fixed shift of 13)

Broken ByKnowing the system

Modern LessonObfuscation ≠ encryption

#### Why This Matters

ROT13 is a special case of the Caesar cipher with shift 13. Because the English alphabet has 26 letters, applying ROT13 twice returns the original — so the same operation encrypts and decrypts. It became the conventional way on early Usenet to hide spoilers, punchlines, and offensive jokes from readers who did not want to see them.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

ROT13 became an early Usenet convention; this exhibit does not establish its first inventor or first use. It was never meant to be secure. Its role was social: a small mechanical step the reader had to take to opt in to seeing potentially objectionable content. Newsreader software offered ROT13 decoding as a convenience. The cipher remains in active use today in puzzle games and in spoiler tags.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Shift each letter forward by 13:

```text
HELLO → URYYB
URYYB → HELLO   (apply twice = original)
```

Because 13 + 13 = 26 = 0 (mod 26), the operation is its own inverse.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Knowing It Is ROT13

Complexity: None

There is no key. The transformation is fixed and public. ROT13 provides zero confidentiality. Its only value is mild reader effort — enough to prevent accidental viewing, not enough to deter even a curious reader.

Variants Equally Weak

Complexity: None

ROT5 (digits) and ROT47 (printable ASCII) are similar conventions for hiding text. These are fixed public mappings, easily reversed once the convention is known.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from ROT13 | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Self-inverse over the alphabet | XOR with the same key in stream ciphers |
| Convention as opt-in viewing | Modern spoiler-tags and content-warning toggles |
| Obfuscation vs. encryption | Modern crypto distinguishes confidentiality from mere encoding |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| Origin | Early Usenet culture (1980s) |
| Year | 1980s popularisation; exact first use not established |

### Rasterschlüssel 44 (RS44)

Enable JavaScript for the animation. The worked example below gives the same documented procedure.

#### Why This Matters

A large settings count is not evidence of security. Following a complete original example makes conventions observable: a changed boundary, pairing rule or final cell changes the ciphertext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The *Rasterschlüssel 44* was a German paper-and-pencil field cipher intended to replace Double Playfair in 1944. This exhibit follows [*Schlüsselanleitung zum Rasterschlüssel 44*, Ausgabe 27. März 1944](<https://cryptocellar.org/wmc/schluesselanleitung-zum-rs44.pdf>), with the second addendum’s clarification of the beginning boundary and column counting. It does not implement the October 1944 change to a directly selected readout column.

A daily key supplied the black-and-white stencil, permuted column ranks, coordinate labels, name alphabets and indicator substitution. Operators wrote on thin grid paper over the stencil. A planned 1 August introduction appears in contemporary Allied reports; actual adoption varied across services and units.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Exact Procedure

- Select an indicated beginning row and physical column. If their intersection is black, advance in row order to the next white cell. Include the beginning itself when it is white.

- Enter prepared plaintext left to right through white cells only. Continue through successive rows, wrapping from the bottom to the top if necessary. The stencil has 24 × 25 cells, with exactly ten writing cells in each row: 240 available cells.

- Add the digits of the tactical-time minute and message length. From the indicated beginning column, move that many physical columns to the right, wrapping at column 25. The first step excludes the beginning column; returning to it after a full circuit counts normally.

- Read the occupied cells top to bottom in the selected column, then by ascending numerical column rank, cycling from 25 to 1. Skip every unoccupied cell, including an unused gap when the message wraps.

- For decryption, mark the same occupied cells from the length and starting position. Fill them in that column order, then read in the original writing order.

The transmitted body was 60–200 letters, leaving at least 40 white cells unused. Shorter messages required operator-chosen *Wahlwörter*, with doubled boundary letters. Longer messages were divided into separately keyed parts of differing lengths. The teaching mode permits shorter bodies without silently adding fillers.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Original Manual Example

Printed pp. 12–13 and Fig. 2 on p. 18 give a complete 77-letter example. Beginning: row `ae` (5), column `bb` (14); tactical time 1203. The digit sum is 0 + 3 + 7 + 7 = 17, so readout begins in physical column `ee` (6), rank 19.

```text
Prepared plaintext:
FEINDGREIFTSEITELFXVIERFUENFUHRBEIAAIGQALFISIGQALFISEEMITAQTPANZNAQSUEDWESTAN

Ciphertext body:
DIANMRQTVFNNRISIFFGPUEFZGNAEEHAEUTAIIEADAGQQLWIBSFFXUTITEEAAENIQSSIRLIEFESELT
```

The test suite also reproduces the 64-letter wrap example on printed pp. 14–15 and Fig. 4, p. 20. These expected ciphertexts were transcribed from the manual, not generated by the new engine.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Cryptanalysis and Limits

Captain Walter J. Fried’s reports document Allied work during 1944. Report F-79 (22 August) describes fitting messages to a captured stencil. F-93 (18 September) reports recovering stencil rows from retransmissions and messages sent twice from the same starting point, then exploiting stereotyped traffic and cribs. It also describes constructing 36 sliding masks to test probable plaintext against known column order.

These are conditional attacks, not a claim that every isolated message was solved. Captured material, repeated arrangements and operator habits mattered. The daily stencil and 25-column permutation create many possible settings, but counting them as “bits of security” ignores their structure and the traffic available to an attacker. Letter frequencies are preserved.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Reconstruction and Teaching Limits

The default stencil and ranks are factual transcriptions of the manual’s worked key. You can vary the beginning and minute; the engine also accepts a validated custom stencil and rank permutation. This page fixes the daily stencil so the published answer stays reproducible.

The demo accepts prepared A–Z text. It does not reproduce German preprocessing (CH/CK → Q, ß → SZ, umlauts written out, number words), place-name substitution, encoded message headers, key distribution, coordinate-use marks, emergency procedures or operator-chosen filler words. Accent stripping is a museum input convenience and is *not* historical German message preparation. No padding or escape scheme is added.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

The diagrams here are drawn by this site’s renderer. No archival scans or third-party images are reproduced.

Modern · 1977

### RSA

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 2 4 5v6c0 5 3.5 9 8 11 4.5-2 8-6 8-11V5z"></path><path d="m9 12 2 2 4-4"></path></svg>
```

Secure (Modern)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

An early practical public-key construction supporting distinct encryption and signature schemes, with public and private keys.

OriginRon Rivest, Adi Shamir, Leonard Adleman (MIT, 1977); Clifford Cocks (GCHQ, 1973, classified)

Year1977

TypePublic-key encryption & digital signature (asymmetric)

StatusIn daily use; NIST is preparing a post-quantum migration (RSA breaks under Shor's algorithm on a sufficiently large quantum computer)

Modern RoleTLS certificates, code signing, PGP/GPG, SSH host keys, JWT signatures, document signing

#### Try a pair of keys

**Toy model — no real security.** Choose two different primes between 2 and 97. This is unpadded textbook arithmetic with deliberately tiny numbers, not secure RSA encryption. It does not authenticate the person offering a public key.

Prime p [Input rsa-p: type=number; initial value=11]  Prime q [Input rsa-q: type=number; initial value=17]  Public exponent e [Input rsa-e: type=number; initial value=7]  Message number [Input rsa-message: type=number; initial value=42]

Use 1 < e < φ(n), coprime to φ(n). The message must be from 0 to n−1. The model computes n = pq, φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1), and the inverse d of e modulo φ(n).

Encrypt and decrypt

Start with the example, then change a prime or the message.

The construction is described in [RFC 8017, §3–5](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017#section-3>); its complete encryption schemes require additional encoding.

Enable JavaScript to run the toy model. The arithmetic and its limits are described below.

#### Why This Matters

RSA provided an early practical construction for public-key encryption and digital signatures. These are different schemes built from related arithmetic, not merely one encryption operation run backwards. Secure encodings, key separation, authentication and application context are essential. A valid signature establishes a relationship to a key; it does not by itself establish a person's identity or resolve every non-repudiation dispute.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Rivest, Shamir and Adleman developed RSA at MIT in 1977, following the public-key research of Diffie and Hellman. Their construction was publicly described in 1977 and published in Communications of the ACM in 1978. Clifford Cocks had found a related construction at GCHQ in 1973, but that work remained classified until 1997.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Pick two large primes *p* and *q* (each ~1024 bits for RSA-2048). Compute *n = p·q* and *φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1)*. Choose a public exponent *e* coprime to *φ(n)* — almost always 65537. Compute the private exponent *d ≡ e<sup>−1</sup> mod φ(n)*.

Public key is *(n, e)*; private key is *(n, d)*. To encrypt message *m*: *c = m<sup>e</sup> mod n*. To decrypt: *m = c<sup>d</sup> mod n*. The math works because of Euler's theorem: *m<sup>ed</sup> ≡ m mod n* for any *m* coprime to *n*. Factoring *n* lets an attacker compute a private exponent. The Chinese remainder theorem extends this correctness argument to all message representatives from 0 to *n*−1, not only those coprime to *n*.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-shield"></use></svg>
```

Security & Cryptanalysis

Factoring the modulus breaks RSA, but general RSA inversion has not been proved equivalent to factoring. Security claims must also specify the encoding and attack model: textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable. RFC 8017 defines schemes such as RSA-OAEP for encryption and RSA-PSS for signatures and recommends using a key pair for one scheme. A sufficiently capable quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break RSA. [Read a quantum resource estimate with its hardware, retry and timing assumptions](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/modern-attack-evidence.html#quantum-resources>). NIST finalized ML-KEM for key establishment and ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for signatures in 2024; these serve different roles rather than providing one universal RSA replacement.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Where You Use It Today

| Where | How RSA is Used |
| --- | --- |
| TLS / HTTPS certificates | RSA is supported alongside other certificate signature algorithms; key size and policy depend on the deployment |
| Code signing | RSA signatures are supported in several software-signing ecosystems; the selected scheme varies |
| PGP / GPG | RSA remains supported; modern OpenPGP implementations also support other key types |
| SSH host keys | RSA keys can use SHA-256 or SHA-512 signatures. OpenSSH 8.8 disabled the SHA-1-based `ssh-rsa` signature scheme by default |
| JWT signatures | `RS256` is an RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signature option; applications must restrict accepted algorithms |

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Exhibit 12 of 174 19th Century

### Running Key Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A book-length key removes short repetition, but keeps language patterns

Source text identification · Statistical analysis

InventorNo single inventor established here

YearHistorical running-key family

Key TypeFull-length key text (book or speech)

Broken BySource text identification · Statistical analysis

Modern LessonA long key is not necessarily a random key

#### Why This Matters

A running key replaces Vigenère’s short repeating keyword with a long passage. Removing that short period does not make the key random: natural language remains biased and structured. A book passage therefore does not give the perfect secrecy of a one-time pad.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The running key cipher applies Vigenère's arithmetic but replaces the short repeating keyword with a message-length passage from a pre-agreed text — a book, a speech, or a newspaper article. Kasiski's usual search for a repeated keyword period is no longer the same route to an attack. Accidental repetitions can still occur, and the structure of the plaintext and key text remains available to statistical analysis.

A shared book offers an inconspicuous source of key material: both parties need the same edition and an agreed starting position. It does not provide a secret, uniformly random, independent pad, and sharing the book does not remove the need to manage those choices securely.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

```text
Plain: ATTACKATDAWN
Key:   FROMTHISBOOK
Cipher: each letter shifted by key letter

A+F=F, T+R=K, T+O=H, A+M=M,
C+T=V, K+H=R, A+I=I, T+S=L...
```

An attacker can test guesses for the source passage and starting position. Even without finding the book, statistical attacks can exploit language patterns in both the plaintext and key. Keeping the source unidentified is therefore not a sufficient security condition.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 380 150" style="width:100%;max-width:380px;height:auto" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Running key cipher using book text as key">
  <style>text{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace;fill:#EDE5D4}rect{rx:4}</style>
  <!-- Book -->
  <rect x="10" y="5" width="80" height="55" fill="rgba(201,168,76,.06)" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.2)" stroke-width="1" rx="3"></rect>
  <text x="25" y="22" font-size="7" fill="#706878">From this</text>
  <text x="25" y="32" font-size="7" fill="#706878">book we</text>
  <text x="25" y="42" font-size="7" fill="#706878">take our</text>
  <text x="25" y="52" font-size="7" fill="#706878">key text</text>
  <text x="50" y="72" font-size="7" fill="#C9A84C">⇓ key source</text>
  <!-- Alignment -->
  <g transform="translate(10,82)">
    <text x="0" y="14" font-size="9" fill="#5A90C8">Plain:</text>
    <text x="50" y="14" font-size="10">A  T  T  A  C  K  A  T</text>
    <text x="0" y="32" font-size="9" fill="#C9A84C">Key:</text>
    <text x="50" y="32" font-size="10" fill="#C9A84C">F  R  O  M  T  H  I  S</text>
    <line x1="50" y1="36" x2="220" y2="36" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.3)" stroke-width=".5"></line>
    <text x="0" y="52" font-size="9" fill="#5AC8A0">Cipher:</text>
    <text x="50" y="52" font-size="10" fill="#5AC8A0">F  K  H  M  V  R  I  L</text>
  </g>
  <!-- Comparison -->
  <rect x="240" y="5" width="130" height="65" fill="rgba(201,168,76,.04)" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,.12)" stroke-width=".5" rx="5"></rect>
  <text x="250" y="22" font-size="8" fill="#C9A84C">Key = book text</text>
  <text x="250" y="36" font-size="8" fill="#706878">Key length = msg length</text>
  <text x="250" y="50" font-size="8" fill="#C85A5A">But NOT random →</text>
```

Book text used as a key matches message length — but English letter patterns make it weaker than a true one-time pad

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Source Text Attack

Complexity: Depends on the candidate sources and positions

If an attacker identifies the edition and passage used for the key, they can reconstruct that keystream and decrypt the message. A likely book title narrows the search, but the starting position and text preparation still matter.

Statistical Cryptanalysis

Complexity: Hard

Even without knowing the source, the key text has English statistical structure. Both the plaintext and key obey English letter frequencies. This creates detectable second-order patterns that sophisticated statistical attacks can exploit — making the running key cipher weaker than a true one-time pad.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Running Key Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Key length = message length | Necessary but not sufficient for a one-time pad: its secret key must also be uniformly random, independent of the message, and used only once |
| Non-repeating key | Modern stream constructions must avoid reusing keystream under their specified key-and-nonce rules |
| Key source = security weakness | True randomness: OTP keys must be random, not drawn from patterned text |

Reading: Joshua Holden, [*The Mathematics of Secrets: Cryptography from Caesar Ciphers to Digital Encryption*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#holden>) (2017), §5.1 on running-key attacks and §5.2 on one-time pads. A long key and a uniformly random key are different requirements.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall XIII: Cipher Culture](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/culture.html>)› Sator Square

Hall XIII · Culture Roman Empire · 1st–4th c. CE

### Sator Square

A 1st-century Roman five-letter palindromic word square — SATOR · AREPO · TENET · OPERA · ROTAS — readable forwards, backwards, up, and down. The whole square’s 25 letters can form a PATER NOSTER cross, with two A’s and two O’s left over.

Palindromic word square; proposed Christian interpretations remain hypotheses.

RegionRome / Pompeii / Roman Britain

YearEarliest extant example: Pompeii, before 79 CE

Earliest findWall graffito, Pompeii, before 79 CE

TrackB (palindrome verifier)

#### Interactive Exhibit

The widget verifies the four-direction palindrome and runs the famous PATER NOSTER anagram check. Type your own five-by-five word-square candidate to test it. Track B — verification tool.

```text
S A T O R
A R E P O
T E N E T
O P E R A
R O T A S
```

 Test a 5×5 word square (5 words × 5 letters)  [Input input: type=text; initial value=SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS]  Verify symmetry

##### Why This Matters

The square reads SATOR, AREPO, TENET, OPERA, ROTAS in rows and columns. AREPO’s meaning is uncertain. Its letters can also form two PATER NOSTER arms sharing one N, with two A’s and two O’s left over. That anagram is real; interpreting it as an intentional Christian message is a historical hypothesis, not a consequence of the letter count.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Pompeii preserves examples dating before the eruption of 79 CE. The Archaeological Park’s record identifies a first-century graffito from a column of the Palestra Grande (inventory 20565). Its lettering and location are archaeological evidence; proposed religious readings need further interpretation. The version beginning ROTAS has the same symmetry as the SATOR-first arrangement shown here.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

The square is a word puzzle with several symmetries. The PATER NOSTER rearrangement supplies a possible interpretation, but an anagram alone does not establish the maker’s intended message or prove that the object was used for secret communication.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

A word square can be used as a puzzle, an emblem or a literary reference without functioning as an encryption system. Checking its letter counts establishes a mathematical property, while identifying its original purpose is a separate historical question.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

          (function () {
            window.encode = function () {
              var raw = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').toUpperCase().trim().split(/\s+/);
              var out = document.getElementById('output');
              if (raw.length !== 5 || raw.some(function (w) { return !/^[A-Z]{5}$/.test(w); })) {
                out.textContent = 'Need exactly 5 words of 5 letters each.'; return;
              }
              var rows = raw;
              var cols = [0,1,2,3,4].map(function (c) { return rows.map(function (r) { return r[c]; }).join(''); });
              var rowsBack = rows.map(function (r) { return r.split('').reverse().join(''); }).reverse();
              var colsBack = cols.map(function (c) { return c.split('').reverse().join(''); }).reverse();
              var rowEqCol = rows.join('|') === cols.join('|');
              var rowsPalin = rows.join('|') === rowsBack.join('|');
              var allLetters = rows.join('').split('').sort().join('');
              // Two arms share one N; two A and two O remain outside the cross.
              var expected = ('PATERNOSTER' + 'PATERNOSTER'.replace('N','') + 'AAOO').split('').sort().join('');
              var pnCheck = allLetters === expected;
              out.textContent =
                'Rows = Columns?       ' + (rowEqCol ? '\u2705' : '\u274c') + '\n' +
                'Rows = reversed rows? ' + (rowsPalin ? '\u2705' : '\u274c') + '\n' +
                'PATER NOSTER cross + AAOO? ' + (pnCheck ? '\u2705 (anagram possible)' : '\u274c') + '\n\n' +
                (rowEqCol && rowsPalin ? 'Square is fully bi-axial \u2014 a true Sator-class word square.' :
                                          'Not a Sator-class square.');
            };
            document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode(); });
          })();
```

Exhibit 01 of 174 Ancient Sparta · interpretation debated

### Scytale

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A traditional rod-and-strip reconstruction, with a debated historical interpretation

Simple transposition model; historical origin and military use are debated.

OriginSparta, Ancient Greece

YearAncient accounts; reconstructed method not securely dated

Key TypeRod diameter (physical key)

Broken ByBrute force — try different rod diameters

Modern LessonTransposition & key space

#### Why This Matters

The traditional scytale reconstruction illustrates transposition: letters are rearranged rather than substituted. Ancient references to staffs and dispatches do not securely establish this as the first military cipher or date the reconstructed method to 500 BCE.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

 Historical Context

Later accounts, especially Plutarch’s *Life of Lysander*, describe a staff and written strip. The earlier sources and their cryptographic interpretation are disputed. The physical reconstruction below is useful for teaching, but should not be presented as an uncontested account of Spartan practice.

Traditional reconstructions interpret the Spartan staff-and-dispatch accounts as secret military communication. In the transposition model, an unwound strip disrupts the reading order; that demonstration does not settle how the ancient object was used.

The familiar scytale reconstruction illustrates transposition cryptography — the idea that you can hide a message not by changing its letters, but by rearranging their order. AES ShiftRows also rearranges positions, but this structural comparison does not establish a direct design lineage.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

 How It Works

A leather strip (skytale) is wound tightly around a wooden rod. The message is written along the length of the rod. When the strip is unwound, the letters are scrambled. A matching rod restores the intended arrangement physically; an analyst may also recover the arrangement without that rod.

**Key = rod diameter**

```text
Example (3-row rod, message ATTACKATDAWN):

Written along the rod, three turns of the strip:
Row 1: A T T A
Row 2: C K A T
Row 3: D A W N

Unwound, the strip is read down each wrap
of the rod: ACD TKA TAW ATN
(transposition rearranges letter positions)

Unwound strip reads: ACDTKATAWATN
Wrapping on a matching rod restores this reading order;
the equivalent rectangle can also be reconstructed.
```

ℹ️

**About this demo:** To guarantee that Decrypt exactly restores your original message, this demo reversibly escapes the letters X, Q, and Z (as ZA, ZB, ZC) before enciphering, so padding and filler X can never be confused with a real letter. Messages containing X, Q, or Z therefore produce slightly different ciphertext than a strictly classical scytale would. The rectangle is completed with X padding.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

 How It Was Broken

Brute Force — Try Different Rod Diameters

Complexity: Small dimension search in this teaching model

In this transposition model, an attacker can try plausible dimensions and examine the results. The size of that search depends on message length and handling assumptions. No ancient account of a first documented brute-force attack is established here.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

 What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Scytale | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Physical key (rod diameter) | Cryptographic key: a specific parameter shared by sender and receiver |
| Transposition (rearrange, not replace) | AES ShiftRows: cyclic row shifts for diffusion |
| Brute force possible (small key space) | AES-256: 2²⁵⁶ possible keys — exhaustive search infeasible |
| Physical device = key distribution problem | Authenticated Diffie–Hellman can establish a shared secret; unauthenticated exchange remains vulnerable to an active intermediary |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

 Can You Break This?

A short Scytale message. Use what you just learned.

ACDTKATAWATN

Hint: 3-row rod. You can check your answer with the demo above.

 Reveal Answer

Rod width = 3 · Plaintext: ATTACKATDAWN

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

 Difficulty to Break

Trivial 5%

Try candidate dimensions; recognizing the message depends on context.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-quill"></use></svg>
```

 Quick Facts

| Exhibit | 1 of 174 |
| --- | --- |
| Era | Ancient Sparta · interpretation debated |
| Trust | Broken |
| Origin | Spartan accounts; interpretation debated |
| Year | Ancient accounts; reconstructed method not securely dated |
| Broken By | Brute force |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

Was the Scytale Really a Transposition Cipher?

The familiar museum interpretation treats the scytale as an early transposition system: wrap, write, unwrap, and the letters scramble. That reading is pedagogically useful and matches how this exhibit's demo works.

But Satoshi Tomokiyo's revisionist reading of the ancient sources argues that Plutarch, Thucydides, and Aulus Gellius do not clearly describe transposed text at all. On that reading, the scytale may have been closer to a messenger-authentication device or integrity check: a physical token proving that a dispatch belonged with a specific staff, not a true cipher in the later sense.

The safe conclusion is not that the standard story is false, but that the evidence is thinner than most textbook summaries imply. The scytale is both an early cipher lesson and a useful reminder that cryptographic history is reconstructed from imperfect sources.

**References:** Satoshi Tomokiyo, *Scytale Not As a Transposition Cipher*, *Cryptiana*; Plutarch, *Life of Lysander* 19; Thucydides 1.131; Aulus Gellius, *Noctes Atticae* 17.9.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Hall XI: Modern Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/modern-crypto.html>)› SHA-256

Modern · 2002

### SHA-256

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 2 4 5v6c0 5 3.5 9 8 11 4.5-2 8-6 8-11V5z"></path><path d="m9 12 2 2 4-4"></path></svg>
```

Secure (Modern)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

A 256-bit digest for messages shorter than 2<sup>64</sup> bits — one-way, collision-resistant, and the verification engine of the digital world.

OriginNSA (designed); published by NIST as FIPS 180-2 in 2002

Year2002

TypeCryptographic hash function (Merkle-Damgård construction over the SHA-2 compression function) — **not a cipher**

StatusSecure; SHA-3 (Keccak) standardised 2015 as a structural alternative, not a replacement

Modern RoleCertificate signatures, software checksums, selected password KDFs, Bitcoin proof-of-work and selected signature schemes

#### Why This Matters

A cryptographic hash maps a variable-length message to a fixed-length digest. Different inputs must sometimes share a digest; collision resistance means that finding such a pair should be computationally infeasible. SHA-256 is widely used for checksums, signatures and Bitcoin proof-of-work. It has no decryption operation, but an attacker can still guess a low-entropy input and compare its digest. A bare hash also does not authenticate its sender.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

NIST published SHA-1 in 1995 and FIPS 180-2 in August 2002, adding SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. SHA-224 was added in a 2004 change notice. The widely publicized MD5 collisions of 2004 and SHA-1 attacks from 2005 therefore came after this SHA-2 standardization. NIST later selected Keccak through a public competition; SHA-3 was standardized in 2015 as a structurally different family, not because full SHA-256 had been practically broken.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The input is padded so its length is congruent to 448 mod 512, then a 64-bit length is appended. The padded message is split into 512-bit blocks. Each block is processed by the *compression function*, which mixes the block into a 256-bit internal state through 64 rounds of bitwise operations: rotations, XORs, AND/OR/NOT, modular addition, and round constants derived from the cube roots of the first 64 primes. After the last block the internal state is the hash output.

Two security goals are preimage resistance (finding an input for a specified digest) and collision resistance (finding any two distinct inputs with the same digest). Generic classical work factors for an ideal 256-bit hash are about 2<sup>256</sup> and 2<sup>128</sup> respectively. These are search-model estimates, not a guarantee that a guessable password takes that much work to recover.

#### Hash bytes, preserve field boundaries

The tuples `["ab", "c"]` and `["a", "bc"]` both become `abc` when their fields are simply joined. Both hash inputs are the same bytes, `61 62 63` in hexadecimal. Their equal digest is an encoding ambiguity, **not a collision attack on SHA-256**.

For this two-field teaching format, encode each field as its four-byte unsigned big-endian UTF-8 byte length followed by its UTF-8 bytes. A receiver checks each length and recovers exactly two fields, rejecting truncation or extra data. Lengths count bytes: `é` encodes as `c3 a9`, so its length is 2.

Swipe or scroll the table horizontally to see every column. Keyboard: focus the table area and use the arrow keys.

Unambiguous encoding for two UTF-8 fields (hexadecimal)

| Fields | Length-prefixed bytes |
| --- | --- |
| `["ab", "c"]` | `00 00 00 02 61 62 00 00 00 01 63` |
| `["a", "bc"]` | `00 00 00 01 61 00 00 00 02 62 63` |

These encoded messages have different SHA-256 digests. Encoding removes this field-boundary ambiguity; it does not make hash collisions mathematically impossible. A complete protocol also defines field types, context and allowed representations. TupleHash is a standardized tuple-hashing construction based on cSHAKE, distinct from SHA-256 and from this teaching encoding.

Inspect an existing application in [Crypto Lab: Context Ward](<https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-context-ward/>): switch to **Full lab** to examine length-prefixed leaf bytes and sealed fields. Its fixed teaching keys and scripted agent are not a production security guarantee.

Source: David Wong, *Real-World Cryptography* (2021 edition), §2.5.4, “Avoid ambiguous hashing with TupleHash,” PDF pp. 120–123 in the reflowed edition, which has no printed pagination. The two-field byte example is a museum adaptation.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-shield"></use></svg>
```

Security & Cryptanalysis

No practical collision attack is known against full SHA-256. Its Merkle–Damgård structure permits length extension: from H(secret ‖ data) and its length, an attacker can derive a digest for an extended message without learning the secret. Therefore that construction is not a safe message authentication code. Use an appropriate keyed construction such as HMAC-SHA-256; changing to an unkeyed SHA-3 hash does not itself provide authentication. Idealized Grover search reduces the generic preimage query exponent, but does not give an inexpensive real-world attack or settle every post-quantum application.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Where You Use It Today

| Where | How SHA-256 is Used |
| --- | --- |
| TLS / HTTPS | SHA-256 is common; certificate signatures can use other approved hashes and signature algorithms |
| Git | Git supports SHA-1 repositories and a SHA-256 object format; repository format determines the identifier |
| Bitcoin | Proof-of-work searches for a double-SHA-256 digest, interpreted as an integer, below the current target |
| Password storage | Used in PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 and scrypt. Argon2 instead uses BLAKE2b internally; raw SHA-256 is unsuitable for password storage |
| Software integrity | `sha256sum`, package manager checksums, signed releases on every modern OS |
| Digital signatures | RSA-PSS and ECDSA can use SHA-256. Ed25519 uses SHA-512 as specified in RFC 8032 |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

| Era | Modern · 2002 |
| --- | --- |
| Status | Secure; SHA-3 (Keccak) standardised 2015 as a structural alternative, not a replacement |
| Origin | NSA (designed); published by NIST as FIPS 180-2 in 2002 |
| Year | 2002 |
| Type | Cryptographic hash function (Merkle-Damgård construction over the SHA-2 compression function) — **not a cipher** |
| Modern Role | Certificate signatures, software checksums, selected password KDFs, Bitcoin proof-of-work and selected signature schemes |

Modern · 1979

### Shamir's Secret Sharing

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 2 4 5v6c0 5 3.5 9 8 11 4.5-2 8-6 8-11V5z"></path><path d="m9 12 2 2 4-4"></path></svg>
```

Secure (Modern)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Split a secret among *n* people so that any *k* of them can rebuild it — and any *k*−1 of them learn nothing whatsoever.

OriginAdi Shamir, ‘How to Share a Secret', *Communications of the ACM* (1979); George Blakley independently the same year

Year1979

TypeThreshold secret-sharing scheme — **not a cipher** (there is no key and nothing is encrypted)

Rests onUniform independent coefficients, distinct nonzero share coordinates and private share handling; no computational hardness assumption

StatusUsed in secret backup, threshold key-management designs and cryptocurrency custody

#### Why This Matters

Almost everything else in this museum protects a secret by making it hard to compute. Shamir's scheme protects one by making it *undetermined*: with too few shares, every possible secret remains exactly as likely as it was before you started. No amount of computing power changes that, because there is nothing left to compute.

It addresses a different task from ordinary encryption: distribute control of a secret among several people while allowing some shares to be unavailable.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Adi Shamir — the S in RSA — published ‘How to Share a Secret' in 1979, a paper of barely two pages. George Blakley published a different construction, using intersecting hyperplanes, in the same year. In Shamir's construction, each share value is one field element, accompanied by its public coordinate. The field must be large enough to provide distinct nonzero coordinates for all participants. Reconstruction uses polynomial interpolation.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The interpolation fact is precise: *k distinct* x-coordinates and their values determine exactly one polynomial of degree *at most k*−1. Fewer points leave its value at zero undetermined when none is itself at zero. Over a finite field, this gives a finite set of candidate secrets; the secrecy argument additionally depends on how the random coefficients are chosen.

So hide the secret as a polynomial's constant term. Pick *k*−1 random coefficients above it, evaluate the polynomial at *x* = 1, 2, 3, … and hand out those values as shares. Any *k* shareholders can interpolate back to the curve and read off its value at zero. Any *k*−1 hold points that fit *every* candidate secret equally well.

Choose the *k*−1 coefficients independently and uniformly from a finite field, with distinct nonzero share coordinates. For any fewer than *k* shares, every candidate secret then has equally many compatible coefficient choices. The shares leave the secret's prior distribution unchanged. Merely taking arbitrary numbers modulo a prime does not supply that guarantee.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-flask"></use></svg>
```

Split a secret, then rebuild it

Arithmetic runs modulo the prime 257, so the secret is one of 257 field values (0–256), not exactly one byte. This small browser model is for learning, not secure key custody. Choose a threshold, deal the shares, then tick shareholders to bring them into the room.

secret (0–256)  [Input secret: type=number; initial value=123]   threshold k  [Input kIn: type=number; initial value=3]   shareholders n  [Input nIn: type=number; initial value=5]   Deal shares

Deal the shares to begin.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What k−1 shares actually reveal

The grid shows the consequence of the interpolation theorem. With fewer than *k* distinct nonzero shares, all 257 candidate secrets remain possible; once enough consistent shares are present, reconstruction selects one. The display applies this theorem rather than exhaustively enumerating every polynomial.

With *k*−1 shares, the answer is yes for all 257 — the shares are consistent with every secret, so they single out none. Add one more share and exactly one survives.

Each cell is one candidate secret from 0 to 256. Gold means ‘still possible given the shares revealed'.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-shield"></use></svg>
```

Security & Cryptanalysis

Under its stated randomness and share-handling assumptions, Shamir's secrecy is information-theoretic. An adversary with fewer than *k* shares learns nothing about the secret, even with unlimited computing power. That theorem does not protect a faulty implementation, predictable coefficients, compromised share storage or too many collected shares.

What it does not do is guard against dishonesty. With exactly the threshold number of shares and no integrity check, a wrong share can produce an incorrect secret without an error signal. Extra shares can reveal inconsistency if the reconstruction checks them; basic interpolation alone does not authenticate their origin. The scheme assumes participants are honest but may be unavailable. Robust reconstruction and **verifiable secret sharing** add protections under their own assumptions; detecting an inconsistent set does not by itself identify the dishonest party.

Two other practical cautions: the dealer sees the secret and must be trusted or eliminated by a distributed key-generation protocol, and the random coefficients must be genuinely random — predictable coefficients collapse the whole argument.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Where You Use It Today

Secret-sharing constructions are used for backups and threshold key-management systems. Hardware security modules and cryptocurrency custody products may use them, but a product's exact mechanism must be checked rather than inferred from a quorum rule. Protocols such as FROST also use threshold shares to produce a signature jointly; trusted-dealer and distributed key-generation arrangements have different trust requirements.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-key"></use></svg>
```

At a glance

**Secret:** the constant term of a polynomial.

**Share:** one point on that polynomial.

**Threshold:** *k* distinct points fix a polynomial of degree at most *k*−1.

**Security:** information-theoretic. Not a hard problem — an undetermined one.

**Blind spot:** basic sharing supplies no built-in share authentication.

The mathematics is in the [Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/interpolation.html>): drag points and watch the curve lock into place.

#### Primary Sources

Adi Shamir, [“How to Share a Secret” (1979)](<https://doi.org/10.1145/359168.359176>); [RFC 9591 (FROST, 2024)](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9591.html>).

#### Sources and Reading

Alfred J. Menezes, Paul C. van Oorschot and Scott A. Vanstone, *Handbook of Applied Cryptography* (1997), §12.7.2, Mechanism 12.71 and Notes 12.72–12.76, pp. 525–527.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  var PM=window.ProtocolMath, P=PM.SHAMIR_P;
  function el(id){return document.getElementById(id);}
  var shares=[], inRoom=[], k=3, secret=123;

  function clampInt(id,lo,hi){
    var v=parseInt(el(id).value,10);
    if(isNaN(v)) v=lo;
    v=Math.max(lo,Math.min(hi,v));
    el(id).value=v; return v;
  }

  function deal(){
    secret=clampInt("secret",0,P-1);
    k=clampInt("kIn",2,6);
    var n=clampInt("nIn",2,8);
    if(n<k){ n=k; el("nIn").value=n; }
    var coeffs=[];
    for(var i=0;i<k-1;i++) coeffs.push(Math.floor(Math.random()*P));
    shares=PM.shamirSplit(secret,k,n,P,coeffs).shares;
    inRoom=shares.map(function(){return false;});
    renderShares(); update();
  }

  function renderShares(){
    var box=el("shareList");
    box.innerHTML="";
    shares.forEach(function(s,i){
      var lab=document.createElement("label");
      lab.style.cssText="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;padding:8px 12px;border:1px solid var(--gold-b,#5a4a2a);border-radius:6px;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;cursor:pointer;";
      var cb=document.createElement("input");
      cb.type="checkbox"; cb.checked=inRoom[i];
      cb.setAttribute("aria-label","Bring shareholder "+s.x+" into the room");
      cb.addEventListener("change",function(){ inRoom[i]=cb.checked; update(); });
      var sp=document.createElement("span");
      sp.textContent="#"+s.x+" → "+s.y;
      lab.appendChild(cb); lab.appendChild(sp);
      box.appendChild(lab);
    });
  }

  // Is candidate `g` consistent with the revealed shares? With fewer than k
  // shares, a degree-(k-1) curve through them and (0,g) always exists, so the
  // honest answer is yes for every g. With k or more, only the true secret fits.
  function consistent(present,g){
    if(present.length===0) return true;
    if(present.length<k) return true;
    return PM.shamirCombine(present.slice(0,k),P)===g;
  }

  function update(){
    var present=shares.filter(function(s,i){return inRoom[i];});
    var grid=el("grid"); grid.innerHTML="";
    var possible=0;
    for(var g=0;g<P;g++){
      var ok=consistent(present,g);
      if(ok) possible++;
      var c=document.createElement("div");
      c.style.cssText="aspect-ratio:1;border-radius:2px;background:"+
        (ok? (g===secret&&present.length>=k? "var(--red,#c94f3d)":"var(--gold,#d4a24c)") : "rgba(255,255,255,.06)");
      grid.appendChild(c);
    }
    var o=el("out");
    if(present.length===0){
      o.innerHTML="No shares in the room. All <b>"+possible+"</b> secrets remain possible.";
    } else if(present.length<k){
      o.innerHTML="<b>"+present.length+"</b> of <b>"+k+"</b> shares present &mdash; below the threshold.<br>"+
        "Reconstruction is impossible, and <b>"+possible+" of "+P+"</b> candidate secrets remain consistent. "+
        "That is all of them: these shares have ruled out nothing.";
    } else {
      var got=PM.shamirCombine(present.slice(0,k),P);
      o.innerHTML="<b>"+present.length+"</b> shares present, threshold <b>"+k+"</b> met.<br>"+
        "Lagrange interpolation at x = 0 returns <b style=\"color:var(--red,#c94f3d)\">"+got+"</b>"+
        (got===secret?" &mdash; the original secret, exactly.":" (unexpected)")+"<br>"+
        "<b>"+possible+" of "+P+"</b> candidates now survive.";
    }
  }

  el("deal").addEventListener("click",deal);
  ["secret","kIn","nIn"].forEach(function(id){
    el(id).addEventListener("change",deal);
  });
  deal();
})();
```

An eighteenth-century garden monument with eight unexplained letters, O · U · O · S · V · A · V · V, and D · M below.

Unresolved inscription; an encoding method is not established

RegionShugborough Hall, Staffordshire, England

YearMid-18th-century monument; inscription date uncertain

Commissioned byThomas Anson, MP, of Shugborough

TrackB (acrostic test bench)

#### Interactive Exhibit

Type a Latin or English phrase whose word initials you think match **O U O S V A V V**. The widget will check the first letter of each word against the inscription. Track B — many interpretations are *consistent*; a match alone does not *prove* an interpretation.

 Your candidate phrase (8 words)  [Input input: type=text; initial value=Optimae Uxoris Optimae Sororis Viduus Amantissimus Vovit Virtutibus]  Test acrostic

##### Why This Matters

On the side of the Shepherd's Monument at Shugborough Hall, beneath a marble relief of Poussin's painting *Et in Arcadia Ego* (mirror-reversed), are carved eight letters: **O · U · O · S · V · A · V · V**, framed below by the letters **D · M**. Their meaning is unresolved. Calling the inscription a cipher already assumes an encoding process that has not been established. A proposed expansion needs historical evidence beyond matching eight initials.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

The monument belongs to the eighteenth-century landscape at Shugborough. The National Trust identifies Peter Scheemakers’s relief and dates the probable addition of columns and entablature to 1763; that date is not a demonstrated date for carving the inscription. Many expansions of its initials have been proposed, including a Latin memorial phrase beginning *Optimae Uxoris Optimae Sororis*. A matching set of initials does not authenticate an attribution, date or intention; none is treated as established here.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Technical Notes

Eight initials and a two-letter footer permit many possible expansions. An acrostic match is therefore weak evidence by itself. Independent documents or archaeological context could strengthen an interpretation; the problem is unresolved, not proven permanently impossible.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Modern Echo

The inscription is preserved at the National Trust’s Shugborough estate. It illustrates the need for independent evidence when interpreting short inscriptions whose encoding rules, if any, are unknown.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    (function () {
      var TARGET = ['O','U','O','S','V','A','V','V'];
      window.encode = function () {
        var raw = (document.getElementById('input').value || '').trim();
        var words = raw.split(/\s+/);
        var out = document.getElementById('output');
        if (words.length !== 8 || words.some(function(w) { return !/^[A-Za-z]/.test(w); })) { out.textContent = 'Enter exactly 8 words beginning with letters.'; return; }
        var lines = ['Target: O \u00b7 U \u00b7 O \u00b7 S \u00b7 V \u00b7 A \u00b7 V \u00b7 V', ''];
        var matches = 0;
        for (var i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
          var w = words[i] || '(missing)';
          var first = (w[0] || '').toUpperCase();
          var hit = first === TARGET[i];
          if (hit) matches++;
          lines.push(' ' + (i+1) + '. ' + TARGET[i] + ' \u2190 ' + first + '  ' + (hit ? '\u2713' : '\u2717') + '   ' + w);
        }
        lines.push('');
        lines.push('Match: ' + matches + ' / 8' +
          (matches === 8 ? '   (initials match \u2014 not authenticated)' :
           matches >= 5 ? '   (close, but not consistent)' :
                          '   (does not fit the inscription)'));
        out.textContent = lines.join('\n');
      };
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { window.encode(); });
    })();
```

WWII · 1940

### SIGABA (ECM Mark II)

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

An American WWII machine with fifteen rotors and irregular stepping; no successful Axis cryptanalytic break is documented in the cited public record.

Never publicly broken by cryptanalysis in wartime service; obsolete today.

OriginWilliam F. Friedman & Frank Rowlett (US Army SIS); Laurance Safford (US Navy OP-20-G)

YearApproved 1940; in service 1941–1959

Key Type15 rotors arranged as 3 banks of 5 (cipher × 5, control × 5, index × 5)

Broken ByNo documented successful enemy wartime cryptanalytic break

Modern LessonRotor-control design changes the structure available to an analyst

#### Why This Matters

SIGABA used separate control and index rotor banks to decide which cipher rotors advanced. Individual stepping patterns can repeat; the design does not promise that no pattern occurs twice. Its operational record differs from a mathematical proof of security, and standard Enigma stepping itself includes a double-step rather than being a perfect odometer.

In the public record, this system was never publicly broken by cryptanalysis in wartime service. That historical record does not establish security today; this obsolete system is presented for historical study.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

SIGABA was used for important American military communications during World War II. Its five cipher rotors were controlled by two additional banks of five rotors. No successful Axis cryptanalytic reading is established in the public record cited here. Numbers describing possible settings are not automatically equivalent to bits of attack resistance.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

Three banks of five rotors. The **cipher bank** performs the actual substitution. The **control bank** steps regularly, odometer-fashion. The control bank's outputs feed the **index bank** — five rotors whose contacts encode the question ‘which of the five cipher rotors steps next?’ The result: any given keystroke advances 1–4 of the cipher rotors in a pattern that depends on the entire current rotor state. The simulation in this exhibit models that pseudorandom advance and the resulting per-keystroke substitution.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

Why It Has Resisted

Why It Held

No measured attack-cost estimate is established by this exhibit

SIGABA differs from Enigma in both stepping and signal path, including the absence of an Enigma-style reflector. Those differences matter to attacks. They do not justify saying that analysis has “nothing to grip,” or that absence of a wartime break proves a machine secure for later use.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from SIGABA (ECM Mark II) | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Make the schedule itself secret | Same lesson reappears in modern stream ciphers (key schedule must be cryptographically strong) |
| Different signal paths impose different constraints | SIGABA lacks the Enigma-style reflector; the security of either machine depends on its complete design and use |
| Compartmented design teams | Friedman and Safford collaborated across services — the rare case of US inter-service cryptographic cooperation actually working |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Break This Cipher

Synthetic teaching exercise, generated by this widget; not an intercepted SIGABA message.
Ciphertext: `LBVIICVKBEYCICOAV`

Hint: the rotor seed is the machine's own name.

 Reveal Answer

**Plaintext:** CLIMB MOUNT NIITAKA
 **Rotor Seed:** SIGABA

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Hall VII · Mechanical Machines WWII · 1943–1946

### SIGSALY — The Encrypted Speech System

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

About 50 tons of equipment and matched key records — a pioneering system for secure Allied voice communication.

DevelopmentBell Telephone Laboratories; operational in 1943

TrustHistorical Only

Machine sizeAbout 50 tons; roughly 40 racks of equipment per terminal

SynchronizationMatched phonograph records carrying key material

NetworkTwelve terminals; initial Pentagon–London service, 15 July 1943

Modern LessonAn early operational use of digital speech parameters and one-time keys

#### 🔓 Interactive Explorer

Typed character codes are combined with a public deterministic sequence modulo six. This does not process speech, implement a vocoder or generate a secret random pad.

 Text for arithmetic illustration  [Input input: type=text; initial value=ATTACK AT DAWN CONFIRM]  Encode

##### Why This Matters

SIGSALY was a pioneering secure digital voice system developed at Bell Laboratories. A vocoder represented speech by changing parameters, which were quantised and combined with matched key material. The one-time-pad principle required the random key values to remain secret and never be reused.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Context: Churchill-Roosevelt Communications

The earlier A-3 transatlantic speech scrambler was vulnerable to interception and analysis. Bell Laboratories developed SIGSALY for high-level Allied voice communications, and it entered service in 1943. The National Cryptologic Museum’s account describes forty equipment racks and substantial operating requirements. The vulnerability of A-3 and the deployment of SIGSALY are separate historical events.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How SIGSALY Worked

SIGSALY quantised vocoder parameters, including information about the speech spectrum and pitch, into discrete levels. The commonly quoted 50-per-second rate concerns these parameters, not direct sampling of an audio waveform at 50 Hz. Modular addition and subtraction with synchronised key records concealed and recovered the parameter stream.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Shannon's Foundation

Shannon’s wartime cryptographic work led to the published 1949 paper *Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems*. It formalised perfect secrecy and analysed key requirements. It did not prove that the one-time pad was the only possible perfectly secret cipher; his separate 1948 communication-theory paper should not be conflated with it.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

Global Network

The NSA history records twelve terminals. The initial Pentagon–London service opened on 15 July 1943; later installations included Paris, North Africa, Hawaii, Guam, Manila and Australia. The number twelve refers to terminals, not rooms per installation. Each terminal needed substantial equipment and power, and the communicating ends needed matching, synchronised key records.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Development | Bell Telephone Laboratories; operational in 1943 |
| --- | --- |
| Trust | Historical Only |
| Machine size | About 50 tons; roughly 40 racks of equipment per terminal |
| Synchronization | Matched phonograph records carrying key material |
| Network | Twelve terminals; initial Pentagon–London service, 15 July 1943 |
| Modern Lesson | An early operational use of digital speech parameters and one-time keys |

#### Sources and Reading

National Cryptologic Museum, [“SIGSALY”](<https://www.nsa.gov/History/National-Cryptologic-Museum/Exhibits-Artifacts/Exhibit-View/Article/2719206/sigsaly/>) (4 August 2021), on Bell Laboratories, the 1943 system and its equipment. Claude E. Shannon, *Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems* (1949), supplies the separate mathematical context for perfect secrecy. The text widget demonstrates neither the historical speech system nor that secrecy guarantee.

#### Embedded script 2 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

    // Arithmetic illustration only: typed characters are not speech parameters.
    function sigDemo(t) {
      // Reduce character codes modulo six and add a public deterministic sequence.
      const bytes = [];
      for (let i=0; i<Math.min(t.length,20); i++) {
        const q = t.charCodeAt(i) % 6; // invented character mapping, not a vocoder
        const k = (i * 37 + 19) % 6; // predictable, public and repeated
        bytes.push((q + k) % 6); // modulo-six addition
      }
      return 'Illustrative residues: [' + bytes.join(' ') + '] — typed character codes plus a public deterministic sequence modulo 6; not speech encryption or a one-time pad.';
    }
```

### Slidex British WWII tactical code card

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```
