Hall VII · Machines Victorian London · 1867

### Wheatstone Cryptograph A clock-face polyalphabetic · 1867

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M3 7a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h11v12a2 2 0 0 0 2 2H6a3 3 0 0 1-3-3V7z"></path><path d="M16 5a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v8h3a0 0 0 0 1 0 0v2a2 2 0 0 1-2 2"></path></svg>
```

Historical Only](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Two geared clock dials, an outer plain alphabet, an inner mixed alphabet — the polyalphabetic cipher you can demonstrate without writing anything down.

Historical unequal-dial device. The current equal-dial widget is a fixed-substitution teaching model, not its mechanism.

OriginCharles Wheatstone, London

Year1867 Paris Universal Exposition

Key TypeMixed-alphabet keyword (inner dial)

MechanismTwo geared hands on concentric dials

Modern LessonMechanisation does not, by itself, add security

#### Why This Matters

Charles Wheatstone (1802–1875) is best known for the Wheatstone bridge, the concertina, and (with Cooke) the first commercial electric telegraph. He was also an enthusiastic cryptographer: the **Playfair cipher** we know by Lord Playfair's name was actually invented by Wheatstone, and his cryptograph — a brass clockwork enciphering machine the size of a pocket watch — was unveiled at the 1867 Paris Universal Exposition.

Wheatstone’s device illustrates mechanically changing substitution. This exhibit does not establish that no version was ever used operationally, and similarity to later machines is not proof of direct descent.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The cryptograph is two concentric dials. The outer dial carries the standard alphabet (plus a 27th mark for word-space on the original brass version). The inner dial carries a **mixed** alphabet derived from a keyword — Polybius-style: write the keyword, drop duplicates, then append the unused letters in order.

The two hands are geared 27:26 — a full revolution of the outer hand advances the inner hand one extra step. To encrypt a letter you sweep the outer hand around to that plaintext letter; the inner hand simultaneously walks across the mixed alphabet, and you read off the ciphertext letter under the inner hand.

The mismatch between 27 and 26 positions changes the relative alignment as the hands move. Alignments eventually recur; “never returns” is not literal. Movement depends on the next plaintext letter, so this is not a simple fixed-period Vigenère key.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Structured search over the cipher-clock model

Reported computational attack; depends on model and text

Historical cipher clocks can be attacked using their structured movement and a search over substitution arrangements, as described in Thomas Kaeding’s *Automated ciphertext-only attack on the Wheatstone Cryptograph and related devices* (2020, revised 2022). The public abstract supports this high-level description; this exhibit does not claim to reproduce its full experiments. There is no established claim here that twenty or thirty guessed keywords cover most historical operators.

Mechanical capture

Complexity: Steal the device

A captured device may disclose its alphabet arrangement and mechanism. Decoding still requires the applicable starting state and conventions. Unequal-dial movement depends on the message, so capturing it does not turn the historical cryptograph into an ordinary repeating-key Vigenère table.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

The cryptograph illustrates why mechanisation and a long cycle are not sufficient measures of security. Kerckhoffs’s later design principle asks whether a system remains secure when its mechanism is known. The equal-dial browser model has different behaviour from Wheatstone’s historical device.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Quick Facts

| Origin | Charles Wheatstone, London |
| --- | --- |
| Year | 1867 Paris Universal Exposition |
| Key Type | Mixed-alphabet keyword (inner dial) |
| Mechanism | Two geared hands on concentric dials |
| Modern Lesson | Mechanisation does not, by itself, add security |

### Herbert Yardley

He led the American Black Chamber, then disclosed its cryptanalytic work in a 1931 book.

🇺🇸

#### Herbert Yardley

1889 – 1958

Herbert Yardley was a pioneer of American cryptanalysis — a self-taught cryptographer from Indiana who talked his way into Army intelligence in WWI and led an important American peacetime codebreaking organization. The 'American Black Chamber' (officially the Cipher Bureau) operated 1919–1929 in New York, funded jointly by the State Department and the Army. Its greatest success was reading Japanese diplomatic traffic during the 1921–22 Washington Naval Conference, giving American negotiators advance knowledge of Japan's bottom-line positions. In 1929, Secretary of State Henry Stimson closed the bureau — reportedly saying 'Gentlemen do not read each other's mail.' Two years later, Yardley published an account of the bureau’s work.

##### Why This Person Matters

Yardley led an important peacetime codebreaking organization and later disclosed its activities in *The American Black Chamber* (1931). The Cipher Bureau had already closed in 1929; the book did not cause that closure, and other American cryptologic work continued. The disclosures alarmed former colleagues and foreign governments. A 1933 law subsequently restricted publication of diplomatic cryptographic secrets.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Building the Black Chamber

Yardley joined the State Department as a telegraph code clerk, quickly recognized vulnerabilities in US diplomatic codes, and wrote a paper demonstrating he could read the President's messages. Promoted to Army intelligence (MI-8) in WWI, he ran a code-and-cipher section that broke German, Mexican, and other traffic. After the Armistice he persuaded both the Army and the State Department to fund a permanent joint bureau — unprecedented in American history — located in a Manhattan brownstone. Yardley later claimed successes against the systems of two dozen countries. NSA’s history notes that missing records prevent full verification of that claim.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Washington Naval Conference

The Washington Naval Conference of 1921–22 sought limits on the major powers’ fleets. Yardley’s bureau supplied decrypts revealing Japanese discussions and negotiating instructions. NSA’s history distinguishes timely intelligence from translations that arrived after their contents had appeared in the press. This access helped American negotiators assess Japan’s flexibility, but it did not make every translation timely or make the treaty the work of the codebreakers alone. [Source: NSA, “The Black Chamber.”](<https://www.nsa.gov/History/Cryptologic-History/Historical-Events/Article-View/article/2740622/the-black-chamber/>)

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

The Book and Its Consequences

*The American Black Chamber* (1931) revealed American successes against diplomatic codes. NSA’s historical account connects the disclosures with increased Japanese adoption of cipher machines, but this was not a single-step progression from Yardley to PURPLE. Diplomatic decrypts supplied foreign-policy intelligence; they were not a readable Japanese naval order for the Pearl Harbor attack.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Modern · 1985

### Zero-Knowledge Proofs

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 2 4 5v6c0 5 3.5 9 8 11 4.5-2 8-6 8-11V5z"></path><path d="m9 12 2 2 4-4"></path></svg>
```

Secure (Modern)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

Convince someone that a statement is true while revealing nothing at all beyond the fact of its truth — not even a hint of why.

OriginShafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali & Charles Rackoff, ‘The Knowledge Complexity of Interactive Proof-Systems' (1985)

Year1985; Schnorr's protocol 1989; zk-SNARKs from 2012

TypeInteractive proof system — **not a cipher** (proves knowledge, transmits none of it)

RecognitionGoldwasser and Micali received the 2012 Turing Award, in part for this work

StatusUnderlies private cryptocurrencies, blockchain rollups, and modern anonymous credentials

#### Why This Matters

A zero-knowledge proof can establish a statement without revealing additional information about its secret witness. Unlike encryption, its purpose is not to deliver the secret to the verifier. The exact guarantee depends on the protocol and on the verifier model.

The consequence is a whole category of systems that were previously unbuildable — proving you are over eighteen without revealing your birthday, proving a transaction is valid without revealing who paid whom, proving a computation ran correctly without repeating it.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

Historical Context

Goldwasser, Micali and Rackoff introduced the idea in their 1985 paper. Their contribution was not a protocol so much as a *definition*: a way to say precisely what ‘revealed nothing' means. Claus-Peter Schnorr gave a compact and practical instance in 1989, and its non-interactive form became the template for a great many modern signature schemes. Later succinct argument systems, including zk-SNARKs, developed different efficiency and setup tradeoffs and became building blocks for blockchain applications.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

A zero-knowledge proof must satisfy three properties at once, and the third is the hard one:

- **Completeness** — an honest prover convinces the verifier with the probability required by the protocol. Perfect completeness means this probability is one.

- **Soundness** — false statements are accepted only with bounded probability. A proof of knowledge additionally formalizes possession of a witness.

- **Zero knowledge** — the verifier learns nothing they could not have produced alone.

This Schnorr identification example has perfect completeness, a knowledge-soundness argument and honest-verifier zero knowledge. The prover knows *x*; everyone knows *y* = *g*<sup>*x*</sup>. The prover commits to a random *r* by sending *t* = *g*<sup>*r*</sup>. The verifier replies with a random challenge *c*. The prover answers *s* = (*r* + *cx*) mod *q*, where *q* is the group order, and the verifier checks:

g<sup>s</sup> = t · y<sup>c</sup> (mod p)

An honest transcript can be simulated without the witness, which is the honest-verifier zero-knowledge argument. Two accepting responses to distinct challenges for the same commitment allow extraction of the discrete logarithm. Impersonation security additionally relies on that logarithm being hard to compute in the selected group.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-flask"></use></svg>
```

Run the protocol

Arithmetic runs in a group of prime order 233 modulo 467 — small enough to print every value. Its small group and teaching randomness are not secure parameters. Choose a secret, then play as an honest prover or as a cheat who does not know it.

secret x  [Input x: type=number; initial value=77]   Prove honestly Cheat (guess the response) Let a cheat try 500 times

Press **Prove honestly**.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-mask"></use></svg>
```

Why a transcript proves nothing — the simulator

Here is the argument that makes ‘zero knowledge' precise, and it is genuinely surprising. Take the protocol's steps *out of order*: choose the challenge and the response first, then work backwards to the commitment that makes the check succeed. The resulting transcript passes verification perfectly — and it was produced by someone with no secret at all.

For this interactive protocol with an honestly sampled uniform challenge, the simulator produces the same transcript distribution without the secret. This establishes *honest-verifier zero knowledge*; it is not by itself a proof for every malicious verifier. A recording of this exchange is not transferable evidence of knowledge, because a third party could have simulated it. That differs from a properly constructed non-interactive signature, whose public verification is intended to be transferable.

Forge a transcript with no secret Answer two challenges on one commitment

Forge a transcript and check it against the same verifier.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-shield"></use></svg>
```

Security & Cryptanalysis

The displayed attack guesses a uniform response, succeeding with probability 1/233 for each fixed commitment and challenge. This is not an upper bound on all attackers: the tiny group here lets an attacker enumerate the secret and then always answer correctly. In a real protocol, impersonation bounds depend on the discrete-log assumption, challenge space and attack model.

The Fiat–Shamir transform derives a challenge by hashing the commitment together with the public statement and required application context. A signature must bind the message as well. Domain separation and unambiguous encodings matter. The prover can try different commitments, but should not be able to choose a useful challenge cheaply under the proof's hash model. A random-oracle proof is a conditional security argument, not a proof that a concrete hash is an ideal oracle.

Succinct proof systems add their own concerns. Many pairing-based zk-SNARKs require a trusted setup whose discarded randomness would forge arbitrary proofs if retained — the reason for elaborate multi-party ceremonies. Transparent systems such as STARKs avoid that setup entirely, at the cost of larger proofs. Pairing-based constructions also inherit the discrete logarithm's vulnerability to quantum attack, while suitably designed hash-based systems avoid that particular attack; their post-quantum security still depends on parameters and assumptions.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Where You Use It Today

Zcash uses zero-knowledge proofs for shielded transactions. Validity rollups can prove that batches of transactions executed correctly; optimistic rollups use a different mechanism. Anonymous credentials can prove attributes without disclosing the full credential. Schnorr and EdDSA signatures use related commitment-and-challenge ideas, but it is misleading to call every signature a zero-knowledge transcript with the guarantees of this interactive demonstration.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-key"></use></svg>
```

At a glance

**Claim:** ‘I know *x* with *g*<sup>*x*</sup> = *y*.'

**Three messages:** commit, challenge, respond.

**Completeness:** honest provers always pass.

**Displayed attack:** uniform response guessing succeeds with probability 1/233; the tiny group permits better attacks.

**Honest-verifier zero knowledge:** a simulator matches the honest transcript distribution without knowing the witness.

The mathematics is in the [Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/pairings.html>): pairings used by some succinct proof systems, and [the oracle](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/random-oracle.html>) Fiat–Shamir leans on.

#### Primary Sources

[RFC 8235 (Schnorr NIZK proof, 2017)](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8235.html>); [RFC 8032 (EdDSA, 2017)](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032.html>). These specify related but distinct constructions; this page implements only the small interactive teaching model.

#### Sources and Reading

Dan Boneh and Victor Shoup, *A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography*, version 0.6 (January 2023), §19.1, Theorem 19.1, and §19.1.1: Schnorr identification, extraction and honest-verifier zero knowledge.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  var PM=window.ProtocolMath, G=PM.GROUP;
  function el(id){return document.getElementById(id);}
  function ri(lo,hi){return lo+Math.floor(Math.random()*(hi-lo+1));}
  function getX(){
    var v=parseInt(el("x").value,10);
    if(isNaN(v)) v=1;
    v=Math.max(1,Math.min(G.q-1,v));
    el("x").value=v; return v;
  }
  function pass(ok){
    return "<b style=\"color:"+(ok?"var(--green,#5AC8A0)":"var(--red,#c94f3d)")+"\">"+(ok?"ACCEPTED":"REJECTED")+"</b>";
  }

  function honest(){
    var x=getX(), y=PM.powmod(G.g,x,G.p);
    var r=ri(0,G.q-1), t=PM.schnorrCommit(r,G);
    var c=ri(0,G.q-1), s=PM.schnorrRespond(r,c,x,G);
    var ok=PM.schnorrVerify(t,c,s,y,G);
    el("proofOut").innerHTML=
      "public key &nbsp;y = g<sup>x</sup> = "+y+"<br>"+
      "1. prover commits &nbsp;t = g<sup>r</sup> = <b>"+t+"</b> &nbsp;<span style=\"opacity:.6\">(r is secret)</span><br>"+
      "2. verifier challenges &nbsp;c = <b>"+c+"</b><br>"+
      "3. prover responds &nbsp;s = r + cx = <b>"+s+"</b><br>"+
      "check g<sup>s</sup> = t&middot;y<sup>c</sup> &rarr; "+pass(ok)+
      "<br><span style=\"opacity:.75\">s is x masked by the fresh random r — the verifier never sees x.</span>";
  }

  function cheat(){
    var x=getX(), y=PM.powmod(G.g,x,G.p);
    var t=PM.schnorrCommit(ri(0,G.q-1),G);
    var c=ri(0,G.q-1), s=ri(0,G.q-1);
    var ok=PM.schnorrVerify(t,c,s,y,G);
    el("proofOut").innerHTML=
      "A prover who does <b>not</b> know x commits, then guesses:<br>"+
      "&nbsp;&nbsp;t = "+t+" &nbsp;&middot;&nbsp; c = "+c+" &nbsp;&middot;&nbsp; guessed s = "+s+"<br>"+
      "check &rarr; "+pass(ok)+
      "<br><span style=\"opacity:.75\">"+(ok
        ? "A 1-in-233 success for this guessing strategy. This tiny group also permits complete secret recovery."
        : "As expected. Only one response in 233 works for this commitment and challenge.")+"</span>";
  }

  function cheatRuns(){
    var x=getX(), y=PM.powmod(G.g,x,G.p), wins=0, T=500;
    for(var i=0;i<T;i++){
      var t=PM.schnorrCommit(ri(0,G.q-1),G);
      if(PM.schnorrVerify(t,ri(0,G.q-1),ri(0,G.q-1),y,G)) wins++;
    }
    el("proofOut").innerHTML=
      "500 attempts by a prover with no secret: <b>"+wins+"</b> succeeded.<br>"+
      "Expected for uniform response guessing, 1/q = 1/233 &rarr; about "+(500/G.q).toFixed(1)+".<br>"+
      "<span style=\"opacity:.75\">This experiment measures one strategy. A large challenge space alone does not establish security; the group and protocol assumptions matter.</span>";
  }

  function simulate(){
    var x=getX(), y=PM.powmod(G.g,x,G.p);
    var c=ri(0,G.q-1), s=ri(0,G.q-1);
    var sim=PM.schnorrSimulate(c,s,y,G);
    if(!sim){ el("simOut").textContent="Degenerate draw; press again."; return; }
    var ok=PM.schnorrVerify(sim.t,sim.c,sim.s,y,G);
    el("simOut").innerHTML=
      "Built <b>backwards</b>, with no knowledge of x:<br>"+
      "&nbsp;&nbsp;pick response s = "+sim.s+" and challenge c = "+sim.c+" first<br>"+
      "&nbsp;&nbsp;solve for the commitment &nbsp;t = g<sup>s</sup>&middot;y<sup>&minus;c</sup> = <b>"+sim.t+"</b><br>"+
      "the same verifier's check &rarr; "+pass(ok)+
      "<br><span style=\"opacity:.75\">Identical in form to an honest transcript, and produced without the secret. "+
      "This is what 'zero knowledge' means: the verifier saw nothing they could not have written themselves.</span>";
  }

  function extract(){
    var x=getX();
    var r=ri(0,G.q-1);
    var c1=ri(0,G.q-1), c2=ri(0,G.q-1);
    if(c1===c2) c2=(c1+1)%G.q;
    var s1=PM.schnorrRespond(r,c1,x,G), s2=PM.schnorrRespond(r,c2,x,G);
    var got=PM.schnorrExtract(s1,c1,s2,c2,G);
    el("simOut").innerHTML=
      "One commitment, two different challenges answered:<br>"+
      "&nbsp;&nbsp;(c&#8321;, s&#8321;) = ("+c1+", "+s1+") &nbsp;&middot;&nbsp; (c&#8322;, s&#8322;) = ("+c2+", "+s2+")<br>"+
      "x = (s&#8321; &minus; s&#8322;) / (c&#8321; &minus; c&#8322;) = <b style=\"color:var(--red,#c94f3d)\">"+got+"</b>"+
      (got===x?" &mdash; the secret itself.":"")+
      "<br><span style=\"opacity:.75\">This is why the protocol proves <em>knowledge</em>: anyone who could answer two challenges on one commitment must hold x. "+
      "It is also why r must never be reused &mdash; the same arithmetic that breaks a repeated ECDSA nonce.</span>";
  }

  el("honest").addEventListener("click",honest);
  el("cheat").addEventListener("click",cheat);
  el("cheatRuns").addEventListener("click",cheatRuns);
  el("simulate").addEventListener("click",simulate);
  el("extract").addEventListener("click",extract);
  honest();
})();
```

### Zimmermann Telegram German codes 0075 / 13040 · 1917

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

A diplomatic telegram deciphered by Room 40 whose publication contributed to American entry into the First World War.

Broken (Room 40)

OriginGerman Foreign Office (Arthur Zimmermann, State Secretary)

Sent16 January 1917

CodesCode 0075 to Washington; re-encoded in 13040 for the onward Mexico leg

Broken byNigel de Grey & Reverend William Montgomery, Room 40, January 1917

OutcomeUS declares war on Germany, 6 April 1917

#### Two versions, two ways of obtaining evidence

Follow the two legs separately. Re-encoding created a different numerical text of the same proposal; obtaining that second text also gave Hall a way to disclose the proposal while shielding the earlier access.

##### 1 · Berlin to Washington — code 0075

Zimmermann’s instruction went to Ambassador Bernstorff in Washington over transatlantic communications. Britain intercepted traffic passing through its cable access; Room 40 worked on the newer code 0075. This was the sensitive access Hall wanted to protect.

##### 2 · Washington to Mexico — code 13040

Bernstorff’s office forwarded the proposal to the German minister in Mexico, re-encoded in the older code 13040. British agents obtained a copy from the telegraph system in Mexico and supplied it to Room 40. This was acquisition of a forwarded copy, not a second interception at the same British cable point.

##### What could be shown?

The Mexican version provided both more readable code groups and a plausible source for disclosure. Comparing a translation with a commercial telegram record could help establish authenticity without explaining every British interception.

Sources: David Kahn, *The Codebreakers*, chapter 9 (the book’s chapter 4 notes); Jay Bellamy, [“The Zimmermann Telegram,” National Archives](<https://www.archives.gov/publications/prologue/2016/winter/zimmermann-telegram>). This route view follows those accounts; it does not claim a single physical path for every transmitted copy.

#### Why This Matters

On 16 January 1917, Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann instructed Germany’s ambassador in Washington to propose an alliance with Mexico if the United States entered the war. The terms included German support for Mexico to recover Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. British interception and decipherment exposed the proposal. Its publication on 1 March increased pressure for US entry into the war, alongside Germany’s unrestricted submarine campaign and other events.

Britain also needed to protect its intelligence sources. Ambassador Walter Page’s telegram of 24 February records the text received from Britain and the account that copies had been bought in Mexico. That contemporary diplomatic account can be compared with the later declassified cryptologic history.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

How It Works

The Berlin-to-Washington transmission used diplomatic code **0075**. Washington re-encoded the onward message to Mexico in the older code **13040** because the Mexican embassy did not hold 0075. Room 40 had recovered much more of the older code. A copy obtained in Mexico helped fill gaps in the reading and gave Britain a way to disclose the telegram without identifying the initial interception source.

The two code numbers describe successive transmission legs, not an additive layer applied to one ciphertext. The museum widget separately demonstrates a small codebook with additive superencipherment; that added operation is a teaching choice, not a reconstruction of this telegram’s procedure.

The widget has a fixed table of 126 entries (123 distinct words) and sentinel-marked letter fallback for other words. Its entries, arithmetic and fallback conventions are modern examples.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

How It Was Broken

Diplomatic codebook reconstruction

Accumulated traffic and partial code recovery

The 0075 reading was incomplete when the telegram arrived. The more extensively recovered 13040 version helped resolve missing passages. Captures of German naval codebooks aided other Room 40 work; they are not the diplomatic codebooks used for this telegram.

Hall’s deception operation

Complexity: Statecraft, not cryptanalysis

Admiral Sir William “Blinker” Hall, head of Room 40, used a British agent in Mexico to obtain a copy of the cable from a commercial telegraph office in Mexico City — an entirely real document that allowed the British to share the plaintext with the Americans while concealing the initial interception route and Room 40’s role.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Zimmermann lesson | Modern echo |
| --- | --- |
| A readable parallel message can help interpret another encoding | Cross-system exposure depends on what the attacker knows; two encodings alone do not guarantee recovery |
| Access to communications routes can enable interception | BGP hijack, undersea cable taps, lawful intercept architectures |
| Using intelligence can risk revealing its source | The Bletchley “ULTRA” disclosure problem; modern source protection in SIGINT |
| Shared codebooks require protected distribution | Public-key systems offer different key-establishment and authentication methods |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

Source: [NSA, *The Zimmermann Telegram*, p. 45 and the translated 1917 German investigation](<https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/news-features/declassified-documents/cryptologic-quarterly/the_zimmermann_telegram.pdf>). The two codes belonged to successive transmission legs, not two encryption layers applied to the same ciphertext.

### Zodiac Cipher

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="trust-label__icon" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true"><rect x="4" y="11" width="16" height="10" rx="2"></rect><path d="M8 11V7a4 4 0 0 1 7.5-2"></path></svg>
```

Broken](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html#trust-labels>)

340 characters. 51 years unsolved. Cracked during a pandemic lockdown.

Oranchak, Blake & Van Eycke (2020)

AuthorThe Zodiac Killer (unidentified)

Year1969 (solved 2020)

Key TypeHomophonic substitution + diagonal transposition

Broken ByOranchak, Blake & Van Eycke (2020)

Modern LessonLayered ciphers · n-gram scoring

#### Why This Matters

Z-340 remained unsolved for 51 years. Its 2020 solution combined a search for transposition patterns with homophonic-substitution solving and manual investigation. The result illustrates how an incorrect model can obstruct an attack, even when the individual cipher techniques are familiar.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

 Historical Context

Between 1969 and 1970, an unidentified serial killer called the Zodiac sent four encrypted messages to San Francisco Bay Area newspapers, taunting police and demanding publication. The killer claimed the ciphers contained his identity.

The first cipher, Z-408 (408 characters), was solved in 1969 by Donald and Bettye Harden. It contained no name. The second cipher, Z-340 (340 characters), defied cryptanalysts, amateur solvers, and FBI investigators for 51 years.

On December 11, 2020, David Oranchak, mathematician Sam Blake, and software developer Jarl Van Eycke publicly announced the solution. They had submitted it to the FBI on December 5; the FBI independently verified the decryption. They had worked remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

 How It Works

The Z-340 uses a layered cipher combining homophonic substitution with diagonal transposition — the key insight that eluded solvers for half a century.

```text
Cipher type: Homophonic substitution + diagonal transposition

Step 1: The Z-340 uses a homophonic alphabet —
        common letters map to multiple symbols
        to flatten frequency patterns

Step 2: Undo the recovered section-specific
        transposition — the first section reads
        diagonally rather than left-to-right

Z-408 first row (17 symbols — the row used by
the interactive demo below):
HER>pl^VPk|1LTG2d

The diagonal transposition is why the cipher
resisted 51 years of analysis — solvers were
looking for patterns in the wrong reading order
```

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

 Decode It Yourself — Z-408 Fragment

The Z-408 cipher was solved in 1969. Below are the first 17 symbols of the real ciphertext. Click a symbol, then type its letter in the box to build the plaintext — or press **Reveal Answer** to see the known solution.

 Ciphertext symbols (first 17 of Z-408)

Assign letter for ****:  [Input zLetterInput: type=text; initial value=]  Clear

 Plaintext (your decryption)

· · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · ·

Reveal Answer Reset

✅

**Known Solution (Z-408, first 17 symbols):**

ILIKEKILLINGPEOPL

The Zodiac enciphered no word spaces, so the row runs straight on: the full Z-408 begins *"I LIKE KILLING PEOPLE BECAUSE IT IS SO MUCH FUN…"* — solved by Donald and Bettye Harden within a week of publication in 1969.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-skull"></use></svg>
```

 How It Was Broken

Computational Search + N-gram Scoring (2020)

Complexity: Very Hard · Oranchak, Blake & Van Eycke

Oranchak had suspected a transposition component since 2012. Working with Blake (who explored candidate transpositions) and Van Eycke (who built the AZdecrypt cipher-solving tool), the team identified the specific diagonal reading pattern through computational search. Candidate routes, recognizable fragments, homophonic search and correction of section-specific disruptions worked together. The exact physical procedure used to encipher the message remains uncertain.

📝

The solution expresses taunts about the investigation and the killer’s claimed beliefs about an afterlife. It does not disclose the killer’s identity.

The Zodiac's identity was not revealed.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

 What It Teaches Modern Cryptography

| Concept from Zodiac Cipher | Modern Evolution |
| --- | --- |
| Homophonic substitution (multiple symbols per letter) | Compare randomized or nonce-based encryption; padding alone does not hide repeated plaintexts |
| Layered cipher (transposition + substitution) | Modern cipher analysis studies how operations interact; layering alone does not establish security |
| 51 years + short ciphertext = hard | Ciphertext length matters: more data = more statistical signal for an attacker |
| Solved by n-gram scoring + computation | Language-scored search can attack classical ciphers; success depends on the cipher, data and search budget |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

 Can You Break This?

A short cipher message. Use what you just learned.

XLI UYMGO FVSAR JSB

Hint: Not the Zodiac's cipher — this one is simpler. Sixteen letters gives limited frequency evidence, but there are only 25 shifts to try. Which one reads as English?

 Reveal Answer

Shift = 4 · Plaintext: THE QUICK BROWN FOX


The Remaining Zodiac Ciphers: Z-13 and Z-32

The main Z-408 message and Z-340 are deciphered, but the meaning of Z-408’s final 18 characters remains uncertain and the Zodiac story is not closed. Two later messages remain open: **Z-13**, the short "My name is" cipher, and **Z-32**, usually interpreted as a location cipher. Their brevity is the main obstacle. At 13 and 32 characters, they do not provide enough depth for the kind of statistical leverage that broke Z-340. That is why Round 3 also routes them into [Hall XII: Unsolved Ciphers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/unsolved.html>) as active research problems, even though this main exhibit focuses on the solved 408- and 340-character messages.

#### Follow the Evidence

[Investigate the source, competing hypotheses and verification](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#z340>), then preserve your own readings in the [Evidence Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html>).

#### Sources and Reading

David Oranchak, Sam Blake and Jarl Van Eycke, [“The Solution of the Zodiac Killer’s 340-Character Cipher”](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17350>) (2024), §§1.3 and 5, for the distinction between the two messages, the remaining Z-408 tail and the solution process.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

// Z-408 demo — first 17 symbols and their known solutions
(function(){
  const SYMS = ['H','E','R','>','p','l','^','V','P','k','|','1','L','T','G','2','d'];
  const ANSWER = 'ILIKEKILLINGPEOPL';
  const map = {}; // sym → assigned letter
  let selectedSym = null;

  function render(){
    const grid = document.getElementById('zGrid');
    if(!grid) return;
    grid.innerHTML = '';
    SYMS.forEach((s,i)=>{
      const cell = document.createElement('div');
      cell.className = 'z-sym' + (map[s] ? ' z-mapped' : '') + (s === selectedSym ? ' z-selected' : '');
      cell.textContent = s;
      cell.setAttribute('title', map[s] ? 'Assigned: ' + map[s] : 'Click to assign a letter');
      cell.setAttribute('tabindex','0');
      cell.setAttribute('role','button');
      cell.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Symbol ' + s + (map[s] ? ', assigned ' + map[s] : ', unassigned'));
      cell.addEventListener('click', ()=>{ selectSym(s); });
      cell.addEventListener('keydown', e=>{ if(e.key==='Enter'||e.key===' '){ e.preventDefault(); selectSym(s); } });
      grid.appendChild(cell);
    });
    // plaintext
    const plain = SYMS.map(s=> map[s] ? '<span style="color:var(--green)">' + map[s] + '</span>' : '<span style="color:var(--tx3)">·</span>').join(' ');
    document.getElementById('zPlaintext').innerHTML = plain;
    // stats
    const filled = Object.keys(map).length;
    const uniqueSyms = [...new Set(SYMS)].length;
    document.getElementById('zStats').textContent = filled + ' of ' + uniqueSyms + ' unique symbols assigned · ' + SYMS.filter(s=>map[s]).length + ' of 17 positions decoded';
  }

  function selectSym(s){
    selectedSym = s;
    const assign = document.getElementById('zAssign');
    const label = document.getElementById('zSelLabel');
    const input = document.getElementById('zLetterInput');
    assign.style.display = 'flex';
    label.textContent = '"' + s + '"';
    input.value = map[s] || '';
    input.focus();
    render();
  }

  window.zAssignLetter = function(v){
    if(!selectedSym) return;
    const letter = v.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z ]/g,'');
    if(letter) map[selectedSym] = letter; else delete map[selectedSym];
    render();
  };

  window.zClearSelected = function(){
    if(selectedSym) delete map[selectedSym];
    document.getElementById('zLetterInput').value='';
    render();
  };

  window.zReveal = function(){
    SYMS.forEach((s,i)=>{ map[s] = ANSWER[i]; });
    selectedSym = null;
    document.getElementById('zAssign').style.display='none';
    document.getElementById('zSolution').style.display='block';
    render();
  };

  window.zReset = function(){
    for(const k in map) delete map[k];
    selectedSym = null;
    document.getElementById('zAssign').style.display='none';
    document.getElementById('zSolution').style.display='none';
    render();
  };

  document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', render);
})();
```

### Classical Codebreaking Topic Guide

From a chamber guide to the museum collection

Looking for a topic from Simon Singh’s [Black Chamber guide](<https://simonsingh.net/The_Black_Chamber/chamberguide.html>)? All 27 subject entries have a route below. Some are techniques or subtopics within an exhibit, rather than separate exhibits. This is a topic crosswalk, not a claim that the sites have identical tools or explanations.

[Start the guided lesson](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html>) · [Teaching resources](<https://ciphermuseum.com/teaching.html>)

#### Find the topic

Black Chamber subject labels and corresponding Cipher Museum material

| Guide topic | Museum destination | What to explore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transposition | [Transposition hall](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/transposition.html>) | Rearrange positions while retaining the letters. |
| Rail Fence Cipher | [Rail Fence](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rail-fence.html>) | Explore rails and routes; conventions affect the result. |
| Latin Square | [Sator Square](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/sator-square.html>) | This is the square Singh calls the Latin Square. Its symmetry and PATER NOSTER anagram are demonstrable; an intended Christian message remains an interpretation. It is not a general mathematical Latin square. |
| Substitution | [Substitution hall](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/substitution.html>) | Replace symbols or groups of symbols. |
| Caesar Cipher | [Caesar](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/caesar.html>) | Use and attack a fixed alphabet shift. |
| Kama-sutra Cipher | [Kama-sutra / paired substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kama-sutra.html>) | Pair letters; the same mapping works in both directions. Read the exhibit’s historical qualifications. |
| Pigpen Cipher | [Pigpen](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/pigpen.html>) | Use a geometric symbol alphabet. |
| Mono-alphabetic Cipher | [Monoalphabetic Substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/monoalphabetic.html>) | One fixed alphabet permutation retains word patterns and letter counts. |
| Codes, Ciphers and Keys | [Glossary](<https://ciphermuseum.com/glossary.html>) | Read the definitions of code, cipher, key, plaintext and ciphertext; the nomenclator exhibit shows mixed systems. |
| Cracking the Substitution Cipher | [First codebreak](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html#first-desk>) | Follow an original notice from first clue to a consistent reading. |
| Letter Frequencies | [Cryptanalysis Techniques](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cryptanalysis.html>) | Count letters and inspect the limits of frequency evidence. |
| Hints and Tips | [Contextual clues](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html#first-desk>) | Highlight doubles, short words and repeated words; request progressive hints. |
| Substitution Cracking Tool | [Manual substitution desk](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-detective.html#manual-substitution>) | Enter partial mappings, lock guesses, undo changes and compare word patterns. |
| Mary Queen of Scots | [Babington Plot](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/babington.html>) | The 1586 correspondence and its use as evidence. The 2023 recovery of the Castelnau letters is a separate investigation, linked below. |
| More Advanced Ciphers | [Cipher Comparison](<https://ciphermuseum.com/comparison.html>) | Compare families and assumptions; complexity alone does not establish security. |
| Digraph Cipher | [Playfair](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/playfair.html>) | One example of encrypting letter pairs. Four-square is another; “digraph cipher” is a category, not a synonym for Playfair. |
| Homophonic Cipher | [Homophonic Substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/homophonic.html>) | Several symbols may represent a common letter; try the new same-message frequency comparison. |
| Playfair Cipher | [Playfair](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/playfair.html>) | Explore its square, pair preparation, rectangle rule and decryption ambiguity. |
| Vigenère Cipher | [Vigenère](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) | Repeating-key arithmetic and its historical qualifications. |
| Swapping Cipher Alphabets | [Vigenère encryption trace](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) | Each key position selects a Caesar alphabet. The trace aligns key, plaintext and ciphertext. |
| Vigenère Square | [Tabula recta](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) | Inspect the rows, columns and their intersections. |
| Vigenère Square Tool | [Vigenère interactive](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) | Enter a message and keyword, then inspect the trace and table. |
| Why is Vigenère so strong? | [Why repeating alphabets hide some patterns](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) | Different key positions can disguise the same plaintext letter differently, but the repeated key leaks periodic structure. This is a broken historical cipher, not strong modern encryption. |
| Cracking the Vigenère Cipher | [Guided Vigenère attack](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html#vigenere-lesson>) | Move from repetitions to candidate periods, column shifts and a checked plaintext. |
| Cracking Principle | [Kasiski and coincidence techniques](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cryptanalysis.html>) | Repeated sequences suggest periods; accidental repetitions and multiples can mislead. |
| Vigenère Cracking Tool | [Inspect and test every step](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html#vigenere-lesson>) | Highlight repeats, choose a period, inspect 26 shifts per column and test a key. Cipher Detective also offers an automated solver. |
| 1900–2000 | [Modern Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/modern.html>) | Continue through machines, computer ciphers, key exchange and public-key systems. Use the timeline for chronology. |

#### Useful connections

- [Nomenclators](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/nomenclator.html>) combine letter substitutions with codes for words or names.

- [Four-square](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/four-square.html>) also encrypts pairs; a [2×2 Hill construction](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hill.html>) provides a different mathematical way to process two-letter blocks.

- [Mary Stuart’s recovered Castelnau letters](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/mary-stuart-castelnau-letters.html>) and [historical investigations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html>) distinguish a recovered reading from the evidence used to verify it.

- [Enigma](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/enigma.html>), [Diffie–Hellman](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/diffie-hellman.html>) and [RSA](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rsa.html>) take the story beyond hand ciphers. [Follow the timeline](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html>).

The guide’s remaining entries—home, contact, Crypto Corner, CD-ROM and the author’s site—are navigation or resources, not missing cipher topics. [Further Reading](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html>) links to Singh’s book and online tutorial.

### First Codebreak — Facilitator’s Answers

Use your browser’s Print command to print or save as PDF. [Open the interactive lessons](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html>) · [Student worksheet](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-worksheet.html>)

**Answer sheet — contains spoilers.** Keep this separate from the student handout. All answers verify deliberately constructed exercises, not historical evidence.

#### 1. The library notice

LOOK FOR THE BOOK OF MAPS IN THE SCHOOL ROOM. DO NOT GO TO THE OLD DOOR. BRING THE BOOK TO THE READING ROOM AT NOON.

Plain alphabet: ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ Cipher alphabet: QWERTYUIOPASDFGHJKLZXCVBNM

Read this table left to right for encryption; reverse its mappings for the worksheet’s cipher-to-plaintext key. Only letters that appear in the notice can be recovered from this exercise.

O occurs 24 times, so G is the most frequent cipher letter. G → E is wrong here. FGGF matches NOON’s doubled middle and repeated outside letter. ZIT → THE, WGGA → BOOK and KGGD → ROOM provide mutually consistent mappings. NOON alone is a crib hypothesis, not a unique solution to an arbitrary four-letter cryptogram.

Ask learners to identify a rejected guess and two supporting clues. The supplied plaintext check verifies this fixture; readability alone would not establish the authenticity of a historical message.

#### 2. The repeating-key dispatch

Generating key: **LAMP**. Its minimal period is four. Repeating that keyword twice produces an equivalent eight-position stream.

THE READING ROOM WILL OPEN AT NINE. BRING THE MAP AND THE LETTER TO THE LIBRARY. THE READING ROOM WILL CLOSE AT FIVE. CHECK THE NAME ON THE LETTER BEFORE YOU GIVE IT TO THE READER. KEEP A COPY OF THE MESSAGE AND NOTE THE TIME IT ARRIVED. THE MAP SHOWS THE ROAD TO THE OLD SCHOOL AND THE BRIDGE OVER THE RIVER. THE READER WILL WAIT IN THE LIBRARY UNTIL THE OTHER COPY ARRIVES. COMPARE THE TWO COPIES AND RECORD EVERY CHANGE. A CLEAR MESSAGE IS ONLY PART OF THE EVIDENCE.

The repeated group TTT begins at positions 34 and 54: a distance of 20 suggests factors including 2, 4, 5 and 10. Its occurrence at position 98 provides a distance of 64 from position 34. Their common factors still do not prove a key; test the columns and full plaintext. IZT at positions 26 and 52 has distance 26 and illustrates an accidental repeat that does not align with the generating period.

At period four, this exercise’s best English chi-square shifts happen to recover LAMP. That is a property of this fixture, not a promise for short columns or other languages. The online tool shows all 26 candidates and checks the reconstructed text.

#### 3. Language and homophone observations

Results depend on the selected sample. The five displayed texts are original, short modern-language samples normalized to A–Z. Word choice, topic, length and normalization can change their frequencies. They must not be presented as historical or population-wide language models.

There are 24 O letters. With four equally likely alternatives, each O-token has expected count 24/4 = 6. Actual counts fluctuate; one draw need not flatten the chart. Other letters retain fixed tokens, and higher-order structure remains. Uniform-looking counts do not prove secrecy.

#### 4. Facilitation and scope

For a 15-minute session, use the first activity only: introduce the mapping rule, let pairs try clues, then discuss a rejected guess. Add the remaining activities when time permits. Never require a learner to reveal their own private information for a puzzle.

Use [the topic guide](<https://ciphermuseum.com/classical-guide.html>) for related exhibits. The format was inspired by [Simon Singh’s Black Chamber](<https://simonsingh.net/The_Black_Chamber/chamberguide.html>); the text, examples and implementation are original. Technical reading is listed on [the lesson page](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html>).

### First Codebreak — Student Activities

Use your browser’s Print command to print or save as PDF. [Open the interactive lessons](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html>) · [Facilitator’s answers (spoilers)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-answers.html>)

Name / team: ____________________ Date: __________

For the first activity, allow about 15 minutes. Work with a partner: one proposes a guess, the other looks for a contradiction. Use the optional extensions for a longer session.

#### 1. Where is the book?

One cipher letter always represents the same plaintext letter. Spaces and punctuation are genuine boundaries retained for this exercise.

SGGA YGK ZIT WGGA GY DQHL OF ZIT LEIGGS KGGD. RG FGZ UG ZG ZIT GSR RGGK. WKOFU ZIT WGGA ZG ZIT KTQROFU KGGD QZ FGGF.

##### Working key: cipher letter → plaintext letter

A → ___ B → ___ C → ___ D → ___ E → ___ F → ___ G → ___ H → ___ I → ___ J → ___ K → ___ L → ___ M → ___ N → ___ O → ___ P → ___ Q → ___ R → ___ S → ___ T → ___ U → ___ V → ___ W → ___ X → ___ Y → ___ Z → ___

##### Clue ladder — read one at a time

- Circle words containing doubled letters. Underline repeated words. Count the cipher letters.

- The most frequent symbol need not represent E. What would make you reject that guess?

- The meeting time is a four-letter word with the pattern 0.1.1.0. Find a cipherword with that shape.

- Test THE for ZIT. Does the same mapping work everywhere?

- This is a library notice: try BOOK for WGGA and ROOM for KGGD.

Your plaintext:

Which two clues support your reading? What did you revise?

#### 2. Follow a repeating key

This optional extension uses repeating-key Vigenère with A=0. Only A–Z letters are present. The message is 369 letters long. Use the online column tools or work together on paper.



- Find two occurrences of a three-letter group. Record their positions, counting from 1.

- Measure the distance and list candidate periods that divide it. Test another repeated group. Why might the clues disagree?

- For each candidate period, put letters at equal key positions in the same column.

- Try Caesar shifts on each column. Test the combined key on the complete message.

Repeated group: ______ Positions: ______ Distance: ______ Candidate periods: ______

Candidate key: ______ What verifies or contradicts it?

What could a key that repeats the same shorter keyword tell you about the true period?

#### 3. Change an assumption

Compare two language samples in the online lesson. Record the most frequent letter and a short word in each. Does one short sample represent its whole language?

Give O four possible numerical tokens in the homophone experiment. Run it twice. Why do the observed counts change? What structure remains?

#### 4. Exchange an original puzzle

Write a short notice, choose a substitution key, and keep the plaintext and key on a separate answer sheet. Give another pair only the ciphertext, cipher family and any intentional hints. Use the museum Workbench to check the answer. These historical puzzle methods are unsuitable for protecting private information.

Community

### Community Codebreaks

Explore practice prompts and historical research leads, then prepare a sourced contribution draft to share through the project issue tracker.

Practice Idea

#### Design a Lighthouse Cipher

Create a nautical puzzle by combining Polybius coordinates with a second transformation, and give another learner enough clues to reverse it.

Suggested difficulty: Intermediate

 [Start with the Polybius exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/polybius.html>)

Study Topic

##### Breaking Confederate Vigenère

Study the historical brass-disk convention, then compare its repeated-key weaknesses with ordinary Vigenère analysis.

Techniques to try: Kasiski · Index of Coincidence

 [Open the Confederate Vigenère exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/confederate-vigenere.html>)

Research Lead

##### Room 40 and the Zimmermann Telegram

Trace how accumulated codebook recovery and an older-code retransmission helped Room 40 read and safely disclose the telegram.

WWI · Diplomatic codebooks · Source links in exhibit

 [Open the Zimmermann exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zimmermann.html>)

Practice Idea

##### Create an Enigma Challenge

Choose rotor, ring, plugboard, and starting settings in the exhibit, encrypt a short dispatch, and challenge a classmate with a crib.

Suggested difficulty: Advanced

 [Open the Enigma exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/enigma.html>)

Study Topic

##### Hill Cipher: When Linear Algebra Attacks

Use matrix inversion modulo 26 to see how enough suitably independent known-plaintext blocks can recover a Hill key and why linearity is the cipher's central weakness.

Technique: Modular matrix algebra

 [Open the Hill cipher exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hill.html>)

Historical Topic

##### The Uncracked Dorabella Cipher

Edward Elgar's 1897 cipher letter to Dora Penny remains unsolved after more than 125 years — an 87-character mystery in 24 unique symbols.

Status: Unsolved · Primary-source image linked in exhibit

 [Open the Dorabella exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/dorabella.html>)

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

'use strict';
(function(){
  var form = document.getElementById('commForm');
  var success = document.getElementById('commSuccess');

  function downloadDraft(){
    /* Basic validation */
    if(!form.checkValidity()){ form.reportValidity(); return; }

    var entry = {
      name: document.getElementById('commName').value.trim(),
      type: document.getElementById('commType').value,
      title: document.getElementById('commTitle').value.trim(),
      body: document.getElementById('commBody').value.trim(),
      sources: document.getElementById('commSources').value.trim(),
      date: new Date().toISOString()
    };

    var lines = [
      'Cipher Museum contribution draft',
      '',
      'Title: ' + entry.title,
      'Type: ' + entry.type,
      'Author: ' + entry.name,
      'Created: ' + entry.date,
      '',
      entry.body,
      '',
      'Sources:',
      entry.sources || '(none supplied)'
    ];
    var blob = new Blob([lines.join('\n')], {type: 'text/plain;charset=utf-8'});
    var url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
    var download = document.createElement('a');
    var safeTitle = entry.title.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-').replace(/^-|-$/g, '') || 'contribution';
    download.href = url;
    download.download = 'cipher-museum-' + safeTitle + '-draft.txt';
    download.click();
    setTimeout(function(){ URL.revokeObjectURL(url); }, 0);

    form.style.display = 'none';
    success.style.display = 'block';
  }

  form.addEventListener('submit', function(e){ e.preventDefault(); downloadDraft(); });
  document.getElementById('downloadDraft').addEventListener('click', downloadDraft);
})();
```

```javascript
    { name:'VENONA',               href:'ciphers/venona.html',               era:'World War II',  year:1943,  type:'Intelligence',    key:'OTP pad reuse analysis',    security:"Broken",      hall:'XI', trust:{"key":"broken","text":"Broken","description":"Cryptographically broken — historically important but unsafe to use today."} },
    { name:'SIGSALY',              href:'ciphers/sigsaly.html',              era:'World War II',  year:1943,  type:'Machine',         key:'Thermal noise + OTP',       security:"Historical Only", hall:'XI', trust:{"key":"historical","text":"Historical Only","description":"Obsolete or historical system; notes distinguish cryptanalysis from capture or other operational compromise."} },
    { name:'Microdot',             href:'ciphers/microdot.html',             era:'World War II', year:1941, dateLabel:'1941 FBI account; earlier origins',  type:'Steganography',   key:'Physical size reduction',   security:"Historical Only",    hall:'XI', trust:{"key":"historical","text":"Historical Only","description":"Obsolete or historical system; notes distinguish cryptanalysis from capture or other operational compromise."} }
  ];

  var tbody = document.getElementById('cipher-tbody');
  var searchInput = document.getElementById('cipher-search');
  var typeFilter = document.getElementById('type-filter');
  var eraFilter = document.getElementById('era-filter');
  var securityFilter = document.getElementById('security-filter');
  var hallFilter = document.getElementById('hall-filter');
  var solvedFilter = document.getElementById('solved-filter');
  var countEl = document.getElementById('cipher-count');

  var eraClasses = { 'Ancient':'ancient','Medieval':'medieval','Renaissance':'renaissance','Baroque':'renaissance','18th Century':'renaissance','Early 20th Century':'wwi','19th Century':'19c','World War I':'wwi','World War II':'wwii','Modern':'modern' };

  function solvedStatus(c) {
    if (c.type === 'Unsolved' || c.hall === 'XII' || /\/(?:beale|kryptos|zodiac|cicada-3301)\.html$/.test(c.href)) return 'Open puzzles';
    return 'Other exhibits';
  }

  // Build rows
  CIPHERS.forEach(function(c, i) {
    var tr = document.createElement('tr');
    tr.dataset.index = i;
    var yearDisplay = c.dateLabel || (c.year === null ? 'Date not established' : c.year < 0 ? Math.abs(c.year) + ' BCE' : c.year);
    tr.innerHTML =
      '<td><a href="' + c.href + '">' + c.name + '</a></td>' +
      '<td><span class="comp-era era-' + (eraClasses[c.era]||'') + '">' + c.era + '</span></td>' +
      '<td>' + yearDisplay + '</td>' +
      '<td>' + c.type + '</td>' +
      '<td>' + c.key + '</td>' +
      '<td>' + (window.TrustLabels.badge(c.trust) || '—') + '</td>' +
      '<td>' + c.hall + '</td>';
    tbody.appendChild(tr);
  });

  // Sort
  var sortCol = 'year';
  var sortDir = 1;
  var ths = document.querySelectorAll('.comp-table th[data-col]');
  ths.forEach(function(th) {
    th.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var col = th.dataset.col;
      if (col === sortCol) { sortDir *= -1; }
      else { sortCol = col; sortDir = 1; }
      ths.forEach(function(t) { t.classList.remove('sorted-asc','sorted-desc'); });
      th.classList.add(sortDir === 1 ? 'sorted-asc' : 'sorted-desc');
      sortTable();
    });
  });

  function sortTable() {
    var rows = Array.from(tbody.querySelectorAll('tr'));
    rows.sort(function(a, b) {
      var ai = +a.dataset.index, bi = +b.dataset.index;
      var ca = CIPHERS[ai], cb = CIPHERS[bi];
      var va, vb;
      // An undated specification is not year zero; keep it after dated entries.
      if (sortCol === 'year' || sortCol === 'era') {
        if (ca.year === null || cb.year === null) return ca.year === cb.year ? 0 : ca.year === null ? 1 : -1;
      }
      if (sortCol === 'year') { va = ca.year; vb = cb.year; }
      else if (sortCol === 'name') { va = ca.name.toLowerCase(); vb = cb.name.toLowerCase(); }
      else if (sortCol === 'era') { va = ca.year; vb = cb.year; }
      else if (sortCol === 'security') {
        va = ca.security; vb = cb.security;
      }
      else { va = ca[sortCol] ? ca[sortCol].toLowerCase() : ''; vb = cb[sortCol] ? cb[sortCol].toLowerCase() : ''; }
      if (va < vb) return -1 * sortDir;
      if (va > vb) return 1 * sortDir;
      return 0;
    });
    rows.forEach(function(r) { tbody.appendChild(r); });
  }

  // Filter
  function applyFilters() {
    var search = searchInput.value.toLowerCase();
    var type = typeFilter.value;
    var era = eraFilter.value;
    var security = securityFilter.value;
    var hall = hallFilter.value;
    var solved = solvedFilter.value;
    var visible = 0;
    var rows = tbody.querySelectorAll('tr');
    rows.forEach(function(row) {
      var c = CIPHERS[+row.dataset.index];
      var show = true;
      if (search && c.name.toLowerCase().indexOf(search) === -1 && c.type.toLowerCase().indexOf(search) === -1 && c.key.toLowerCase().indexOf(search) === -1) show = false;
      if (type && c.type !== type) show = false;
      if (era && c.era !== era) show = false;
      if (security && c.security !== security) show = false;
      if (hall && c.hall !== hall) show = false;
      if (solved && solvedStatus(c) !== solved) show = false;
      row.classList.toggle('hidden', !show);
      if (show) visible++;
    });
    countEl.textContent = 'Showing ' + visible + ' of ' + CIPHERS.length;
  }

  searchInput.addEventListener('input', applyFilters);
  typeFilter.addEventListener('change', applyFilters);
  eraFilter.addEventListener('change', applyFilters);
  securityFilter.addEventListener('change', applyFilters);
  hallFilter.addEventListener('change', applyFilters);
  solvedFilter.addEventListener('change', applyFilters);

  // Initial sort by year
  document.querySelector('th[data-col="year"]').classList.add('sorted-asc');
  sortTable();
  applyFilters();
})();
```

 Special Exhibit · The Science of Breaking Codes

### Cryptanalysis Techniques

"To know how to defend, you must first know how to attack."

Ten approaches to classical cryptanalysis, with seven hands-on demonstrations. Success depends on the cipher, evidence, language, key and message length; no technique here defeats a correctly used one-time pad.

 [Open Codebreaker's Workbench →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/workbench.html>) [Open Cipher Detective →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-detective.html>)

The Toolkit

#### 10 Techniques That Break Classical Ciphers

Technique 01

Frequency Analysis

Al-Kindi · Baghdad · ~850 AD

Long English samples often have frequencies near E=12.7%, T=9.1%, A=8.2%, with variation by text. A fixed one-to-one substitution preserves the sample’s counts while relabeling letters. Compare counts and sequences to propose mappings; frequency alone does not guarantee key recovery. Homophonic and syllabic systems need additional analysis.

Technique 02

Kasiski Examination

Friedrich Kasiski · 1863

In repeating-key Vigenère, the same plaintext at the same key phase produces the same ciphertext. Repeated ciphertext fragments can suggest key periods through factors of their spacing. Accidental repeats also occur, so candidate periods need further tests.

Technique 03

Index of Coincidence

William Friedman · published 1922

Measures the probability that two distinct sampled positions contain the same letter. Long English samples often lie near 0.066; independent uniform A–Z text has expected IC 1/26 ≈ 0.0385. These are reference values, not bounds: an observed IC can range from 0 to 1. Coincidence statistics can suggest repeating-key periods, but do not identify a cipher by themselves.

Technique 04

Crib-Based Cryptanalysis

Polish Mathematicians · WWII Bletchley

Cribs are hypotheses about plaintext, suggested by message formats, context or repeated phrases. Against Enigma, analysts tested those hypotheses against machine constraints and additional traffic. Known plaintext is an attack model that modern encryption must withstand; it is not automatically a fatal weakness.

Technique 05

Known Plaintext Attack

Universal · Classical through Modern

Known plaintext can expose a classical cipher's key. For a 2×2 Hill cipher, two matched plaintext/ciphertext *blocks* suffice when the plaintext-block matrix P is invertible modulo 26: gcd(det(P), 26) = 1. Otherwise, more observations or other analysis are needed. Enigma cribs impose different, rotor-machine constraints.

Technique 06

Hill Climbing Search

Modern · Computer Era

Start with a random key. Decrypt. Score the result using English language statistics — common digrams like TH, HE, IN. Make random changes to the key. Keep improvements, discard downgrades. Use multiple starting points to explore candidates. Such searches can attack substitution, Playfair and transposition, but may stall at local optima or favor incorrect plaintext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg viewBox="0 0 520 236" style="max-width:560px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;background:#1a1a2e;border:1px solid #2e2e3a;border-radius:6px;" role="img" aria-label="Hill climbing: greedy steps reach a local peak and stall below the global best"><line x1="20" y1="200" x2="500" y2="200" stroke="#555" stroke-width="1"></line><path d="M20 190 C 80 150, 110 92, 150 92 C 190 92, 210 150, 260 165 C 300 176, 330 60, 375 46 C 410 36, 460 90, 500 130" fill="none" stroke="#e8d5a3" stroke-width="1.6"></path><circle cx="60" cy="168" r="4" fill="#d4af37" stroke="#141422" stroke-width="1"></circle><circle cx="90" cy="140" r="4" fill="#d4af37" stroke="#141422" stroke-width="1"></circle><circle cx="118" cy="110" r="4" fill="#d4af37" stroke="#141422" stroke-width="1"></circle><circle cx="140" cy="95" r="4" fill="#d4af37" stroke="#141422" stroke-width="1"></circle><circle cx="150" cy="92" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#C85A5A" stroke-width="1.6"></circle><text x="150" y="74" style="font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:10px;fill:#C85A5A;text-anchor:middle">stuck: every single swap scores worse</text><text x="375" y="30" style="font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:10px;fill:#8b7355;text-anchor:middle">global best — never reached</text><circle cx="375" cy="46" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#555" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="3,2"></circle><text x="260" y="224" style="font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:10px;fill:#8b7355;text-anchor:middle">key space, one small change per step  →</text><text x="30" y="20" style="font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:10px;fill:#8b7355;text-anchor:start">fitness (English-ness of the decrypt)</text></svg>
```

Hill climbing search — iteratively refining key guesses by scoring decrypted output against English language statistics.

[Substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/monoalphabetic.html>) [Playfair](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/playfair.html>) Transposition

Technique 07

Simulated Annealing / Genetic Algorithms

Modern · AI-Assisted

Genetic algorithms explore populations of candidate keys; simulated annealing sometimes accepts worse-scoring moves. These methods can help attack classical ciphers, but time and success depend on the problem and settings. A high language score does not prove a correct plaintext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]


Simulated annealing — one possible escape from a local optimum; a finite run need not reach the global best.

[Double Transposition](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/double-transposition.html>) [Playfair](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/playfair.html>) [Hill Cipher](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hill.html>)

Technique 08

Stepping-Switch Cryptanalysis

Frank Rowlett & Genevieve Grotjan · SIS · 1939–1940

Japan's Purple machine routed plaintext through banks of telephone-style stepping switches rather than rotors. The US Signals Intelligence Service had no machine to study, so they hunted statistical regularities in intercept traffic — looking for cycles in how the switches advanced. Genevieve Grotjan’s September 1940 insight was a crucial step in the team’s reconstruction of the switch behavior. SIS built an analog machine, enabling decryption of Purple diplomatic messages. MAGIC was the wider intelligence product, not the name of this single attack. Practise the depth-and-alignment step on synthetic messages in [Diagnosing a Machine from Evidence](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/purple-diagnosis.html>).

[Purple](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/purple.html>) Stepping-switch machines

Technique 09

Computer-Assisted Manuscript Decipherment

Knight, Megyesi & Schaefer · USC ISI / Uppsala · 2011

Knight, Megyesi and Schaefer combined careful transcription, symbol statistics and linguistic reasoning to decipher Copiale. Their 2011 paper describes unsuccessful early automatic-decryption attempts, then progress after treating the Roman letters as spaces and grouping likely homophones. This was a combination of computation and human analysis, not an EM algorithm automatically discovering the answer. [Original Copiale paper](<https://aclanthology.org/W11-1202/>).

[Copiale](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/copiale.html>) [Homophonic](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/homophonic.html>)

Technique 10

Chaocipher Reconstruction

Moshe Rubin & George Lasry · 2010–2014

The disclosure of Byrne’s Chaocipher algorithm in 2010 made independent implementation and attack possible. Subsequent research studied known-plaintext and ciphertext-only attacks under specified conditions. Distinguish revealing an algorithm from recovering a secret starting state. [Researchers’ record of attacks and solved exhibits](<https://www.chaocipher.com/chaocipher-current-state-of-research.htm>).

[Chaocipher](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/chaocipher.html>)

⚡

**Search speed depends on the problem:** Short repeating keys and long, ordinary-language messages can be easy for automated solvers. Short texts, unusual vocabulary, layered ciphers and poorly chosen scoring models can remain difficult. The demonstrations here are examples, not measured performance guarantees.

Al-Kindi’s surviving treatise describes frequency-based cryptanalysis. A monoalphabetic substitution preserves counts while relabeling symbols; polyalphabetic substitution changes that relationship, but need not make a short sample uniform. Language frequencies are evidence for hypotheses, not a guarantee of successful decryption.

Index of Coincidence

0.0385 (uniform reference) Reference comparison scale ~0.066 (English reference)

**Additive-cipher crib test.** Slide a guessed plaintext word across a Vigenère or running-key ciphertext. At each position this tool computes a possible key fragment, (ciphertext − crib) mod 26, with A = 0. A repeating fragment is a hypothesis to test against other text, not confirmation of the crib or key. [Enigma crib attacks](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/enigma.html>) instead test rotor and plugboard constraints; this subtraction is not the Enigma attack.

Ciphertext (letters only)

Crib (guessed plaintext word)  [Input cribWord: type=text; initial value=]

 Drag Crib

For an additive cipher such as Vigenère, known plaintext reveals the keystream *only at the matching positions*: Key[i] = (Cipher[i] − Plain[i]) mod 26. Align both inputs at their first letter. A repeating fragment suggests a possible period; finite observations do not prove that the rest of the key repeats.

To explore a hypothesis, enter a period no longer than the observed keystream. Any extension beyond the known plaintext remains unverified.

Watch a small Caesar-key search score candidate shifts against English frequencies. It illustrates greedy search, not a guaranteed solve: a short or unusual message may score best under an incorrect key.

Ciphertext  [Input hillInput: type=text; initial value=KHOOR ZRUOG]

 Run Hill Climb

The objective is the mean reference frequency assigned to each letter: `sum(reference frequency of each letter) / letter count`. Higher scores are preferred. This measures a preference for common letters, not distance from an English frequency distribution.

Counterexample: `HELLOWORLD` and its reversal `DLROWOLLEH` both score 5.85; `EEEEEEEEEE` scores 12.7. A score optimum can be wrong even when every key has been checked.

 Restore supplied known-answer example

Simulated annealing sometimes accepts worse-scoring candidates to escape local optima. This Caesar example illustrates the rule; a finite run does not guarantee the globally best score or the authentic plaintext.

Historical Record

#### 12 Famous Codebreaks in History

Selected attacks and advances, with their evidence and limitations.

850 AD

Al-Kindi Breaks Substitution

Al-Kindi · Baghdad

Technique: Frequency Analysis

An early surviving systematic account of frequency analysis. Its effectiveness depends on the cipher and available text.

1850s

Babbage Breaks Vigenère

Charles Babbage

Technique: Repeating Sequence Analysis

Babbage worked on attacks against repeating-key polyalphabetic ciphers but did not publish his method. Kasiski independently published an approach in 1863.

1863

Kasiski Publishes the Method

Friedrich Kasiski

Technique: Pattern Repetition Analysis

Kasiski published a method using repeated ciphertext groups to investigate the period of repeating-key polyalphabetic ciphers. Publication did not make every polyalphabetic system immediately readable.

1932

Polish Mathematicians Break Enigma

Rejewski, Różycki, Zygalski · Warsaw

Technique: Permutation Analysis · Known Plaintext

Rejewski reconstructed military Enigma in 1932; Polish analysts subsequently developed several attacks and aids, including the bomba in 1938. Their July 1939 exchange with Britain and France shared methods and reconstructed machines.

1940

US SIS Breaks Japanese Purple

Friedman's SIS team · Grotjan's insight · Washington DC

Technique: Statistical Analysis · Machine Reconstruction

Purple provided valuable Japanese diplomatic intelligence. It did not reveal a complete operational plan for the Pearl Harbor attack; diplomatic and naval communications used different systems.

1974 · 1990

DES and Differential Cryptanalysis

IBM & NSA · rediscovered by Eli Biham & Adi Shamir

Technique: Differential Cryptanalysis

IBM’s designers knew a form of differential cryptanalysis while developing DES and used it in selecting the S-boxes. Biham and Shamir later developed the technique publicly. Its effectiveness depends on the cipher and the available data.

WWII

Bletchley Park Breaks Enigma

Alan Turing · Gordon Welchman

Technique: Crib Attacks · Electromechanical Bombe

Polish mathematicians reconstructed military Enigma before the war. Later Allied bombe machines used crib-derived constraints to eliminate settings. The intelligence contribution was substantial; a precise number of years removed from the war cannot be measured.

1941–1944

From the Lorenz Depth to Colossus

Bill Tutte · Tommy Flowers

Technique: Known Plaintext · Early Computer Search

Tiltman’s 1941 work and Tutte’s structural reconstruction preceded Colossus. The electronic machine became operational in February 1944 and accelerated statistical wheel-setting searches.

1943–80

VENONA: Reused Pad Material

US Army Signal Intelligence

Technique: Key Reuse Exploitation

Duplicated Soviet pad material enabled attacks on some traffic. Analysts also had to reconstruct codebook meanings; recovery was partial and often took years. VENONA’s success did not break the perfect-secrecy guarantee of a correctly used one-time pad.

1993

Linear Cryptanalysis vs DES

Mitsuru Matsui

Technique: Linear Cryptanalysis

Linear approximations enabled a statistical attack on DES under a large known-plaintext requirement. The often-cited 2⁴³ figure is a data requirement for a particular attack, not an unconditional reduction of all attack costs to 2⁴³.

1996

RSA Timing Attack

Paul Kocher

Technique: Side-Channel Timing Analysis

Kocher described how data-dependent execution times can leak secret information from implementations, including RSA. Such attacks require suitable observations and vulnerable implementations; they do not solve the underlying factoring problem.

2017

SHA-1 Collision (SHAttered)

Google · CWI Institute

Technique: Collision Attack

The SHAttered team produced two different PDFs with the same SHA-1 digest. This demonstrated a practical collision and reinforced a migration already underway; collision resistance and preimage resistance are different properties.

🔍

**The Big Pattern:** These cases combine mathematical analysis with **operational evidence**, **protocol weaknesses** and **implementation behavior**. Reused pad material, predictable plaintext and timing leakage create different attack opportunities. Predictable plaintext is not itself an error: modern encryption should protect it under the stated attack model.

#### From papers to inspectable evidence

[Evidence Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html>) · [historical decipherment investigations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html>) · [Modern attack conditions](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/modern-attack-evidence.html>)

#### Reading the search score

George Lasry, *A Methodology for the Cryptanalysis of Classical Ciphers with Search Metaheuristics* (2018 published thesis), §§3.2.1–3.2.4, printed pp. 29–34 / PDF pp. 50–55, and §4.5, printed pp. 56–57 / PDF pp. 77–78, distinguishes objectives, selectivity and resilience to key errors. The small Caesar landscape above is an original teaching example; it does not reproduce the thesis’s large-key experiments.

#### Reading

Joshua Holden, *The Mathematics of Secrets: Cryptography from Caesar Ciphers to Digital Encryption* (2017 edition), chapter 2 and §§5.1–5.2; David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet* (revised edition, 1996); Robert L. Benson, *The VENONA Story* (Center for Cryptologic History edition, 2001), pp. 1–3, 7 and 14–17. The demonstrations illustrate hypotheses and search rules, not guaranteed recoveries.

#### Evidence from Another Encryption

In the [paired-message investigation](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/kisses.html>), a solved weak copy supplies a crib for another historical cipher. Then compare [Banburismus evidence scores](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/joan-clarke.html#banburismus-experiment>) and [Rejewski’s cycle structure](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/enigma.html#cycle-structure>).

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)
