```javascript

function escapeLabText(text) {
  return text.replace(/[&<>"']/g, ch => ({"&":"&amp;", "<":"&lt;", ">":"&gt;", '"':"&quot;", "'":"&#39;"}[ch]));
}

function showTab(id, button) {
  const targetPanel = document.getElementById('tab-' + id);
  const targetButton = button || document.getElementById('tab-btn-' + id);
  document.querySelectorAll('.lab-panel').forEach(panel => {
    const isActive = panel === targetPanel;
    panel.classList.toggle('active', isActive);
    panel.hidden = !isActive;
  });
  document.querySelectorAll('[id^="tab-btn-"]').forEach(tab => {
    const isActive = tab === targetButton;
    tab.classList.toggle('active', isActive);
    tab.setAttribute('aria-selected', isActive ? 'true' : 'false');
    tab.tabIndex = isActive ? 0 : -1;
  });
  if (targetButton) {
    targetButton.focus();
  }
}

document.querySelectorAll('.lab-tab').forEach((tab, index, tabs) => {
  tab.addEventListener('keydown', event => {
    const previous = (index - 1 + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
    const next = (index + 1) % tabs.length;
    if (event.key === 'ArrowLeft') {
      event.preventDefault();
      tabs[previous].click();
    } else if (event.key === 'ArrowRight') {
      event.preventDefault();
      tabs[next].click();
    } else if (event.key === 'Home') {
      event.preventDefault();
      tabs[0].click();
    } else if (event.key === 'End') {
      event.preventDefault();
      tabs[tabs.length - 1].click();
    }
  });
});

// ── Frequency Analysis ──────────────────────────────
const ALPHA = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
const ENG_FREQ = [8.2,1.5,2.8,4.3,12.7,2.2,2.0,6.1,7.0,0.15,0.77,4.0,2.4,6.7,7.5,1.9,0.095,6.0,6.3,9.1,2.8,0.98,2.4,0.15,2.0,0.074];

function buildLabFreqSVG() {
  const svg = document.getElementById('labFreqSVG');
  if (!svg) return;
  const bw = 16, gap = 6, h = 140, base = 155, maxEng = 12.7;
  let html = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < 26; i++) {
    const x = i * (bw + gap);
    const eh = (ENG_FREQ[i] / maxEng) * h;
    // English reference bar (outline)
    html += '<rect x="' + x + '" y="' + (base - eh) + '" width="' + bw + '" height="' + eh + '" fill="none" stroke="rgba(201,168,76,0.3)" stroke-width="1" rx="1"/>';
    // Input frequency bar (filled, initially zero height)
    html += '<rect id="svgbar_' + ALPHA[i] + '" x="' + x + '" y="' + base + '" width="' + bw + '" height="0" fill="#C9A84C" rx="1" style="transition:y .3s,height .3s;"/>';
    // Letter label
    html += '<text x="' + (x + bw / 2) + '" y="' + (base + 12) + '" text-anchor="middle" fill="#706878" font-family="monospace" font-size="8">' + ALPHA[i] + '</text>';
  }
  svg.innerHTML = html;
}
buildLabFreqSVG();

function labFreqUpdate() {
  const txt = document.getElementById('labFreqInput').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
  const result = document.getElementById('labFreqResult');
  const hint = document.getElementById('labFreqHint');
  const icEl = document.getElementById('labFreqIC');
  const reading = document.getElementById('labFreqReading');
  if (!txt.length) { hint.textContent=''; result.textContent=''; icEl.textContent='—'; if(reading)reading.textContent=''; resetSVGBars(); return; }
  const counts={}, len=txt.length, maxEng=12.7, h=140, base=155;
  for (const ch of txt) counts[ch]=(counts[ch]||0)+1;
  let maxCh='E',maxPct=0;
  for (let i=0;i<26;i++){
    const ch=ALPHA[i], pct=((counts[ch]||0)/len)*100;
    const barH=(pct/maxEng)*h;
    const el=document.getElementById('svgbar_'+ch);
    if(el){el.setAttribute('y',base-barH);el.setAttribute('height',barH);el.setAttribute('fill',pct>8?'#C9A84C':pct>4?'#9A7A40':'#7a6530');}
    if(pct>maxPct){maxPct=pct;maxCh=ch;}
  }
  // Compute IC inline
  let icSum=0;
  for (const k in counts) icSum+=counts[k]*(counts[k]-1);
  const ic=len>1?icSum/(len*(len-1)):0;
  icEl.textContent=len>1?ic.toFixed(4):'— (needs two letters)';
  const guessShift=(maxCh.charCodeAt(0)-69+26)%26;
  hint.textContent=`Most frequent: ${maxCh} (${maxPct.toFixed(1)}%) → If this is E, shift = ${guessShift}`;
  result.innerHTML=`<strong>Total letters:</strong> ${len}<br><strong>Most common:</strong> ${maxCh} = ${maxPct.toFixed(1)}%<br><strong>Caesar hypothesis if the most frequent symbol represents E:</strong> ${guessShift}`;
  if (reading) {
    reading.innerHTML = `Your text's most common letter is <strong style="color:var(--gold-lt)">${maxCh}</strong> (${maxPct.toFixed(1)}%). In many long English samples, the most common letter is <strong style="color:var(--gold-lt)">E</strong> (12.7%). If this is a monoalphabetic substitution, <strong>${maxCh}</strong> is a candidate for <strong>E</strong> in the plaintext; short or unusual samples may differ.`;
  }
}
function resetSVGBars(){for(let i=0;i<26;i++){const el=document.getElementById('svgbar_'+ALPHA[i]);if(el){el.setAttribute('y',155);el.setAttribute('height',0);}}}

// ── Index of Coincidence ────────────────────────────
function calcIC() {
  const txt = document.getElementById('iocInput').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
  const display = document.getElementById('icValue');
  const bar = document.getElementById('icBar');
  const interp = document.getElementById('icInterpret');
  if (txt.length < 2) { display.textContent='—'; bar.style.width='0%'; interp.textContent=''; return; }
  const counts={};
  for (const ch of txt) counts[ch]=(counts[ch]||0)+1;
  const n=txt.length;
  let sum=0;
  for (const k in counts) sum+=counts[k]*(counts[k]-1);
  const ic=(sum/(n*(n-1)));
  display.textContent=ic.toFixed(4);
  const pct=Math.min(100,Math.max(0,((ic-0.0385)/(0.066-0.0385))*100));
  bar.style.width=pct+'%';
  let msg='';
  if(ic > 0.080) msg='The observed IC is above the usual long-English reference. Repetitive or short text can produce high values; this does not identify a cipher.';
  else if(ic >= 0.060) msg='This IC is near the long-English reference. Plaintext, transposition and fixed substitution can all preserve this structure; other constructions can also produce it.';
  else if(ic >= 0.045) msg='This IC lies between common English and uniform-letter reference values. A repeating-key cipher is one hypothesis, not a diagnosis.';
  else msg='This IC is near or below the uniform-letter reference. Short samples can even have IC 0; the value does not prove randomness or a long key.';
  msg += ' Observed IC ranges from 0 to 1. The bar clips values outside its reference comparison scale. Consider message length, language and other evidence.';
  interp.innerHTML=msg;
}

// ── Kasiski Examination ─────────────────────────────
function runKasiski() {
  const txt = document.getElementById('kasiskiInput').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
  const result = document.getElementById('kasiskiResult');
  const hits = document.getElementById('kasiskiHits');
  if (txt.length < 20) { result.textContent='Enter at least 20 characters.'; hits.innerHTML=''; return; }

  const repeats={};
  for (let len=3;len<=6;len++) {
    for (let i=0;i<=txt.length-len;i++) {
      const seq=txt.substr(i,len);
      if (!repeats[seq]) repeats[seq]=[];
      repeats[seq].push(i);
    }
  }

  const found=[];
  for (const seq in repeats) {
    if (repeats[seq].length>1) {
      const positions=repeats[seq];
      const spacings=[];
      for (let i=1;i<positions.length;i++) spacings.push(positions[i]-positions[i-1]);
      found.push({seq,positions,spacings});
    }
  }

  if (!found.length) { result.textContent='No repeated sequences found. Text may be too short, or cipher is not Vigenère with a short key.'; hits.innerHTML=''; return; }

  // GCD analysis
  const allSpacings=found.flatMap(f=>f.spacings);
  const gcds={};
  for (const s of allSpacings) {
    for (let k=2;k<=Math.min(s,15);k++) {
      if (s%k===0) gcds[k]=(gcds[k]||0)+1;
    }
  }
  const sorted=Object.entries(gcds).sort((a,b)=>b[1]-a[1]);
  const likelyKey=sorted[0]?sorted[0][0]:null;

  result.innerHTML=`Found <strong>${found.length}</strong> repeated sequences. Top spacing-factor candidate (2–15): <strong style="color:var(--gold)">${likelyKey || "none"}</strong>. This heuristic counts overlapping repeats; accidental repeats and tied factors require further tests.`;
  hits.innerHTML=found.slice(0,8).map(f=>
    `<div class="kasiski-hit">"${f.seq}" at positions ${f.positions.join(', ')} — spacings: ${f.spacings.join(', ')}</div>`
  ).join('');
}

// ── Crib Dragging ───────────────────────────────────
// Require at least two complete periods. A match describes only this fragment;
// it does not establish either the guessed plaintext or the complete key.
function fragmentPeriod(fragment) {
  for (let period = 1; period <= Math.floor(fragment.length / 2); period++) {
    let fits = true;
    for (let i = period; i < fragment.length; i++) {
      if (fragment[i] !== fragment[i % period]) { fits = false; break; }
    }
    if (fits) return period;
  }
  return null;
}

function runCribDrag() {
  const ct = document.getElementById('cribCipher').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
  const crib = document.getElementById('cribWord').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
  const out = document.getElementById('cribResult');
  if (ct.length < 2 || crib.length < 1) { out.textContent='Enter ciphertext and a crib word.'; return; }
  if (crib.length > ct.length) { out.textContent='Crib is longer than ciphertext.'; return; }
  let html = '<div style="display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:.4rem;max-height:300px;overflow-y:auto;">';
  for (let pos = 0; pos <= ct.length - crib.length; pos++) {
    let key = '';
    for (let j = 0; j < crib.length; j++) {
      key += ALPHA[(ct.charCodeAt(pos + j) - crib.charCodeAt(j) + 26) % 26];
    }
    const period = fragmentPeriod(key);
    const style = period !== null ? 'border-color:var(--gold);background:var(--gold-glow);' : '';
    html += '<div style="font-family:var(--fm);font-size:.75rem;background:var(--s3);border:1px solid var(--s4);border-radius:var(--r);padding:.5rem .75rem;color:var(--tx2);' + style + '">';
    html += '<span style="color:var(--tx3);min-width:60px;display:inline-block;">Pos ' + pos + ':</span> ';
    html += 'Key fragment = <span style="color:var(--gold-lt);font-weight:700;">' + key + '</span>';
    if (period !== null) html += ' <span style="color:var(--gold);margin-left:.5rem;">Period ' + period + ' fits this fragment (hypothesis)</span>';
    html += '</div>';
  }
  html += '</div><p style="margin-top:.75rem;color:var(--tx2);">A highlighted period fits at least two repeats within the guessed span. Check the proposed key against plaintext outside the crib. No highlight does not rule out a longer period or a running key.</p>';
  out.innerHTML = html;
}

// ── Known Plaintext Attack ──────────────────────────
function runKPA() {
  const plain = document.getElementById('kpaPlain').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
  const cipher = document.getElementById('kpaCipher').value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
  const out = document.getElementById('kpaResult');
  if (!plain.length || !cipher.length) { out.textContent='Enter both plaintext and ciphertext.'; return; }
  const len = Math.min(plain.length, cipher.length);
  let key = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
    key += ALPHA[(cipher.charCodeAt(i) - plain.charCodeAt(i) + 26) % 26];
  }
  let html = '<strong>Observed keystream (' + len + ' positions):</strong> <span style="color:var(--gold-lt);font-family:var(--fm);letter-spacing:.1em;overflow-wrap:anywhere;">' + key + '</span>';
  html += '<br><strong>Supported plaintext span:</strong> <span style="font-family:var(--fm);overflow-wrap:anywhere;">' + plain.slice(0, len) + '</span>';
  if (plain.length > cipher.length) html += '<br>Extra plaintext has no matching ciphertext and was not used.';
  if (cipher.length > len) html += '<br><strong>Unknown remainder:</strong> ' + (cipher.length - len) + ' ciphertext positions; the observed fragment alone does not decrypt them.';
  const period = fragmentPeriod(key);
  if (period !== null) {
    html += '<br><strong>Period hypothesis:</strong> ' + period + ' (fragment ' + key.slice(0, period) + '). This fits the observed span; it does not prove the complete key repeats.';
  } else {
    html += '<br>No period with two complete repeats fits the observed span. Longer periods and nonrepeating keys remain possible.';
  }

  const periodInput = document.getElementById('kpaPeriod');
  const requested = periodInput.value.trim();
  // Browsers expose unfinished number input (for example "1e") as an empty
  // value with badInput set. Do not mistake that state for an omitted period.
  if (periodInput.validity.badInput) {
    html += '<br><strong>Cannot test that period:</strong> enter a whole number from 1 to ' + len + ', or clear the field.';
  } else if (requested) {
    const assumed = Number(requested);
    if (!Number.isInteger(assumed) || assumed < 1 || assumed > len) {
      html += '<br><strong>Cannot test that period:</strong> enter a whole number from 1 to ' + len + '.';
    } else {
      const candidate = key.slice(0, assumed);
      const fits = Array.from(key).every((letter, i) => letter === candidate[i % assumed]);
      if (!fits) {
        html += '<br><strong>Period ' + assumed + ' rejected:</strong> it contradicts the observed keystream.';
      } else {
        let extrapolated = '';
        for (let i = len; i < cipher.length; i++) {
          extrapolated += ALPHA[(cipher.charCodeAt(i) - candidate.charCodeAt(i % assumed) + 26) % 26];
        }
        html += '<br><br><strong>Assumed key:</strong> ' + candidate + ' (period ' + assumed + ').';
        if (extrapolated) html += '<br><strong>Unverified extension under this assumption:</strong> <span style="font-family:var(--fm);overflow-wrap:anywhere;">' + extrapolated + '</span>';
        else html += '<br>There is no ciphertext beyond the known span to extend.';
        html += '<br>Validate this hypothesis against independent plaintext or other evidence.';
      }
    }
  }
  out.innerHTML = html;
}

// The score stays unchanged: this lesson exposes its limitations.
function caesarToyScore(text) {
  const letters = text.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g, '');
  if (!letters.length) return null;
  return Array.from(letters).reduce((sum, c) => sum + ENG_FREQ[c.charCodeAt(0) - 65], 0) / letters.length;
}
function caesarToyDecrypt(text, shift) {
  return text.toUpperCase().replace(/[A-Z]/g, c => ALPHA[(c.charCodeAt(0) - 65 - shift + 26) % 26]);
}
const CAESAR_LESSON_EXAMPLES = {
  hill: { ciphertext: 'KHOOR ZRUOG', plaintext: 'HELLO WORLD', shift: 3 },
  anneal: { ciphertext: 'WKLV LV D WHVW PHVVDJH', plaintext: 'THIS IS A TEST MESSAGE', shift: 3 }
};
function renderCaesarLandscape(prefix, input, state) {
  const out = document.getElementById(prefix + 'Landscape');
  if (!/[A-Z]/i.test(input)) {
    out.textContent = 'Enter at least one A–Z letter to define a score. No search or language conclusion is available.';
    return;
  }
  const rows = Array.from({length: 26}, (_, shift) => ({shift, text: caesarToyDecrypt(input, shift), score: caesarToyScore(caesarToyDecrypt(input, shift))}));
  const maximum = Math.max(...rows.map(row => row.score));
  const optima = rows.filter(row => Math.abs(row.score - maximum) < 1e-10).map(row => row.shift);
  const example = CAESAR_LESSON_EXAMPLES[prefix];
  const known = input.toUpperCase().trim() === example.ciphertext ? example : null;
  let html = '<h3>All 26 shifts under this objective</h3><p><strong>Search stopping point:</strong> ' +
    (state ? 'shift ' + state.stop + ' (last accepted state).' : 'not run.') +
    ' <strong>Score optimum after checking all 26:</strong> shift' + (optima.length > 1 ? 's ' : ' ') + optima.join(', ') +
    '. <strong>Supplied known answer:</strong> ' + (known ? 'shift ' + known.shift + ', ' + known.plaintext + '.' : 'none for this edited input.') + '</p>';
  if (state) html += '<p><strong>Best sampled shift:</strong> ' + state.best + '. <strong>Evaluated path:</strong> ' + state.path.join(' → ') + '. Rejected proposals are included; they do not become the stopping point.</p>';
  html += '<p>The exhaustive score check is a reference for this 26-key lesson, separate from the search trajectory. It does not validate a plaintext.</p>' +
    '<div style="overflow-x:auto;" role="region" tabindex="0" aria-label="Caesar shift scores; scroll horizontally if needed"><table class="caesar-landscape-table" style="width:100%;text-align:left;"><caption>Higher mean letter-frequency scores are preferred. Markers distinguish the search state, model optimum and supplied answer.</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Shift</th><th scope="col">Score</th><th scope="col">Role</th><th scope="col">Candidate</th></tr></thead><tbody>';
  for (const row of rows) {
    const roles = [];
    if (state && row.shift === state.stop) roles.push('Stopping point');
    if (state && row.shift === state.best) roles.push('Best sampled');
    if (optima.includes(row.shift)) roles.push('Score optimum');
    if (known && row.shift === known.shift) roles.push('Supplied answer');
    html += '<tr data-shift="' + row.shift + '" data-score="' + row.score + '"><th scope="row">' + row.shift + '</th><td>' + row.score.toFixed(4) +
      '<br><meter min="0" max="12.7" value="' + row.score + '" aria-label="Shift ' + row.shift + ' score" style="width:6rem;">' + row.score.toFixed(4) + '</meter></td><td>' + roles.join('; ') +
      '</td><td style="font-family:var(--fm);word-break:break-word;">' + escapeLabText(row.text) + '</td></tr>';
  }
  out.innerHTML = html + '</tbody></table></div>';
}
for (const prefix of ['hill', 'anneal']) {
  const field = document.getElementById(prefix + 'Input');
  function refresh() { document.getElementById(prefix + 'Output').textContent = ''; renderCaesarLandscape(prefix, field.value); }
  field.addEventListener('input', refresh);
  document.getElementById(prefix + 'Example').addEventListener('click', () => { field.value = CAESAR_LESSON_EXAMPLES[prefix].ciphertext; refresh(); });
  refresh();
}

// ── Hill Climbing ───────────────────────────────────
async function runHillClimb() {
  const input = document.getElementById('hillInput').value.toUpperCase();
  const out = document.getElementById('hillOutput');
  const btn = document.getElementById('hillBtn');
  if (!/[A-Z]/.test(input)) { out.textContent = ''; renderCaesarLandscape('hill', input); return; }
  document.getElementById('hillInput').disabled = true;
  document.getElementById('hillExample').disabled = true;
  btn.disabled = true;
  out.innerHTML = '';

  const score = caesarToyScore;
  const decrypt = caesarToyDecrypt;

  let current = 0;
  let bestScore = score(decrypt(input, 0));
  let steps = [{shift: 0, score: bestScore, text: decrypt(input, 0), action: 'Start'}];

  for (let iter = 0; iter < 30; iter++) {
    const neighbors = [(current + 1) % 26, (current + 25) % 26];
    let improved = false;
    for (const n of neighbors) {
      const ns = score(decrypt(input, n));
      steps.push({shift: n, score: ns, text: decrypt(input, n), action: ns > bestScore ? 'Climb ↑' : 'Reject ↓'});
      if (ns > bestScore) {
        bestScore = ns;
        current = n;
        improved = true;
        break;
      }
    }
    if (!improved) break;
  }

  for (let i = 0; i < steps.length; i++) {
    const s = steps[i];
    const line = document.createElement('div');
    const color = s.action === 'Climb ↑' ? 'var(--green)' : s.action === 'Reject ↓' ? 'var(--red)' : 'var(--gold)';
    line.style.cssText = 'padding:.3rem .6rem;border-radius:3px;';
    line.innerHTML = '<span style="color:' + color + ';min-width:70px;display:inline-block;">' + s.action + '</span> Shift ' + s.shift.toString().padStart(2,'0') + ' (score ' + s.score.toFixed(1) + '): <span style="color:var(--tx);">' + escapeLabText(s.text) + '</span>';
    if (i === steps.length - 1 && s.action !== 'Reject ↓') {
      line.style.background = 'var(--gold-glow)';
      line.innerHTML += ' <span style="color:var(--green);font-size:.7rem;margin-left:.5rem;">← Converged</span>';
    }
    out.appendChild(line);
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 120));
  }
  renderCaesarLandscape('hill', input, {stop: current, best: current, path: steps.map(step => step.shift)});
  document.getElementById('hillInput').disabled = false;
  document.getElementById('hillExample').disabled = false;
  btn.disabled = false;
}

// ── Simulated Annealing ─────────────────────────────
async function runAnneal() {
  const input = document.getElementById('annealInput').value.toUpperCase();
  const out = document.getElementById('annealOutput');
  const btn = document.getElementById('annealBtn');
  if (!/[A-Z]/.test(input)) { out.textContent = ''; renderCaesarLandscape('anneal', input); return; }
  document.getElementById('annealInput').disabled = true;
  document.getElementById('annealExample').disabled = true;
  btn.disabled = true;
  out.innerHTML = '';

  const score = caesarToyScore;
  const decrypt = caesarToyDecrypt;

  let current = Math.floor(Math.random() * 26);
  const initialShift = current;
  let currentScore = score(decrypt(input, current));
  let bestShift = current, bestScore = currentScore;
  let temp = 10.0;
  const cooling = 0.85;
  let steps = [];

  for (let iter = 0; iter < 30 && temp > 0.1; iter++) {
    const neighbor = (current + (Math.random() < 0.5 ? 1 : 25)) % 26;
    const ns = score(decrypt(input, neighbor));
    const delta = ns - currentScore;
    const accept = delta > 0 || Math.random() < Math.exp(delta / temp);
    const action = delta > 0 ? 'Better ↑' : (accept ? 'Accept ↔' : 'Reject ↓');
    steps.push({shift: neighbor, score: ns, text: decrypt(input, neighbor), action, temp: temp.toFixed(2)});
    if (accept) {
      current = neighbor;
      currentScore = ns;
      if (ns > bestScore) { bestScore = ns; bestShift = neighbor; }
    }
    temp *= cooling;
  }

  for (let i = 0; i < steps.length; i++) {
    const s = steps[i];
    const line = document.createElement('div');
    const color = s.action === 'Better ↑' ? 'var(--green)' : s.action === 'Accept ↔' ? 'var(--orange)' : 'var(--red)';
    line.style.cssText = 'padding:.3rem .6rem;border-radius:3px;';
    line.innerHTML = '<span style="color:var(--tx3);min-width:55px;display:inline-block;">T=' + s.temp + '</span> <span style="color:' + color + ';min-width:65px;display:inline-block;">' + s.action + '</span> Shift ' + s.shift.toString().padStart(2,'0') + ': <span style="color:var(--tx);">' + escapeLabText(s.text) + '</span>';
    out.appendChild(line);
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 120));
  }

  const final = document.createElement('div');
  final.style.cssText = 'margin-top:.75rem;padding:.6rem;background:var(--gold-glow);border-radius:3px;';
  final.innerHTML = '<strong style="color:var(--gold);">Best sampled candidate:</strong> Shift ' + bestShift + ' → <span style="color:var(--tx);font-family:var(--fm);letter-spacing:.1em;">' + escapeLabText(decrypt(input, bestShift)) + '</span> <span style="color:var(--green);font-size:.7rem;">(score ' + bestScore.toFixed(1) + ')</span>';
  out.appendChild(final);
  renderCaesarLandscape('anneal', input, {stop: current, best: bestShift, path: [initialShift, ...steps.map(step => step.shift)]});
  document.getElementById('annealInput').disabled = false;
  document.getElementById('annealExample').disabled = false;
  btn.disabled = false;
}
```

```javascript

  // Chrome-less embeddable demo: /embed.html?cipher=caesar
  // The cipher name is validated against a strict pattern, then handed to the
  // same demo-loader that renders exhibit-page demos.
  (function () {
    'use strict';
    var cipher = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('cipher') || '';
    var valid = /^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]{0,39}$/.test(cipher);
    var el = document.getElementById('embed-demo');
    if (valid) {
      el.setAttribute('data-cipher', cipher);
      document.getElementById('embed-title').textContent = 'Interactive Demo — ' + cipher;
      document.title = cipher + ' Demo — The Cipher Museum';
    } else {
      el.innerHTML = '<p class="embed-error">No cipher specified. Use embed.html?cipher=caesar (or vigenere, playfair, railFence…)</p>';
    }
    // If the loader doesn't recognise the cipher, replace the spinner text.
    window.addEventListener('load', function () {
      setTimeout(function () {
        if (el.hasAttribute('data-cipher') && !el.querySelector('input, select, textarea, button')) {
          el.innerHTML = '<p class="embed-error">Unknown cipher "' + el.getAttribute('data-cipher').replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9]/g, '') + '". Check the demo name on its exhibit page.</p>';
        }
      }, 400);
    });
  })();
```

- [Teaching](<https://ciphermuseum.com/teaching.html>)

A first visit · No previous experience needed

### Your first codebreak

A book has been left in the wrong room. Read the notice, test a guess, and find out where to go.

Allow about 15 minutes for the first lesson. The three extensions can be explored separately. Every message here is an original, invented teaching exercise. Your work stays in this tab and resets when you reload.

[1. Read the notice](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html#first-desk>)[2. Follow a repeating key](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html#vigenere-lesson>)[3. Compare languages](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html#language-lesson>)[4. Spread the counts](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html#homophone-lesson>)[Print the activities](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-worksheet.html>)[Find a cipher topic](<https://ciphermuseum.com/classical-guide.html>)

The interactive lessons require JavaScript. The [worksheet](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-worksheet.html>), [answers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-answers.html>), and [topic guide](<https://ciphermuseum.com/classical-guide.html>) also work without it.

#### 1. Where is the book?

This notice uses a one-to-one substitution: each letter always becomes the same cipher letter. Spaces and punctuation were retained. Your task is to propose a partial key and check it across the whole notice.

##### The intercepted notice

##### Look for a clue

Highlight doubled lettersHighlight short wordsHighlight repeated words

Count the cipher letters

A substitution preserves the counts but changes their labels. A particular text need not follow an average English frequency table.

Try the tempting guess G → E

##### Build your key

Enter a plaintext letter below a cipher letter. A dot means unknown. Lock a guess to preserve it; unlock it before changing it. The same plaintext letter cannot be assigned twice.

##### Your current reading

UndoClear unlocked guessesCheck the message

##### Help when you need it

Show the next clueReveal one missing letter

 What changed your mind? Name two clues that support your reading.

A readable result needs a consistent key and supporting evidence. The check here compares your result with the answer to this invented exercise. It cannot authenticate a document or prove who wrote it.

Continue with your own message in the [manual substitution desk](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-detective.html#manual-substitution>), or try [the Curator’s Sealed Letter](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html>) to investigate what a recovered message can prove.

#### 2. Follow a repeating key

This longer library dispatch uses repeating-key Vigenère. Only A–Z letters count toward the key position. Spaces and punctuation have been removed. The original exercise was written with recurring phrases so you can examine key alignment.

##### Find repeated fragments

Find repeated trigrams

##### Try a period

Candidate repeating-key period
- 1

- 2

- 3 [selected]

- 4

- 5

- 6

- 7

- 8

- 9

- 10

For a proposed period of four, column 1 contains letters 1, 5, 9…; column 2 contains 2, 6, 10… . If the period fits the key, each column uses one Caesar shift. Try key letters below and watch the columns and message change.

“Best English fit” minimizes chi-square against a fixed, rounded English letter-frequency reference. Lower is a closer fit, not a probability of correctness. Short columns and unusual language can mislead. Inspect every shift, then test the complete message.

Candidate key: ****

Check reconstructed messageReveal the supplied key

Explain why the repeating key creates useful groups. Why could a multiple of the true period also work? Continue to the [Vigenère table and encryption trace](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) and the [cryptanalysis techniques](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cryptanalysis.html>).

#### 3. Which language are you assuming?

Compare the letter counts, short words and within-word pairs in five small, original library messages. Change the language and inspect the sample that produced the numbers.

Reference sample

##### Letter counts and percentages

##### Most frequent within-word pairs

##### Words of one to three letters in this sample

All five samples are modern teaching prose, written in uppercase A–Z with accents omitted. Counts do not include spaces or punctuation; letter pairs do not cross word boundaries. These small samples are not representative language corpora or historical frequency tables.

Return to the notice: the most frequent ciphertext symbol represents O, not E. The subject and wording matter as well as the language. For historical work, explore the separately documented profiles and abstention rules in the [Evidence Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html>).

#### 4. Give a common letter more disguises

Use the same notice from lesson 1. First, every letter receives one numerical token. Then give its unusually frequent O several alternatives. The charts count whole three-digit tokens, not individual digits; both charts use the same scale.

Possible tokens for O
- 1

- 2

- 4 [selected]

- 8
Draw another sample

##### One token per letter

##### O receives alternatives

Inspect the numerical ciphertext

Giving O extra symbols can reduce its individual peaks. Other letters still repeat, and sequences still carry structure. A flatter chart does not establish secure encryption.

This deliberately simple allocation adapts to one invented notice; it is not a historical key. Random choices use a teaching simulation, not a cryptographic random generator. Real proportional allocations must consider the wider alphabet and the expected message distribution.

Continue to [Homophonic Substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/homophonic.html>) and the [one-time pad](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/one-time-pad.html>) to see why a statistical appearance and a secrecy proof are different things.

#### For a classroom or library group

Work in pairs: one person proposes a guess and the other tries to find a contradiction. Swap roles after the third clue. Use the first notice for a short session; add the Vigenère exercise for a longer workshop.

[Printable activities, without answers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-worksheet.html>) · [Separate facilitator’s answers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-answers.html>) · [Classical topic guide](<https://ciphermuseum.com/classical-guide.html>)

To exchange messages, each pair can use the [Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/workbench.html>) to encrypt an original short notice. Give the other pair only the ciphertext and cipher family; retain a separate answer copy. These are puzzle ciphers, unsuitable for protecting private information.

#### Sources and scope

Simon Singh’s [Black Chamber](<https://simonsingh.net/The_Black_Chamber/chamberguide.html>) inspired the guided teaching format. See its [hints](<https://simonsingh.net/The_Black_Chamber/hintsandtips.html>) and [repeating-key explanation](<https://simonsingh.net/The_Black_Chamber/crackingprinciple.html>). These museum messages, lesson text and implementation are original.

Technical background: Al Sweigart, *Cracking Codes with Python* (2018), chapter 17, for word-pattern constraints; Menezes, van Oorschot and Vanstone, *Handbook of Applied Cryptography* (1997), §§7.3.2–7.3.3, for substitution and polyalphabetic systems. The English chi-square reference is a more coarsely rounded version of the museum Detective’s existing reference. [Continue reading](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html>).

### Further Reading

Read a chapter, try an exhibit, then return to the book with a question

**Note:** The Cipher Museum does not sell, endorse, or affiliate with any publisher or retailer. Book links identify official author or publisher information pages; book texts and ebook downloads are not linked. Research and archival links are identified separately. No affiliate codes are used. ISBNs are provided to help you locate copies through your preferred library or bookseller.

#### Chapter-to-Exhibit Reading Trails

Choose a book or a case-study topic below. Each stop pairs a specific chapter or section with a museum activity and a question to investigate. These are concept companions, not reproductions of the books or complete implementations of their programming chapters. Use the stated edition: numbering can change between editions.

[Sweigart · learn by doing](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#sweigart>) [Gaines · classical codebreaking](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#gaines>) [Holden · the mathematics](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#holden>) [Esslinger · historical evidence](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#esslinger>) [Traffic analysis · three sources](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#traffic-analysis-books>) [Ancient scripts · six books](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#ancient-scripts-books>) [Purple · three books](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#purple-books>) [Working is not secure · three books](<https://ciphermuseum.com/further-reading.html#security-claims-books>)

For a route without a book, use the museum's [guided tours](<https://ciphermuseum.com/tours/index.html>).

*Cracking Codes with Python*Al Sweigart · No Starch Press, 2018

Use Al Sweigart’s *Cracking Codes with Python* (2018), following the chapter references below. The museum illustrates cipher behavior; the book teaches the Python programs, file handling and testing.

- **Chapters 5–6 · Caesar shifts and exhaustive search**

Try [Caesar](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/caesar.html>), then compare all shifts in [Cipher Detective](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-detective.html>). What lets you recognize a promising plaintext?

Chapter 5 · Chapter 6

- **Chapters 7–12 · Transposition and testing**

Use [Columnar Transposition](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html>) to track moved letters. The museum's keyed-column variant differs from the book's width-key program; chapters 9–11 also cover software tests, files and English detection.

Chapter 7 · Chapter 12

- **Chapters 13–15 · Modular arithmetic and affine keys**

Try valid and invalid multipliers in [Affine](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/affine.html>). Why must the multiplier have an inverse modulo 26?

Chapter 13 · Chapter 15

- **Chapters 16–17 · Substitution and word patterns**

Explore [Monoalphabetic Substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/monoalphabetic.html>), then build a partial key in [Cipher Detective](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-detective.html#manual-substitution>). Which word candidates remain compatible with one shared mapping?

Chapter 16 · Chapter 17

- **Chapters 18–20 · Vigenère and repeated-key evidence**

Try [Vigenère](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) and the Kasiski tab in the [Cryptanalysis Lab](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cryptanalysis.html>). Does a repeated fragment prove a key length, or suggest candidates?

Chapter 18 · Chapter 20

- **Chapter 21 · One-time pads**

Visit [One-Time Pad](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/one-time-pad.html>). Separate the conditions for perfect secrecy from the effects of key reuse and ciphertext tampering.

Chapter 21

- **Chapters 22–24 · Primes and public-key encryption**

Follow the small-number example in [RSA](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rsa.html>). The arithmetic is educational: production RSA requires secure parameters, padding and implementation protections beyond this trail.

Chapter 22 · Chapter 24

*Cryptanalysis: A Study of Ciphers and Their Solution*Helen Fouché Gaines · corrected Dover edition, 1956; original work, 1939

A classical cryptanalysis workbook, not present-day deployment guidance. Find the [publisher's edition](<https://store.doverpublications.com/products/9780486200972>) (ISBN 978-0-486-20097-2); use your library copy for the chapter exercises.

- **Chapters VI–VII · Columnar transposition and multiple anagramming**

Reorder several same-key intercepts in the [multiple-anagramming exercise](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html#multiple-anagramming>). Can one ordering explain every message? Compare the different-key control.

- **Chapters VIII–IX · Substitution fundamentals**

Use [Monoalphabetic Substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/monoalphabetic.html>) and [Cipher Detective](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-detective.html#manual-substitution>) to combine letter frequencies with word constraints. A frequent letter is evidence, not a guaranteed mapping.

- **Chapters XII and XIV–XV · Vigenère and period hypotheses**

Move from [Vigenère](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) to the [Cryptanalysis Lab](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cryptanalysis.html>). Compare Kasiski evidence with a guessed plaintext fragment; keep an inferred key period separate from verified text.

*The Mathematics of Secrets: Cryptography from Caesar Ciphers to Digital Encryption*Joshua Holden · Princeton University Press, 2017

See the [author's book page, contents and errata](<https://wordpress.rose-hulman.edu/holden/the-mathematics-of-secrets/>). These stops use the 2017 edition (ISBN 978-0-691-14175-6).

- **Sections 1.6–1.7 · Hill matrices and known plaintext**

Visit [Hill](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hill.html>). Check the determinant of the known-plaintext matrix: two matched blocks alone do not guarantee a unique 2 × 2 key.

- **Sections 3.5–3.7 · Columnar transposition and anagramming**

Try the [shared-column exercise](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html#multiple-anagramming>). Compare plausible neighboring letters across messages; a contact score is not a probability of correctness.

- **Sections 5.1–5.2 · Running keys and one-time pads**

Compare [Running-Key](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/running-key.html>) and [One-Time Pad](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/one-time-pad.html>). Why does a long passage without a short period still differ from independent, uniformly random key material?

*Learning and Experiencing Cryptography with CrypTool and SageMath*Bernhard Esslinger · Artech House, 2024

Use the 2024 Artech House edition (ISBN 978-1-68569-017-5) for the chapter and section numbers below. The museum is a separate implementation; it does not run the book's CrypTool or SageMath exercises.

- **Chapter 2, sections 2.1–2.2 · Transposition and substitution**

Compare [Columnar Transposition](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html>) with [Monoalphabetic Substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/monoalphabetic.html>). Which changes symbol positions, and which changes the symbols themselves?

- **Chapter 3, sections 3.4.1–3.4.2 and 3.5.1 · Transcription and tokenization**

Prepare a source in [Cipher Detective](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-detective.html#transcription-workspace>) before analyzing it. Preserve uncertain symbols and original lineation, then inspect what an A–Z projection leaves out. For manuscript transcription at larger scale, explore [CrypTool's CTTS project](<https://www.cryptool.org/en/ctts/>).

- **Chapter 3, sections 3.5.2–3.5.3 · Heuristic search and scoring**

Compare hill climbing and simulated annealing in the [Cryptanalysis Lab](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cryptanalysis.html#hill-climbing>). A search score reflects a language model; it does not certify a historically correct reading.

##### Trails behind the case studies

These trails group the books cited by the museum’s newer case studies. Each stop names the book and its edition and links the exhibit it supports. The books are cited by title, not linked: find them through a library or bookseller.

*Traffic analysis: what a network reveals before its messages are read*Borrmann et al. · Diffie and Landau · Thirsk

Three sources behind [Reading the Radio Log](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html>). The exercise’s radio log is invented; these books supply the method and the history.

- **Borrmann et al. · Externals, net structure and deception**

Donald A. Borrmann and colleagues, *The History of Traffic Analysis: World War I – Vietnam* (Center for Cryptologic History, National Security Agency, 2013). Work the [network and callsign stages](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#connect>) of the radio log. Which of your conclusions rests on an observation, and which on a callsign match you chose?

- **Borrmann et al. · First World War examples**

Compare the book’s cases with the exercise’s [history notes](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#history>). What does a silent radio tell you, and what does it leave unknown about the unit that carried it?

- **Diffie and Landau · Communications intelligence and call records**

Whitfield Diffie and Susan Landau, *Privacy on the Line: The Politics of Wiretapping and Encryption*, updated and expanded edition (MIT Press, 2007). After the radio log’s [debrief](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#debrief>), ask which of its externals still has a counterpart in a record of the numbers a telephone line calls.

- **Thirsk · A log-reader’s account**

James Thirsk’s account in Ralph Erskine and Michael Smith (eds), *The Bletchley Park Codebreakers* (Biteback, 2011). Read it after the exercise’s [section on limits](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#limits>). What did wartime log-readers record that a two-day teaching log leaves out?

*Ancient scripts: decipherment as hypothesis and test*Chadwick · Ventris and Chadwick · Parkinson · Collier and Manley · Coe · Kettunen and Helmke

Six books behind the Linear B, Egyptian and Maya cases in [Historical Investigations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html>). These are writing systems, not ciphers: each was recovered by testing hypotheses about how the script works. The [writing-systems tour](<https://ciphermuseum.com/tours/tour.html?tour=writing-systems>) visits the same cases in order.

- **Chadwick · From Kober’s structural work to tablet Ta 641**

John Chadwick, *The Decipherment of Linear B* (Cambridge University Press, 1958). Work the [Linear B case](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#linear-b>). Which evidence built the grid, and which tablet tested it afterwards?

- **Ventris and Chadwick · The decipherment and the spelling rules**

Michael Ventris and John Chadwick, *Documents in Mycenaean Greek* (Cambridge University Press, 1956). Return to the [Linear B case](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#linear-b>). Once the spelling rules are known, which readings still stay ambiguous?

- **Parkinson · Young, Champollion and how the signs work**

Richard Parkinson, *Cracking Codes: The Rosetta Stone and Decipherment* (University of California Press, 1999). Work the [Egyptian case](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#egyptian>). Which two observations broke the idea of one picture to a word?

- **Collier and Manley · Sound signs, determinatives and reading direction**

Mark Collier and Bill Manley, *How to Read Egyptian Hieroglyphs* (University of California Press, 1998). In the [Egyptian case](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#egyptian>), sort the signs by role. Which add sound, and which only place a word in a class of meaning?

- **Coe · Landa, Knorozov and Proskouriakoff**

Michael D. Coe, *Breaking the Maya Code*, 3rd edition (Thames & Hudson, 2012). Work the [Maya case](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#maya>). Why did Landa’s “alphabet” give nonsense when it was applied letter by letter, and what changed when Knorozov read its signs as syllables?

- **Kettunen and Helmke · Spelling harmony**

Harri Kettunen and Christophe Helmke, *Introduction to Maya Hieroglyphs*, 20th edition (Wayeb, 2025). Back in the [Maya case](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#maya>), take a spelling such as ba-ki for baak. Which vowel is spoken, and what does the silent one signal?

*Purple: diagnosing a machine from evidence*Stamp and Low · Rowlett · Mundy

Three books behind [Diagnosing a Machine from Evidence](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/purple-diagnosis.html>). The worksheet’s messages and wiring are invented and simplified; it does not reproduce the historical attack or the Purple machine.

- **Stamp and Low · Depth, matched plaintext and partial permutations**

Mark Stamp and Richard M. Low, *Applied Cryptanalysis: Breaking Ciphers in the Real World* (Wiley, 2007). Do the [worksheet](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/purple-diagnosis.html#worksheet>). Which entries in your partial permutation were supplied as plaintext, and which did you infer?

- **Rowlett · From a first pattern to corroboration**

Frank B. Rowlett, *The Story of Magic: Memoirs of an American Cryptologic Pioneer* (Aegean Park Press, 1998). After testing an alignment on the [held-out message](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/purple-diagnosis.html#worksheet>), ask what the team looked for once the first instance of the relationship had been found.

- **Mundy · The team behind the work**

Liza Mundy, *Code Girls: The Untold Story of the American Women Code Breakers of World War II* (Hachette, 2017). Read the worksheet’s [team note](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/purple-diagnosis.html#team>) and the [Purple](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/purple.html>) exhibit. Who else worked on Purple, and what did each contribute?

*Working is not secure: a functional test is not a security test*Flannery · Bauer · Piper and Murphy

Three books behind [Working Is Not Secure](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/working-is-not-secure.html>) and its [guided route](<https://ciphermuseum.com/tours/tour.html?tour=working-not-secure>). The page’s message, key and tests are original, and no attack from these books is reproduced.

- **Flannery · A working scheme, an attack and a negative result**

Sarah Flannery with David Flannery, *In Code: A Mathematical Journey* (Profile Books, 2000). Read the page’s [negative result](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/working-is-not-secure.html#negative>). Why was a report on the attack worth including in her next project?

- **Bauer · The maxims of cryptology**

Friedrich L. Bauer, *Decrypted Secrets: Methods and Maxims of Cryptology*, 4th edition (Springer, 2007). After the [worked example](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/working-is-not-secure.html#example>), ask which of the maxims its key-space claim ignores.

- **Piper and Murphy · Practical security**

Fred Piper and Sean Murphy, *Cryptography: A Very Short Introduction* (Oxford University Press, 2002). The example has 26! (about 4 × 10<sup>26</sup>) keys, yet its security claim fails in the [verdict](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/working-is-not-secure.html#verdict>). Why does a large key space bound only exhaustive key search?

#### Interactive Companion Exhibits

Standalone hands-on exhibits that go deeper on a single idea than the main halls can. Free, open-source, and browser-based.

Interactive Exhibit · Companion

DeckBook

A Cipher Museum companion exhibit

A card-based one-time keybook: the deck order is the key. Watch a Vigenère-style stream cipher run one card at a time, then break it yourself — reuse a key across two messages and crib-drag the plaintext back out — and finish with a shareable intercept challenge. A hands-on deep dive into one-time keys, key reuse, and why key distribution is the hard problem, all client-side and installable offline.

 [Open DeckBook →](<https://systemslibrarian.github.io/DeckBook/>) InteractiveOne-Time PadKey ReuseFree

#### Canonical Histories

Six starting points for exploring cryptographic history and practice.

History · Essential

*The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*

David Kahn

1967 · revised 1996 · ISBN 978-0684831305

A wide-ranging history of cryptology, from ancient writing systems to twentieth-century intelligence. The revised 1996 edition adds discussion of computer-era cryptography. Use it for historical context, with later specialist research for developments and corrections published since then.

 [Publisher page →](<https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Codebreakers/David-Kahn/9780684831305>) EssentialHistory

Popular Science · Essential

*The Code Book: The Science of Secrecy from Ancient Egypt to Quantum Cryptography*

Simon Singh

1999 · Anchor paperback, 2000 · ISBN 978-0385495325

A narrative introduction to the history of cryptography, including Mary, Queen of Scots, Enigma, public-key cryptography and quantum ideas. It pairs well with the museum’s introductory exhibits; its historical narrative is not a current implementation guide.

 [Author site →](<https://simonsingh.net/books/the-code-book/>)

[The Black Chamber](<https://simonsingh.net/The_Black_Chamber/index.html>) is Singh’s online introduction to classical ciphers and codebreaking. Its guided substitution and Vigenère material inspired the format of our original [beginner activities](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html>). Use the [topic guide](<https://ciphermuseum.com/classical-guide.html>) to find corresponding museum exhibits.

 EssentialIntroductory

Academic · Historical Cryptanalysis

*Secret History: The Story of Cryptology*

Craig P. Bauer

2nd ed. 2021 · ISBN 978-1138061231

A history-oriented textbook with mathematical explanations and cryptanalysis exercises. Use the second edition’s contents to locate the relevant system. Developments after its 2021 publication, including the 2023 Castelnau-letter decipherment, require separate sources.

 [Publisher page →](<https://www.routledge.com/Secret-History-The-Story-of-Cryptology/Bauer/p/book/9781138061231>) TextbookMathematics

Academic · Technical History

*Decrypted Secrets: Methods and Maxims of Cryptology*

Friedrich L. Bauer

4th ed. 2007 · ISBN 978-3540245025

A technical and historical reference on cryptography and cryptanalysis. Its fourth edition discusses classical cipher systems, mechanical methods and mathematical concepts such as redundancy and unicity distance. Read modern security recommendations alongside newer standards.

 [Springer page →](<https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-540-48121-8>) ReferenceCryptanalysis

Illustrated Overview · Browsable

*The Story of Codes: The History of Secret Communication*

Stephen Pincock & Mark Frary

ISBN 978-1911130895 · Elwin Street illustrated edition

An illustrated popular introduction to secret communication, by Stephen Pincock and Mark Frary. Useful for discovering topics and visual examples. Verify technical procedures and disputed historical interpretations against the cited scholarship or original documents.

 [Publisher page →](<https://www.elwinstreet.com/story-of-codes>) IllustratedIntroductory

Engineering Reference

*Cryptography Engineering: Design Principles and Practical Applications*

Niels Ferguson, Bruce Schneier, Tadayoshi Kohno

2010 · ISBN 978-0470474242

An updated version of Ferguson and Schneier's *Practical Cryptography* (2003), with Tadayoshi Kohno as co-author. Explores how to build secure systems from cryptographic components, including implementation risks, key management, and protocol design. Read its engineering principles alongside current standards and implementation guidance.

 [Author page →](<https://www.schneier.com/books/cryptography-engineering/>) TechnicalModern

#### Modern Cryptography Textbooks

Textbooks and a narrative history connecting historical cryptography with modern theory and practice. Use the specified edition or version when following a chapter citation.

Graduate Textbook

*Introduction to Modern Cryptography*

Jonathan Katz & Yehuda Lindell

Revised 3rd ed. 2025 · ISBN 978-1032496795

A graduate textbook on definitions, constructions and proofs for modern cryptography. Covers symmetric and public-key cryptography, authentication and security models. Use the revised third edition for this listing; chapter numbering can differ in earlier editions.

 [Publisher page →](<https://www.routledge.com/Introduction-to-Modern-Cryptography-Revised-Third-Edition/Katz-Lindell/p/book/9781032496795>) GraduateProvable Security

Graduate Textbook

*A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography*

Dan Boneh & Victor Shoup

Version 0.6 · January 2023

A graduate treatment of cryptographic definitions, constructions and security proofs. The museum cites version 0.6 for topics including discrete-log assumptions, Schnorr identification and threshold secret sharing. Read the assumptions and security model with each theorem; the small-number exhibits are teaching examples.

 GraduateSecurity Proofs

Foundational Textbook

*Cryptography: Theory and Practice*

Douglas R. Stinson & Maura B. Paterson

4th ed. 2018 · ISBN 978-1138197015

A mathematical textbook spanning classical and modern cryptography, with exercises and topics including perfect secrecy, block ciphers and public-key systems. Maura B. Paterson co-authors the fourth edition; distinguish it from earlier editions credited to Stinson alone.

 [Publisher page →](<https://www.routledge.com/Cryptography-Theory-and-Practice/Stinson-Paterson/p/book/9781138197015>) TextbookMathematical

History · Public-Key Era

*Crypto: How the Code Rebels Beat the Government—Saving Privacy in the Digital Age*

Steven Levy

2001 · ISBN 978-0140244328

A narrative history of public-key cryptography and disputes over access to encryption, including PGP, the Clipper Chip and export controls. It provides historical context for the modern exhibits; its 2001 account is not current security or policy guidance.

 [Publisher page →](<https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/332850/crypto-by-steven-levy/>) HistoryModern

#### Biography & Narrative History

Biography

*Alan Turing: The Enigma*

Andrew Hodges

1983 · centenary ed. 2014 · ISBN 978-0691164724

The standard biography of Turing, written by a mathematician who treats the technical material seriously. Covers Bletchley Park in depth, Turing's contributions to the Bombe design, his postwar computing and morphogenesis work, and his prosecution and death. The centenary edition includes a new preface and updated bibliographic notes. The basis of the (significantly less accurate) film *The Imitation Game*.

 [Author site →](<https://www.turing.org.uk/book/>) BiographyWWII

Biography

*The Woman Who Smashed Codes: A True Story of Love, Spies, and the Unlikely Heroine Who Outwitted America’s Enemies*

Jason Fagone

2017 · ISBN 978-0062430489

An account of Elizebeth Smith Friedman’s career, drawing on declassified government files and library archives. It follows her cryptanalytic work and the recognition of her contributions. Companion to the [Elizebeth Friedman exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/elizebeth-friedman.html>).

 [Author site →](<https://www.jasonfagone.com/woman-who-smashed>) BiographyWomen in Crypto

Memoir

*Between Silk and Cyanide: A Codemaker’s War, 1941–1945*

Leo Marks

1998 · ISBN 978-0684864228

Leo Marks’s memoir of code work for Britain’s Special Operations Executive. It discusses poem codes, agents’ communications and the pressures of wartime key handling. As a retrospective personal account, it should be compared with archival and scholarly sources. Companion to the [Leo Marks exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/leo-marks.html>).

 MemoirSOEWWII

Popular History

*Seizing the Enigma: The Race to Break the German U-Boat Codes, 1939–1945*

David Kahn

1991 · revised edition, 2012 · ISBN 978-1591148074

Kahn's focused account of Allied capture operations against German naval Enigma material — pinches from weather ships, trawlers, and submarines. Explains why physical capture of key material was as important as mathematical cryptanalysis and how the two combined in the Battle of the Atlantic. A shorter, more readable Kahn than *The Codebreakers*.

 HistoryNavalWWII

Popular History

*Battle of Wits: The Complete Story of Codebreaking in World War II*

Stephen Budiansky

2000 · ISBN 978-0684859323

A history of Allied codebreaking during the Second World War, including work in Britain and the United States and its use in the Atlantic and Pacific theatres. Compare the narrative with the specialist histories and primary records listed by individual exhibits.

 HistoryWWII

Modern Intelligence History

*GCHQ: The Uncensored Story of Britain's Most Secret Intelligence Agency*

Richard J. Aldrich

2010 · ISBN 978-0007278473

A history of British signals intelligence, including wartime codebreaking, the Cold War and intelligence alliances. The 2010 edition predates the 2013 Snowden disclosures; do not treat it as an account of that later episode or as the authorized GCHQ history.

 Intelligence HistoryCold War

#### Specialist Histories

Deeper dives into specific institutions, programs, and cipher families.

Bletchley Park · Insider Account

*Codebreakers: The Inside Story of Bletchley Park*

F. H. Hinsley & Alan Stripp (eds.)

1993 · ISBN 978-0192802132

A collection of accounts by people who worked at Bletchley Park, edited by F. H. Hinsley and Alan Stripp. Covers several sections and methods of the wartime operation. These retrospective testimonies are valuable primary accounts, but individual recollections still need comparison with contemporary records.

 Primary SourceBletchley

Bletchley Park · Memoir

*The Hut Six Story: Breaking the Enigma Codes*

Gordon Welchman

1982 · revised 1997 · ISBN 978-0947712341

Gordon Welchman’s account of Hut 6, including the diagonal board, traffic analysis and the organization of Enigma work. A technical participant’s memoir, to read alongside other accounts of the Polish, British and Allied contributions.

 MemoirBletchley

Polish Enigma History

*Enigma: How the Poles Broke the Nazi Code*

Władysław Kozaczuk & Jerzy Straszak

2004 · ISBN 978-0781809412

An account of the Polish Cipher Bureau and the work of Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski. Distinguish this 2004 book from Kozaczuk’s longer 1984 *Enigma*, whose edition and appendices differ.

 PolishWWII

Pacific Theatre · Codebreaking

*Combined Fleet Decoded: The Secret History of American Intelligence and the Japanese Navy in World War II*

John Prados

1995 · Naval Institute Press reprint, 2001 · ISBN 978-1557504319

A history of intelligence and the Japanese navy during the Pacific war, connecting signals intelligence with other sources and naval operations. Companion reading for the museum’s [JN-25](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/jn-25.html>) and [Purple](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/purple.html>) exhibits.

 PacificSIGINT

Cold War SIGINT · VENONA

*Venona: Decoding Soviet Espionage in America*

John Earl Haynes & Harvey Klehr

1999 · ISBN 978-0300084627

Haynes and Klehr’s analysis of the Soviet intelligence messages released through VENONA. Compare their historical interpretations with the actual translations and their gaps; partial decryption and an identification argument are different forms of evidence.

 Cold WarVENONA

History of Intelligence

*Spycatcher: The Candid Autobiography of a Senior Intelligence Officer*

Peter Wright with Paul Greengrass

1987 · ISBN 978-0670821556

Peter Wright’s controversial memoir of British counterintelligence, including his suspicions about Roger Hollis. Those allegations are not an established “unmasking.” Read the book as an attributed personal account and compare its claims with other records.

 Intelligence HistoryCold War

#### Academic Journals & Proceedings

Peer-Reviewed Journal

*Cryptologia*

Taylor & Francis · Founded 1977

A peer-reviewed journal publishing technical, historical, educational and cultural work on cryptology. It includes the 2023 decipherment of Mary Stuart’s letters to Castelnau. Access varies by article; open-access papers and subscription material are both present.

 [Journal page →](<https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/ucry20>) Peer-ReviewedHistoryMathematics

Conference Proceedings · Open Access

*HistoCrypt*

Annual conference · First held 2018

A conference devoted to historical cryptology, including manuscript analysis, cryptanalysis and digital humanities. The conference site links proceedings and programs. Check the actual paper record for its publication venue and date rather than assuming every historical decipherment appeared here.

 [Conference site →](<https://histocrypt.org/>) Open AccessConference

Academic Project · Open Access

DECODE — Decipherment of Coded Manuscripts

Historical cryptology research collaboration

A research database of historical encrypted manuscripts and related keys, within the DECRYPT research collaboration. Its records help locate material for transcription and cryptanalysis. Consult the project site for participating institutions, access arrangements and current holdings.

 [DECODE database →](<https://de-crypt.org/>) DatabaseOpen Access

Modern Cryptography Journal

*Journal of Cryptology*

Springer · IACR · Founded 1988

A peer-reviewed research journal associated with the IACR, covering cryptographic theory and related topics. It is distinct from the ePrint preprint archive: an ePrint posting is not evidence of journal peer review or acceptance. Consult the publisher for each article’s access status.

 [Journal page →](<https://link.springer.com/journal/145>) Modern CryptoPeer-Reviewed

Journal of Record

*IEEE Annals of the History of Computing*

IEEE · Founded 1979

A journal of computing history, including research on early computers, codebreaking equipment and the people and institutions that developed them. Use individual article citations for specific historical claims.

 [Journal page →](<https://www.computer.org/csdl/magazine/an>) Computing HistoryMachines

IACR Conferences

Crypto · Eurocrypt · Asiacrypt

IACR · Annual

IACR conferences presenting peer-reviewed cryptographic research. Their proceedings and author preprints provide routes into modern theory and practice. Access arrangements vary by publication and year; consult the conference or IACR publication pages.

 [IACR home →](<https://iacr.org/>) Modern CryptoOpen Access

#### Researcher Profiles

- George Lasry

Cryptanalyst · Co-author, Mary Queen of Scots nomenclator decipherment (2023)

A researcher in computer-assisted historical cryptanalysis and a co-author, with Norbert Biermann and Satoshi Tomokiyo, of the 2023 Castelnau-letter decipherment. His publications include attacks and methods for several classical systems. See the [Lasry exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/lasry.html>).

 [Publications →](<https://dblp.org/pid/147/8139.html>) ResearchHistorical Cryptanalysis

- Beáta Megyesi

Professor, Stockholm University · Historical cryptology and DECRYPT

A computational linguist working on historical cryptology, transcription and decipherment. She co-authored the 2011 Copiale paper and contributes to the DECRYPT research collaboration. Her faculty page provides current affiliations and research projects.

 [Faculty page →](<https://www.su.se/english/profiles/b/beba5639>) ResearchNLP · Computational

- Satoshi Tomokiyo

Independent researcher · Historical cipher manuscripts

An independent researcher on historical ciphers and a co-author of the 2023 Castelnau-letter paper. His *Cryptiana* site discusses diplomatic cipher documents, nomenclators and archival sources, often with detailed manuscript references.

 [Cryptiana research site →](<https://cryptiana.web.fc2.com/code/crypto.htm>) ResearchRenaissance Ciphers

- Nick Pelling

Researcher · Voynich manuscript; historical unsolved ciphers

Author of *The Curse of the Voynich* and the *Cipher Mysteries* blog. The site discusses Voynich and other unresolved cases. Distinguish research hypotheses and commentary from independently established findings.

 [Cipher Mysteries blog →](<https://ciphermysteries.com/>) ResearchUnsolved Ciphers

- Klaus Schmeh

Cryptanalyst · Co-author, *Codebreaking: A Practical Guide* (Robinson, 2020)

A writer and researcher on cryptology, and co-author with Elonka Dunin of *Codebreaking: A Practical Guide*. His archived blog documents historical cipher cases and research discussions; the linked archive is a resource to explore, not a guarantee that every proposed solution is established.

 [Klausis Krypto Kolumne (archived) →](<https://scienceblogs.de/klausis-krypto-kolumne/>) ResearchPractical Cryptanalysis

- James Gillogly

Cryptanalyst · Beale Papers and Kryptos K1–K3

A cryptanalyst known for work on the Beale ciphers and for independently solving the first three Kryptos sections in 1999. Consult his specific papers for the methods and limits of each result; the last Kryptos section is a separate problem.

 ResearchStatistical Analysis

- Elonka Dunin

Cryptanalyst · Kryptos; co-author, *Codebreaking: A Practical Guide* (Robinson, 2020)

A cryptography writer and researcher known for her Kryptos work and collection of famous unsolved-code resources. She co-authored *Codebreaking: A Practical Guide* with Klaus Schmeh. See the [Dunin exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/dunin.html>) and her site for specific publications and projects.

 [Personal site →](<https://www.elonka.com/>) ResearchKryptosAdvocacy

#### Primary Source Archives

- NSA Center for Cryptologic History

Fort Meade, Maryland

The NSA's public history arm publishes declassified monographs, oral history transcripts, and the back issues of the internal *Cryptolog* journal. The VENONA documents (2,900 decrypted messages), the Friedman Documents collection, and the technical histories of SIGABA, SIGSALY, and early NSA computing are free downloads. The single richest primary-source archive for 20th-century American cryptologic history.

 [nsa.gov/history →](<https://www.nsa.gov/History/Cryptologic-History/>) Primary SourcesFree

- Bletchley Park Trust Archive

Milton Keynes, UK

Bletchley Park preserves records, objects and accounts of the wartime codebreaking operation. Its Roll of Honour is a research resource, not a complete census. The working Colossus and Bombe reconstructions are at the separately operated National Museum of Computing on the Bletchley Park estate; check each institution’s visitor information.

 [bletchleypark.org.uk →](<https://bletchleypark.org.uk/>) Primary SourcesWWII

- UK National Archives — HW Department

Kew, London

The National Archives uses the department reference **HW** for records of GCHQ and its predecessor, the Government Code and Cypher School. It contains multiple series, including signals intelligence and technical histories. The official research guide explains how to search them and check viewing or download arrangements.

 [GCHQ and GCCS records guide →](<https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/intelligence-and-security-services/>) Primary SourcesWWII

- US National Archives — Record Group 457

College Park, Maryland

RG 457 is the primary NSA / ASA / AFSA record group — the largest collection of US SIGINT materials available to researchers. Contains VENONA working papers, original MAGIC (“Purple”) intercept files, raw WWII intercept traffic, and NSA's own historical studies of major programs. Many materials require FOIA requests; others are open access. The definitive first stop for primary-source American SIGINT research.

 [RG 457 finding aid →](<https://www.archives.gov/research/intelligence/nsa/records.html>) Primary SourcesSIGINT

- Friedman Collection — George C. Marshall Foundation

Virginia Military Institute, Lexington, VA

The foundation’s collection descriptions identify separate William F. Friedman and Elizebeth S. Friedman holdings. Consult their finding aids for the actual scope and access conditions. Other Friedman papers are held by additional archives; a general collection link does not establish that every named document is digitized.

 [Collection descriptions — see Elizebeth and William Friedman →](<https://www.marshallfoundation.org/research-library/library-collections/>) Primary SourcesBiography

- Voynich Manuscript — Beinecke MS 408

Yale University Library

Full high-resolution scans of every page of the Voynich Manuscript are freely available through the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library. The standard research corpus. Researchers should also consult René Zandbergen's *voynich.nu*, the most thorough public source on provenance, hand identification, and transcript history — in more depth than any single publication.

 [Beinecke digital scans →](<https://collections.library.yale.edu/catalog/2002046>) Primary SourcesUnsolvedFree

- Crypto Museum

Paul Reuvers & Marc Simons · Eindhoven, Netherlands · cryptomuseum.com

The most comprehensive online archive of cipher machines, spy radios, burst encoders, and intelligence-related communications equipment. Detailed technical reconstructions, photographs, and operator documentation for hundreds of cipher machines from the early 1900s through the Cold War. The Cipher Museum's Hagelin family sidebar (M-209 exhibit) and SIGSALY exhibit cite Crypto Museum Foundation documentation directly. Cipher Museum is listed in Crypto Museum's Virtual Museums directory (April 2026).

 [cryptomuseum.com →](<https://www.cryptomuseum.com/>) Peer InstitutionHardwareFree

#### Web Resources & Software

Analysis Software · Open Source

CrypTool 2

CrypTool Project

An open-source visual workbench for experimenting with many classical and modern cryptographic methods. It includes cipher operations and cryptanalysis tools. Check its current component list and documentation for a particular historical variant rather than assuming it implements every museum exhibit.

 [cryptool.org →](<https://www.cryptool.org/en/ct2/>) SoftwareFree

Browser-based Toolkit

CyberChef

GCHQ · Open Source

GCHQ’s open-source toolkit chains data transformations into recipes. It includes encoding, hashing, encryption and analysis operations. Many operations process data locally; review any network-capable operation and the hosting context before entering sensitive material.

 [CyberChef app →](<https://gchq.github.io/CyberChef/>) SoftwareFree

Research Website

Cipher Mysteries

Nick Pelling

Nick Pelling’s research blog on unsolved manuscripts, codes and related historical questions. Useful for following arguments and locating references. Proposed interpretations should be checked against the evidence and distinguished from accepted decipherments.

 [ciphermysteries.com →](<https://ciphermysteries.com/>) WebsiteUnsolved Ciphers

Voynich Reference

voynich.nu

René Zandbergen

René Zandbergen’s reference site on the Voynich manuscript, including provenance, manuscript structure, transcriptions and research history. It provides links to evidence and competing interpretations; distinguish established physical observations from theories about the text.

 [voynich.nu →](<https://www.voynich.nu/>) WebsiteVoynich

Challenge Platform

MysteryTwister

CrypTool Project

A cryptographic challenge platform with graded problems and a separate category for open challenges. Read each challenge’s instructions, available hints and solution status; open problems may have no verified solution to check against.

 [mysterytwister.org →](<https://www.mysterytwister.org/>) ChallengesFree

Academic Preprints

Cryptology ePrint Archive

IACR

The IACR’s public archive for research preprints in cryptology. Papers may be revised or withdrawn and are not peer reviewed merely by appearing here. Check version dates, errata and any later publication before using a result as settled guidance.

 [eprint.iacr.org →](<https://eprint.iacr.org/>) PreprintsModern CryptoFree

Online Course

Stanford Cryptography I

Dan Boneh · Coursera

Dan Boneh’s *Cryptography I* course introduces symmetric encryption, integrity, public-key encryption and key exchange. The linked listing is for that course only. Course access, assignments and certificates depend on the platform’s current terms; Boneh and Shoup’s textbook is freely available separately.

 [Coursera →](<https://www.coursera.org/learn/crypto>) CourseFree

Reference · Federal

NIST Computer Security Resource Center

National Institute of Standards and Technology

The authoritative source for current US cryptographic standards: AES (FIPS 197), SHA-2 / SHA-3 (FIPS 180-4 / 202), the post-quantum standards ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA (FIPS 203/204/205, finalized 2024), and the SP 800 guidance series. The historical archive of NIST's cipher competitions — AES, SHA-3, post-quantum — is itself an unmatched primary-source record of how modern cipher standards are made.

 [csrc.nist.gov →](<https://csrc.nist.gov/>) StandardsFree

Commentary

Schneier on Security

Bruce Schneier

Bruce Schneier’s commentary on cryptography, security engineering and policy, with a related *Crypto-Gram* newsletter. Useful for discovering developments and arguments; follow links to original research and standards for technical claims.

 [schneier.com →](<https://www.schneier.com/>) CommentaryPolicy

#### Books Behind the New Experiments

I. J. Good, Donald Michie and Geoffrey Timms, *General Report on Tunny* (1945), §§23A–C, printed pp. 78–80 (collected PDF pp. 81–83), supports the known-pattern setting method in the [Colossus counting experiment](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/colossus.html>). Its synthetic traffic and modern null simulations are identified separately.

George Lasry, *A Methodology for the Cryptanalysis of Classical Ciphers with Search Metaheuristics* (2018), §§4.5–4.7 and §§5.3.2–5.3.4, printed pp. 57–60 and 69–78 (PDF pp. 78–81 and 90–99), supports evaluation discipline and the [bounded columnar search](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html>). The museum's adaptations and measured limits are stated on the exhibit.

These citations identify the complete works and relevant pages; no ebook copies are linked.
