#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function () {
  "use strict";
  const svg = document.getElementById("stage");
  const NS = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  const W = 700, H = 460;

  // curve: y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B  (A=1, B=1 -> smooth, single connected branch)
  const A = 1, B = 1;

  // world<->screen mapping
  const xmin = -1.4, xmax = 3.2, ymin = -4.2, ymax = 4.2;
  const sx = (x) => (x - xmin) / (xmax - xmin) * W;
  const sy = (y) => H - (y - ymin) / (ymax - ymin) * H;

  function make(tag, attrs) {
    const e = document.createElementNS(NS, tag);
    for (const k in attrs) e.setAttribute(k, attrs[k]);
    return e;
  }

  // ---- grid + axes ----
  const grid = document.getElementById("grid");
  function axisLine(x1, y1, x2, y2, w, op) {
    grid.appendChild(make("line", { x1, y1, x2, y2,
      stroke: "#2e2e3a", "stroke-width": w, "stroke-opacity": op }));
  }
  for (let gx = Math.ceil(xmin); gx <= xmax; gx++)
    axisLine(sx(gx), 0, sx(gx), H, 1, gx === 0 ? 0.9 : 0.35);
  for (let gy = Math.ceil(ymin); gy <= ymax; gy++)
    axisLine(0, sy(gy), W, sy(gy), 1, gy === 0 ? 0.9 : 0.35);

  // ---- curve path (single connected branch for A=1, B=1) ----
  const fx = (x) => x * x * x + A * x + B;
  const topBranch = [], botBranch = [], step = 0.012;
  for (let x = xmin; x <= xmax; x += step) {
    const v = fx(x);
    if (v >= 0) {
      const r = Math.sqrt(v);
      topBranch.push([x, r]);
      botBranch.push([x, -r]);
    }
  }
  let d = "";
  topBranch.forEach((p, i) => { d += (i ? "L" : "M") + sx(p[0]).toFixed(1) + " " + sy(p[1]).toFixed(1) + " "; });
  for (let j = botBranch.length - 1; j >= 0; j--) {
    d += "L" + sx(botBranch[j][0]).toFixed(1) + " " + sy(botBranch[j][1]).toFixed(1) + " ";
  }
  document.getElementById("curvePath").setAttribute("d", d.trim());

  // ---- interaction state ----
  const cons = document.getElementById("construction");
  const pts = document.getElementById("points");
  const readout = document.getElementById("readout");
  let picks = []; // world-space points on curve

  function onCurveNear(px, py) {
    let best = null, bestd = Infinity;
    for (let xx = xmin; xx <= xmax; xx += 0.004) {
      const v = fx(xx);
      if (v < 0) continue;
      const r = Math.sqrt(v);
      for (const c of [[xx, r], [xx, -r]]) {
        const dd = (sx(c[0]) - px) ** 2 + (sy(c[1]) - py) ** 2;
        if (dd < bestd) { bestd = dd; best = c; }
      }
    }
    return best;
  }

  const dot = (x, y, color, r) => make("circle",
    { cx: sx(x), cy: sy(y), r: r || 6, fill: color, stroke: "#1c1c22", "stroke-width": 2 });

  function label(x, y, txt, color) {
    const t = make("text", { x: sx(x) + 11, y: sy(y) - 9, fill: color,
      "font-family": "ui-monospace, monospace", "font-size": "15", "font-weight": "700" });
    t.textContent = txt;
    return t;
  }

  // add two points via chord-and-tangent (handles the doubling case)
  function addPoints(P, Q) {
    if (Math.abs(P[0]-Q[0]) < 1e-9 && Math.abs(P[1]+Q[1]) < 1e-9) {
      return { third: null, sum: null, slope: null };
    }
    let m;
    if (Math.abs(P[0] - Q[0]) < 1e-9 && Math.abs(P[1] - Q[1]) < 1e-9) {
      m = (3 * P[0] * P[0] + A) / (2 * P[1]);      // tangent slope (P = Q)
    } else {
      m = (Q[1] - P[1]) / (Q[0] - P[0]);           // chord slope
    }
    const x3 = m * m - P[0] - Q[0];
    const y3 = m * (P[0] - x3) - P[1];
    return { third: [x3, -y3], sum: [x3, y3], slope: m };
  }

  function drawConstruction() {
    cons.innerHTML = "";
    if (picks.length < 2) return;
    const [P, Q] = picks;
    const { third, sum, slope: m } = addPoints(P, Q);

    if (sum === null) {
      cons.appendChild(make("line", {x1:sx(P[0]), y1:0, x2:sx(P[0]), y2:H, stroke:"#C85A5A", "stroke-width":2}));
      readout.textContent = "P + Q = ∞ — the point at infinity (the group identity).";
      return;
    }
    const yL = P[1] + m * (xmin - P[0]);
    const yR = P[1] + m * (xmax - P[0]);
    cons.appendChild(make("line", { x1: sx(xmin), y1: sy(yL), x2: sx(xmax), y2: sy(yR),
      stroke: "#C85A5A", "stroke-width": 2, "stroke-opacity": 0.85 }));

    cons.appendChild(dot(third[0], third[1], "#d98a7a", 5));

    cons.appendChild(make("line", { x1: sx(third[0]), y1: sy(third[1]),
      x2: sx(sum[0]), y2: sy(sum[1]),
      stroke: "#C85A5A", "stroke-width": 1.6, "stroke-dasharray": "4 4", "stroke-opacity": 0.8 }));

    cons.appendChild(dot(sum[0], sum[1], "#C85A5A", 7));
    cons.appendChild(label(sum[0], sum[1], "P+Q", "#C85A5A"));

    // aria-live readout announces the full result to screen readers
    readout.innerHTML = "P+Q = ( <b>" + sum[0].toFixed(2) + "</b>, <b>" + sum[1].toFixed(2) + "</b> )";
  }

  function redrawPoints() {
    pts.innerHTML = "";
    picks.forEach((p, i) => {
      pts.appendChild(dot(p[0], p[1], "#F3EEDF", 6));
      pts.appendChild(label(p[0], p[1], i === 0 ? "P" : "Q", "#F3EEDF"));
    });
  }

  // register a chosen point, update visuals + announce
  function choose(p) {
    if (!p) return;
    if (picks.length >= 2) { picks = []; cons.innerHTML = ""; }
    picks.push(p);
    redrawPoints();
    if (picks.length === 2) {
      drawConstruction();
    } else {
      readout.innerHTML = "P = ( <b>" + p[0].toFixed(2) + "</b>, <b>" +
        p[1].toFixed(2) + "</b> ) &nbsp;·&nbsp; select a second point for Q";
    }
  }

  function pointFromEvent(clientX, clientY) {
    const rect = svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    const cx = (clientX - rect.left) * (W / rect.width);
    const cy = (clientY - rect.top) * (H / rect.height);
    return onCurveNear(cx, cy);
  }

  // ---- pointer (mouse) ----
  svg.addEventListener("click", (e) => choose(pointFromEvent(e.clientX, e.clientY)));

  // ---- touch: only intercept a deliberate tap, never a scroll ----
  // Track the start point; if the finger moves beyond a small threshold we treat
  // it as a scroll and leave the page's default behaviour untouched.
  let touchStart = null;
  const TAP_SLOP = 12; // px of movement still counted as a tap

  svg.addEventListener("touchstart", (e) => {
    if (e.touches.length !== 1) { touchStart = null; return; }
    const t = e.touches[0];
    touchStart = { x: t.clientX, y: t.clientY, scrolled: false };
    // note: do NOT preventDefault here — that would trap a scroll gesture
  }, { passive: true });

  svg.addEventListener("touchmove", (e) => {
    if (!touchStart) return;
    const t = e.touches[0];
    if (Math.hypot(t.clientX - touchStart.x, t.clientY - touchStart.y) > TAP_SLOP) {
      touchStart.scrolled = true; // it's a scroll — let the page move
    }
  }, { passive: true });

  svg.addEventListener("touchend", (e) => {
    if (!touchStart || touchStart.scrolled) { touchStart = null; return; }
    // confirmed tap: now it's safe to suppress the emulated click and act
    e.preventDefault();
    const t = e.changedTouches[0];
    choose(pointFromEvent(t.clientX, t.clientY));
    touchStart = null;
  }, { passive: false });

  // ---- reset ----
  document.getElementById("reset").addEventListener("click", () => {
    picks = [];
    cons.innerHTML = "";
    pts.innerHTML = "";
    readout.innerHTML = "y² = x³ + x + 1 &nbsp;·&nbsp; <b>tap the curve</b>";
  });

  // ---- preload a demonstrative pair ----
  document.getElementById("pick").addEventListener("click", () => {
    const Px = -0.6, Qx = 1.2;
    picks = [[Px, Math.sqrt(fx(Px))], [Qx, -Math.sqrt(fx(Qx))]];
    redrawPoints();
    drawConstruction();
  });

  // ---- keyboard / screen-reader fallback ----
  // Populate two <select>s with real on-curve points; adding announces via aria-live.
  const selP = document.getElementById("selP");
  const selQ = document.getElementById("selQ");
  const sampleXs = [-0.6, -0.2, 0.4, 1.0, 1.6, 2.4]; // spread across the domain
  const kbPoints = [];
  sampleXs.forEach((x) => {
    const v = fx(x);
    if (v < 0) return;
    const r = Math.sqrt(v);
    kbPoints.push([x, r]);
    kbPoints.push([x, -r]);
  });
  kbPoints.forEach((p, i) => {
    const text = "( " + p[0].toFixed(2) + ", " + p[1].toFixed(2) + " )";
    const oP = document.createElement("option"); oP.value = i; oP.textContent = text; selP.appendChild(oP);
    const oQ = document.createElement("option"); oQ.value = i; oQ.textContent = text; selQ.appendChild(oQ);
  });
  selP.value = "0";
  selQ.value = String(Math.min(3, kbPoints.length - 1));

  document.getElementById("addKb").addEventListener("click", () => {
    const P = kbPoints[+selP.value];
    const Q = kbPoints[+selQ.value];
    picks = [P, Q];
    redrawPoints();
    drawConstruction(); // updates the aria-live readout with P+Q
  });
})();
```

[← Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/index.html>) Exhibit 146 · easy → · hard ←

The Conceptual Keystone

### Easy one way,
*hard* the other

Many computational cryptographic constructions depend on functions that are easy to evaluate and difficult to invert on properly sampled inputs. Their security is conjectured, not proved merely by drawing an arrow. Information-theoretic systems such as the one-time pad do not require this computational assumption.

**An assumption, not a proof.** We *believe* these functions are hard to reverse; we cannot prove it. Computational public-key schemes rely on particular hardness assumptions. Some proposed schemes have been broken, so each construction needs its own analysis.

§1

#### Multiply, then try to undo it

Multiplying suitably chosen large primes and attempting to recover them illustrates a candidate one-way relationship. For the tiny values shown, factoring is easy. The plot compares multiplication with a trial-division estimate, not with the fastest known general factoring algorithms.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="curve" viewBox="0 0 700 380" id="owf" role="img" aria-label="Cost of multiplying versus factoring as numbers grow."></svg>
```

size (bits)  [Input br: type=range; initial value=16]   Factor it (watch it crawl)

—

The bar estimates trial division up to √n. The Factor button counts actual trial divisions for this tiny sample. More advanced factoring algorithms are substantially faster at large sizes; do not extrapolate this bar into an RSA security estimate.

§2

#### The trapdoor twist

Some public-key constructions add a trapdoor. RSA's relevant operation is modular exponentiation: knowing the prime factors lets the owner compute a private exponent and invert that operation. Decryption is not division of the ciphertext by a prime.

public: n = p·q · trapdoor: the pair (p, q)

Trapdoor functions are one design pattern, not a description of every public-key scheme. Diffie–Hellman key agreement, for example, has a different structure.

Where this touches your keys

##### The bet under everything

Factoring breaks RSA, and solving discrete logs breaks classical DH and ECC. Post-quantum designs use several families, including lattice, code and hash-based assumptions. Security claims must name the particular construction and problem, rather than treating all these as the same trapdoor.

A cryptographic hash is intended to resist preimage search without a secret inversion trapdoor. This does not mean an attacker cannot recover a low-entropy input by guessing. No proof establishes that a concrete hash such as SHA-256 is a one-way function against every efficient attacker.

Next: [Reduction & Proof](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/reduction.html>) — how we argue one wall is at least as tall as another.

Continue with [RSA](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rsa.html>) or explore [security reductions](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/reduction.html>).

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  var NS="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  function el(t,a){var e=document.createElementNS(NS,t);for(var k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;}
  function randPrime(bits){
    var lo=Math.pow(2,bits-1), hi=Math.pow(2,bits)-1;
    function isP(n){if(n<2)return false;for(var i=2;i*i<=n;i++)if(n%i===0)return false;return true;}
    for(var tries=0;tries<9999;tries++){var c=Math.floor(lo+Math.random()*(hi-lo));c|=1;if(isP(c))return c;}
    return 3;
  }
  var owf=document.getElementById("owf"), br=document.getElementById("br"), oread=document.getElementById("oread");
  var W=700,H=380,pad=54;

  function draw(){
    var bits=+br.value; owf.innerHTML="";
    var half=Math.max(2,Math.floor(bits/2));
    var p=randPrime(half), q=randPrime(half), n=p*q;
    // forward cost ~ constant; factoring cost ~ sqrt(n) trial divisions (worst case bar)
    var fwd=1;
    var facCost=Math.sqrt(n);
    var maxBar=Math.sqrt(Math.pow(2,48));
    function barH(v){ return Math.min(1, Math.log(v+1)/Math.log(maxBar+1))*(H-2*pad); }
    owf.appendChild(el("line",{x1:pad,y1:H-pad,x2:W-pad,y2:H-pad,stroke:"#F3EEDF","stroke-width":1.5}));
    // forward bar
    var fh=Math.max(6,barH(fwd));
    owf.appendChild(el("rect",{x:180,y:H-pad-fh,width:120,height:fh,fill:"#5AC8A0"}));
    var t1=el("text",{x:240,y:H-pad+22,fill:"#5AC8A0","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"13","text-anchor":"middle","font-weight":"700"});
    t1.textContent="multiply"; owf.appendChild(t1);
    // factor bar
    var gh=Math.max(6,barH(facCost));
    owf.appendChild(el("rect",{x:400,y:H-pad-gh,width:120,height:gh,fill:"#C85A5A"}));
    var t2=el("text",{x:460,y:H-pad+22,fill:"#C85A5A","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"13","text-anchor":"middle","font-weight":"700"});
    t2.textContent="factor"; owf.appendChild(t2);
    // n label
    var tn=el("text",{x:W/2,y:pad-14,fill:"#F3EEDF","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"15","text-anchor":"middle","font-weight":"700"});
    tn.textContent=p+" × "+q+" = "+n; owf.appendChild(tn);
    oread.innerHTML="n = <b>"+n+"</b> ("+(Math.floor(Math.log2(n))+1)+" bits) · trial-division estimate ≈ √n ≈ <b>"+Math.round(facCost)+"</b> steps";
    owf._current={n:n,p:p,q:q};
  }
  function runFactor(){
    var st=owf._current; if(!st)return; var n=st.n, count=0, found=null;
    for(var i=2;i*i<=n;i++){ count++; if(n%i===0){ found=[i,n/i]; break; } }
    oread.innerHTML="factored n = <b>"+n+"</b> = "+found[0]+" × "+found[1]+" after <b>"+count+"</b> trial divisions";
  }
  br.addEventListener("input",draw);
  document.getElementById("fac").addEventListener("click",runFactor);
  draw();
})();
```

[← Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/index.html>) Exhibit 156 · e(aP,bQ)=e(P,Q)ᵃᵇ

A Tool Used by Some zk-SNARKs

### Multiplying the
*unmultipliable*

Pairings connect elliptic-curve groups to a target group so that scaling two input points becomes exponentiation by the product of their scalars. This algebraic relationship supports some proof and signature schemes. Hiding those scalars requires suitable source and target groups and security assumptions.

**A model of one identity.** This page illustrates bilinearity with small modular powers. It neither hides its inputs nor implements a pairing or privacy protocol.

§1

#### A bridge between two worlds

A bilinear pairing e takes two points from elliptic-curve groups and maps them into a finite field, in a way that turns point-scaling into exponentiation. Scale the inputs by hidden scalars a and b, and the output is the base pairing raised to the *product* a·b.

e(aP, bQ) = e(P, Q)<sup>a·b</sup>

The identity enables checks on products of scalars without directly computing those scalars. It does not by itself establish zero knowledge or prevent attacks in either group.

§2

#### Explore the bilinearity identity

This interaction is an **exponent model of bilinearity**. It compares (5ᵃ)ᵇ mod 23 with 5ᵃᵇ mod 23 using the displayed scalars. It does not compute elliptic-curve points, a real pairing, or a zero-knowledge proof. The symbolic labels show where those objects occur in the actual pairing identity.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="curve" viewBox="0 0 700 470" id="pair" role="img" aria-label="Two computation paths that both arrive at e(P,Q) to the power ab, showing the pairing identity."></svg>
```

a  [Input aR: type=range; initial value=3]   b  [Input bR: type=range; initial value=5]

—

Both paths compute the same tiny modular exponentiation. This checks an exponent identity; the displayed P, Q and e(P,Q) are symbolic stand-ins, not calculated elliptic-curve points or pairing values.

Keyboard alternative: set scalars a and b, then evaluate both paths. a =  [Input aIn: type=number; initial value=3]   b =  [Input bIn: type=number; initial value=5]   Evaluate both paths

§3

#### How proof systems use pairings

Pairings enable compact verification in systems such as Groth16 and appear in KZG polynomial commitments. BLS signature aggregation is another application, but is not itself a zk-SNARK. Zero knowledge requires additional protocol structure and randomization; bilinearity or a polynomial commitment alone does not provide it.

A pairing checks an algebraic relationship. The surrounding protocol must supply soundness, zero knowledge and any required setup guarantees.

Pairings power several of the most influential and compact proof systems, but they are one major family rather than a requirement for succinctness. STARKs verify with hashes and no pairing at all; Bulletproofs and Halo-style systems get short proofs and recursion from ordinary discrete-log groups. The distinction matters here more than most places in this hall: a sufficiently capable fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm would defeat the discrete-log assumptions used by pairing-friendly curves. Hash-based proof systems are candidates for post-quantum use, subject to their specific construction, parameters and quantum security analysis. Succinct verification has more than one foundation, and they don't share a fate.

Where this touches your keys

##### Under the privacy protocols

Some zk-SNARKs, identity-based encryption constructions and signature schemes use pairings. The target is typically a multiplicative subgroup of an extension field. The required security assumptions and parameter choices concern both source and target groups; a pairing is an algebraic tool, not an independent promise of privacy.

Applied in: [Zero-Knowledge Proofs](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zero-knowledge-proofs.html>) — where the pairing-based zk-SNARK family puts this identity to work.
Builds on: [Elliptic Curves](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/elliptic-curves-real.html>), [Group Theory](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/group-theory.html>). Exponent identity tested in `crypto-algebra.js`.

**Sources and scope:** [Groth, On the Size of Pairing-based Non-interactive Arguments (2016)](<https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/260>); [Boneh, Lynn and Shacham, Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing (2001)](<https://crypto.stanford.edu/~dabo/pubs/papers/weilsigs.pdf>).

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  const CA=window.CryptoAlgebra;
  const NS="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  const mk=(t,a)=>{const e=document.createElementNS(NS,t);for(const k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;};
  const pair=document.getElementById("pair");
  const pread=document.getElementById("pread");
  const aR=document.getElementById("aR"), bR=document.getElementById("bR");
  const aIn=document.getElementById("aIn"), bIn=document.getElementById("bIn");

  const BASE=5, MOD=23; // toy target group: e(P,Q) modelled as BASE in Z_23*

  function node(x,y,label,val,color){
    const g=mk("g",{});
    g.appendChild(mk("rect",{x:x-64,y:y-26,width:128,height:52,rx:4,fill:"#1c1c22",stroke:color,"stroke-width":2}));
    const l=mk("text",{x,y:y-32,fill:"#D5CDDF","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"11","text-anchor":"middle"});
    l.textContent=label; g.appendChild(l);
    const v=mk("text",{x,y:y+7,fill:color,"font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"18","font-weight":"700","text-anchor":"middle"});
    v.textContent=val; g.appendChild(v);
    pair.appendChild(g); return g;
  }
  function arrow(x1,y1,x2,y2,label){
    pair.appendChild(mk("line",{x1,y1,x2,y2,stroke:"#F3EEDF","stroke-width":1.8}));
    const ang=Math.atan2(y2-y1,x2-x1);
    pair.appendChild(mk("polygon",{points:(x2)+","+(y2)+" "+(x2-10*Math.cos(ang-0.4))+","+(y2-10*Math.sin(ang-0.4))+" "+(x2-10*Math.cos(ang+0.4))+","+(y2-10*Math.sin(ang+0.4)),fill:"#F3EEDF"}));
    if(label){const t=mk("text",{x:(x1+x2)/2,y:(y1+y2)/2-8,fill:"#D4B765","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"12","text-anchor":"middle","font-weight":"700"});t.textContent=label;pair.appendChild(t);}
  }

  function draw(a,b){
    pair.innerHTML="";
    const r=CA.pairingCheck(a,b,BASE,MOD);
    // LEFT PATH: scale points then pair
    node(150,90,"P, Q (base points)","P, Q","#F3EEDF");
    arrow(150,116,150,164,"scale by a, b");
    node(150,190,"aP, bQ (scalars hidden)","aP, bQ","#C85A5A");
    arrow(150,216,300,300,"pair e(\u00b7,\u00b7)");
    // RIGHT PATH: pair then exponentiate
    node(550,90,"e(P, Q) base pairing","e(P,Q) = "+BASE,"#5AC8A0");
    arrow(550,116,550,164,"raise to a\u00b7b = "+(a*b));
    node(550,190,"e(P,Q)^(ab)","= "+r.viaProduct,"#5AC8A0");
    arrow(550,216,400,300,"");
    // MEETING POINT
    const meet=node(350,340,"both paths agree",""+r.viaProduct,r.equal?"#5AC8A0":"#C85A5A");
    // check mark
    const chk=mk("text",{x:350,y:400,fill:r.equal?"#5AC8A0":"#C85A5A","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"15","font-weight":"700","text-anchor":"middle"});
    chk.textContent=r.equal?"\u2713 e(aP,bQ) = e(P,Q)^(ab) = "+r.viaProduct:"mismatch"; pair.appendChild(chk);

    pread.innerHTML="a="+a+", b="+b+" \u00b7 e(aP,bQ) = <b>"+r.viaChain+"</b> = e(P,Q)^"+(a*b)+" = <b>"+r.viaProduct+"</b> "+(r.equal?"<b style='color:#5AC8A0'>\u2713</b>":"\u2717");
    aIn.value=a; bIn.value=b; aR.value=a; bR.value=b;
  }
  function fromSliders(){ draw(+aR.value,+bR.value); }
  aR.addEventListener("input",fromSliders);
  bR.addEventListener("input",fromSliders);
  document.getElementById("evalBtn").addEventListener("click",()=>{
    let a=parseInt(aIn.value,10), b=parseInt(bIn.value,10);
    a=Math.max(1,Math.min(10,isNaN(a)?3:a)); b=Math.max(1,Math.min(10,isNaN(b)?5:b));
    draw(a,b);
  });
  draw(3,5);
})();
```

[← Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/index.html>) Exhibit 153 · R_q = Z_q[X]/(Xⁿ+1)

The Structure Inside ML-KEM & ML-DSA

### Numbers that
are *polynomials*

The lattice exhibits showed why hard problems on a grid protect a key. But the deployed post-quantum standards don't use plain grids — they use lattices built from *polynomials*, where a whole list of numbers multiplies as a single object and wraps around a ring boundary. That structure is what makes ML-KEM fast enough to ship.

**The missing bridge.** Between the finite-fields exhibit (numbers mod q) and the lattice exhibits (geometry) sits this: arithmetic on polynomials whose coefficients are numbers mod q, and which themselves wrap modulo Xⁿ+1. ML-KEM’s security is related to Module-LWE. ML-DSA also relies on a short-integer-solution variant, SelfTargetMSIS; the two schemes do not have identical assumptions.

§1

#### A coefficient list that acts as one number

A polynomial like 3 + 2X + 5X² + X³ is just its list of coefficients, [3, 2, 5, 1]. In the ring R_q = Z_q[X]/(Xⁿ+1) two rules apply: every coefficient is reduced *mod q*, and any power Xⁿ or higher wraps back down — because Xⁿ is defined to equal −1. That single rule, Xⁿ = −1, is what makes the ring "negacyclic."

Xⁿ = −1 → Xⁿ⁺ᵏ wraps to −Xᵏ, coefficients mod q

§2

#### Watch the multiplication wrap

Multiplying two polynomials would normally push degrees up to 2n−2. The ring folds everything above degree n−1 back down with a sign flip, and reduces mod q, so the product is another length-n list. Edit either polynomial's coefficients and watch the product — and the terms that wrapped — recompute.

Keyboard alternative: enter comma-separated coefficients for polynomials a and b, then multiply. a =  [Input aIn: type=text; initial value=1,2,3,4]   b =  [Input bIn: type=text; initial value=0,1,0,1]   Multiply in R_q

§3

#### Why a ring and not just a grid

A single ring element already packs n numbers. Stack a few of them into a *module* and you have a lattice with enormous dimension but a tiny, structured description — you store a handful of polynomials, not a giant matrix. Polynomial structure reduces storage and enables efficient arithmetic. It is one engineering approach; other post-quantum families use different structures and size tradeoffs.

The polynomial ring is how you get a thousand-dimensional lattice into a few kilobytes — security from geometry, efficiency from structure.

Where this touches your keys

##### The arithmetic inside every ML-KEM operation

Polynomial multiplication, accelerated by Number Theoretic Transforms, is important to ML-KEM and ML-DSA. ML-KEM relies on Module-LWE; ML-DSA uses module-lattice assumptions including Module-LWE and Module-SIS-related problems. The schemes also perform hashing, sampling, encoding and other operations. This exhibit implements ring arithmetic, not either complete standard.

Bridges: [Finite Fields](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/finite-fields.html>) (coefficients mod q) → here → [Lattices](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/lattices-svp.html>) (the geometry). Tested logic in `crypto-algebra.js`.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  const CA=window.CryptoAlgebra;
  const NS="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  const mk=(t,a)=>{const e=document.createElementNS(NS,t);for(const k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;};
  const ring=document.getElementById("ring");
  const rread=document.getElementById("rread");
  const nsel=document.getElementById("nsel"), qsel=document.getElementById("qsel");
  const aIn=document.getElementById("aIn"), bIn=document.getElementById("bIn");

  let n=4, q=17, A=[1,2,3,4], B=[0,1,0,1];

  function parse(str,len){
    const parts=str.split(",").map(s=>parseInt(s.trim(),10));
    const out=new Array(len).fill(0);
    for(let i=0;i<len;i++) out[i]=isNaN(parts[i])?0:CA.mod(parts[i],q);
    return out;
  }

  // compute product AND track which product terms came from a wrap (deg>=n)
  function mulTraced(a,b){
    const c=new Array(n).fill(0), wrapped=new Array(n).fill(false);
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++)for(let j=0;j<n;j++){
      let k=i+j, sign=1;
      if(k>=n){k-=n; sign=-1; wrapped[k]=true;}
      c[k]=CA.mod(c[k]+sign*a[i]*b[j],q);
    }
    return {c,wrapped};
  }

  function draw(){
    ring.innerHTML="";
    // viewBox is 700 wide: last column starts at colX+2*colGap-30 and must
    // end (plus its "wrapped" tag) inside 700, so keep the geometry tight
    const colX=80, colGap=235, rowY=80, rowGap=44, boxW=175;
    // headers
    const head=(x,label,color)=>{const t=mk("text",{x,y:50,fill:color||"#F3EEDF","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"14","font-weight":"700"});t.textContent=label;ring.appendChild(t);};
    head(colX,"a(X)"); head(colX+colGap,"b(X)"); head(colX+2*colGap,"a\u00b7b in R_q","#C85A5A");

    const {c,wrapped}=mulTraced(A,B);
    // draw coefficient rows for A, B, C
    function col(x,arr,wrapMark){
      for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
        const y=rowY+i*rowGap;
        const wrap=wrapMark&&wrapMark[i];
        ring.appendChild(mk("rect",{x:x-30,y:y-20,width:boxW,height:32,rx:3,
          fill:"#1c1c22",stroke:wrap?"#C85A5A":"#2e2e3a","stroke-width":wrap?2:1}));
        const deg=mk("text",{x:x-20,y:y+2,fill:"#D5CDDF","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"12"});
        deg.textContent="X"+(i===0?"\u2070":i===1?"\u00b9":i===2?"\u00b2":i===3?"\u00b3":"^"+i); ring.appendChild(deg);
        const v=mk("text",{x:x+30,y:y+2,fill:wrap?"#C85A5A":"#F3EEDF","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"15","font-weight":"700"});
        v.textContent=arr[i]; ring.appendChild(v);
        if(wrap){
          const tag=mk("text",{x:x+70,y:y+2,fill:"#C85A5A","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"11"});
          tag.textContent="\u21b5 wrapped"; ring.appendChild(tag);
        }
      }
    }
    col(colX,A,null); col(colX+colGap,B,null); col(colX+2*colGap,c,wrapped);
    // wrap illustration arc
    const anyWrap=wrapped.some(Boolean);
    if(anyWrap){
      const note=mk("text",{x:colX-30,y:rowY+n*rowGap+8,fill:"#C85A5A","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"12"});
      note.textContent="X\u207f = \u22121, so high-degree terms fold back with a sign flip";
      ring.appendChild(note);
    }
    rread.innerHTML="a\u00b7b = [ <b>"+c.join(", ")+"</b> ] in Z_"+q+"[X]/(X"+(n===4?"\u2074":"^"+n)+"+1)";
    aIn.value=A.join(","); bIn.value=B.join(",");
  }

  function reparse(){ A=parse(aIn.value,n); B=parse(bIn.value,n); draw(); }
  nsel.addEventListener("change",()=>{ n=+nsel.value; A=parse(aIn.value,n); B=parse(bIn.value,n); draw(); });
  qsel.addEventListener("change",()=>{ q=+qsel.value; A=A.map(v=>CA.mod(v,q)); B=B.map(v=>CA.mod(v,q)); draw(); });
  document.getElementById("mulBtn").addEventListener("click",reparse);
  document.getElementById("rand").addEventListener("click",()=>{
    A=Array.from({length:n},()=>Math.floor(Math.random()*q));
    B=Array.from({length:n},()=>Math.floor(Math.random()*q));
    draw();
  });
  draw();
})();
```

[← Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/index.html>) Exhibit 144 · π(x) ~ x/ln x

Prime Density and Key Generation

### How to find a
prime in the *dark*

RSA key generation commonly samples large candidates and tests for primality. The Prime Number Theorem explains their approximate density and therefore the expected number of attempts. It does not itself prove that a particular candidate is prime or impose a fixed running time.

**A key-generation connection.** Prime density explains why random candidate search is practical. Generating a key still requires appropriate primality testing and parameter checks; the other algebraic foundations in this hall are also essential to their respective constructions.

§1

#### Primes thin out — but slowly

Among small numbers, primes are everywhere. As you climb, they thin. The Prime Number Theorem pins down exactly how fast: the count of primes below *x*, written π(x), grows like x⁄ln x. Equivalently, a number near *x* is prime with probability about 1⁄ln x.

π(x) ≈ x / ln x · density near x ≈ 1 / ln x

The slider shows small, exactly countable ranges. Cryptographic primes are vastly larger; the asymptotic theorem helps explain their density, not a direct enumeration on this screen.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="curve" viewBox="0 0 700 420" id="pnt" role="img" aria-label="Prime counting function versus x over ln x."></svg>
```

x up to  [Input xr: type=range; initial value=1000]

—

Ink dots: the **true** π(x), counted by sieve. Teal line: the theorem's estimate x⁄ln x. Their ratio tends to 1 as x grows; the error need not decrease monotonically, and the absolute difference can grow.

§2

#### The keygen coin-flip

For a common two-prime 2048-bit RSA modulus, key generation selects two suitable primes of roughly 1024 bits each and checks the product’s size. The theorem says a random 1024-bit *integer* is prime with probability about 1⁄ln(2¹⁰²⁴) ≈ 1⁄710. Restricting this sampling model to odd candidates approximately doubles the density: roughly **1 in 355 odd candidates** is prime. Sieve out small factors like 3 and 5 first and the rate improves again. So you test a few hundred candidates with a fast primality check, and finish with an expected runtime that depends on the implementation and hardware.

at 1024 bits: ~1 in 710 integers · ~1 in 355 *odd* candidates

Keep the claim narrow: this theorem explains why RSA can *find* its primes quickly. It says nothing about why factoring their product is hard — that bet is made in [The One-Way Function](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/one-way-function.html>), and the arithmetic that makes the resulting key *work* is in [Euler & Fermat](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/euler-fermat.html>).

Prime density explains why random sampling is practical. Reliable random generation, primality testing, parameter choices and implementation are also necessary; a density theorem is not a complete key-generation algorithm.

Where this touches your keys

##### Why random prime search is practical

Random sampling with primality testing is a common strategy, but other constructions also exist. The theorem describes asymptotic density; expected runtime depends on candidate filtering, the primality test and the machine.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  var NS="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  function el(t,a){var e=document.createElementNS(NS,t);for(var k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;}
  function sieve(n){var s=new Array(n+1).fill(true);s[0]=s[1]=false;
    for(var i=2;i*i<=n;i++)if(s[i])for(var j=i*i;j<=n;j+=i)s[j]=false;return s;}

  var pnt=document.getElementById("pnt"), xr=document.getElementById("xr"), pread=document.getElementById("pread");
  var W=700,H=420,pad=52;

  function draw(){
    var X=+xr.value; pnt.innerHTML="";
    var s=sieve(X);
    // compute pi(x) samples
    var samples=[], cumcount=0, maxpi=0;
    for(var x=2;x<=X;x++){ if(s[x])cumcount++; if(x%Math.max(1,Math.floor(X/120))===0||x===X){ samples.push([x,cumcount]); } maxpi=cumcount; }
    var estMax=X/Math.log(X);
    var yMax=Math.max(maxpi,estMax)*1.08;
    function px(x){return pad+(x/X)*(W-2*pad);}
    function py(v){return H-pad-(v/yMax)*(H-2*pad);}
    // axes
    pnt.appendChild(el("line",{x1:pad,y1:H-pad,x2:W-pad,y2:H-pad,stroke:"#F3EEDF","stroke-width":1.5}));
    pnt.appendChild(el("line",{x1:pad,y1:pad,x2:pad,y2:H-pad,stroke:"#F3EEDF","stroke-width":1.5}));
    // estimate curve x/ln x
    var d="";
    for(var x=2;x<=X;x+=Math.max(1,Math.floor(X/200))){ var v=x/Math.log(x);
      d+=(d?"L":"M")+px(x).toFixed(1)+" "+py(v).toFixed(1)+" "; }
    pnt.appendChild(el("path",{d:d.trim(),fill:"none",stroke:"#5AC8A0","stroke-width":2.4}));
    // true pi(x) dots
    samples.forEach(function(pt){
      pnt.appendChild(el("circle",{cx:px(pt[0]).toFixed(1),cy:py(pt[1]).toFixed(1),r:2.4,fill:"#F3EEDF","fill-opacity":0.8}));
    });
    // labels
    var lx=el("text",{x:W-pad,y:H-pad+22,fill:"#D5CDDF","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"12","text-anchor":"end"});
    lx.textContent="x = "+X; pnt.appendChild(lx);
    var ly=el("text",{x:pad+8,y:pad-8,fill:"#D5CDDF","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"12"});
    ly.textContent="count of primes ≤ x"; pnt.appendChild(ly);
    // legend
    var lg=el("text",{x:px(X*0.55),y:py(X*0.55/Math.log(X*0.55))-10,fill:"#5AC8A0","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"13","font-weight":"700"});
    lg.textContent="x / ln x"; pnt.appendChild(lg);
    pread.innerHTML="π("+X+") = <b>"+maxpi+"</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; x/ln x ≈ <b>"+Math.round(estMax)+"</b>";
  }
  xr.addEventListener("input",draw);
  draw();
})();
```

[← Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/index.html>) Exhibit 154 · the perfect hash

The Assumption Beneath Fiat–Shamir

### The oracle that
can't be *predicted*

Much of cryptography leans on a fiction so useful it's treated as bedrock: a hash function that behaves like a perfectly random one. Feed it anything, get back noise you could never have guessed — and the same input always returns the same noise. From that single idea, signatures are built.

**A model, held on purpose.** No real function is a true random oracle. A random-oracle proof studies a complete scheme with access to an ideal random function. Replacing that oracle with a real hash is an additional design step, not an automatic transfer of the proof. The visible avalanche effect below is a much weaker property.

§1

#### Two demands on a hash

Preimage resistance asks that finding an input for a specified digest be infeasible; collision resistance asks that finding any two distinct inputs with one digest be infeasible. Neither property follows merely from outputs looking unrelated to their inputs.

pre-image: given h, find m with H(m)=h · collision: find m₁ ≠ m₂ with H(m₁)=H(m₂)

§2

#### The avalanche

Here's the property you can see. Flip a *single* input bit and, in a good hash, roughly *half* the output bits flip — with no pattern linking which. Toggle any input bit below and watch the change cascade through the mixing rounds. A one-bit nudge should scramble the whole output.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="curve" viewBox="0 0 700 460" id="ava" role="img" aria-label="Avalanche effect: flipping one input bit cascades to change about half the output bits."></svg>
```

Flip a random bit New input

—

Click any input bit (top row) to toggle it. The vermilion output bits are the ones that changed versus the previous output. A good mixer changes about **half**, unpredictably — that's the avalanche.

**Not a security test.** A broken hash can still show an avalanche effect. Even a deliberately weak function can pass this visual check while remaining easy to invert or collide. The toy mixer here is one of them. Seeing the scramble is not evidence of one-wayness; it only tells you the output isn't obviously tracking the input.

Keyboard alternative: enter a bit position 0 to 15 to toggle, then apply. toggle bit #  [Input bitIn: type=number; initial value=0]   Toggle bit

§3

#### From random oracle to signature

The Fiat–Shamir transform replaces the verifier's challenge with a hash of the commitment, public statement and required application context; a signature also binds its message. A proof in the random-oracle model treats that hash as an ideal random function. Correct transcript binding and the proof's assumptions matter, and substituting a real hash does not automatically transfer the proof.

A Fiat–Shamir signature binds the message and required transcript context into a hash-derived challenge. Unforgeability belongs to the complete construction under its stated assumptions; it is not a property of the challenge alone.

§4

#### Why abort a signature attempt?

ML-DSA forms a response shaped like *z = y + c·s*: a random mask plus a secret-dependent shift. Unlike uniform masking around a finite group, a mask drawn from a bounded interval has edges. Publishing a response near an edge can reveal information about that shift.

**A scalar example.** Choose the integer mask *y* uniformly from −4 through 4, and let the shift *t* be −1, 0 or 1. The response is *z = y + t*. These are inclusive integer ranges:

- For *t = −1*, responses range from −5 through 3.

- For *t = 0*, responses range from −4 through 4.

- For *t = 1*, responses range from −3 through 5.

Seeing *z = 5* identifies *t = 1*. Instead, discard the attempt unless *−3 ≤ z ≤ 3*, then resample the mask. For every allowed shift, exactly seven of the nine masks survive. Conditional on acceptance, each of the seven responses has probability 1/7, independent of the shift. The common interior removes this edge information.

This illustrates one reason for Fiat–Shamir *with aborts*. Actual ML-DSA operates on polynomial vectors, imposes a strict response-norm bound and performs further rejection checks. The scalar example is not its signing algorithm or a security proof. Compare the [Schnorr identification example](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zero-knowledge-proofs.html>), where masking uses modular arithmetic.

Explore the existing [Dilithium Reject lab](<https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-dilithium-reject/>): “Why Each Check Exists” explains the bounds, and “Watch the Loop” shows signing attempts. Retry histograms alone do not demonstrate exploitable secret leakage.

Where this touches your keys

##### Used by several signature families

Schnorr-style signatures and ML-DSA use Fiat–Shamir ideas. ML-DSA uses SHAKE-based hashing and a construction often described as Fiat–Shamir with aborts. SLH-DSA belongs to a hash-based signature family with different assumptions and tradeoffs. These are distinct constructions, not one security argument applied to every signature.

Related: [One-Way Functions](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/one-way-function.html>) (pre-image resistance in general), [Reduction & Proof](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/reduction.html>) (what a proof in this model claims).

**Sources and scope:** Alfred Menezes, *A Gentle Introduction to Lattice-Based Cryptography*, version 3.3, September 16, 2026, §7.1.4, Issue #5, pp.73–74; [RFC 8235 (2017)](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8235.html>); NIST [FIPS 204](<https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final>), Algorithm 7, and [FIPS 205](<https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final>) (2024). The interval example is conceptual; the interactive 16-bit mixer is an illustration, not a cryptographic hash.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  const NS="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  const mk=(t,a)=>{const e=document.createElementNS(NS,t);for(const k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;};
  const ava=document.getElementById("ava");
  const aread=document.getElementById("aread");

  // toy 16-bit mixer with several rounds; deterministic, strong avalanche
  function mix(x){
    x&=0xFFFF;
    x=(x^(x<<7))&0xFFFF;
    x=(x^(x>>>3))&0xFFFF;
    x=(x^(x<<5))&0xFFFF;
    x=(x*0x9E37)&0xFFFF;
    x=(x^(x>>>8))&0xFFFF;
    x=(x^(x<<2))&0xFFFF;
    return x&0xFFFF;
  }
  const bits=v=>Array.from({length:16},(_,i)=>(v>>>(15-i))&1);

  let input=0b1011001110100101;
  let prevOut=mix(input);

  function draw(changedInputBit){
    ava.innerHTML="";
    const out=mix(input);
    const inB=bits(input), outB=bits(out), prevB=bits(prevOut);
    const W=700, x0=70, cell=36, gap=2, topY=120, botY=300;
    const lab=(y,txt)=>{const t=mk("text",{x:x0,y:y-18,fill:"#D5CDDF","font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"13","font-weight":"700"});t.textContent=txt;ava.appendChild(t);};
    lab(topY,"input  (click a bit to flip)");
    lab(botY,"output  (vermilion = changed)");

    // input row (clickable)
    inB.forEach((b,i)=>{
      const x=x0+i*(cell+gap);
      const changed=(changedInputBit===i);
      const g=mk("g",{cursor:"pointer",class:"inbit","data-i":i});
      g.appendChild(mk("rect",{x,y:topY,width:cell,height:cell,rx:3,
        fill:b?"#F3EEDF":"#1c1c22",stroke:changed?"#C85A5A":"#2e2e3a","stroke-width":changed?2.5:1}));
      const t=mk("text",{x:x+cell/2,y:topY+cell/2+5,fill:b?"#1c1c22":"#F3EEDF",
        "font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"15","font-weight":"700","text-anchor":"middle"});
      t.textContent=b; g.appendChild(t);
      g.addEventListener("click",()=>toggle(i));
      ava.appendChild(g);
    });

    // connecting "mixing" lines
    ava.appendChild(mk("text",{x:W/2,y:(topY+botY)/2+18,fill:"#D4B765",
      "font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"13","text-anchor":"middle","font-style":"italic",
    })).textContent="6 rounds of shift \u00b7 xor \u00b7 multiply";

    // output row
    let flips=0;
    outB.forEach((b,i)=>{
      const x=x0+i*(cell+gap);
      const changed=(b!==prevB[i]); if(changed)flips++;
      ava.appendChild(mk("rect",{x,y:botY,width:cell,height:cell,rx:3,
        fill:changed?"#C85A5A":(b?"#F3EEDF":"#1c1c22"),stroke:"#2e2e3a","stroke-width":1}));
      const t=mk("text",{x:x+cell/2,y:botY+cell/2+5,fill:(changed||b)?"#1c1c22":"#F3EEDF",
        "font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace","font-size":"15","font-weight":"700","text-anchor":"middle"});
      t.textContent=b; ava.appendChild(t);
    });

    aread.innerHTML="input 0x"+input.toString(16).toUpperCase().padStart(4,"0")+
      " \u2192 output 0x"+out.toString(16).toUpperCase().padStart(4,"0")+
      " \u00b7 <b>"+flips+"/16</b> output bits changed";
  }

  function toggle(i){
    prevOut=mix(input);
    input^=(1<<(15-i));
    draw(i);
  }
  document.getElementById("flipRand").addEventListener("click",()=>toggle(Math.floor(Math.random()*16)));
  document.getElementById("newIn").addEventListener("click",()=>{
    input=Math.floor(Math.random()*0x10000); prevOut=mix(input); draw(-1);
  });
  document.getElementById("toggleBtn").addEventListener("click",()=>{
    const b=parseInt(document.getElementById("bitIn").value,10);
    if(!isNaN(b)&&b>=0&&b<=15) toggle(b);
  });
  draw(-1);
})();
```

[← Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/index.html>) Exhibit 148 · A ≤ B

What "Provably Secure" Actually Claims

### Standing on a
*borrowed* difficulty

Cryptographers rarely prove a scheme is hard to break. They prove a conditional implication: that breaking it would let you solve a problem everyone already believes is hard. Security is borrowed from a difficulty we trust — and the loan is made by a *reduction*.

**A conditional claim.** A proof names an assumption, adversary model and quantitative reduction loss. It neither proves that assumption nor licenses reversing the reduction arrow.

§1

#### The contrapositive machine

Suppose a precisely defined reduction could turn a successful scheme-breaker into a solver for a specified hard problem. If the transformation preserved sufficient running time and success probability, the problem's assumed hardness would bound the attacker. The animation is a hypothetical logic diagram, not an implementation or a proof that RSA inversion is equivalent to factoring.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="curve" viewBox="0 0 700 420" id="red" role="img" aria-label="A reduction: a scheme-breaker is used to build a factoring machine."></svg>
```

Run the reduction Reset

Suppose a break exists…

Read it as a machine: feed a hard factoring instance in, wrap it as a fake scheme challenge, let the hypothetical breaker crack it, and read the factors back out. If the reduction is efficient enough, a sufficiently fast breaker would contradict the specified factoring-hardness assumption.

§2

#### The chain of trust

The direction of the implication matters. A reduction using an attacker to solve a problem supports a conditional security claim. The opposite direction—using a problem solver to break a scheme—shows a possible attack but is not that security proof. A broken assumption can invalidate a proof without automatically yielding an attack on every scheme.

- RSAknown attack directionfactoring the modulus breaks RSA. General RSA inversion is not known to be equivalent to factoring.

- ECC · DHscheme-specific assumptionsCDH, DDH or other group assumptions, according to the protocol and security goal. A discrete-log solver is enough to break DH.

- ML-KEM · ML-DSAmodule-lattice assumptionsspecific Module-LWE and Module-SIS-related problems and additional construction assumptions; not an equivalence to arbitrary exact SVP.

A reduction says how an attacker would imply a solver under stated conditions. It does not require an attacker to literally run that solver first.

Where this touches your keys

##### Why anyone trusts a primitive

Public-key security estimates combine formal definitions, conditional reductions and concrete cryptanalysis. A reduction has an attack model, parameter restrictions and a loss in time or success probability; it may not be tight. No reduction proves the underlying hardness assumption itself.

AES is supported by decades of public cryptanalysis rather than a proof from an independently established hard problem. Higher-level symmetric constructions can still have reductions to assumptions about their block cipher or hash. Both the mathematical model and practical attack evidence matter.

Foundations referenced here: [One-Way Functions](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/one-way-function.html>), [Lattices & the SVP](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/lattices-svp.html>).

**Sources and scope:** Dan Boneh and Victor Shoup, *A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography*, version 0.6 (January 2023), Chapter 10; NIST [FIPS 203](<https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/203/final>) and [FIPS 204](<https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final>).

```javascript

(function(){
  "use strict";
  var NS="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  function el(t,a){var e=document.createElementNS(NS,t);for(var k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;}
  var red=document.getElementById("red"), rread=document.getElementById("rread");

  var steps=[
    {box:"factoring\ninstance n",x:90,color:"#F3EEDF",note:"Start with a hard problem: factor n."},
    {box:"wrap as fake\nscheme challenge",x:270,color:"#D4B765",note:"Disguise n as a challenge for the scheme."},
    {box:"the BREAKER\n(hypothetical)",x:450,color:"#C85A5A",note:"Hand it to the attacker who 'breaks' the scheme."},
    {box:"read off\np and q",x:630,color:"#5AC8A0",note:"Its answer hands you the factors. Contradiction."}
  ];

  function drawUpTo(n){
    red.innerHTML="";
    var y=210;
    for(var i=0;i<steps.length;i++){
      var s=steps[i], active=(i<n);
      var op=active?1:0.22;
      // connector
      if(i>0){
        var prev=steps[i-1];
        red.appendChild(el("line",{x1:prev.x+62,y1:y,x2:s.x-62,y2:y,
          stroke:"#F3EEDF","stroke-width":2,"stroke-opacity":active?0.9:0.15}));
        if(active) red.appendChild(el("polygon",{points:(s.x-62)+","+y+" "+(s.x-74)+","+(y-6)+" "+(s.x-74)+","+(y+6),fill:"#F3EEDF"}));
      }
      var g=el("g",{opacity:op});
      g.appendChild(el("circle",{cx:s.x,cy:y,r:56,fill:"#1c1c22",stroke:s.color,"stroke-width":2.5}));
      var lines=s.box.split("\n");
      lines.forEach(function(ln,li){
        var t=el("text",{x:s.x,y:y-6+li*18,fill:s.color,"font-family":"ui-monospace,monospace",
          "font-size":"12","font-weight":"700","text-anchor":"middle"});
        t.textContent=ln; g.appendChild(t);
      });
      red.appendChild(g);
    }
    rread.textContent = n>0 ? steps[Math.min(n-1,3)].note : "Suppose a break exists…";
  }

  var cur=0, iv=null;
  document.getElementById("play").addEventListener("click",function(){
    if(iv)clearInterval(iv); cur=0;
    if(window.matchMedia&&window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches){
      drawUpTo(steps.length);   // same end state, no animation
      return;
    }
    iv=setInterval(function(){ cur++; drawUpTo(cur); if(cur>=steps.length)clearInterval(iv); },700);
  });
  document.getElementById("rreset").addEventListener("click",function(){ if(iv)clearInterval(iv); cur=0; drawUpTo(0); });
  drawUpTo(0);
})();
```

 Hall I · Ancient traditions and later comparisons

### World Origins of Cryptography

Writing, concealment and encipherment across Egyptian, Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Indian and Arabic traditions

Early writing traditions include concealment, signaling, language decipherment and deliberate encipherment. These are related topics, not interchangeable evidence of encryption. This hall identifies the historical sources and the limits of each modern demonstration.

Ancient Egypt Ancient Israel Ancient Greece Ancient Rome Classical India Abbasid Baghdad

📜

**What this hall teaches:** The surviving sources describe different problems: hiding a message, signalling it, substituting symbols and deciphering an unfamiliar script. Similarity between methods does not by itself establish a shared origin or direct transmission between cultures.

🧭

**Suggested route:** Start with Egyptian Substitution and the Rosetta Stone to separate unusual writing from language decipherment. Continue through Histiaeus, Scytale, Atbash and Caesar, then compare al-Kindi’s documented cryptanalytic methods.

[Exhibit 64 Egypt · ~1900 BCE

Egyptian Substitution Hieroglyphs

Unusual writing in Khnumhotep II’s tomb: an early example discussed in cryptographic histories, without an established modern secrecy purpose.

Track B Visualization

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/egyptian-substitution.html>) [Exhibit 71 Egypt · 196 BCE

Rosetta Stone

The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) records a decree in two languages and three scripts. It supported the decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs; it is not an encryption system.

Track B Decipherment

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rosetta-stone.html>) [Exhibit 65 Greece · ~499 BCE

Histiaeus's Tattooed Messenger

Histiaeus of Miletus (~499 BCE) — the Greek tyrant who tattooed a secret revolt order on a slave's shaved scalp, then waited for the hair to regrow before sending him.

Historical Only Track B Steganography

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/histiaeus-tattoo.html>) [Exhibit 1 Sparta · interpretation debated

Scytale

The traditional scytale reconstruction illustrates transposition, but the dates and cryptographic interpretation of ancient evidence are disputed.

WRAP: HELPMEIAMUNDERATTACK
 READ: HDUEANPTTDMAECREITAK

Broken Transposition

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/scytale.html>) [Exhibit 2 Ancient Rome · 1st century BCE

Caesar Cipher

Suetonius describes Caesar’s use of a three-letter shift. The modern 26-letter exercise has only 26 shifts to test; it does not require a ninth-century attack.

PLAIN: HELLO
 SHIFT: +3
 CIPH: KHOOR

Broken Live Demo

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/caesar.html>) [Exhibit 3 Ancient Greece · ~150 BC

Polybius Square

Polybius describes alphabetic torch signalling using five tablets for the Greek alphabet. The displayed I/J grid is a modern Latin-alphabet adaptation.

A→11 B→12 C→13
 HELLO = 23 15 31 31 34

Broken Foundation Cipher

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/polybius.html>) [Exhibit 41 Ancient Hebrew tradition

Atbash

Atbash — the ancient Hebrew reflection cipher (A<->Z, B<->Y, C<->X), self-inverse and used in the Book of Jeremiah (25:26, 51:41) for SHESHACH.

A↔Z B↔Y C↔X …
 HELLO = SVOOL

Broken Self-Inverse

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/atbash.html>) [Exhibit 67 India · ~400 CE

Kama Sutra Cipher

Mlecchita-vikalpa, secret writing among the Kama Sutra’s arts. The interactive illustrates a modern paired-letter substitution, not a recovered ancient alphabet.

Broken Live Demo

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kama-sutra.html>) [Exhibit 66 Greece · 4th c. BCE

Aeneas Tacticus

Aeneas’s water-clock signaling, preserved in Polybius: synchronized vessels selected preset military messages, not letters of an alphabet.

Live Demo

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/aeneas-tacticus.html>) [Exhibit 68 Baghdad · ~850 CE

Arabic Nomenclators

Arabic cryptanalytic scholarship and a teaching model of nomenclators: frequency analysis, codewords, and the need to identify a particular historical key.

Broken Live Demo

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/arabic-nomenclators.html>) [Exhibit 42 Usenet · 1980s

ROT13

ROT13 (~1983, Usenet) — the self-inverse Caesar with shift 13, designed as a spoiler obscurer rather than a cipher. One operation toggles text in and out.

Broken Self-Inverse

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rot13.html>)

What This Hall Teaches

#### Foundational Concepts

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Modular Arithmetic

The Caesar cipher wraps around the alphabet using modulo 26. `(position + shift) mod 26`. Modular arithmetic appears throughout cryptography; AES uses binary finite-field operations rather than addition modulo 26.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

Coordinate Encoding

Polybius’s coordinate notation separates a symbol into row and column information. Later fractionating ciphers rearrange such coordinates; modern bitslicing is a different implementation technique.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

Frequency Analysis (the weakness)

Fixed substitutions preserve symbol counts while relabeling them. Frequency comparisons can suggest a key, especially with longer text, but short samples may not follow average language frequencies.

[Next Hall → Hall II: Classical Substitution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/substitution.html>)

 Hall VI · Special Exhibition · 1861 – 1865

### The American Civil War Gallery

The telegraph transformed warfare — and cryptography with it

The American Civil War made extensive use of electric telegraphy for military command. It was not the first war to use telegraphs. Operators had to balance speed, interception risks and key distribution; the three systems here show different approaches rather than a single cause of the war’s outcome.

Union Cipher Confederate

⚡

**Telegraphy and interception:** Electrical messages could cross long distances quickly, while intermediaries and wiretaps created security risks. Sensitive military traffic used codes and ciphers, but not every telegram was encrypted.

[Exhibit 24 Union · 1861

Stager Cipher

The Union’s Stager system combined word transposition, code words and operational procedures. Wartime success is a historical claim, not a proof of mathematical security.

ROUTE: up 1, down 4, up 2, down 3, up 5, down 6

↑1

↓4

↑2

↓3

↑5

↓6

rapture

Sept

twenty

nine

1862

for

Historical Only Lincoln's Cipher

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/stager.html>) [Exhibit 25 Confederate · 1862

Confederate Vigenère

Confederate repeating-key ciphers and Union solutions, including the MANCHESTER BLUFF dispatch of 25 May 1863. Some solutions were delayed or obstructed by transmission errors.

Documented example key:

Manchester Bluff

Broken Jefferson Davis

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/confederate-vigenere.html>) [Exhibit 26 Confederate · 1862

Confederate Dictionary Code

Dictionary codes replace words with references in an agreed book. Repeated references and language patterns can still leak information; this widget is a simplified model.

Historical coordinate example: 146.L.20
 Page 146, left column, twentieth word; edition must match

Broken Jefferson Davis

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/dictionary-code.html>)

The Cryptographic Balance of Power

#### Contrasting Systems and Operational Evidence

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

 Union Cryptography

- **Stager Cipher:** Purpose-built for telegraph security. Route transposition + code-word substitution evolved continuously throughout the war, through a series of numbered cipher books ending with Cipher No. 4 (1865).

- **Professional management:** The U.S. Military Telegraph Corps, under Stager and Eckert, controlled all cipher usage. Operators were trained and supervised.

- **Reported operational success:** Historical accounts credit the Union system’s protection of traffic. This does not prove mathematical immunity or establish the fate of every intercepted telegram.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

 Confederate Cryptography

- **Repeating-key substitution:** Confederate use preceded Kasiski’s 1863 publication. Documented Union solutions do not establish that the analysts used his method.

- **Key reuse:** A recovered key could expose other traffic using that key. It did not automatically reveal every Confederate military message.

- **Dictionary codes:** Correspondents needed matching editions and lookup conventions. Kahn documents specific dictionary arrangements; an unsupported story about two generals using mismatched editions is not evidence.

🏛️

**Reading the evidence:** Word-route ciphers, codeword substitutions and dictionary references are different procedures. The linked exhibits distinguish historical records from their synthetic browser examples. Source: David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), Chapter 7, “Crises of the Union.”

 Hall X · The Human Stories

### Hall of Codebreakers

Codebreakers, cipher designers and the teams behind important cryptanalytic achievements

  Cryptanalytic results depend on evidence, methods, teamwork and operating conditions.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

 Al-Kindi

~850 AD

**Person:** Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi, Baghdad

**Technique:** Frequency analysis

Al-Kindi’s surviving treatise gives an early systematic account of frequency analysis. A fixed letter substitution preserves counts, allowing language statistics and word patterns to guide a search. That does not mean every ciphertext has enough information for a unique solution.

💡

Letter frequencies vary by language, genre and sample length. Comparing them can suggest candidate substitutions; words and higher-order patterns help test those guesses. The most common symbol need not encode the most common letter in a short message.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-swords"></use></svg>
```

 Thomas Phelippes and Mary Queen of Scots[Full exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/babington.html>)

1586

**Person:** Thomas Phelippes, agent of Sir Francis Walsingham

**Technique:** Frequency analysis + contextual knowledge

Mary's encrypted correspondence with Babington Plot conspirators was intercepted and decoded. She was executed February 8, 1587. The break is one of history's clearest examples of cryptanalysis determining a human life.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-key"></use></svg>
```

 Étienne Bazeries and the Great Cipher

1893

**Person:** Commandant Étienne Bazeries (1846–1931), French Army cryptanalyst

**Technique:** Syllabic-substitution analysis on a 587-symbol nomenclator, with contextual cribbing against historical Louis XIV correspondence

In the 1890s Bazeries reconstructed a Rossignol-era nomenclator using syllable hypotheses, contextual readings and repeated groups. The royal systems developed during the seventeenth century; Bonaventure should not be credited with creating one alongside his father in the 1620s. Kahn describes homophones, nulls and an erasure instruction affecting the previous sign. These special entries complicate analysis, but no one trap explains the whole history of the decipherment.

Bazeries’s decipherment of Louis XIV correspondence also led him to propose an identity for the Man in the Iron Mask. That historical interpretation is disputed; deciphering a letter does not settle every inference about its subject. He also designed a cipher cylinder and published *Les Chiffres Secrets Dévoilés* (1901 edition).

💡

The Great Cipher break is the canonical example of **cryptanalysis as historiography**: the tool was invented to decrypt diplomacy in real time, but its lasting payoff was unlocking a 200-year-old archive. See the exhibit: [Hall II · Great Cipher (17th century)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/great-cipher.html>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

 Room 40 and the Zimmermann Telegram

1917

**People:** Room 40, British Naval Intelligence

**Technique:** Code book reconstruction from partial recoveries

Germany secretly offered Mexico an alliance against the United States. Britain decoded it, waited strategically, then shared it with Washington. The telegram helped bring America into WWI. The war ended 20 months later.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

 The Polish Breaking of Enigma

1932

**People:** Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki, Henryk Zygalski

**Technique:** Permutation group mathematics + known message indicators

Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski combined mathematical analysis, intercepted indicators and intelligence supplied through French cooperation to reconstruct and attack military Enigma. They shared their results with French and British colleagues near Warsaw in July 1939. See [GCHQ’s account of that meeting](<https://www.gchq.gov.uk/information/the-pyry-forest-meeting>).

🇵🇱

Rejewski's breakthrough came from analyzing the message indicator system — the first six characters of each Enigma message. By collecting enough indicators, he found patterns that revealed the mathematical structure of the rotors. Pure mathematics, applied to an engineering problem, by a 27-year-old mathematician.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

 Turing, Welchman, and the Bombe

1940

**People:** Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman, engineering teams and bombe operators

**Technique:** Crib-based electromechanical search

British bombe machines tested constraints derived from possible plaintext, building on the Polish breakthrough and later Allied work. ULTRA intelligence contributed to wartime operations. Estimates of how much it shortened the war are counterfactual judgments, not measured results.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-signal"></use></svg>
```

 Traffic Analysts and Log-Readers[Try the exercise →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html>)

WWI–WWII

**People:** Traffic analysts, including James Thirsk, who wrote about his wartime work as a “log-reader”

**Technique:** Traffic analysis: callsigns, frequencies, schedules, routing and direction finding

Not every result needed a decrypt. Traffic analysts studied the externals of radio traffic: who called whom, when, on which frequency and from where. That work helped locate units, guide interception and support cryptanalysts. Its results could also be misread: on the day of Jutland in 1916, a callsign located in harbour was taken to mean the German fleet was still in port. Try the method on an invented log in [Reading the Radio Log](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

 Tiltman, Tutte, Flowers, and Colossus[Full exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bill-tutte.html>)

1941–1944

**People:** John Tiltman (message/key recovery), Bill Tutte and the Research Section (structure), Tommy Flowers and team (engineering)

**Technique:** Statistical wheel-pattern analysis

Tiltman recovered messages and key from a repeated-key transmission in 1941. Tutte and the Research Section inferred the machine’s structure by early 1942. Flowers and his team later built Colossus, operational in February 1944, to accelerate statistical wheel-setting.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-flag"></use></svg>
```

 William Friedman and Purple

1940

**Person:** William F. Friedman, US Army Signal Intelligence

**Technique:** Statistical analysis + machine reconstruction

The SIS team reconstructed PURPLE’s logical behavior and achieved its major breakthrough in September 1940. It produced valuable Japanese diplomatic intelligence before Pearl Harbor, but those diplomatic messages did not disclose the operational attack plan. Diplomatic and naval intelligence must not be treated as interchangeable.

⚠️

Breaking an encryption system does not guarantee access to every relevant message, a correct translation or the right interpretation. Intelligence collection, distribution and operational decision-making are separate stages.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-shield"></use></svg>
```

 The Navajo Code Talkers

1942–1945

**People:** 420 Navajo Marines, US Marine Corps

**Cipher:** Navajo language plus a constructed military code

Navajo Marines used a specially developed military vocabulary and alphabet-spelling code as well as their language. The original 29 code developers received Congressional Gold Medals in 2001; later code talkers received silver medals. The code’s reported wartime success is a historical result, not a mathematical proof of secrecy.

[View the Navajo Code Talkers exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/navajo-code-talkers.html>)

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

 Joan Clarke and Naval Enigma[Full exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/joan-clarke.html>)

1940–1945

**Person:** Joan Elisabeth Lowther Clarke (later Murray), 1917–1996

**Technique:** Banburismus — Bayesian sequential analysis of Enigma indicators

Recruited from Cambridge mathematics in 1940, Clarke became one of the most productive cryptanalysts in Hut 8 and rose to deputy head — extraordinary in a service that paid female staff at clerical rates and barred them from "officer" titles. She was a fluent practitioner of Banburismus, the Bayesian sequential procedure invented by Turing to slash the Bombe's workload by ranking which wheel orders to test first. On the most stubborn naval traffic she shared the load with Turing himself; on shorter runs she worked alone.

Clarke’s Naval Enigma work contributed to intelligence used in the Atlantic campaign. Access varied by network and period, including the 1942 U-boat blackout. She received the MBE in 1946. Her postwar career included a move to Scotland after marriage in 1952, a return to Cheltenham in 1962, formal retirement in 1977 and later clerical work. The linked biography distinguishes those dates and supplies the sources.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

 Bill Tutte: Inferring the Lorenz Structure[Full exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bill-tutte.html>)

1941–1942

**Person:** William Thomas "Bill" Tutte, 1917–2002, Cambridge graph theorist

**Technique:** Statistical period-finding on a 4,000-character depth produced by an operator's August 1941 mistake

After a repeated-key Lorenz transmission in August 1941, John Tiltman recovered plaintext and key material. Tutte and the Research Section analysed the resulting stream and inferred the twelve-wheel structure by early 1942. This work distinguished five chi wheels, five psi wheels and two motor wheels, enabling later statistical attacks without first possessing the machine.

Tutte’s statistical work helped make machine-assisted Tunny attacks possible. Colossus was a collective engineering and operational achievement, and manual work continued alongside it. Tutte later made major contributions to graph theory and combinatorics. His codebreaking role remained little known for many years; the Tutte Institute for Mathematics and Computing in Canada commemorates his work.

💡

See also: [Hall VII · Lorenz exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/lorenz.html>) for the machine; Story 6 above for Tommy Flowers and Colossus.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

 Elizebeth Smith Friedman: Rum-Runners and Nazi Spies[Full exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/elizebeth-friedman.html>)

1923–1946

**Person:** Elizebeth Smith Friedman, 1892–1980

**Technique:** Hand cryptanalysis of commercial codes, polyalphabetics, and one-part nomenclators across 12,000+ messages

Elizebeth Friedman developed cryptanalytic methods at Riverbank and later led important Coast Guard work against smuggling traffic. Her team’s work included expert testimony and wartime analysis of clandestine communications. American cryptanalysis had earlier practitioners too; it was not invented by one couple.

During WWII Friedman’s Coast Guard team analyzed clandestine networks in the Western Hemisphere. Its cryptanalytic contributions are distinct from the investigative work that disrupted those networks. Her archival papers and the biographical sources linked in the exhibit help recover that history.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-compass"></use></svg>
```

 Agnes Meyer Driscoll: Madame X of US Naval Intelligence[Full exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/agnes-driscoll.html>)

1920s–1940s

**Person:** Agnes Meyer Driscoll, 1889–1971, US Navy civilian cryptanalyst

**Technique:** Analysis of Japanese naval codes and additive encipherment; manual codebook reconstruction

Driscoll joined the Navy in 1918 and became an important analyst of Japanese naval systems, including the Red Book, Blue Book and early JN-25. She helped train later Navy cryptanalysts. Her JN-25 work preceded the Pacific teams’ 1942 Midway intelligence successes; wartime assignments also included work against German Enigma.

Driscoll worked on the Navy’s CM cipher machine before leaving briefly for the Hebern company in 1923. Her career combined machine knowledge and manual analysis. See the [NSA biographical account](<https://www.nsa.gov/Press-Room/Digital-Media-Center/Biographies/Biography-View-Page/Article/1623020/agnes-meyer-driscoll/>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-scroll"></use></svg>
```

 Leo Marks and the SOE Agent Codes[Full exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/leo-marks.html>)

1942–1945

**Person:** Leopold Samuel "Leo" Marks, 1920–2001, Head of Codes, Special Operations Executive

**Technique:** Prepared keying material, letter one-time pads and communications security checks

Marks worked on SOE agents’ communications, including efforts to recover messages corrupted by operator errors and reduce the need for dangerous retransmission. Prepared keys and agreed security checks addressed different operational risks; no indicator scheme guaranteed survival under error, interception or coercion.

Marks advocated prepared worked-out keys and letter one-time pads as improvements to SOE communications. These are distinct methods, and silk describes a carrier rather than a cryptographic construction. His memoir, *Between Silk and Cyanide: A Codemaker’s War, 1941–1945* (1998 edition), gives his retrospective account. A poem-derived transposition key is not a random one-time pad.

💡

See also: [Hall IX · One-Time Pad](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/one-time-pad.html>) for the mathematics of letter one-time pads; silk could also carry other kinds of prepared keying material.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

 VENONA and the Soviet OTP

1943–1980

**People:** Meredith Gardner and the US Army Signal Intelligence Service

**Technique:** Depth attack on reused pad pages

VENONA analysts exploited duplicated Soviet pad material. These messages used decimal code groups and no-carry arithmetic, so subtracting aligned ciphertext digits cancels the reused pad; it is not literally bytewise XOR. Recovering code groups and identifying people required further analysis. See the [NSA’s VENONA history](<https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/coldwar/venona_story.pdf>).

⚡

The pad-production and distribution process violated the one-use condition. Negative results against a correctly used one-time pad say nothing about traffic encrypted with duplicated pages. VENONA’s partial recoveries came from this operational weakness, not a contradiction of Shannon’s theorem.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

 Oranchak, Blake, Van Eycke and the Zodiac Z-340

2020

**People:** David Oranchak, Sam Blake, Jarl Van Eycke

**Technique:** Computational search + n-gram statistical scoring

The Z340 solution announced in December 2020 combined computer searches, homophonic substitution analysis and recognition of a transposition structure with irregularities. David Oranchak, Sam Blake and Jarl Van Eycke solved the message; this did not identify the sender.

[View the Zodiac Cipher exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zodiac.html>)

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]
