```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-flag"></use></svg>
```

 Frank Rowlett and the SIS Purple Team

1939–1940

**Person:** Frank B. Rowlett, US Army Signal Intelligence Service

**Technique:** Stepping-switch analysis using traffic and related plaintext evidence

Frank Rowlett led day-to-day SIS work against PURPLE with colleagues including Genevieve Grotjan and William Friedman. Statistical relationships in traffic and related plaintext evidence helped reconstruct the machine’s behavior without a captured PURPLE machine.

Rowlett also contributed to the development of SIGABA. No successful enemy wartime cryptanalytic break of that system is publicly documented; that is narrower than a guarantee that the design can never be attacked.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

 Genevieve Grotjan and September 20, 1940

1940

**Person:** Genevieve Grotjan Feinstein, SIS junior cryptanalyst

**Technique:** Pattern recognition across aligned worksheets

On the afternoon of September 20, 1940, Grotjan asked Rowlett to look at a worksheet she had prepared. Aligning intercept plaintext-ciphertext pairs, she had identified a recurring relationship in the consonant cipher alphabet — the alignment that revealed how Purple's stepping switches were wired. Rowlett later described the moment as “one of the great breaks of the war.” Grotjan had been with SIS for less than two years. *Code Girls* and the Army Intelligence and Security Command’s historian give this date; Rowlett’s memoir, *The Story of Magic*, recalls the day as shortly before Labor Day.

💡

Grotjan also contributed to the work that became VENONA. She left government service in 1947, before NSA was established, and later taught mathematics. See the [NSA biography](<https://www.nsa.gov/Press-Room/Digital-Media-Center/Biographies/Biography-View-Page/Article/1621585/genevieve-grotjan-feinstein/>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

 Boris Hagelin and the M-209

1934–1983

**Person:** Boris C. W. Hagelin, Swedish-born cipher-machine designer

**Contribution:** Pin-and-lug rotor mechanics for hand-portable cipher machines

Boris Hagelin developed commercially important pin-and-lug machines, including the family from which the M-209 was derived. Crypto AG’s later supplier-compromise history is a separate question from the public cryptanalysis of particular Hagelin mechanisms. The [Hagelin exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hagelin-c36.html>) distinguishes those issues.

[View the M-209 exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/m209.html>)

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

 The Copiale Team

2011

**People:** Kevin Knight (USC ISI), Beáta Megyesi and Christiane Schaefer (Uppsala University)

**Technique:** Transcription, statistics and manual cryptanalysis

Knight, Megyesi and Schaefer combined transcription, statistical exploration and manual cryptanalysis to decipher the Copiale manuscript in 2011. Early automatic hypotheses did not directly solve it: recognizing how ordinary Roman letters and abstract symbols functioned was crucial. See their [original paper](<https://aclanthology.org/W11-1202/>).

[View the Copiale Cipher exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/copiale.html>)

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

 The Chaocipher Verifiers

2010–2014

**People:** Moshe Rubin (algorithm reconstruction, 2010), George Lasry (cryptanalytic verification)

**Technique:** Documentary reconstruction + simulated annealing

Byrne kept Chaocipher’s mechanism secret. The family’s 2010 donation made its algorithm available; later published key-recovery work studied attacks under specified message and crib conditions. Algorithm disclosure, recovery of a particular key and a general claim of security are different results.

[View the Chaocipher exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/chaocipher.html>)

#### Sources and Reading

David Kahn, *The Codebreakers: The Comprehensive History of Secret Communication from Ancient Times to the Internet*, revised edition (1996), for the historical survey and Great Cipher account. Leo Marks, *Between Silk and Cyanide: A Codemaker’s War, 1941–1945*, 1998 edition, for his retrospective SOE account. Donald A. Borrmann and colleagues, [*The History of Traffic Analysis: World War I – Vietnam*](<https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/13/2002761879/-1/-1/0/TRAFFIC_ANALYSIS.PDF>) (NSA Center for Cryptologic History, 2013), for the traffic-analysis panel. Individual exhibits identify archival and institutional sources for their biographies; the summaries here preserve those sources’ limits.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Museum Map](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html>)› Hall XIII

 Hall XIII · Cipher Culture

### Cipher Culture

Cryptography as art, music, fiction, public mystery, and game — the cipher leaves the chancery and enters the world.

  "Long before computers, cipher craft was a parlour game, a religious puzzle, a love note, a signature, and a riddle posed to the public square."

[XIII · 1 Bach's BACH Motif The four notes B♭ – A – C – B♮ spell 'BACH' in German musical notation — a self-signature Bach embedded in his final unfinished fugue. 1750 and later uses](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bach-motif.html>) [XIII · 2 Conan Doyle: The Dancing Men The fictional stick-figure cipher Sherlock Holmes solves in The Adventure of the Dancing Men (1903) — a frequency-analysis primer disguised as a Strand magazine story. 1903](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/dancing-men.html>) [XIII · 3 Poe: The Gold-Bug Poe’s The Gold-Bug (1843) makes a substitution decipherment central to a fictional treasure hunt and explains the reasoning to readers. 1843](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/gold-bug.html>) [XIII · 4 Cicada 3301 Anonymous puzzle rounds beginning in 2012 combined online clues, steganography, ciphers and physical posters. The 2014 Liber Primus rune pages remain only partly deciphered. 2012-2014](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/cicada-3301.html>) [XIII · 5 Alternate-Reality Game Ciphers Alternate-reality games — from The Beast (2001) to Year Zero (2007) and beyond — built on the assumption that players will recognise, transcribe, and crack classical ciphers across forums, phone calls, and physical artifacts. 2001-present](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/krypto-arg.html>) [XIII · 6 MIT Mystery Hunt An annual MIT puzzle hunt, begun in 1981, combining many kinds of puzzles. Size, duration, themes and final objects vary between editions. 1981-present](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/mit-mystery-hunt.html>) [XIII · 7 Sator Square The SATOR square has five palindromically arranged words. Its letters form a PATER NOSTER cross with two A’s and two O’s left over; the intended meaning remains debated. pre-79 CE](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/sator-square.html>) [XIII · 8 Freemason Pigpen Tradition Pigpen uses geometric symbols for letters and appears in fraternal cipher traditions. The fixed substitution is readily reversible once the alphabet is known. Masonic and later puzzle traditions](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/freemason-pigpen.html>)

🎭

**Why a hall for culture?** Cryptography's history is usually told as a duel between makers and breakers — cipher designers, users and later analysts. But cipher craft has always overflowed the chancery. Composers signed their work in notes; novelists embedded keys in plot; later commentaries described paired-letter concealment. This hall makes the cultural side of cryptography visible — the part that explains why the discipline still attracts amateurs as well as cryptographers.

[Open Popular Culture Survey →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/popular-culture-survey.html>)

 Hall VII · 1467 – 1950s

### Mechanical Cipher Machines

When cryptography became hardware — and hardware changed history

From Alberti’s fifteenth-century disk to twentieth-century rotor and pin-and-lug devices, this hall explores the mechanisation of cipher operations. Interception, cryptanalysis, engineering and interpretation were all needed to turn enemy communications into intelligence; machines alone did not win wars or decrypt every message.

146717951932–19451947–1950s

⚙️

**The mechanical advantage:** Hand ciphers require operators to look up tables, count positions, and write carefully. Mechanical devices automate the cipher operation — dramatically increasing speed and reducing errors. The tradeoff: a captured machine reveals everything about the cipher structure. Security must then rely entirely on the key settings.

[Exhibit 27Renaissance · 1467

Alberti Cipher Disk

Alberti’s fifteenth-century cipher disk illustrates changing substitutions using two alphabets. The exhibit distinguishes historical instructions from a regular-step teaching model.

BrokenFirst Cipher Disk

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/alberti-disk.html>) [Exhibit 1731786 · Sweden

Gripenstierna’s Cipher Machine

A documented 57-disk device separated plaintext access from ciphertext copying. The original is lost; later replicas are reconstructions.

Historical Only

Explore exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/gripenstierna.html>) [Exhibit 281795 · USA

Jefferson Disk

Jefferson’s unpublished 1790s proposal used 36 disks. The later 25-disk M-94 illustrates a similar mechanism; direct adoption of Jefferson’s proposal is not established.

BrokenCompare M-94

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/jefferson-disk.html>) [Exhibit 691817 · USA

Wadsworth Cipher

Wadsworth’s 1817 device uses geared disks with 33 and 26 positions. A published 2020 ciphertext-only search studied key recovery for this historical design.

BrokenUnequal Geared Disks

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/wadsworth-cipher.html>) [Exhibit 291918–1945

Enigma Machine

Enigma developed through commercial and military models. Rejewski’s 1932 breakthrough and later Polish and Allied work attacked particular machines, keys and procedures.

BrokenBletchley Park

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/enigma.html>) [Exhibit 30WWII · 1940

Lorenz Cipher

Lorenz SZ40/42: Tiltman recovered messages and key from a 1941 depth; Tutte and the Research Section inferred the structure by early 1942; Colossus accelerated wheel-setting from February 1944.

BrokenBuilt Colossus

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/lorenz.html>) [Exhibit 31WWII · 1942–1945

Navajo Code Talkers

Navajo code talkers used a specialized military vocabulary and spelling alphabet during World War II. Their language and the constructed code were distinct layers.

Historical OnlyPacific Theatre

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/navajo-code-talkers.html>) [Exhibit 461918

Chaocipher

Chaocipher (1918) — John F. Byrne's two-disk dynamic cipher. Disclosed in 2010; published known-plaintext and in-depth ciphertext-only attacks recover its keys.

BrokenDynamic State

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/chaocipher.html>) [Exhibit 47WWII · 1942 production

M-209 (Hagelin C-38)

US production of the portable M-209 began in 1942, following 1940 trials. Its six pin-wheels and 27-bar lug cage illustrate a mechanically complex system with documented cryptanalytic weaknesses.

Broken~140,000 units

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/m209.html>) [Exhibit 52WWII · 1939–1945

Purple (Type 97)

Purple was Japan’s Type 97 diplomatic stepping-switch cipher. Grotjan’s 20 September 1940 breakthrough helped the US Army SIS team reconstruct it.

BrokenMAGIC

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/purple.html>) [Exhibit 99WWII · Pacific

JN-25

JN-25 combined Japanese naval code groups with additive encipherment. Partial recoveries by Allied teams, including Station HYPO, contributed to Midway intelligence.

BrokenMidway intelligence

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/jn-25.html>) [Exhibit 174Early 1930s · Japan

Imperial Japanese Navy IKA

Intercepted traffic revealed a cipher's behaviour. Compare that evidence with an American analog and with physical mechanisms the cited study leaves unknown.

Historical Only

Explore exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/ika.html>) [Exhibit 981931–1938

Red (Type A)

Red (Type A) was a Japanese diplomatic cipher using a half-rotor mechanism. It preceded the stepping-switch system PURPLE.

BrokenBridge to MAGIC

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/red-type-a.html>) [Exhibit 57 1940

SIGABA (ECM Mark II)

SIGABA used fifteen rotors in cipher, control and index banks. No successful enemy wartime cryptanalytic break is publicly documented; the widget is a simplified model.

15 rotors · 3 banks of 5 · 1–4 cipher rotors step per keystroke

Historical OnlyPseudo-random stepping

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/sigaba.html>) [Exhibit 58 1937

Typex

Typex developed from commercial Enigma technology for British use. Models and plugboard arrangements varied; adapted machines also supported Allied Enigma decryption.

Five rotor positions; stepping and connections depend on the model

Historical OnlyBritish rotor system

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/typex.html>) [Exhibit 1611947

NEMA

Swiss NEMA rotor machine (1947) — four cipher wheels, independent stepping wheels, and a moving reflector. Explore historical military encryption and decryption.

Historical Only

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/nema.html>) [Exhibit 1621930s–1950s

Hagelin C-36 / C-52

Hagelin C-36 and C-52 lineage — pin-and-lug cipher machines, the M-209 connection, published known-plaintext attacks, and the Crypto AG supplier history.

Broken

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hagelin-c36.html>)

#### Machines for Codebreaking

[Exhibit 1681940

Turing–Welchman Bombe

A crib becomes a network of constraints; machinery searches for settings that survive.

Historical context →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bombe.html>)[Exhibit 1691944

Colossus

Electronic counting accelerated the statistical search behind the Tunny breakthrough.

Historical context →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/colossus.html>)

The Arc of History

#### From Bronze Disk to Electronic Computer

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

Alberti → Vigenère → Enigma

Alberti’s disk, repeating-key tables and electrical rotor machines all illustrate changing substitutions. Their mechanisms and historical development differ: the familiar repeating-key table is associated with Bellaso (1553), while Vigenère described an autokey system (1586).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

Lorenz → Colossus → Computing

Tiltman’s manual recovery and Tutte’s structural analysis came first. Later statistical searches over Lorenz wheel settings benefited from electronic counting: Colossus was operational in February 1944. This was an important early application of programmable electronics.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-key"></use></svg>
```

Physical Keys → Digital Keys

Enigma required physical rotor choices, positions, ring settings and plugboard connections. Modern systems use several kinds of keys and lengths, with different distribution and authentication methods. Both need disciplined management of secret material.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Museum Map](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html>)› Hall V

 Hall V · 1880s — Cold War · 1880 – 1970

### Military & Spy Ciphers

When lives depend on secrecy — the peak of hand-cipher design

Military hand systems balance speed, key logistics, operator training and resistance to attack. The examples here had different operational roles and weaknesses; none should be used for present-day security.

WWI WWII Cold War 4 Hard-to-Break Exhibits

⚔️

**The military cryptographer's dilemma:** A cipher must be strong enough that the enemy cannot read it — but simple enough that a soldier can encrypt and decrypt in the field without a computer, under stress, with minimal training. Every cipher in this hall represents a different solution to that impossible trade-off.

[Exhibit 19 1880s · Russia

Nihilist Cipher

Nihilist additive substitution combines plaintext and repeating-key Polybius coordinates by ordinary addition. Its association with nineteenth-century Russian revolutionaries does not establish a particular inventor or first break.

H=23, key=31 → 54  E=15, key=14 → 29

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/nihilist.html>) [Exhibit 20 WWI · Germany · March 1918

ADFGX Cipher

Germany’s ADFGX field cipher appeared in March 1918; Painvin obtained solutions in April. Its square-plus-transposition construction required continuing key recovery.

Plain → Polybius(ADFGX) → Columnar transpose
 H → AF E → DA

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/adfgx.html>) [Exhibit 21 WWI · Germany · June 1918

ADFGVX Cipher

ADFGVX combined a 6×6 substitution square with columnar transposition. Painvin’s June 1918 solutions exploited particular traffic and keys, not every later message automatically.

6×6 grid · Letters AND digits · Same two-step process

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/adfgvx.html>) [Exhibit 22 1890s · France

Bazeries Cipher

Bazeries is associated with both a cipher cylinder and hand-cipher procedures. This exhibit uses a labelled substitution-and-reversal model; it is not the cylinder.

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bazeries.html>) [Exhibit 23 Cold War · 1950s

VIC Cipher

The Hollow Nickel message became readable with information from Häyhänen’s 1957 defection. The exhibit distinguishes historical VIC from its simplified browser model.

Checkerboard → chain addition → double transposition

Historical OnlyHistorical Recovery

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vic.html>) [Exhibit 55 18th–20th c.

Book Cipher

Book ciphers use a shared text and agreed indexing rules. Arnold’s historical correspondence and the Beale pamphlet’s claimed treasure story have different evidential status.

"RIVER" → look up in shared book → (page, line, word) = (127, 14, 6)

BrokenOut-of-band key

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/book-cipher.html>) [Exhibit 45 Soviet Hand Systems

Straddling Checkerboard

A straddling checkerboard gives some letters one digit and others two. It is a component of VIC, not a secure cipher by itself; an exact first-use date is not established here.

E→3 T→9 A→6 HELLO → 71 3 18 18 02

BrokenVIC Building Block

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/straddling-checkerboard.html>)

🇫🇷

Painvin’s work against ADFGX and ADFGVX contributed useful intelligence during the 1918 fighting. Repeated traffic and painstaking manual analysis mattered. Attributing the result of an entire offensive to one decipherment overstates what the evidence can establish.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Layering → Multiple Rounds

ADFGVX combines coordinate substitution and transposition. AES likewise composes operations, but its mathematical structure and security analysis differ. AES has 10, 12 or 14 rounds depending on key size; the final round omits MixColumns.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-quill"></use></svg>
```

Checkerboard → Variable-Length Encoding

The VIC cipher's straddling checkerboard assigns shorter codes to common letters (like Huffman coding) while also obscuring the alphabet mapping. This dual purpose — compression and encryption — is a sophisticated design insight that modern protocols use separately.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

Operational Disclosure and Cryptanalysis

VIC’s full key procedure became known through a defection. That differs from recovering a key by cryptanalysis. Operational compromise can expose a system even when a particular mathematical attack has not been demonstrated.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

 Comparative Tactical Systems Table

|  System |  Primary Use |  Field Speed |  Attack considerations |  Operational Failure Mode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  [Nihilist](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/nihilist.html>) |  Cell-based covert messaging |  Medium |  Moderate |  Key reuse exposes additive structure |
|  [ADFGX](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/adfgx.html>) / [ADFGVX](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/adfgvx.html>) |  WWI operational traffic |  Fast once drilled |  Traffic and key procedures matter |  Message volume + reused structure enabled Painvin's break |
|  [Bazeries](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bazeries.html>) |  Officer-level secure correspondence |  Slow in field conditions |  Depends on the particular procedure |  Complex procedure encourages operator shortcuts |
|  [Book Cipher](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/book-cipher.html>) |  Long-form clandestine dispatches |  Slow |  Variable |  Known edition and indexing conventions can expose a book code |
|  [VIC](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vic.html>) |  Cold War espionage bursts |  Slow but disciplined |  Historical case, not a quantified security level |  Defector information enabled the documented message recovery |

Legend: this table compares practical trade-offs for operators in the field, not abstract mathematical strength alone.

🛰️

**Appendix: modern tactical authentication.** Contemporary military systems separate *confidentiality* from *authentication*. Historical hand ciphers in this hall mostly protect secrecy, but modern tactical traffic also requires authentication mechanisms and freshness checks, such as message authentication codes, signatures and challenge-response protocols, with suitable key management. The enduring lesson is procedural: even strong ciphers fail without authenticated operator workflows.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Museum Map](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html>)› Hall XI

 Hall XI · 1976 – Present

### Modern Cryptography

Different cryptographic tasks, constructions and security assumptions

The earlier halls distinguish cryptanalytic breaks, operational misuse, obsolescence, and unresolved systems; a correctly used one-time pad remains unbreakable. The constructions here serve different purposes. DES and AES are symmetric block ciphers; DES is now unsafe because its 56-bit key is too small. RSA supports distinct public-key encryption and signature schemes, with appropriate encoding and padding such as OAEP and PSS. Diffie–Hellman is key agreement, and SHA-256 is a hash function. These building blocks explain encryption, shared-secret establishment, signatures, and integrity; none alone provides a complete secure system.

For the broader landscape — ChaCha20, ECDH, post-quantum standardisation, and the cipher-vs-protocol taxonomy — see the [Modern Cryptography wing](<https://ciphermuseum.com/modern.html>). For the design rule that underpins every card in this hall, see [Kerckhoffs's Principle](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kerckhoffs.html>).

Modern Era Mathematically Founded

[Exhibit 59 1977 · NBS / NSA

DES (Data Encryption Standard)

DES was standardized in 1977. Its 56-bit key became vulnerable to practical exhaustive search, demonstrated by EFF’s Deep Crack in 1998.

Broken Withdrawn 2005

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/des.html>) [Exhibit 60 1976 · Stanford

Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange

Diffie–Hellman derives a shared group element over a public channel. Authentication, appropriate groups and key derivation are needed for secure protocol use.

Secure (Modern) CDH and authentication

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/diffie-hellman.html>) [Exhibit 61 1977 · MIT

RSA

RSA uses a public modulus and exponents to support public-key constructions. Secure encryption and signatures need specified padding, adequate parameters and correct implementation.

Secure (Modern) RSA assumption and encoding

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rsa.html>) [Exhibit 62 2001 · FIPS 197

AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)

AES standardises a 128-bit block cipher with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. Secure use also requires an appropriate mode, key management and implementation.

Secure (Modern) FIPS 197

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/aes.html>) [Exhibit 63 2002 · NSA / NIST

SHA-256

SHA-256 produces a 256-bit digest for messages shorter than 2^64 bits. Hashing has distinct roles in signatures, integrity checks and other protocols; a bare hash is not authentication.

Secure (Modern) FIPS 180-2

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/sha256.html>) [Exhibit 158 1992 · Vanstone

ECDSA

ECDSA signs with elliptic-curve arithmetic. The toy model shows how nonce reuse can expose a signing key under the stated conditions; it is not a production implementation.

Secure (Modern) FIPS 186

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/ecdsa.html>) [Exhibit 159 1979 · Adi Shamir

Shamir's Secret Sharing

Shamir’s finite-field construction lets k valid shares reconstruct a secret. Fewer shares preserve its prior distribution when coefficients are chosen uniformly and independently with distinct nonzero share coordinates.

Secure (Modern) CACM 1979

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/shamir-secret-sharing.html>) [Exhibit 160 1985 · GMR

Zero-Knowledge Proofs

Zero-knowledge formalizes what a proof reveals. This small Schnorr model illustrates honest-verifier zero knowledge and extraction from repeated commitments, not production security.

Secure (Modern) Turing Award 2012

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zero-knowledge-proofs.html>)

#### The mathematics beneath this hall

[§142 · Foundations Finite Fields Beneath AES: finite-field inversion for nonzero bytes, a special zero rule and an affine transform](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/finite-fields.html>) [§143 · Foundations Modular Arithmetic Beneath Diffie-Hellman: the cyclic group a shared secret is built inside](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/modular-arithmetic.html>) [§145 · Foundations Euler & Fermat Beneath RSA: the congruence that makes decryption undo encryption](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/euler-fermat.html>) [§154 · Foundations The Random Oracle An idealised model used in some hash-based security analyses; SHA-256 is a concrete function](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/random-oracle.html>)

🎓

**The museum’s closing lesson:** Modern cryptography specifies security goals, attack models and assumptions. Public designs, suitable parameters and careful implementations matter together. Historical weaknesses do not imply that every classical system is broken, or that modern primitives are secure under every use.

#### Research case studies: what was actually attacked?

[UA-8295: altered firmware and forensic evidence](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/ua-8295.html>) · [SoDark: eight-round radio linking protection](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/sodark.html>) · [NFC: authentication, configuration and counterfeit hardware](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/nfc-deployment.html>)

[Compare GPU search, GPRS faults and conditional-linear DES](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/modern-attack-evidence.html>). Each result identifies the target, attacker access and limits of the evidence.

[← Previous Hall Hall X: Hall of Codebreakers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/codebreakers.html>) [Next Hall → Hall XII: Unsolved Ciphers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/unsolved.html>)

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Museum Map](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html>)› Hall III

 Hall III · Renaissance — 19th century

### The Polyalphabetic Revolution

"Le chiffre indéchiffrable" — The unbreakable cipher. Until it wasn't.

Polyalphabetic systems use changing substitution alphabets. They obscure simple letter-frequency relationships, but repeating keys create structure that analysts can exploit. Bellaso, Vigenère, Babbage, Kasiski and Friedman contributed different constructions or methods; the history is more varied than a single cipher remaining universally trusted for 300 years.

Renaissance 19th Century Running Key: Hard to Break

🔑

**The key insight:** A key selects which alphabet applies at each position. The same plaintext letter can therefore map to different ciphertext letters. Repeated key positions may still be separated into simpler substitution problems.

[Exhibit 8 1553

Vigenère Cipher

The modern repeating-key cipher bears Vigenère’s name; Bellaso’s 1553 publication belongs to its earlier history. Babbage and Kasiski developed attacks in the nineteenth century.

Plain: ATTACKATDAWN
 Key: LEMONLEMONLE
 Cipher: LXFOPVEFRNHR

BrokenLive Demo

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>) [Exhibit 9 1857

Beaufort Cipher

Beaufort cipher (1857) — Sir Francis Beaufort's reciprocal Vigenère variant where encrypt and decrypt are the same operation. Broken by Kasiski examination.

Reciprocal: Encrypt(Encrypt(P)) = P
 C = (Key − Plain) mod 26

BrokenReciprocal Rule

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/beaufort.html>) [Exhibit 10 1563

Porta Cipher

Porta cipher (1563) — della Porta's reciprocal polyalphabetic table where each key letter swaps two halves of the alphabet. Falls to Kasiski just like Vigenère.

13 tableau rows · Key letter pair selects row
 Reciprocal: same operation decrypts

BrokenRenaissance

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/porta.html>) [Exhibit 11 17th Century

Gronsfeld Cipher

A numeric-key Vigenère variant traditionally associated with Gronsfeld in the seventeenth century. Ten shifts per position reduce the key choices.

Key: 3 1 4 1 5
 Shift by digit value — only 10 options per position

BrokenTen Shifts per Digit

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/gronsfeld.html>) [Exhibit 12 19th Century

Running Key Cipher

Running Key cipher (19th c.) — a Vigenère variant using a long passage of natural text as the key. Broken by Friedman with high-probability-trigram dragging.

Plain: ATTACKATDAWN
 Key: FROMTHISBOOK

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/running-key.html>) [Exhibit 53 1586

Autokey

Plaintext autokey extends a primer with message letters. It removes a fixed repeating keyword but retains exploitable language structure and error propagation.

Plain: ATTACKATDAWN
 Key: KEYATTACKATD

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/autokey.html>)

The Fatal Flaw

#### How the Repeating Key Betrays Itself

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-lens"></use></svg>
```

The Kasiski Examination

The same plaintext sequence under the same repeating-key alignment produces the same ciphertext. Repeated ciphertext sequences can therefore suggest distances divisible by the period. Coincidental repeats also occur, so candidate periods need testing. The repeated string below is an illustration of the inference, not a guarantee that its key length is known.

```text
Ciphertext:
LXFOPVEFRNHRLXFOPVEFRNHR
      ↑               ↑
   pos 6           pos 18
   Distance = 12 → test divisors of 12; coincidence is also possible
```

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

Index of Coincidence

The index of coincidence measures the chance that two positions chosen without replacement contain the same letter. English samples often lie near 0.066, while independent uniform A–Z samples approach 1/26. Repeating-key substitution can move the overall score toward the latter, but length, language and key period matter: IC supplies evidence, not a certain cipher identification.

| Text Type | IC Value |
| --- | --- |
| Random | ~0.038 |
| Illustrative Vigenère sample | ~0.052 |
| English | ~0.066 |

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Vigenère → Stream Ciphers

Vigenère repeats a short sequence of letter shifts. ChaCha20 instead generates pseudorandom bit blocks from a key, nonce and counter, then combines them with plaintext using XOR. Its security is computational, and its usage rules prevent keystream reuse. “Non-repeating” does not mean that individual output blocks can never coincide.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-book"></use></svg>
```

Running Key → One-Time Pad

The running key cipher is one step from the one-time pad. The difference: a book passage is not random. If the source text has linguistic structure, that structure leaks into the ciphertext and enables statistical attacks.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-key"></use></svg>
```

Keys, Periods and Usage Limits

The Vigenère lesson: short repeating keys are fatal. Modern systems can reuse a suitably strong key for multiple messages, but must respect each scheme’s nonce, counter, and usage limits. Key derivation can separate session keys; it does not automatically guarantee unique key material.

 Hall VIII · 1605 – Present

### Puzzle & Novelty Ciphers

Cryptographically weak. Historically fascinating. Explore encoding, concealment and communication.

Not every cipher was designed to win wars or protect state secrets. Some were tools of secret societies, some were intellectual exercises, and one was the difference between isolation and survival for prisoners of war. This hall honors ciphers whose significance lies not in their cryptographic strength but in their human story.

🗂️

**Looking for the museum's open mysteries?** The major unsolved historical exhibits that once crowded this hall — Voynich, Beale, Dorabella, and Kryptos — now live together in [Hall XII: Unsolved Ciphers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/unsolved.html>), where the museum can present them as active research problems rather than novelty pieces.

💡

Bacon’s biliteral alphabet represents letters by patterns of two forms and can hide them in a carrier. That is a useful early example of binary representation, but it does not establish a direct historical line to Shannon’s information theory or electronic computing.

[Exhibit 32~1700s · Freemasons

Pigpen Cipher

Pigpen cipher (~1700) — Freemason geometric substitution where each letter becomes the lines and dots of its grid cell. Trivial once the glyph table is seen.

BrokenFreemason

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/pigpen.html>) [Exhibit 331605

Bacon's Cipher

Bacon’s biliteral alphabet represents letters with patterns of two forms and can hide them in a carrier. Binary representation is distinct from a direct historical origin for ASCII.

BrokenTwo-form Encoding

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bacon.html>) [Exhibit 34Vietnam War · 1960s

Tap Code

Tap Code (1965) — the 5x5 Polybius square tapped through walls as row-then-column knocks. Used by US POWs in the Hanoi Hilton during the Vietnam War.

BrokenPOW Communication

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/tap-code.html>) [Exhibit 351969 · Solved 2020

Zodiac Cipher (Z-340)

Zodiac killer ciphers (1969) — homophonic substitution as in Z-408 (broken in 1969 by the Hardens) and Z-340 (broken in 2020 by Oranchak, Blake, and Van Eycke).

Broken51-Year Mystery

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zodiac.html>) [Exhibit 48c. 1760–1780 · Deciphered 2011

Copiale Cipher

Knight, Megyesi and Schaefer deciphered the Copiale manuscript in 2011 using transcription, statistics and manual analysis. The exhibit separates that result from its invented demonstration alphabet.

BrokenSecret Society

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/copiale.html>) [Exhibit 1401994 · Refuted 1999

Bible Code (ELS)

Equidistant-letter claims require controls for flexible search choices. McKay and colleagues examined the statistical experiment and showed how alternative name choices produced striking results in a control text. The Moby-Dick demonstrations were a separate challenge to prophecy claims.

Statistical Fallacy

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bible-code.html>)

✊

**The Tap Code's real value:** Every guard who knew the pattern could intercept tap code messages. The system was not cryptographically secure. But that wasn't the point. The Tap Code's value was human — it maintained communication, solidarity, and command structure among men in solitary confinement. Sometimes a cipher's purpose is not secrecy. It's connection.

 Hall II · Ancient roots — 20th century

### Classical Substitution

The arms race between letter-mappers and frequency counters

Fixed substitutions preserve recognizable structure. Al-Kindi’s surviving treatise explains frequency analysis; later homophonic, digraph and algebraic constructions change what patterns remain. Their attacks require different evidence and methods.

Medieval Renaissance Victorian 3 Hard-to-Break Exhibits

💀

Frequency analysis compares observed counts with language models. It is useful against fixed substitutions but does not by itself solve every system in this hall. The exhibits distinguish statistical guesses, known plaintext and exhaustive key search.

[Exhibit 4 Ancient roots · medieval analysis

Monoalphabetic Substitution

Monoalphabetic substitution maps each letter to a fixed substitute. Al-Kindi described frequency analysis in the ninth century; useful attacks depend on the text and available evidence.

Plain: ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
 Cipher: QWERTYUIOPASDFGHJKLZXCVBNM

BrokenFrequency Analysis

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/monoalphabetic.html>) [Exhibit 5 Renaissance · ~1400

Homophonic Substitution

Homophonic substitution assigns multiple symbols to a plaintext letter to reduce frequency peaks. Historical nomenclators combined this idea with codewords and other conventions.

E → 12, 37, 44 T → 21, 90
 A → 05, 63 Z → 99

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/homophonic.html>) [Exhibit 6 Victorian · 1854

Playfair Cipher

Playfair cipher (1854) — Charles Wheatstone's keyed 5x5 digram cipher promoted by Lord Playfair. Used by the British in WWI; broken by digram analysis.

Key MONARCHY: HE → CF · PL → QP

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/playfair.html>) [Exhibit 43 1902 treatise

Four-Square Cipher

Four-Square appears in Delastelle’s 1902 treatise. Two keyed and two standard 5×5 squares substitute letter pairs; digraph structure can support cryptanalysis.

Two keyed squares (top-right, bottom-left) · two plain squares

BrokenDigraph

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/four-square.html>) [Exhibit 44 ACA specification

Two-Square Cipher

Two-square uses two keyed 5×5 squares to encipher letter pairs. This demo follows the ACA horizontal rectangle rule and discloses its extra filler-escape convention.

Two keyed squares stacked or side-by-side

BrokenDigraph

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/two-square.html>) [Exhibit 54 1400s–1800s

Nomenclator

Nomenclator (1400s) — The 400-year diplomatic compromise: a small substitution alphabet plus a large code dictionary. Hall II of The Cipher Museum.

THE KING ARRIVES IN VIENNA → 60 70 23 09 12 12 64 1899

BrokenHybrid Code+Cipher

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/nomenclator.html>) [Exhibit 7 1929

Hill Cipher

Hill’s 1929 cipher mixes groups of letters using an invertible matrix modulo 26. Suitable matched plaintext blocks can expose the key by linear algebra.

Cipher = Key Matrix × Plaintext Vector (mod 26)

BrokenHard to Break

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hill.html>) [Exhibit 166December 1941

German Double Playfair

German Double Playfair: reconstruct the December 1941 Doppelkastenschlüssel manual, including 17-column pairing, two substitution stages and its published example.

Broken

→](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/double-playfair.html>) [Exhibit 38 Baroque · 17th century

The Great Cipher

The Rossignols’ syllabic nomenclator was deciphered by Bazeries in the 1890s. His proposed Man in the Iron Mask identification remains disputed.

Illustrative key: LE → 124 ROI → 301 (null) → 412
 DELETE PREV → 891

BrokenDeciphered in the 1890s

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/great-cipher.html>) [Exhibit 39 Elizabethan · 1586

Babington Plot Cipher

The 1586 Babington Plot: intercepted nomenclator letters, a forged postscript, and the difference between compromised keys and an insecure transport channel.

Synthetic tokens illustrate letters, codewords, nulls and a doubling instruction
 QUEEN → ⟨w28⟩ DOUBLETH → ⟨x2⟩

BrokenCost a queen her head

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/babington.html>)

What This Hall Teaches

#### The Substitution Arms Race

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

Frequency Analysis

Al-Kindi's 850 AD technique. Monoalphabetic substitution preserves language-frequency patterns. With enough suitable ciphertext, frequency counts and word patterns can reveal the substitution; short messages need not have a unique solution. The Caesar cipher is a trivial special case.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

Homophonic Defense

Assign multiple ciphertexts to common letters to flatten frequency peaks. A sophisticated attacker can still detect the homophonic system through structural patterns and solve it with enough ciphertext.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

Digraph Encryption → AES Blocks

Playfair encrypts letter pairs; AES encrypts 128-bit blocks. Both operate on blocks, but this alone does not establish security. AES combines nonlinear and linear operations under a modern security model.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

Matrix Multiplication → Modern Mixing

Hill’s cipher and AES MixColumns both mix multiple input symbols using linear algebra, but they use different fields and play different roles. A linear layer alone does not provide the nonlinear security of a complete modern block cipher.

 Hall IV · 19th – Early 20th Century

### Transposition & Fractionation

Rearranging the message instead of replacing its letters

Transposition changes symbol positions. Fractionation splits symbols into coordinate components before rearranging them. These methods provide useful comparisons with modern permutations and mixing layers, while their historical variants retain exploitable structure.

19th Century WWI 3 Hard-to-Break Exhibits

🚂

**Transposition vs Substitution:** Substitution replaces letters (A→Q), preserving positions. Transposition keeps letters but moves them (position 1→7). Both methods preserve statistical information — substitution preserves frequency, transposition preserves frequency too. The letters are all still there. Only their arrangement changes.

Rail Fence Cipher — "HELLOWORLD" on 3 rails

[Exhibit 13 Classical transposition

Rail Fence Cipher

Rail Fence transposes a message along a zigzag route. Rail count, offset conventions and message length define the search; there is no universal ten-rail maximum.

Two successive columnar transpositions: historical military use, attack conditions, and modern computerized cryptanalysis; not an unbroken cipher until 2013.

H→23, E→15 → rows: 2 1 | cols: 3 5 → new pairs: 21,35 → FP

Fractionated Morse — converts text to Morse, regroups dots, dashes, and separators in trigrams, then substitutes via a keyed alphabet. Broken by trigram stats.

Modern Connection

#### Comparing Historical Rearrangement with AES

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

ShiftRows in AES

AES ShiftRows rotates three rows of its byte-state array; the first row stays in place. It works with MixColumns and the other round operations to spread dependencies. This is a conceptual connection to permutation, not evidence of direct descent from columnar transposition.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

Compare MixColumns with Fractionation

AES MixColumns is a **linear** transformation over GF(2⁸). It combines bytes within each column. Bifid instead rearranges coordinate components; the mechanisms are different, although both illustrate mixing.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Diffusion

Diffusion spreads the influence of input information across output components. A pure transposition only moves whole symbols and preserves their frequencies. AES combines permutation and linear mixing with nonlinear substitution and key addition.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Museum Map](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html>)› Hall IX

 Hall IX · 1882 – Present

### The Unbreakable

Where classical cryptography reached its limits — and mathematics drew the line

Many historical ciphers succumbed to cryptanalysis; others were exposed by operational mistakes, became obsolete, or remain unresolved. Claude Shannon proved perfect secrecy for a correctly used one-time pad: a secret, uniformly random, independent message-length key used once. Its demanding key-distribution requirements limit its use. This hall examines that guarantee and how pad reuse undermined it.

What came next — AES, RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and the systems that protect the digital world — lives in the [Modern Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/modern.html>) wing.

Theoretical Security WWII

[Exhibit 36 1882 · Theoretical

One-Time Pad

A one-time pad offers perfect secrecy with a secret, uniform, independent message-length key used once. Try ciphertext tampering to see why secrecy is not authentication.

Plain: HELLO
 Key: XMCKL (illustrative pad)
 Cipher: EQNVZ

Secure (Modern) If Rules Followed

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/one-time-pad.html>) [Exhibit 37 1917 · AT&T

Vernam Cipher

Vernam’s teleprinter system combines text with a key stream. XOR supplies perfect secrecy only when the pad is uniformly random, independent, secret, long enough and never reused.

Plain: H (01000; illustrative A=1 encoding)
 Key: Q (10001)
 XOR: Y (11001)

Secure (Modern) XOR Foundation

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vernam.html>) [Exhibit 108 1943–1980 · Cold War

VENONA Project

VENONA analysed intercepted Soviet messages, chiefly from the 1940s, by exploiting duplicated pad material. The project ran from 1943 to 1980.

Depth relation: Decimal: C₁ − C₂ = P₁ − P₂ (mod 10, digitwise)
 Failure mode: Key page reuse
 Lesson: Math stayed sound; operations failed

Broken Operational failure

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/venona.html>) [Exhibit 51 1999 · Schneier

Solitaire / Pontifex

Bruce Schneier’s 54-card Solitaire cipher (1999) was designed for Neal Stephenson’s novel *Cryptonomicon* (1999 edition). Crowley measured a bias in consecutive keystream outputs; this is a study exhibit, not a security recommendation.

Key: deck order · Output: 1–26 per card draw
 Bias: 1/22.5 vs 1/26 ideal (Crowley 1999)

Historical Only Statistical Weakness Cryptonomicon

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/solitaire.html>)

The Mathematics of Secrecy

#### Claude Shannon and Perfect Secrecy

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-chart"></use></svg>
```

Shannon's 1949 Proof

Perfect secrecy means observing ciphertext does not change the prior probability of any plaintext: P(M=m | C=c) = P(M=m), for ciphertexts with nonzero probability. Plaintexts need not be equally likely beforehand. An independently uniform one-time pad meets this definition; it is not the only possible perfectly secret construction. Encryption alone does not authenticate a message.

For example, if a message was more likely before interception, it remains more likely afterwards. The ciphertext does not improve that prior guess. This guarantee concerns message content within the defined message space; length and other traffic metadata may still be visible.

Source: Claude E. Shannon, *Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems* (1949), §10, pp. 679–682. Shannon also describes perfectly secret systems using Latin squares.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

Why Its Use Is Limited

A one-time pad has demanding operational requirements:

- The key must be as long as the message — a 1GB file needs a 1GB key

- The key must be truly random — not pseudorandom

- Key distribution must be perfectly secure — if the key channel isn't secure, neither is the cipher

- Every key used once means you can never reuse, recycle, or re-derive it

⚡

**VENONA:** US Army analysts, and later successor organizations including NSA, exploited reused Soviet additive key material. The historical traffic used decimal subtraction without borrowing, not binary XOR; the exhibit shows both the principle and a decimal teaching exercise.

Why Classical Ciphers Failed

#### Shannon's Two Principles — and How Modern Crypto Achieves Them

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

 Confusion

Confusion complicates the relationship between the key and ciphertext statistics. For a Caesar shift, C = P + k mod 26, one aligned plaintext–ciphertext letter pair reveals k. Shannon’s term is a design principle, not a universal numerical score.

**Modern solution:** AES uses a fixed, public nonlinear S-box together with key addition and diffusion over multiple rounds. The S-box alone is a known byte substitution; its output determines its input. Security belongs to the complete construction, not secrecy of that table.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="../images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

 Diffusion

Spreading the influence of each plaintext bit across many ciphertext bits. *Caesar does not spread changes between letters* — changing one letter changes exactly one ciphertext letter. Frequency analysis exploits this directly.

**Modern comparison:** AES combines nonlinear substitution, key mixing and linear diffusion. A full-cipher avalanche measurement describes behavior across inputs, not a promise that every change flips exactly half the bits.

The Complete Journey

#### From Caesar to AES — What Each Generation Taught the Next

|  Classical Cipher Type |  Fatal Weakness |  Modern Solution |  Modern Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Caesar / Substitution | Frequency analysis — letter mapping preserved | Repeated substitution, diffusion and key mixing | AES SubBytes |
| Monoalphabetic | 26! keys but relabel the same frequency counts | Fixed public S-box combined with round-key addition | AES with round keys |
| Polyalphabetic / Vigenère | Repeating key creates detectable periodicity | Pseudorandom keystreams with unique nonce/counter inputs under a key; output bytes can repeat | ChaCha20, AES-CTR |
| Transposition | Letters preserved, just rearranged — anagram attacks work | Substitution and linear diffusion across rounds | AES ShiftRows + MixColumns |
| Playfair / Hill (block) | Small blocks leak digraph statistics; linear algebra solvable | 128-bit blocks, non-linear operations, key mixing | AES (128-bit block) |
| Military layered (ADFGVX) | Substitution + transposition — each layer still attackable | AES uses 10, 12 or 14 rounds; the final round omits MixColumns. Inversion with the key is efficient | AES |
| One-Time Pad | Impractical key management — reuse is catastrophic | Computational security with short keys under stated assumptions; not perfect secrecy | AES modes; authenticated X25519-based protocols |

🎓

**The museum’s lesson:** State the security goal and assumptions explicitly. Perfect secrecy, computational security, authenticity and implementation resistance are different claims. Real systems need appropriate parameters, secure key handling and careful implementation; they do not invariably fail loudly when misused.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)› [Museum Map](<https://ciphermuseum.com/museum-map.html>)› Hall XII

 Hall XII · Open Problems · Living Research

### Unsolved Ciphers

Ten cases involving unresolved inscriptions, incomplete decipherments or uncertain interpretation. Their evidence and solution status differ; consult each exhibit’s dated sources.

  These cases have different evidential limits. The Voynich parchment’s radiocarbon range is not the date its text was written. Kryptos K4’s archival plaintext discovery is distinct from a public cryptanalytic solution. Some other inscriptions are not established encryption systems at all.

🧭

**Unsolved is not the same as unbreakable.** Some cases may be ciphers, others unknown writing, private notation or hoaxes. Archival plaintext discovery, a proposed interpretation and a reproducible cryptanalytic solution are distinct outcomes.

[XII · 1 Voynich Manuscript The Voynich manuscript has an undeciphered script. Parchment dating and sample-dependent text statistics constrain hypotheses without identifying its language or method. Parchment dated 1404–1438](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/voynich.html>) [XII · 2 Kryptos (K4) Kryptos: K1–K3 publicly solved; K4 plaintext recovered from an archive in 2025, without a publicly demonstrated cryptanalytic solution. 1990](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kryptos.html>) [XII · 3 Beale Ciphers (1 & 3) Beale ciphers — three numerical ciphers published in an 1885 Lynchburg pamphlet, said to have been written in the 1820s and to point to a Virginia treasure. Only #2 was solved (Declaration of Independence key); #1 and #3 unsolved. Published 1885; claimed 1820s story](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/beale.html>) [XII · 4 Dorabella Cipher Edward Elgar’s 1897 Dorabella cryptogram contains 87 symbols. No proposed reading has achieved general acceptance. 1897](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/dorabella.html>) [XII · 5 Zodiac Z-13 & Z-32 The short Z13 and Z32 messages lack generally accepted readings. Their ambiguity differs from the solved Z408 and Z340 messages. 1970](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zodiac.html>) [XII · 6 Shugborough Inscription An eighteenth-century garden monument with eight unexplained letters and D · M below. Its encoding method, if any, is unknown. Mid-18th century](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/shugborough.html>) [XII · 7 D'Agapeyeff Challenge Alexander d’Agapeyeff’s 1939 numeric challenge: a verified ciphertext excerpt, overlapping-pair analysis and explicit limits on proposed reconstructions. 1939](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/dagapeyeff.html>) [XII · 8 Somerton Man (Tamám Shud) The Somerton Man inscription and a simplified transcription experiment. A 2022 genealogical identification proposal is separate from interpreting the letters. 1948](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/somerton-man.html>) [XII · 9 McCormick Notes Two handwritten notes found with Ricky McCormick in 1999. The FBI’s 2011 appeal sought contextual evidence and help interpreting their notation. ~1999](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/mccormick.html>) [XII · 10 Phaistos Disc The Phaistos Disc is a Bronze Age stamped inscription from Crete. Its language and reading remain disputed; it is not established as a cipher. ~1700 BCE](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/phaistos-disc.html>)

📐

**How an "unsolved" exhibit can become a "solved" one.** The path runs through one or more of: (a) *statistical attack* — the Oranchak–Blake–Van Eycke solution of Z-340 in 2020; (b) *transcription and manual analysis aided by statistics* — Knight, Megyesi and Schaefer’s 2011 Copiale decipherment; (c) *archival discovery* — a key, plaintext, or contemporary commentary surfaces; (d) *cross-disciplinary linguistics* — Champollion's 1822 Egyptian decipherment is the model. Which approach is useful depends on the object and the evidence available.

[← Previous Hall XI: Modern Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/modern-crypto.html>) [Next → Hall XIII: Cipher Culture](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/culture.html>)

#### The Story of Encryption

[##### Act I · Ancient World to Paper Systems

 c. 1900 BC – 1900

From unusual writing in Khnumhotep II’s tomb—not evidence of secret communication—to classical substitution, transposition and repeating-key systems.

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/ancient.html>) [##### Act II · Machines & War

 1900 – 1945

From WWI field systems to Enigma and Lorenz in WWII, ending with the first codebreaking computers.

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/machines.html>) [##### Act III · Mathematical Security

 1945 – Present

From post-war information theory to modern cryptography: Shannon's 1949 proof and the rise of mathematical security.

 →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/unbreakable.html>) [##### Annex · Hall of Foundations

 The Mathematics Under It All

Exhibits §141–157: the number theory, hardness assumptions, and structures your keys stand on — from finite fields to lattices and pairings, each with a working interactive.

```javascript
// Intersection observer for fade-up animations (graceful fallback for older browsers)
(function(){
  var els = document.querySelectorAll('.fade-up');
  if (typeof IntersectionObserver === 'undefined') {
    els.forEach(function(el){ el.style.animationPlayState = 'running'; });
    return;
  }
  var io = new IntersectionObserver(function(entries) {
    entries.forEach(function(e) { if (e.isIntersecting) { e.target.style.animationPlayState='running'; io.unobserve(e.target); }});
  }, {threshold:.1});
  els.forEach(function(el) { el.style.animationPlayState='paused'; io.observe(el); });
})();
```

#### Embedded script 3 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

'use strict';
(function(){
  var A = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
  var mod = function(a,m){ return((a%m)+m)%m; };

  var engines = {
    caesar: {
      enc: function(t){ return t.split('').map(function(ch){
        var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
        if(i<0) return ch; var o=A[mod(i+3,26)];
        return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
      }).join(''); },
      dec: function(t){ return t.split('').map(function(ch){
        var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
        if(i<0) return ch; var o=A[mod(i-3,26)];
        return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
      }).join(''); }
    },
    rot13: {
      enc: function(t){ return t.split('').map(function(ch){
        var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
        if(i<0) return ch; var o=A[mod(i+13,26)];
        return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
      }).join(''); },
      dec: function(t){ return this.enc(t); }
    },
    atbash: {
      enc: function(t){ return t.split('').map(function(ch){
        var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
        if(i<0) return ch; var o=A[25-i];
        return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
      }).join(''); },
      dec: function(t){ return this.enc(t); }
    },
    vigenere: {
      enc: function(t,k){
        k=(k||'MUSEUM').toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
        if(!k) k='MUSEUM'; var ki=0;
        return t.split('').map(function(ch){
          var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
          if(i<0) return ch;
          var o=A[mod(i+A.indexOf(k[ki%k.length]),26)]; ki++;
          return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
        }).join('');
      },
      dec: function(t,k){
        k=(k||'MUSEUM').toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
        if(!k) k='MUSEUM'; var ki=0;
        return t.split('').map(function(ch){
          var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
          if(i<0) return ch;
          var o=A[mod(i-A.indexOf(k[ki%k.length]),26)]; ki++;
          return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
        }).join('');
      }
    },
    beaufort: {
      enc: function(t,k){
        k=(k||'MUSEUM').toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
        if(!k) k='MUSEUM'; var ki=0;
        return t.split('').map(function(ch){
          var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
          if(i<0) return ch;
          var o=A[mod(A.indexOf(k[ki%k.length])-i,26)]; ki++;
          return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
        }).join('');
      },
      dec: function(t,k){ return this.enc(t,k); }
    },
    affine: {
      enc: function(t){
        return t.split('').map(function(ch){
          var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
          if(i<0) return ch; var o=A[mod(5*i+8,26)];
          return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
        }).join('');
      },
      dec: function(t){
        return t.split('').map(function(ch){
          var c=ch.toUpperCase(); var i=A.indexOf(c);
          if(i<0) return ch; var o=A[mod(21*(i-8),26)];
          return ch===c?o:o.toLowerCase();
        }).join('');
      }
    },
    railfence: {
      enc: function(t){
        var rails=['','',''];
        var r=0,dir=1;
        for(var i=0;i<t.length;i++){
          rails[r]+=t[i];
          if(r===0) dir=1; if(r===2) dir=-1;
          r+=dir;
        }
        return rails.join('');
      },
      dec: function(t){
        var n=t.length,lens=[0,0,0],r=0,dir=1;
        for(var i=0;i<n;i++){ lens[r]++; if(r===0)dir=1;if(r===2)dir=-1;r+=dir; }
        var rows=['','',''],pos=0;
        for(var j=0;j<3;j++){ rows[j]=t.substr(pos,lens[j]); pos+=lens[j]; }
        var idx=[0,0,0]; r=0;dir=1; var out='';
        for(var i=0;i<n;i++){ out+=rows[r][idx[r]++]; if(r===0)dir=1;if(r===2)dir=-1;r+=dir; }
        return out;
      }
    },
    polybius: {
      enc: function(t){
        var grid='ABCDEFGHIKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
        return t.split('').map(function(ch){
          var c=ch.toUpperCase(); if(c==='J') c='I';
          var idx=grid.indexOf(c);
          if(idx<0) return ch;
          return ''+(Math.floor(idx/5)+1)+(idx%5+1);
        }).join(' ');
      },
      dec: function(t){
        var grid='ABCDEFGHIKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
        return t.replace(/([1-5])([1-5])/g,function(_,r,c){
          var idx=(parseInt(r)-1)*5+(parseInt(c)-1);
          return (idx>=0&&idx<25)?grid[idx]:'';
        });
      }
    },
    bacon: {
      // 25-letter Bacon (I/J merged). 25 × 5 = 125 chars.
      // A=AAAAA B=AAAAB C=AAABA D=AAABB E=AABAA F=AABAB G=AABBA H=AABBB
      // I/J=ABAAA K=ABAAB L=ABABA M=ABABB N=ABBAA O=ABBAB P=ABBBA Q=ABBBB
      // R=BAAAA S=BAAAB T=BAABA U=BAABB V=BABAA W=BABAB X=BABBA Y=BABBB Z=BBAAA
      enc: function(t){
        var codes='AAAAAAAAABAAABAAAABBAABAAAABABAABBAAABBBABAAAABAABABABAABABBABBAAABBABABBBAABBBBBAAAABAAABBAABABAABBBABAABABABBABBABABBBBBAAA';
        return t.split('').map(function(ch){
          var c=ch.toUpperCase(); if(c==='J') c='I'; var i=A.indexOf(c);
          if(i<0) return ch; if(i>9) i--;
          return codes.substr(i*5,5);
        }).join(' ');
      },
      dec: function(t){
        var codes='AAAAAAAAABAAABAAAABBAABAAAABABAABBAAABBBABAAAABAABABABAABABBABBAAABBABABBBAABBBBBAAAABAAABBAABABAABBBABAABABABBABBABABBBBBAAA';
        var clean=t.replace(/[^AaBb]/g,'').toUpperCase();
        var out='';
        for(var i=0;i+5<=clean.length;i+=5){
          var chunk=clean.substr(i,5);
          for(var j=0;j<25;j++){ if(codes.substr(j*5,5)===chunk){ var c=j; if(c>=9) c++; out+=A[c]; break; }}
        }
        return out;
      }
    }
  };

  var selCipher = document.getElementById('pg-cipher');
  var elInput   = document.getElementById('pg-input');
  var elOutput  = document.getElementById('pg-output');
  var elKey     = document.getElementById('pg-key');
  var elKeyWrap = document.getElementById('pg-key-wrap');
  var btnSwap   = document.getElementById('pg-swap');
  var btnCopy   = document.getElementById('pg-copy');
  var encrypting = true;

  function update(){
    var name = selCipher.value;
    var eng  = engines[name];
    var text = elInput.value;
    var key  = elKey.value;
    elKeyWrap.style.display = (name==='vigenere'||name==='beaufort')?'':'none';
    if(!text){ elOutput.textContent=''; return; }
    elOutput.textContent = encrypting ? eng.enc(text,key) : eng.dec(text,key);
  }

  selCipher.addEventListener('change', update);
  elInput.addEventListener('input', update);
  elKey.addEventListener('input', update);
  btnSwap.addEventListener('click', function(){
    encrypting = !encrypting;
    btnSwap.textContent = encrypting ? '↕ Decrypt' : '↕ Encrypt';
    var lbl = elInput.previousElementSibling;
    lbl.textContent = encrypting ? 'Plaintext' : 'Ciphertext';
    update();
  });
  btnCopy.addEventListener('click', function(){
    var text = elOutput.textContent;
    if(text && navigator.clipboard){
      navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
      btnCopy.textContent = 'COPIED';
      setTimeout(function(){ btnCopy.textContent='COPY'; }, 1200);
    }
  });

  // Seed with a demo message
  elInput.value = 'The die is cast';
  update();
})();
```

### Metadata and search/social descriptions

- description: Compare Copiale, Mary Stuart, Charles V and Z340 with the Egyptian, Linear B and Maya decipherments: what structure, keys and independent checks can each establish.

Research and evidence

### How a Decipherment Becomes Evidence

Compare Copiale, Mary Stuart, Charles V and Z340 with the Egyptian, Linear B and Maya decipherments: what structure, keys and independent checks can each establish.

A decipherment is a chain of claims: source → transcription → structural hypothesis → key → reading → independent checks. These investigations distinguish historical evidence from museum exercises. The [Charles V case](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#charles-v>) adds a staged lesson in mixed token rules and partial keys. [Open the Evidence Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html>).

#### Copiale: the ordinary letters were the surprise

[The Copiale manuscript](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/copiale.html>) combines familiar Roman letters with unfamiliar symbols. Knight, Megyesi and Schaefer first tested the familiar letters as the message-bearing alphabet. That hypothesis failed. Comparing neighboring contexts helped reveal groups of homophones among the unfamiliar signs; German language hypotheses and human interpretation guided the search.

- **Source:** preserve diacritics and distinguish symbol types before counting them. A familiar-looking letter need not play its familiar role.

- **Competing hypothesis:** treat ordinary Roman letters as ciphertext, then as separators. The successful reading uses unaccented Roman letters as word boundaries. Calling them meaningless nulls loses that function.

- **Mixed key:** the system includes multi-letter values such as CH, SCH and ST, logograms, and a colon that doubles the preceding consonant. A one-letter substitution cannot represent the whole manuscript.

- **Evidence:** test mappings across occurrences and read the resulting German in context. Some material remained unresolved in the 2011 paper; a successful passage does not certify every glyph.

**Try it:** in the workbench, enter an original exercise `g1 g2 g3 g1` with g1→A, g2→CH and g3→space. Compare that typed key with forcing every sign to one letter. This exercise is invented; it is not a transcription from Copiale.

Source: [Knight, Megyesi and Schaefer, “The Copiale Cipher” (2011)](<https://aclanthology.org/W11-1202/>), especially the transcription and decipherment discussion, PDF pp. 2–7. The paper and its manuscript figures supply the historical evidence.

#### Mary Stuart: preserve the dot, then test the story

The [57-letter collection published in 2023](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/mary-stuart-castelnau-letters.html>) contains more than 150,000 transcribed cipher symbols and about 50,000 plaintext words. Its 219 graphical symbol types include distinctions that cannot be compressed into a 26-letter alphabet.

- **Source:** record the archive, shelfmark and folio. The collection spans BnF Français 2988, Français 20506, Cinq Cent de Colbert 470 and Français 3158. Keep letter identity separate from a modern filename.

- **Reading alternatives:** diacritics distinguish symbols. If a mark might be a dot or damage, record both readings and its image region. Do not silently merge the two types to make a solver work.

- **Language hypothesis:** early Italian expectations gave way to French. A modern-English score is not evidence against a French reading.

- **Search and interpretation:** simulated annealing recovered letter homophones. Names, word codes, repeat and erase controls, and other nomenclature required further manual work. Preserve the literal reading before normalizing spelling or translating.

- **Independent corroboration:** surviving plaintext versions and historical correspondence help test the interpretation. They provide evidence beyond the language score used to select a candidate.

**Try it:** transcribe an invented pair as `g17 g17-dot`, save a span with both alternatives, and record why one is preferred. Revise the source and inspect the earlier annotation: its original location is retained. This tests provenance, not recovery of a historical letter.

Source: [Lasry, Biermann and Tomokiyo, “Deciphering Mary Stuart’s lost letters from 1578–1584” (2023)](<https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2022.2160677>), §3.2, §4.2, §5.1 and Appendix A; PDF pp. 9–13, 16–26, 32 and 96–98. Figure 2 shows letter F38 and the importance of the source image.

#### Charles V, 1547: change the model, keep the failed attempts

A letter from Charles V to Jean de Saint-Mauris, preserved in Nancy, resisted early frequency-based guesses. The 2023 decipherment study traces the breakthrough to related letters in Besançon with marginal readings, followed by comparison with earlier reconstructed keys.

- **Test the unit.** One sign need not mean one letter. The reconstructed key includes letters, consonant–vowel units, doubled consonants, word codes and nulls.

- **Preserve the discovery sequence.** Failed guesses explain why the model changed. A later readable passage does not turn an earlier guess into evidence.

- **Mark the limits.** The 2023 key marks some word-code values as context-based guesses; its nomenclator is limited to this letter.

**Two dates, one record:** the letter writes 22 February **1546**. The study dates it **1547** under a January-start year, explaining that the contemporary year could start at Easter. Preserve both the written date and the dating rule; this is not a Julian-to-Gregorian day conversion.

**A readable allegation remains an allegation.** Charles reports an assassination rumour; Saint-Mauris’s reply calls it a rumour. Deciphering that report does not establish that the alleged plot happened.

#### Egyptian hieroglyphs: sound, sense and direction

**Egyptian hieroglyphs are a writing system, not a cipher.** Classical and Renaissance writers stressed the signs as symbols of ideas (Parkinson). That assumption, not encryption, was the obstacle: many of the signs recorded sounds. Scribes could still write unusually on purpose; see the [Khnumhotep II spellings](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/egyptian-substitution.html>).

- **Source.** The [Rosetta Stone](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rosetta-stone.html>) records one decree in two languages and three scripts, and its Greek could be read. In the hieroglyphic text, royal names are enclosed in cartouches (Parkinson).

- **Transcription.** By 1816 Thomas Young had isolated Ptolemy’s name in a cartouche and, helped by the demotic version, gave five of its signs correct sound values and eight others wrong ones (Parkinson). Copies of further cartouches, from an obelisk found at Philae and from the temple of Abu Simbel, widened the comparison (Parkinson).

- **Structural hypothesis.** Young proposed that sound signs were used only for foreign names such as Ptolemy, and that the rest of the script, including the epithets inside the cartouche, worked symbolically (Parkinson). In 1821 Champollion still treated hieroglyphs as symbolic and logographic, one picture to a word (Parkinson).

- **Key.** The key that worked is a mixed system. Some signs write one, two or three consonants; some write a whole word by sound and meaning together; determinatives add no sound but place a word in a class, such as motion; and phonetic complements repeat part of a larger sign’s sound to make its reading clear (Collier and Manley; Parkinson). Vowels are not written (Collier and Manley).

- **Reading.** Signs face the beginning of the line, so you read into their faces, and from top to bottom (Collier and Manley). A transliteration records the consonants, such as *pr*; a translation gives the meaning, “go out” (Collier and Manley). Spoken forms used today add conventional vowels for convenience (Collier and Manley).

- **Independent checks.** Two observations that played no part in framing the hypothesis broke it. In December 1821 Champollion counted 1,419 hieroglyphic signs on the Rosetta Stone against 486 Greek words, far too many signs for one picture per word (Parkinson). Then, among copies from Abu Simbel received on 14 September 1822, a cartouche gave a native king’s name, Ramesses: a sun sign read as Ra, the sun, and final signs already known as *s* (Parkinson). Sound signs were not reserved for foreign names.

**What stays open.** A partial key can mislead: Young’s five correct values came with eight wrong ones (Parkinson). Vowels remain a modern convention.

#### Linear B: structure before sound

**Linear B is a script, not a cipher.** Nobody designed it to hide anything. Its signs record syllables and commodities in Mycenaean palace accounts, in an early form of Greek. When work began, both the sound values and the language were unknown, so there was no key to recover and no sender who wanted secrecy. Counting, grouping and testing predictions overlap with cryptanalysis; success meant a reading that independent evidence could check.

- **Structure first.** Alice Kober collected recurring words and showed that some appear in sets of three related forms, sharing a stem and changing their ending. She deliberately stopped before assigning sounds. From these relationships she drew up the beginning of a grid of signs that seemed to share a consonant or a vowel; Michael Ventris extended it.

- **The structure outlived a wrong interpretation.** Kober read her “triplets” as inflected forms of words. Ventris took a step she had not: he treated them as place names. Her first five proved to be the names of Cretan towns, with adjectives formed from them, and the relationships between signs that she had found still held.

- **The expected language had to give way.** Ventris’s working notes of 1951–52 tested Aegean and Etruscan parallels while Greek readings were still regarded as out of the question, and he favoured an Etruscan connection until mid-1952. He introduced his first full test of Greek, Work Note 20 of 1 June 1952, as a digression. Values from the grid then produced the names of Cretan towns and Greek words. The decipherment was announced on 1 July 1952.

- **The test came from a tablet not used to build the values.** Tablet Ta 641 was excavated at Pylos in 1952, and Carl Blegen studied it in spring 1953. Read with Ventris’s values, the words beside drawings of tripods and pots described those vessels: *ti-ri-po-de* beside tripods, *qe-to-ro-we* beside a four-handled pot, *a-no-we* beside one without handles. Blegen reported this in a letter of 16 May 1953. The tablet did not help form the values; it tested them.

- **Some readings stay open.** Linear B spelling leaves out *l*, *r* and *s* at the end of a syllable, and *m* and *n* before another consonant, so one written word can stand for different Greek words: *pa-te* can be *patēr*, “father”, or *pantes*, “all”. Context settles some cases: one tablet pairs *pa-te* with *ma-te*, “mother”, which points to *patēr*. Others remain open; even on Ta 641, Chadwick noted, the descriptions of the tripods allow several translations with no firm way to choose between them.

- **No confidence score.** Chadwick called the odds against Ta 641’s agreement arising by accident astronomical, and of a later check he wrote that such probabilities are “beyond mathematical analysis”. Ventris and Chadwick also pointed to the system’s success on texts found later. These are arguments, not measured probabilities, and this page does not turn them into a score.

**Original structural exercise:** the Latin labels below are invented, not Linear B signs, ancient words or a historical transcription. It isolates two steps: what repeated structure can and cannot establish, and how a held-out record tests an interpretation. It does not reproduce Kober’s grid or the decipherment.

Training groups — no meanings supplied; numbers are occurrences in an invented inventory

| Family | X form | Y form | Z form |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | A X (2) | A Y (7) | A Z (1) |
| B | B X (1) | B Y (6) | B Z (1) |

Repeated X/Y/Z endings suggest a relationship. Y is by far the commonest ending, which makes it look like the basic form. Neither observation establishes which ending means one item, two items or something else, and neither supplies a sound.

**Held-out exercise inventory:** one jar: C X; two jars: C Y; C Z beside a jar drawing with no numeral. These records were withheld from the training groups, as Ta 641 was absent from the evidence that produced Ventris’s values. They are part of this invented fixture.

Why was the commonest ending not the singular? An inventory mostly counts several items, so a plural can be its commonest form. Frequency is a clue about use, not a meaning.
