What does this reveal?

It records equal-symbol positions, not plaintext. Renaming is one-to-one: different symbols keep different names. In a homophonic cipher, different ciphertext symbols can still stand for the same plaintext letter, so this pattern is not necessarily the plaintext’s pattern. This does not apply as a decipherment method to modern encryption or a properly used one-time pad.

The single-occurrence action replaces the first repeated occurrence with a new symbol. If all symbols are distinct, it replaces the last with the first. With only one symbol, no equality relationship can change. Separating spaces here are token boundaries, not symbols being encoded.

**Research credit:** Nishant Kambhatla, Logan Born and Anoop Sarkar, [*Decipherment as Regression: Solving Historical Substitution Ciphers by Learning Symbol Recurrence Relations* (2023)](<https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-eacl.160/>), §3.1. This activity implements their first-occurrence numbering definition on an original example. It does not run their Transformer model or claim their decipherment performance.

#### 5. What survives when words are replaced?

A repeated label can reveal a useful relationship without revealing an entire message. In this original task, every source has three words drawn from **PINE, OAK, ELM and ASH**. The question is always: **were the first and last original words the same?**

The check enumerates all 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible source triples. For a fixed substitution, the count below assumes the *whole* mapping is known; the labeled examples alone do not establish that a learner has discovered it. For fresh replacement, every output is possible from every source under the stated independent, uniform model.

**Try the counterexample:** choose the many-to-one rule and compare A with B. Then choose C: can you answer the equality question even though several original messages remain possible?

**Scope:** this is a deterministic teaching display, with frozen possible draws for the fresh-replacement condition. It runs no language model and reports no AI accuracy. It distinguishes a task clue from full message or key recovery. Whole-word replacement, a historical letter cipher, and modern encryption are different systems; random replacement here is not an encryption scheme with a decoding key.

**Research credit:** Zhouxiang Fang, Aayush Mishra, Muhan Gao, Anqi Liu and Daniel Khashabi, [*ICL CIPHERS: Quantifying “Learning” in In-Context Learning via Substitution Ciphers* (2025)](<https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1316/>), §§2.2–2.5, pp. 25913–25914. Their comparison uses stable token permutations and fresh per-occurrence replacements; task success need not recover the whole mapping. This four-way comparison, word task, fixtures and exact enumeration are our teaching model, not a replication of their experiment or results.

#### 6. A hidden message still has to reach its reader

Would the recipient recover the intended message? Would the carrier attract attention? Would a discovered message remain secret? These are separate questions. The three original examples below expose the extraction rules and keys so that you can test them.

In her study of seventeenth-century German handbooks, Eveline Szarka discusses Harsdörffer’s ambiguous invoice numbers, musical ciphers whose rhythm or melody might look unusual, and Friderici’s need to keep reserved words out of surrounding text. Those are accounts of proposed methods, not evidence that every proposal was used successfully.

Continue with the [Cardano grille’s selected positions](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/cardano-grille.html>), [null-cipher extraction rules](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/null-cipher.html>), or [Bacon’s two-symbol representation](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bacon.html>).

**Research credit:** Eveline Szarka, [*On the Combination of Cryptography and Steganography in 17th Century Germany* (2023)](<https://ecp.ep.liu.se/index.php/histocrypt/article/view/705>), §§4–6, pp. 163–166, and conclusion p. 167; [publisher PDF](<https://ecp.ep.liu.se/index.php/histocrypt/article/download/705/611/722>). All invoices, word codes, sentences and rhythms in this activity are new teaching fixtures. No source illustration, historical key or musical composition is reproduced.

#### The handbell: when a date rules out a cipher

**Historical case — unresolved.** Rudolf II’s alchemical handbell, made around 1600, carries a Greek-letter inscription. Bean, Gannon and Lang’s 2023 study corrects an earlier transcription and compares possible interpretations.

The same inscription, represented as digits or Latin letters, prompted different suggestions from Mason’s cipher classifier:

Outputs reported in the 2023 paper, not rerun by this museum

| Input representation | Leading suggestions |
| --- | --- |
| Digits | Monome-Dinome; Tridigital |
| Latin letters | Bazeries; Checkerboard |

These tools used ACA-oriented training and English-language assumptions. Their rankings are clues, not calibrated probabilities of the bell’s cipher type.

Could Monome-Dinome explain an inscription from around 1600?

The paper dates Monome-Dinome in its present form to about 1936. That chronology rules out this particular suggestion for the bell. Eliminating a candidate does not identify the correct one.

**Keep the question open:** the paper does not settle whether the inscription encodes recoverable plaintext or represents another kind of meaningful symbolism. No decipherment is supplied here.

Source: Richard Bean, Corinna Gannon and Sarah Lang, [*The cipher of Emperor Rudolf II’s “Alchemical Hand Bell”*](<https://ecp.ep.liu.se/index.php/histocrypt/article/view/690>) (HistoCrypt 2023), pp. 13–17, §§2–3 and 5. The classifier reports and chronology come from that study; the museum has not inspected the artifact.

Sarah Lang’s [*Situating ciphers among alchemical techniques of secrecy*](<https://ecp.ep.liu.se/index.php/histocrypt/article/view/698>) (2023) adds a useful distinction: secrecy can involve cover names, symbolic conventions and social practices as well as reversible encryption. Transcription alone need not reveal meaning.

Continue with [recording uncertain readings](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html#annotations>), [applying your own key](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html#keys>), or [the experimental homophonic search](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html#homophonic>).

A traffic-analysis exercise

### Reading the Radio Log

Two days of invented wireless intercepts. You will not decrypt a single message. Who worked whom, which new callsign was which old station, and what can you honestly claim?

**This log is fictional.** Every callsign, frequency, time, bearing and fragment on this page is invented for teaching. It reconstructs a method, not any real network, army or day.

The method is traffic analysis: the study of the externals of communications—callsigns, frequencies, schedules, routing, volume and where a transmitter is—while message content is left to cryptanalysis. The National Security Agency’s history of the subject describes those elements and their wartime use, and the notes below cite it as the NSA history. Predict, then check: each step records what you chose, so that later evidence can show what your own choices imply. Everything runs in your browser.

[1. Read the log](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#log>) · [2. Who worked whom?](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#connect>) · [3. New callsigns](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#match>) · [4. Observed or inferred?](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#notebook>) · [5. Second-stage evidence](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#stage-two>) · [6. Debrief](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#debrief>) · [Sources](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html#sources>)

The method notes, history and sources remain readable without JavaScript. Enable JavaScript to see the log and run the exercise.

#### 1. Read the log

One invented net, two days. Our receiver listened from 06:00 to 18:00 each day, with the gaps shown. Each station transmits on its own frequency. At midnight every station took a new callsign. Serial numbers restart at 1 each day.

**Groups** is the length of the enciphered text. The text itself is not part of this exercise, so nothing can be decrypted. **R** followed by a number is a receipt for the other station’s message of that number.

| Time | kHz | From | To | Serial | Groups | Intercept operator’s note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Day 2 intercept log (invented; all callsigns changed at midnight)

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

##### What the log does not contain

Missing observations are evidence too. This list is computed from the log and stays on the page throughout the exercise.

#### 2. Who worked whom?

Using only the From and To columns for Day 1, tick each pair of callsigns you saw in contact. Then compare your drawing with the log.

Day 1 pairs heard in contact

Compare with the logClear links

Diagram positions are arbitrary; they are not locations. After comparison: solid lines are in the log, red dashed lines have no supporting row, faint dotted lines are links you missed. A partly read callsign gets its own node.

Choose the pairs you saw working each other, then compare with the log.

##### Net control, and the headquarters question

A military net was typically run by a net control station working its outstations, and the structure of a net could mirror the organization it served (NSA history). Choose the callsign that looks like net control. It is recorded as hypothesis H1, kept apart from what you observed.

 Net control candidate on Day 1
- Choose…

Record as hypothesis H1

No hypothesis recorded yet.

#### 3. Day 2: the callsigns changed

Changing callsigns was meant to break exactly the continuity you need. Analysts often bridged a change through whatever did not change at the same time: frequencies, contact schedules, an operator’s sending style, the pattern of who worked whom (NSA history). Match each Day 2 callsign to a Day 1 callsign, or leave it unresolved, then read what your matches imply.

Record matchesReset matches

Choose a Day 1 callsign, or leave unresolved, for each Day 2 callsign.

#### 4. Observed, inferred or not supported?

Sort each statement by what the log can bear. An observation is in the rows. An inference goes beyond them and could be wrong. Some claims the log cannot support at all.

- Observed in the log

- Inference

Check classificationsReset statements

Classify each statement, then check.

#### 5. Second-stage evidence

Two further sources arrive. Direction finding measures the bearing of a transmitter from a receiving post; bearings from two posts can cross to give an approximate fix (NSA history). Operators’ chatter was generally sent unenciphered, and careless chatter could leak callsigns, schedules or even unit designators. Record your Day 2 matches first, so the new evidence tests your own choices.

Reveal second-stage evidence

On this invented 60 × 48 km grid, our two DF posts are on the west edge. The invented force faces west, so east is its rear. Each bearing is taken as accurate to ±2°, or ±4° for a very brief signal; the circle round each fix is a rough teaching estimate of that error, not a measured confidence region.

Direction-finding results (invented)

| Day | Callsign | Bearings | Result | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

Dashed circles: Day 1 fixes. Solid circles: Day 2 fixes. A red line joins two fixes when your matches imply a move larger than the combined uncertainty.

##### A plain-language fragment

##### What your matches now imply

#### 6. Debrief

The debrief opens with the second-stage evidence. Until then, keep your own reasoning.

Here is the exercise key: the invented truth behind the log. A real analyst never received one, and the key contains no plans or intentions, because nothing in a log of externals could test them.

Exercise key (fictional)

| Station | Day 1 | Day 2 | Role in the key |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

The plausible wrong match built into this log is GA1 = ZB3. GA1 took over ZB3’s old frequency, and matching by frequency is a sound habit that usually works. Here it invents two events at once: a receipt-only station suddenly sending the most traffic on the net, and DH9 vanishing. Direction finding then turns the same mistake into an overnight move of about 20 km that never happened. The schedule (minute 40), the role (long numbered messages, answered by net control at minute 42) and the chatter about a number 5 all point to DH9 instead.

#### After the exercise: the history behind it

**Callsigns are not units.** The NSA history recounts how, on the day of Jutland in May 1916, an Admiralty operations director asked what a callsign located in harbour meant and was told it was the German fleet commander’s. The commander used a different callsign at sea; that one stayed at fleet headquarters. The British commander-in-chief was signalled that direction finding placed the German flagship in harbour.

**Quiet on the air is not quiet on the ground.** In another First World War example, British signals suggested that Australian and Canadian units were still in Flanders while those units moved under signals silence to Amiens. An absence of traffic says something about a radio, not necessarily about a unit.

**Volume is not intention.** Volume was one of the externals analysts studied, and in general more traffic allowed more to be inferred (NSA history). But a count of groups measures activity on the air. In this log the apparent Day 2 rise is mostly longer listening. A real rise could still be routine reports, repeats of garbled messages, an exercise, or dummy traffic sent to mislead.

**Analysts were not working alone.** Traffic analysis informed cryptanalysts about who was talking to whom, and its products were combined with decrypts and other sources (NSA history). James Thirsk’s chapter in *The Bletchley Park Codebreakers* is a participant’s account of this work as a wartime “log-reader”.

#### How this differs from real traffic analysis

- **Scale.** Real logs ran to thousands of entries across many nets. This one has 34 rows.

- **Callsign systems.** Here callsigns change once. Real systems changed periodically to a prearranged plan, which analysts sometimes recovered and could then predict (NSA history).

- **Direction finding.** The ±2° readings and fix circles are a rough model. Real bearings could be much worse, and a fix is an area, not a point.

- **Deception.** Real targets changed procedures, reduced time on the air and sent dummy traffic (NSA history). This log contains no deliberate deception.

- **No answer key.** Real analysts revised hypotheses as evidence accumulated and seldom learned for certain whether they were right.

#### Where this leads

**The history route.** Continue with [Station HYPO](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/station-hypo.html>), where partial JN-25 recovery worked alongside traffic analysis and operational context before Midway, or follow the [Ciphers at War tour](<https://ciphermuseum.com/tours/tour.html?tour=wartime>). The [Hall of Codebreakers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/codebreakers.html>) holds the people behind the methods.

**The modern version.** [Blind Relay](<https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-blind-relay/#corr-h>), in Crypto Lab, runs the same move on modern logs. Its “Correlation without collusion” exhibit joins an Oblivious HTTP relay’s log to the gateway’s log without touching key material, on ciphertext size and on timing. Padding merges the size join into one anonymity set; when traffic is sparse, the timing join still links requests. Where sizes or arrivals coincide, it reports an anonymity set or an overlap instead of guessing, the same discipline as leaving a callsign unresolved here.

The same join, then and now

| In this radio log | In Blind Relay’s logs |
| --- | --- |
| Message length in groups | Ciphertext size |
| Contact schedule: the minute past the hour | Arrival time at relay and gateway |
| Leaving a callsign unresolved | Reporting an ambiguous join instead of guessing |

#### Sources

- Donald A. Borrmann, William T. Kvetkas, Charles V. Brown, Michael J. Flatley and Robert Hunt, *The History of Traffic Analysis: World War I – Vietnam* (Center for Cryptologic History, National Security Agency, 2013): [NSA PDF](<https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/13/2002761879/-1/-1/0/TRAFFIC_ANALYSIS.PDF>); [GovInfo copy](<https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo91580>). Used for the definition and elements of traffic analysis, net structure, deception and dummy traffic, and the First World War examples.

- Whitfield Diffie and Susan Landau, *Privacy on the Line: The Politics of Wiretapping and Encryption*, updated and expanded edition (MIT Press, 2007), [open-access edition](<https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/5572.001.0001>). They call traffic analysis, not cryptanalysis, “the heart of a communications intelligence organization”, and find a narrower form of it in law-enforcement records of the numbers a line calls.

- James Thirsk, “Traffic analysis: a log-reader’s tale”, in Ralph Erskine and Michael Smith (eds), *The Bletchley Park Codebreakers* (Biteback, 2011). It first appeared in *Action This Day* (2001): [contents of the 2001 edition](<https://cryptocellar.org/ActionContents.html>). A participant’s account; this exercise does not reproduce its examples.

The log, bearings, chatter and key are original to this page. No private copy of any source is linked.

Cryptanalysis Techniques

### Codebreaker's Workbench

Encrypt, decrypt, and analyze text with live cipher engines. Watch frequency distributions shift in real time.

[Evidence Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html>) — preserve manuscript readings, compare numerical groupings and search homophonic keys. [Try the historical investigations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html>), [six guided evidence exercises](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/reading-the-evidence.html>) or [a radio log read without decryption](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html>).

Input Text Distribution

IC counts matching letter pairs; it ignores their order. It does not identify a cipher or prove randomness. [See a balanced, predictable counterexample.](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/entropy.html#entropy-rate>)

  var ENGLISH_FREQ = [8.167,1.492,2.782,4.253,12.702,2.228,2.015,6.094,6.966,0.153,0.772,4.025,2.406,6.749,7.507,1.929,0.095,5.987,6.327,9.056,2.758,0.978,2.360,0.150,1.974,0.074];

  /* ─── Populate cipher dropdown ─── */
  var sel = document.getElementById('wbCipher');
  CIPHERS.forEach(function(c){
    var o = document.createElement('option');
    o.value = c.id; o.textContent = c.name;
    sel.appendChild(o);
  });

  /* ─── Cipher config ─── */
  function curCipher(){ return CIPHERS.find(function(c){ return c.id === sel.value; }); }

  sel.addEventListener('change', function(){
    var c = curCipher();
    var keyEl = document.getElementById('wbKey');
    var extraEl = document.getElementById('wbExtra');
    if(c.hasKey){
      keyEl.parentElement.style.display='';
      keyEl.placeholder = c.keyDefault || '';
      keyEl.value = c.keyDefault || '';
      document.querySelector('label[for="wbKey"]').textContent = c.keyLabel || 'Key';
    } else {
      keyEl.parentElement.style.display='none';
    }
    extraEl.innerHTML = '';
    document.getElementById('wbKeyWarning').hidden = true;
  });
  sel.dispatchEvent(new Event('change'));

  /* ─── Encode / Decode ─── */
  function getEngine(id){
    return CE[id];
  }

  function doRun(enc){
    var c = curCipher();
    var e = getEngine(c.id);
    if(!e) { showOutput('Engine not available for: ' + c.name); return; }
    var text = document.getElementById('wbInput').value;
    var key = document.getElementById('wbKey').value || (c.keyDefault || '');
    var warning = document.getElementById('wbKeyWarning');
    warning.hidden = true;
    warning.textContent = '';
    if(c.id === 'runningKey') {
      var keyLength = key.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g, '').length;
      var messageLength = text.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g, '').length;
      if(!keyLength || keyLength < messageLength) {
        warning.textContent = keyLength
          ? 'This key has ' + keyLength + ' letters for ' + messageLength + ' message letters, so the teaching engine repeats it. Supply a full-length passage for a non-repeating running key.'
          : 'No alphabetic key supplied: the engine uses its built-in teaching excerpt and repeats it if needed.';
        warning.hidden = false;
      }
    }
    try {
      var result = enc ? e.encode(text, key) : e.decode(text, key);
      if(typeof result === 'object' && result.out) result = result.out;
      showOutput(result);
    } catch(err) {
      showOutput('Error: ' + err.message);
    }
  }

  function showOutput(text){
    document.getElementById('wbOutput').textContent = text;
  }

  document.getElementById('wbEncode').addEventListener('click', function(){ doRun(true); });
  document.getElementById('wbDecode').addEventListener('click', function(){ doRun(false); });

  document.getElementById('wbSwap').addEventListener('click', function(){
    var inp = document.getElementById('wbInput');
    var out = document.getElementById('wbOutput');
    inp.value = out.textContent;
    out.textContent = '';
    updateFreq();
  });

  document.getElementById('wbClear').addEventListener('click', function(){
    document.getElementById('wbInput').value = '';
    document.getElementById('wbOutput').textContent = '';
    document.getElementById('wbKeyWarning').hidden = true;
    updateFreq();
  });

  document.getElementById('wbCopy').addEventListener('click', function(){
    var text = document.getElementById('wbOutput').textContent;
    var btn = this;
    function unavailable(){
      btn.textContent = 'SELECT OUTPUT TO COPY';
      var output = document.getElementById('wbOutput');
      output.focus();
      var range = document.createRange(); range.selectNodeContents(output);
      var selection = window.getSelection(); selection.removeAllRanges(); selection.addRange(range);
    }
    if(navigator.clipboard && navigator.clipboard.writeText){
      navigator.clipboard.writeText(text).then(function(){
        btn.textContent = 'COPIED';
        setTimeout(function(){ btn.textContent = 'COPY'; }, 1500);
      }, unavailable);
    } else unavailable();
  });

  /* ─── Quick Tools ─── */
  document.getElementById('wbReverse').addEventListener('click', function(){
    var inp = document.getElementById('wbInput');
    inp.value = inp.value.split('').reverse().join('');
    updateFreq();
  });
  document.getElementById('wbUpper').addEventListener('click', function(){
    var inp = document.getElementById('wbInput');
    inp.value = inp.value.toUpperCase();
  });
  document.getElementById('wbStrip').addEventListener('click', function(){
    var inp = document.getElementById('wbInput');
    inp.value = inp.value.toUpperCase().replace(/[^A-Z]/g,'');
    updateFreq();
  });

  /* ─── Frequency Analysis ─── */
  function countFreqs(text){
    var counts = new Array(26).fill(0);
    var total = 0;
    for(var i=0;i<text.length;i++){
      var c = text.charCodeAt(i);
      if(c>=65&&c<=90){ counts[c-65]++; total++; }
      else if(c>=97&&c<=122){ counts[c-97]++; total++; }
    }
    return {counts:counts, total:total};
  }

  function calcIC(counts, total){
    if(total<2) return 0;
    var sum=0;
    for(var i=0;i<26;i++) sum += counts[i]*(counts[i]-1);
    return sum / (total*(total-1));
  }

  function renderBars(containerId, labelId, freqs){
    var container = document.getElementById(containerId);
    var labels = document.getElementById(labelId);
    var maxF = Math.max.apply(null, freqs) || 1;
    container.innerHTML = '';
    labels.innerHTML = '';
    for(var i=0;i<26;i++){
      var pct = (freqs[i]/maxF*100)||0;
      var bar = document.createElement('div');
      bar.className = 'freq-bar';
      bar.style.height = Math.max(pct,1) + '%';
      bar.setAttribute('data-pct', freqs[i].toFixed(1));
      bar.setAttribute('title', A[i]+': '+freqs[i].toFixed(2)+'%');
      container.appendChild(bar);
      var lbl = document.createElement('span');
      lbl.textContent = A[i];
      labels.appendChild(lbl);
    }
  }

  function updateFreq(){
    var text = document.getElementById('wbInput').value;
    var r = countFreqs(text);
    var freqs = r.counts.map(function(c){ return r.total ? (c/r.total*100) : 0; });
    renderBars('freqBars','freqLabels', freqs);
    var ic = calcIC(r.counts, r.total);
    document.getElementById('icVal').textContent = r.total >= 2 ? ic.toFixed(4) : '—';
    var hint = 'At least two A–Z letters are needed for a matching-pair proportion.';
    if(r.total >= 2){
      if(r.total < 20) hint = 'Short sample: the observed coincidence proportion is sensitive to each letter.';
      else if(ic > 0.06) hint = 'Higher observed coincidence: more repeated-letter pairs than the uniform-letter reference (1/26 ≈ 0.0385).';
      else if(ic > 0.04) hint = 'Observed coincidence is above the uniform-letter reference (1/26 ≈ 0.0385).';
      else hint = 'Low observed coincidence: compatible with many sources, including balanced deterministic text.';
    }
    document.getElementById('icHint').textContent = hint;
  }

  /* English reference bars */
  renderBars('refBars','refLabels', ENGLISH_FREQ);

  /* Live update */
  document.getElementById('wbInput').addEventListener('input', updateFreq);
  // Ciphertext is passed in the fragment so it is not sent in the HTTP request.
  function importCiphertext(){
    var params = new URLSearchParams(location.hash.slice(1));
    if(params.has('ct')) {
      document.getElementById('wbInput').value = params.get('ct');
      document.getElementById('wbOutput').textContent = '';
      document.getElementById('wbKeyWarning').hidden = true;
      updateFreq();
    }
  }
  window.addEventListener('hashchange', importCiphertext);
  importCiphertext();
  updateFreq();
})();

A guided route

### Working Is Not Secure

A cipher that encrypts and decrypts perfectly can still fail the one claim that matters. This route separates three questions that are easy to blur: is it correct, is it fast, and is it secure?

The explanation and the route remain readable without JavaScript. Enable JavaScript to run the two tests.

#### Three different questions

- **Correctness:** does decryption give back exactly what was encrypted? A failure here is a bug.

- **Performance:** is it fast and cheap enough to use? Speed is a reason to choose a scheme, never evidence that it is secure.

- **The security claim:** what does it promise against an adversary, and has anyone tried to break that promise? Neither of the first two answers this.

Practical ciphers can be broken in principle, so what matters is how much work an attack really needs. Trying every key is the attack of last resort, which means a large key space bounds only exhaustive key search. Any shortcut that avoids searching keys makes the number of keys irrelevant (Fred Piper and Sean Murphy, *Cryptography: A Very Short Introduction*).

#### A worked example: four questions, two tests

The scheme is a simple substitution cipher: each letter is always replaced by the same other letter. The message and key below are invented for this page.

1. What does the adversary have?

The ciphertext only, plus ordinary knowledge of English. No key and no plaintext.

2. What property is claimed?

That the ciphertext gives nothing away, because there are 26! (about 4 × 10<sup>26</sup>) possible keys: far too many to try.

3. What would a functional test show?

Whether decrypting with the key returns the message exactly. It tests correctness only.

4. What is a separate security test?

An attack that uses only what the adversary has. Here: rank the ciphertext letters by how often they occur, and pair them with English letters ranked the same way. No key is searched.

**Ciphertext:** ``

 Run the functional testRun the security test

**Attacker’s first reading:** ``

##### The verdict

The cipher works: it is correct, and fast enough to do by hand. Its security claim still fails, because the attack never needed to search the key space. The museum’s [substitution exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/monoalphabetic.html>) goes from this first reading to the full key. To play a security game in which the attacker’s advantage is measured over many rounds, try [Hidden Bit](<https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-hidden-bit/>) in Crypto Lab.

#### When the claim fails

Sarah Flannery’s Cayley–Purser algorithm was a working public-key scheme, and it won her the Young Scientist competition. An attack then exposed a security problem in it. In her book *In Code* (2000) she describes including a detailed report on that attack in her later project, and treating the negative result as part of how science moves forward rather than as a failure. The book does not give the technical attack, and this page does not reproduce the attack either.

Friedrich L. Bauer’s maxims of cryptology make the same warning from the other side: do not underrate the adversary, distrust an inventor’s confidence in their own method, and remember that people make mistakes (Bauer, *Decrypted Secrets*, 4th edition).

#### Follow the route

The [Working Is Not Secure tour](<https://ciphermuseum.com/tours/tour.html?tour=working-not-secure>) visits exhibits where each of the four questions decides the outcome: a huge key space undone by language patterns, a perfect-secrecy guarantee that holds only under strict conditions, a machine attacked through its procedures, what a security proof really assumes, and how modern attacks are judged. It returns to the verdict above.

#### Sources

- Sarah Flannery with David Flannery, *In Code: A Mathematical Journey* (Profile Books, 2000).

- Friedrich L. Bauer, *Decrypted Secrets: Methods and Maxims of Cryptology*, 4th edition (Springer, 2007).

- Fred Piper and Sean Murphy, *Cryptography: A Very Short Introduction* (Oxford University Press, 2002).

The message, key and tests are original to this page. Books are cited by title; no copy of any book is linked. Key-size figures from older books are not used as present-day guidance.

 Understanding Encryption

### How Ciphers Work

From pen-and-paper codes to the mathematics behind modern security

#### Start with one message

[Your first codebreak](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html>) guides you through a library notice, repeating-key Vigenère, language assumptions and homophonic counts. Try the first lesson in about 15 minutes.

[Find a classical cipher topic](<https://ciphermuseum.com/classical-guide.html>) · [Print the activities](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-worksheet.html>)

Why History Matters

#### What Classical Ciphers Can Teach

Historical ciphers offer useful comparisons with modern substitution, permutation and key management. These comparisons explain concepts; they do not establish a direct historical path from a classical system to AES or another modern design.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Substitution → S-Boxes

Classical substitutions illustrate a basic idea also present in AES. Its nonlinear S-boxes operate with key mixing and diffusion; a fixed substitution table alone does not provide modern security.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Polyalphabetic → Stream Ciphers

Vigenère's repeating keyword and ChaCha20's pseudorandom keystream illustrate combining a message with a keystream. A ChaCha20 key can protect multiple messages, but nonces must not repeat under that key, and the block counter must not wrap.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

Transposition → Permutation

Classical transpositions permute symbols. AES ShiftRows permutes byte positions and MixColumns combines bytes linearly; these are useful conceptual comparisons, not a claim of direct historical descent.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-gear"></use></svg>
```

Rotor Machines → Block Ciphers

Enigma changes its substitution as it steps. Modern block ciphers use repeated designed round operations. Compare the mechanisms without treating one as a direct implementation of the other.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

Lorenz → Computing

Manual cryptanalysis recovered Lorenz messages and inferred the machine before Colossus. From February 1944, Colossus accelerated statistical searches for wheel settings; it was an important early programmable electronic computer.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

One-Time Pad → Perfect Secrecy

Shannon formalized perfect secrecy: an OTP achieves it for fixed-length messages when the pad is uniformly random, secret, independent of the message and never reused. Practical encryption often targets computational security with shorter keys. Information-theoretic and computational security are different guarantees, with different assumptions.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="section-divider" viewBox="0 0 180 6"><line x1="0" y1="3" x2="180" y2="3"></line></svg>
```

#### Three details that change a protocol

Follow these worked examples, then continue in the linked Crypto Lab activities:

- [A valid tag versus a fresh message](<https://ciphermuseum.com/modern.html#replay-freshness>): replay A/B/A and see what receiver state changes.

- [Field boundaries before hashing](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/sha256.html#structured-hashing>): distinguish different records from different input bytes.

- [Separate keys after key agreement](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/diffie-hellman.html#key-derivation>): compare HKDF purpose labels and output lengths.

[Entrance](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)›Modern Cryptography

 Beyond the Museum

### Modern Cryptography

Not just ciphers — an entirely different discipline

This collection includes ciphers, people, historical and cultural context, mathematical foundations, hashes, signatures, and protocols. A cipher reversibly transforms plaintext into ciphertext with a key, but many exhibits explain other parts of cryptography. This page connects that broader history to modern practice.

The Complete Journey

#### Classical → Modern: Compare Historical Weaknesses with Modern Design

| Classical Cipher Type | Historical Limitation | Modern Solution | Modern Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Caesar / Monoalphabetic | Frequency analysis — letter mapping preserved | Nonlinear substitution combined with diffusion and key mixing | AES SubBytes |
| Homophonic Substitution | One-to-many substitution can retain language and structural clues | Computational security under a defined attack model | AES in an appropriate authenticated mode |
| Polyalphabetic / Vigenère | Repeating key creates detectable periodicity | Pseudorandom keystreams with per-key nonce uniqueness and counter limits | ChaCha20, AES-GCM |
| Transposition (Rail Fence, Columnar) | Letter counts preserved; language and ordering clues can help analysis | Nonlinear substitution combined with diffusion and key mixing | AES ShiftRows + MixColumns |
| Playfair / Hill (block) | Small blocks leak digraph statistics; linear algebra solvable | 128-bit blocks, non-linear operations, round keys | AES (128-bit block) |
| Fractionation (Bifid, ADFGVX) | Coordinate mixing insufficient with static key square | Multiple rounds of mixing with key-derived round keys | AES 10–14 rounds |
| Layered classical systems | Substitution + transposition — each layer still attackable | Multiple designed rounds; security depends on the whole construction | AES, Camellia, SM4 |
| Machine ciphers (Enigma, Lorenz) | Physical key distribution; operator errors; structural flaws | Authenticated public-key methods help establish shared secrets | RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ECDH |
| One-Time Pad | Impractical key management — reuse is catastrophic | Computationally secure with short key; KDFs for key derivation | AES-256, X25519 key exchange |

Shannon's Framework

#### Confusion & Diffusion

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

Confusion

Making the relationship between key and ciphertext as complex as possible. Caesar has a simple key relationship: C = P + 3. One known pair reveals the entire key.

**Modern solution:** AES S-boxes are highly non-linear. The S-box has a precise public algebraic definition. Its nonlinearity works with the other round operations; an S-box alone does not make encryption secure.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

Diffusion

Spreading each plaintext bit's influence across many ciphertext bits. Caesar does not spread changes across letter positions: change one letter, change exactly one ciphertext letter.

**Modern solution:** AES combines ShiftRows and MixColumns to spread byte dependencies. Across suitable inputs, changing one bit of a full AES input changes about half the output bits on average; this is not an exact per-message promise or a standalone security proof.

The Modern Landscape

#### What Replaced Classical Cryptography

⚠️

**Taxonomy note:** Symmetric and public-key encryption schemes both reversibly transform plaintext into ciphertext. RSA encryption and RSA signatures are distinct schemes with different encoding and padding requirements. Diffie–Hellman establishes shared secrets; signatures authenticate messages; hash functions produce digests. These primitives solve different problems and must be combined with appropriate protocols.

🏛️

**Looking for the exhibits?** Explore these constructions — [DES](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/des.html>), [Diffie-Hellman](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/diffie-hellman.html>), [RSA](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rsa.html>), [AES](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/aes.html>), and [SHA-256](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/sha256.html>) — and further exhibits in [Hall XI · Modern Cryptography](<https://ciphermuseum.com/halls/modern-crypto.html>). This page provides the wider context: the journey from classical failure to modern practice, and additional constructions such as ChaCha20, ECDH and post-quantum schemes.

🔐 Ciphers — Plaintext → Ciphertext → Plaintext

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-diamond"></use></svg>
```

AES-256 (Symmetric) → exhibit

128-bit blocks, 256-bit key, 14 rounds. 2²⁵⁶ possible keys; no practical key-recovery attack is known against correctly used full-round AES. Protocol, mode and implementation failures remain separate risks.](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/aes.html>)

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-globe"></use></svg>
```

ChaCha20 (Stream Cipher)

Designed by Daniel Bernstein. Original ChaCha uses a 64-bit nonce and 64-bit block counter. IETF ChaCha20 (RFC 8439) uses a 256-bit key, 96-bit nonce, and 32-bit block counter. Both XOR plaintext with a deterministic pseudorandom keystream: never reuse a nonce under the same key, and never let the block counter wrap. [Original specification](<https://cr.yp.to/chacha/chacha-20080128.pdf>); [RFC 8439 §§2.3, 4](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8439.html#section-2.3>) and [errata](<https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc8439>).

🔑 Key Exchange — Creating a Shared Secret

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-person"></use></svg>
```

Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange → exhibit

Derives a shared secret over a public channel. Computing the shared group element is the computational Diffie–Hellman problem. Discrete logarithms provide one route to solving it; protocol security also needs authentication. *Not a cipher — it does not encrypt data.*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/diffie-hellman.html>)

🔓 Public-Key Cryptography — Asymmetric Encryption & Signatures

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-key"></use></svg>
```

RSA (Asymmetric) → exhibit

Rivest, Shamir, Adleman (1977). Two keys — public (encrypt) and private (decrypt) — based on arithmetic modulo a product of large primes; factoring that composite reveals the private key. Used in TLS, email, and digital signatures.](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rsa.html>)

#️⃣ Hash Functions — One-Way Fingerprints

[[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-lock"></use></svg>
```

SHA-256 (Hash Function) → exhibit

Produces a fixed 256-bit digest of a message shorter than 2⁶⁴ bits. Preimage resistance means finding an input for a chosen digest should be computationally difficult; low-entropy inputs can still be guessed. Generic collision search takes roughly 2¹²⁸ work, rather than having a proven exact lower bound. Used in digital signatures, certificate verification, blockchain. *A hash is not a reversible encryption scheme; guessed inputs can still be tested.*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/sha256.html>)

🔮 The Future — Post-Quantum Cryptography

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-flask"></use></svg>
```

Post-Quantum Cryptography

Sufficiently large, fault-tolerant quantum computers could break conventional RSA and Diffie–Hellman using Shor’s algorithm. NIST standardized the first three algorithms from its post-quantum project in 2024: **ML-KEM** (formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber, key encapsulation) and **ML-DSA** (formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium, signatures), both based on structured lattice problems. NIST also standardized the hash-based SLH-DSA signature scheme in 2024. These are intended to resist known quantum attacks; they are not proofs against every future attack. The mathematics is on exhibit in the Hall of Foundations: [lattices & the SVP](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/lattices-svp.html>), [the closest-vector problem](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/closest-vector.html>), [Learning With Errors](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/learning-with-errors.html>) — an introduction to the mathematical setting of lattice-based standards — and [polynomial rings](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/polynomial-rings.html>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-quill"></use></svg>
```

Elliptic-Curve Signatures → exhibit

[ECDSA](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/ecdsa.html>) signatures verify under a public key rather than concealing content; attribution to a person requires a trusted key association: a private scalar on an elliptic curve, a public point, and a signature anyone can check. Suitable 256-bit elliptic-curve groups and 3072-bit RSA are commonly compared at roughly 128 bits of classical security, under their respective assumptions. Security requires an appropriate curve and implementation. Reused or biased nonces, side-channel leakage, faults and validation errors can compromise a signer. Shor’s algorithm also applies to the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem. The group law is in [the Hall of Foundations](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/elliptic-curves-real.html>).

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-puzzle"></use></svg>
```

Threshold Secret Sharing → exhibit

[Shamir’s Secret Sharing](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/shamir-secret-sharing.html>) (1979) represents the secret in a finite field and samples the remaining polynomial coefficients independently and uniformly. With distinct nonzero share coordinates, k valid shares reconstruct the secret; fewer than k preserve its prior distribution. This information-theoretic property also holds against quantum computation, but does not protect stolen shares or faulty implementations. Threshold signing protocols can build on secret-sharing ideas but require additional protections; plain Shamir sharing does not authenticate shares or perform signatures.

[Inline SVG: original diagram/icon markup]

```html
<svg class="icon" width="17" height="17"><use href="images/icons.svg#i-mask"></use></svg>
```

Zero-Knowledge Proofs → exhibit

[Zero-knowledge proofs](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zero-knowledge-proofs.html>) combine a soundness guarantee with a specified bound on what the verifier can learn beyond the statement. The guarantee depends on the protocol and security model; toy protocols can have a visible nonzero soundness error. The succinct variants — zk-SNARKs and STARKs — validate private transactions and compress whole blocks of computation into a proof small enough to check on a blockchain. The Fiat–Shamir transformation connects certain interactive identification protocols to noninteractive proofs or signatures under additional assumptions. A signature is not automatically a general-purpose zero-knowledge proof.

#### A valid tag can belong to an old message

Suppose A carries counter 1 and B carries counter 2. Each tag covers the counter and message under the same session key. An observer records both. Compare a receiver that remembers only the last token with one that accepts a valid tag only when its counter exceeds the highest accepted counter, initially 0.

Swipe or scroll the table horizontally to see every column. Keyboard: focus the table area and use the arrow keys.

Deliver A, B, then A again; authenticate before updating state

| Delivery | Tag check | Last-token-only rule | Increasing-counter rule |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A (1) | Valid | Accept | Accept; highest = 1 |
| B (2) | Valid | Accept | Accept; highest = 2 |
| A (1), replayed | Valid | Accept | Reject; highest = 2 |
| A changed to counter 3; old tag | Invalid | Reject | Reject; highest = 2 |
| Forget receiver state, keep key; replay A (1) | Valid | Accept | Accept; highest = 1 |

The A/B/A sequence defeats last-token-only checking. Resetting state under the unchanged key defeats the counter rule too. Rejected packets must not advance the accepted counter. This simplified rule rejects out-of-order messages; transports that allow reordering need a defined replay window and session lifecycle, including counter exhaustion. Replaying recorded ciphertext does not require encrypting a new message with a reused nonce: sender nonce uniqueness and receiver freshness are separate requirements.

Try the existing [Crypto Lab: Regex Veil](<https://systemslibrarian.github.io/crypto-lab-fte/>), in its **Freshness** section: open authenticated fragments twice, then reset the used-counter window. It is a local protocol teaching model, not a deployed transport.

Sources: Ross Anderson, *Security Engineering: A Guide to Building Dependable Distributed Systems*, third edition (2020), §4.3, printed pp. 122–124 (PDF pp. 169–171); David Wong, *Real-World Cryptography* (2021 edition), §3.3.3, PDF pp. 140–143 in the reflowed edition, which has no printed pagination. The table is a museum teaching example.

🎓

**The museum's final lesson:** Many historical systems failed through structural weaknesses, key reuse, or operational mistakes; others are obsolete or unresolved. A correctly used one-time pad retains perfect secrecy. Modern cryptography adds computational security and public-key methods, while still depending on sound key management, and extends into protocols, signatures, and proofs.

 Your Guide to the Collection

### Museum Map

13 halls, the Foundations Annex, 174 exhibits — one continuous story: how humanity learned to keep secrets

🧭

**Suggested route:** Start in Hall I and follow the historical connections, then visit the Foundations Annex for the mathematics. The halls cover overlapping traditions and different security goals, rather than one inevitable path from simple ciphers to a single “unbreakable” system.

Reading the Exhibits

#### Trust Labels

Cipher and protocol exhibits carry one of four labels indicating their modern security status. People, places, institutions, principles, fiction, cultural exhibits, and mathematical foundations carry no cipher trust label. Click a label on any exhibit to return here.

Broken

Cryptographically broken — historically important but unsafe to use today.

Historical Only

Obsolete or historical system; notes distinguish cryptanalysis from capture or other operational compromise.

Educational

A didactic construction for learning cryptographic concepts, not for security.

Secure (Modern)

Still considered secure when used correctly with modern key handling.

[Compare GPU search, GPRS faults and conditional-linear DES](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/modern-attack-evidence.html>). Each result identifies the target, attacker access and limits of the evidence.

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

'use strict';
(function(){
  /* "You are here" — reads localStorage for last visited hall */
  var KEY = 'ciphermuseum.lastHall';
  var hallId = '';
  try { hallId = localStorage.getItem(KEY) || ''; } catch(e){}
  if(hallId){
    var room = document.querySelector('[data-hall-id="'+hallId+'"]');
    if(room){
      room.classList.add('bldg-here');
      var label = document.getElementById('youAreHereLabel');
      var wrap = document.getElementById('youAreHere');
      if(label && wrap){
        var name = room.querySelector('.bldg-room-name');
        label.textContent = 'Last visited: ' + (name ? name.textContent : hallId);
        wrap.style.display = '';
      }
      room.scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth',block:'center'});
    }
  }
  /* Record hall visits from referrer */
  var ref = document.referrer;
  if(ref){
    var MAP = {ancient:'ancient',substitution:'substitution',polyalphabetic:'polyalphabetic',
      transposition:'transposition',military:'military','civil-war':'civil-war',
      machines:'machines',puzzle:'puzzle',unbreakable:'unbreakable',codebreakers:'codebreakers',
      'modern-crypto':'modern-crypto',unsolved:'unsolved',culture:'culture'};
    Object.keys(MAP).forEach(function(k){
      if(ref.indexOf('/halls/'+k+'.html')!==-1){
        try{ localStorage.setItem(KEY, MAP[k]); }catch(e){}
      }
    });
    if(ref.indexOf('/cryptanalysis.html')!==-1){
      try{ localStorage.setItem(KEY, 'lab'); }catch(e){}
    }
    if(ref.indexOf('/modern.html')!==-1){
      try{ localStorage.setItem(KEY, 'modern'); }catch(e){}
    }
  }
})();
```

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

(function(){
  var HALLS = [
    {id:'ancient',      label:'Hall I',   name:'World Origins of Cryptography', href:'halls/ancient.html', icon:'𓀂'},
    {id:'substitution', label:'Hall II',  name:'Classical Substitution', href:'halls/substitution.html', icon:'🔤'},
    {id:'polyalphabetic',label:'Hall III',name:'Polyalphabetic',         href:'halls/polyalphabetic.html', icon:'🔑'},
    {id:'transposition',label:'Hall IV',  name:'Transposition',          href:'halls/transposition.html', icon:'⟺'},
    {id:'military',     label:'Hall V',   name:'Military & Spy',         href:'halls/military.html', icon:'🎖'},
    {id:'civil-war',    label:'Hall VI',       name:'Civil War Gallery',      href:'halls/civil-war.html', icon:'⚔'},
    {id:'machines',     label:'Hall VII', name:'Mechanical Machines',     href:'halls/machines.html', icon:'⚙'},
    {id:'puzzle',       label:'Hall VIII', name:'Puzzle Ciphers',          href:'halls/puzzle.html', icon:'🧩'},
    {id:'unbreakable',  label:'Hall IX',    name:'Unbreakable Ciphers',    href:'halls/unbreakable.html', icon:'🔒'},
    {id:'codebreakers', label:'Hall X',       name:'Hall of Codebreakers',   href:'halls/codebreakers.html', icon:'🏛'},
    {id:'foundations',  label:'Annex',    name:'Hall of Foundations',    href:'hall-of-foundations/index.html', icon:'𝔽'}
  ];

  var resetInThisPage = false;
  function getPassed(){
    if(resetInThisPage) return [];
    try {
      var saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('ciphermuseum.path.passed'));
      if(!Array.isArray(saved)) return [];
      return saved.filter(function(id, i){
        return saved.indexOf(id) === i && HALLS.some(function(hall){ return hall.id === id; });
      });
    } catch(e){ return []; }
  }

  function render(){
    var passed = getPassed();
    var total = HALLS.length;
    var done = passed.length;

    /* Summary */
    document.getElementById('summary').innerHTML =
      '<div class="summary-stat"><span class="stat-num">' + done + ' / ' + total + '</span><span class="stat-label">Halls Completed</span></div>' +
      '<div class="summary-stat"><span class="stat-num">' + Math.round((done/total)*100) + '%</span><span class="stat-label">Progress</span></div>' +
      '<div class="summary-stat"><span class="stat-num">' + done + '</span><span class="stat-label">Badges Earned</span></div>';

    /* Grid */
    var grid = document.getElementById('pathGrid');
    grid.innerHTML = '';
    HALLS.forEach(function(h){
      var isPassed = passed.indexOf(h.id) !== -1;
      var card = document.createElement('div');
      card.className = 'path-card' + (isPassed ? ' passed' : '');

      var badgeColor = isPassed ? 'var(--gold)' : 'var(--s5)';
      var fillColor = isPassed ? 'var(--gold-glow)' : 'none';
      card.innerHTML =
        '<svg class="badge-svg" width="72" height="72" viewBox="0 0 80 80">' +
          '<circle cx="40" cy="40" r="36" fill="none" stroke="' + badgeColor + '" stroke-width="2"/>' +
          '<circle cx="40" cy="40" r="28" fill="' + fillColor + '" stroke="' + (isPassed?'var(--gold-dim)':'var(--s5)') + '" stroke-width="1"/>' +
          '<text x="40" y="44" text-anchor="middle" font-size="22">' + h.icon + '</text>' +
        '</svg>' +
        '<div class="card-hall">' + h.label + '</div>' +
        '<div class="card-name">' + h.name + '</div>' +
        '<div class="card-status ' + (isPassed?'done':'pending') + '">' + (isPassed ? '✓ Badge Earned' : '○ Not Yet Completed') + '</div>' +
        '<a class="card-link" href="' + h.href + '">' + (isPassed ? 'Revisit Hall' : 'Visit Hall') + '</a>';
      grid.appendChild(card);
    });
  }

  document.getElementById('resetBtn').addEventListener('click', function(){
    if(confirm('Reset all learning path progress? This cannot be undone.')){
      resetInThisPage = true;
      try {
        localStorage.removeItem('ciphermuseum.path.passed');
        localStorage.removeItem('ciphermuseum.path.active');
      } catch(e) { /* Storage unavailable: reset this page's displayed state. */ }
      render();
    }
  });

  render();
})();
```

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

'use strict';
(function(){
  var DATA = [
    { title:'Poe, The Gold-Bug', medium:'literature', family:'substitution', period:'1843-1903', href:'ciphers/gold-bug.html', note:'Poe’s 1843 short story presents substitution decipherment through Legrand’s explanation of counts, patterns and likely words.' },
    { title:'Conan Doyle, Dancing Men', medium:'literature', family:'substitution', period:'1843-1903', href:'ciphers/dancing-men.html', note:'A cryptographic plot solved by pattern frequency and word shape — Holmes decodes by recognising E and common short words.' },
    { title:'Doyle, The Gloria Scott', medium:'literature', family:'concealment', period:'1843-1903', href:'ciphers/null-cipher.html', note:'Holmes breaks a null cipher hidden in a letter — every third word carries the real message, illustrated in the Null Cipher exhibit.' },
    { title:'The Da Vinci Code', medium:'literature', family:'multi-stage', period:'2000s', href:'ciphers/da-vinci-code.html', note:'Layered clue progression using substitutions and symbolic puzzles; the exhibit distinguishes fictional effects from the underlying cipher techniques.' },
    { title:'National Treasure', medium:'film', family:'multi-stage', period:'2000s', href:'ciphers/national-treasure.html', note:'Adventure-film chain of historical clue extraction and decoding; cipher literacy presented as heroic problem-solving.' },
    { title:'Gravity Falls Credits Ciphers', medium:'television', family:'substitution', period:'2010s', href:'ciphers/gravity-falls.html', note:'Broadcast audience puzzle loop built on Caesar/Atbash/A1Z26 variants; viewers can try the clues themselves.' },
    { title:'Cicada 3301', medium:'internet', family:'multi-stage', period:'2010s', href:'ciphers/cicada-3301.html', note:'Internet-scale collaborative cryptography and steganography hunt spanning three years and multiple continents.' },
    { title:'MIT Mystery Hunt', medium:'puzzle hunt', family:'multi-stage', period:'1980s', href:'ciphers/mit-mystery-hunt.html', note:'Annual team puzzle ecosystem featuring recurring cipher families; over 40 years of collaborative code-solving tradition.' },
    { title:'ARG puzzle practices', medium:'internet', family:'multi-stage', period:'multiple periods', href:'ciphers/krypto-arg.html', note:'ARG-era integration of text ciphers and media-layer clues; community collaborative decryption as social event.' },
    { title:'The BACH Motif', medium:'music', family:'substitution', period:'before 1800', href:'ciphers/bach-motif.html', note:'B-A-C-H uses German note names as a musical signature; the exhibit identifies its appearance in The Art of Fugue.' },
    { title:'Kryptos (Sanborn sculpture)', medium:'art', family:'multi-stage', period:'1990s', href:'ciphers/kryptos.html', note:'CIA headquarters sculpture bearing an 869-character ciphertext (865 letters plus four question marks) — K1–K3 publicly solved; K4 plaintext recovered from archival papers in 2025, distinct from a public cryptanalytic solution.' },
    { title:'Zodiac Killer Ciphers', medium:'historical document', family:'multi-stage', period:'1960s', href:'ciphers/zodiac.html', note:'Z408 solved in 1969; Z340 finally cracked in 2020 by an international team using candidate transpositions and homophonic-substitution search with language scoring.' },
    { title:'Sator Square in Tenet (2020)', medium:'film', family:'wordplay', period:'2010s', href:'ciphers/sator-square.html', note:'Ancient Latin word square revived in pop culture — notably in the film Tenet — as a symbol of palindromic mystery.' },
    { title:'Freemason Pigpen Tradition', medium:'tradition', family:'substitution', period:'before 1800', href:'ciphers/freemason-pigpen.html', note:'Grid-based substitution associated with Masonic manuscripts; the exhibit separates the historical tradition from a modern teaching alphabet.' }
  ];

  var resultWrap = document.getElementById('survey-results');
  var empty = document.getElementById('survey-empty');
  var m = document.getElementById('filter-medium');
  var f = document.getElementById('filter-family');
  var p = document.getElementById('filter-period');

  function render(){
    var mm = m.value, ff = f.value, pp = p.value;
    var rows = DATA.filter(function(item){
      return (mm === 'all' || item.medium === mm)
        && (ff === 'all' || item.family === ff)
        && (pp === 'all' || item.period === pp);
    });

    resultWrap.innerHTML = '';
    if(!rows.length){ empty.style.display = ''; return; }
    empty.style.display = 'none';

    rows.forEach(function(item){
      var card = document.createElement('article');
      card.className = 'survey-card';
      card.innerHTML =
        '<div class="survey-meta">' + item.medium + ' · ' + (item.period === '2010s' ? '2010s+' : item.period) + '</div>' +
        '<h3>' + item.title + '</h3>' +
        '<p style="margin:0 0 .75rem;line-height:1.65;color:var(--tx2);">' + item.note + '</p>' +
        '<a href="' + item.href + '" class="view-all-link">Open exhibit →</a>';
      resultWrap.appendChild(card);
    });
  }

  m.addEventListener('change', render);
  f.addEventListener('change', render);
  p.addEventListener('change', render);
  render();
})();
```

A reader’s mystery from Cipher Museum

### The Curator’s
Sealed Letter

A readable message.
A disputed order. Your finding.

A sealed case has conflicting transfer records. Two instructions disagree about where it should go. Open the file and work out what the records justify. The book’s four optional slips offer another way into the same investigation.

Original modern puzzle · Free · No account required

Start the investigation[Try the four book slips ↓](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html#slips>)[I have the book’s instruction](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html#unlock>)

The interactive case needs JavaScript. You can still [read the four slips and their hints](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html#slips>) below.

#### A second way through the book

The slips appear after chapters 1, 3, 14 and 17 of [*Secrets of the Cipher Museum*](<https://ciphermuseum.com/the-book.html>). You can also try all four here. They use simplified ideas, not historical ciphertexts. The book’s twenty historical investigations stand on their own.

Work at your own pace. Each slip has a small hint and a separate answer reveal. Nothing depends on page numbers, a purchase or a timer. Your answers are checked in this browser and are not submitted to a server. An optional [slip notebook](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html#notebook>) lets you keep the four answers together.

The four slips

#### Follow the marks

Slip 1 · After chapter 1The small key

The first slip has travelled separately from the letter. Its numbers disguise letters, except for two groups that stand for whole words. Someone has helpfully pencilled in an example: 31 24 53 means CAR.

31 08 42 17 24 53 19

08 = O; 17 = P; 19 = E; 24 = A; 31 = C; 42 = M; 53 = R; 65 = TO; 90 = THE.

Use the key to recover the first word. Keep every answer in order; together, the four slips make one instruction.

A nudge

Treat each two-digit group as one entry in the key. The first two groups give CO.

Reveal this slip’s answer

**COMPARE**. 31, 08, 42, 17, 24, 53 and 19 give C, O, M, P, A, R and E. The unused whole-word groups show how a small code vocabulary can sit beside an alphabet.

[Keep this answer in your notebook →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html#notebook>)

A miniature invented nomenclator, prompted by chapter 1. It is not Mary Stuart’s historical cipher.

Slip 2 · After chapter 3The clerk’s route

The second slip contains no disguised letters. The clerk has changed their order. A note on the envelope gives the route: start at the top left, read DOWN to the bottom, then start at the top of the next column to the right.

Read down each column, left to right1 ↓2 ↓3 ↓

| T | C | I |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H | O | E |
| E | P | S |

Read all three columns in that order. Restore the spaces to recover two words.

A nudge

The first column reads T, H, E. Move to the top of the middle column next.

Reveal this slip’s answer

**THE COPIES**. The columns give THE, COP and IES. Joined and respaced, they read THE COPIES. No letter has changed; its position has.

[Keep this answer in your notebook →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html#notebook>)

An invented route puzzle, prompted by chapter 3. It is not a reconstruction of a Union Army message.

Slip 3 · After chapter 14The reused strip

Two slips used the same six secret numbers. Here, letters become numbers (A = 01 through Z = 26). The sender adds one secret number to each letter number. These teaching examples use ordinary addition, without wraparound.

Known letters: L E T T E R

Letter numbers: 12 05 20 20 05 18

First message: 53 22 82 28 40 38

Second message: 43 22 68 23 53 25

The first message is known to say LETTER. Subtract its letter numbers from its sent numbers to recover the secret strip. Subtract that strip from the second message, then turn the results back into letters. For the first position: 53 minus 12 gives the secret number 41; 43 minus 41 gives 02, or B.

A nudge

The recovered strip is 41 17 62 08 35 20. Use it once more on the second message.

Reveal this slip’s answer

**BEFORE**. Removing the recovered strip gives 02 05 06 15 18 05: BEFORE. Knowing one message helps expose the other because the secret numbers were reused.

[Keep this answer in your notebook →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html#notebook>)

A tiny arithmetic illustration prompted by chapter 14, not a VENONA intercept or a secure encryption tool. Actual one-time-pad protection depends on a random secret pad used only once.

Slip 4 · After chapter 17The letters that do nothing

The last slip appears cluttered. Its note is blunt: the lower-case letters are padding. They carry nothing. Keep only the CAPITAL letters, in their existing order. The spaces on the slip were added to mislead.

aYbO cUdT eRfU gShT iTjH kElM

Remove the padding and the false spaces. Restore ordinary word breaks to recover the final three words.

A nudge

The first three capitals are Y, O and U. Keep working from left to right.

Reveal this slip’s answer

**YOU TRUST THEM**. The capitals spell YOUTRUSTTHEM. The spacing becomes YOU TRUST THEM. The familiar-looking lower-case letters were a distraction.

[Keep this answer in your notebook →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html#notebook>)

An invented null-letter puzzle prompted by the change of assumptions in chapter 17. It does not reproduce the Copiale cipher’s symbol system.

Case file 01 · An original fictional investigation

#### The room that changed

A sealed loan case has a disputed transfer record. Two copies of its order name different rooms. Can you protect the case without making a bad accusation?

You are the museum’s duty reader. The transfer was scheduled for nine; it is now after 09:12. A later note places the case in room four, but does not establish how it got there. Any further movement is paused while the paperwork is checked. Ellis, who holds the case keys, has been accused of arranging a theft. The curator needs a finding before authorising further movement. Recover the dispatch, compare the records, and decide what the museum should do.

All people, documents and events in this case are invented. The simplified word code is a teaching puzzle. The times and signatures below are information in the records, not independent verification.

- 1 · Decode

- 2 · Compare

- 3 · Find a source

- 4 · Make a finding

Step 1 of 4: recover the destination.

1 · Read the message

##### A dispatch in numbers

The retained dispatch uses a tiny codebook. Each two-digit group stands for a whole word. Use the entries below to read the message. Which room does it name?

A · Dispatch carbon · Marked 08:10 · Reference CM-17

14 33 18 29 06 41 52 08 27. 19 44 07 25 63.

Filed in the dispatch tray. No signature.

The working codebook

- **06** TO

- **07** KEYS

- **08** AT

- **14** MOVE

- **18** SEALED

- **19** KEEP

- **25** WITH

- **27** NINE

- **29** CASE

- **33** THE

- **41** ROOM

- **44** BOTH

- **52** FOUR

- **63** ELLIS

 The destination in the encoded dispatch [Input dispatch-room: type=text; initial value=]

Enter the room number, as a word or a digit.

Check the dispatch

A nudge

Find the code for ROOM. The group immediately after it gives the destination.

More help

41 means ROOM. Look up the next group, 52.

Show the answer and continue

The dispatch names ROOM FOUR. You can still investigate the records if decoding is not your favourite part.

Use this reading

2 · Compare the documents

##### A readable message is not the end

Here is your reading beside the delivered copy. Keep the supporting records in view. You can establish a difference before you know how it happened.

A · Dispatch carbon · Marked 08:10 · Reference CM-17

##### The retained copy, decoded

MOVE THE SEALED CASE TO ROOM FOUR AT NINE. KEEP BOTH KEYS WITH ELLIS.

Filed in the dispatch tray. No signature.

B · Delivery copy · Marked 08:25 · Reference CM-17

##### The delivered copy

MOVE THE SEALED CASE TO ROOM FIVE AT NINE. KEEP BOTH KEYS WITH ELLIS.

Found beside the receiving desk. No signature.

C · Handling log

##### An opened envelope

08:17 — Envelope received, outer seal intact.
08:20 — Envelope opened for routine inspection. Initial: R.
08:25 — Copy placed at receiving desk.

The log does not identify who wrote either copy.

D · Inventory note · Marked 09:12

##### A later observation

Sealed case present in room four. Seal appears intact. Contents not checked.

This note was made after the scheduled transfer time. It does not record what happened at nine. There is no accompanying record for room five.

What changed in the wording of A and B?

 [Input difference-time: type=radio; initial value=time]  The time of the move [Input difference-room: type=radio; initial value=room]  The destination room [Input difference-keys: type=radio; initial value=keys]  The person keeping the keys

Check the difference

Help me compare

Ignore the document labels for a moment. Read the two instructions word for word. The time and the name at the end agree.

3 · Ask for another source

##### Which record would help most?

You can request one record from the archive. You want evidence about the authorised destination, not another reason to suspect someone.

Choose the most useful next record.

 [Input source-keys: type=radio; initial value=keys]  The key checkout log showing who could open the case [Input source-register: type=radio; initial value=register]  The curator’s signed dispatch register for reference CM-17 [Input source-rumour: type=radio; initial value=rumour]  The porter’s arrival log showing when the envelope reached R

Request this record

A nudge about sources

Which record is connected to this particular instruction and the person who authorised it?

E · Dispatch register · Marked 08:09 · Reference CM-17

##### The record you requested

Authorised destination: ROOM FOUR.
Scheduled move: 09:00.
Key custodian: Ellis.
Signed: M. Vale, curator.

The register supports the retained copy’s destination. Its signature has not been independently authenticated. It does not identify who prepared the delivered copy.

4 · Separate a finding from an accusation

##### What can you tell the curator?

Choose the finding and action these records support.

 [Input verdict-theft: type=radio; initial value=theft]  A and E name room four. Hold further movement and accuse Ellis of changing B: custody of the keys establishes who altered the destination. [Input verdict-clerk: type=radio; initial value=clerk]  B is the later delivered copy. Authorise movement to room five and clear the discrepancy: the later timestamp establishes that the destination was officially revised. [Input verdict-evidence: type=radio; initial value=evidence]  A and E name room four; B names room five. Hold further movement and check authorisation: these records do not establish who changed the wording. [Input verdict-nothing: type=radio; initial value=nothing]  D records an apparently intact seal. Hold further movement until the destination is checked, but clear the theft allegation: that observation establishes that nothing was removed.

Submit your finding

Case file completed

##### Your finding reaches the curator.

**The curator’s response:** “Keep both copies. Keep the transfer on hold until we have checked the register and the chain of custody. Do not treat possession of a key as a verdict against its keeper.”

Your reading established FOUR in the encoded dispatch. Comparison established FIVE in the delivered copy. The register supplied another source supporting FOUR. That is enough to question the disputed order and preserve the evidence. It is not enough to identify an author or a motive.

The later inventory note adds an observation, with a limit: someone recorded an apparently intact seal, but nobody recorded checking the contents. A copying error, an authorised change not reflected in the register, and a deliberate alteration still require investigation.

**Your next checks:** authenticate the register, locate the dispatch original, identify the writers and handlers of both copies, and inspect the case’s contents. You have resolved what the documents disagree about while keeping the unresolved questions visible.

The curator’s response is the fictional ending to this exercise. It is not a new document you were expected to infer or evidence proving a culprit.

##### Take the question into the museum

In the [Babington exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/babington.html>), follow who controls the correspondence channel. At [the one-time pad exhibit](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/one-time-pad.html>), distinguish a sound method from the consequences of reusing its secret material. Then ask the same question of each recovery: what does readable text actually establish?

For the physical side of interception, visit [Cabinet Noir](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/cabinet-noir.html>) to explore how postal offices opened, copied and resealed letters.
