#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

  document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
    var q = document.getElementById('q');
    var kindFilter = document.getElementById('kind-filter');
    var resultsEl = document.getElementById('results');
    var emptyEl = document.getElementById('empty');
    var statusEl = document.getElementById('status');
    var suggestionsEl = document.getElementById('suggestions');
    var indexReady = false;
    statusEl.setAttribute('role', 'status');

    function escapeHTML(s){return String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g,function(c){return {'&':'&amp;','<':'&lt;','>':'&gt;','"':'&quot;',"'":'&#39;'}[c];});}

    function syncUrl(method) {
      var url = new URL(location.href);
      var text = q.value.trim();
      if (text) url.searchParams.set('q', text); else url.searchParams.delete('q');
      if (kindFilter.value) url.searchParams.set('kind', kindFilter.value); else url.searchParams.delete('kind');
      history[method || 'replaceState']({}, '', url.pathname + url.search + url.hash);
    }

    function render() {
      if (!indexReady) return;
      var raw = q.value.trim();
      var kind = kindFilter.value;
      if (!raw) {
        resultsEl.innerHTML = '';
        emptyEl.style.display = 'none';
        suggestionsEl.style.display = '';
        statusEl.textContent = 'Type to search · ' + (window.CipherSearch._count || '174') + ' exhibits · 13 halls · indexed pages';
        return;
      }
      suggestionsEl.style.display = 'none';
      var hits = window.CipherSearch.query(raw);
      if (kind) hits = hits.filter(function (h) { return h.entry.kind === kind; });
      var matchCount = hits.length;
      hits = hits.slice(0, 60);
      if (!hits.length) {
        resultsEl.innerHTML = '';
        emptyEl.style.display = '';
        statusEl.textContent = '0 matches for "' + raw + '"';
        return;
      }
      emptyEl.style.display = 'none';
      statusEl.textContent = matchCount + ' match' + (matchCount === 1 ? '' : 'es') + ' for "' + raw + '"' + (matchCount > hits.length ? ' · showing first ' + hits.length : '');
      var hl = window.CipherSearch.highlight;
      resultsEl.innerHTML = hits.map(function (h) {
        var e = h.entry;
        var meta = [];
        if (e.kind === 'cipher') meta.push('Cipher');
        else if (e.kind === 'hall') meta.push('Exhibit Hall');
        else meta.push('Page');
        if (e.hall && e.hall !== '—') meta.push('Hall: ' + escapeHTML(e.hall));
        if (e.created && e.created !== '—') meta.push('Created: ' + escapeHTML(e.created));
        if (e.trust) meta.push('Trust: ' + window.TrustLabels.badge(e.trust));
        var tags = e.tags.slice(0, 6).map(function (t) {
          return '<span class="sr-tag">' + escapeHTML(t) + '</span>';
        }).join('');
        return '' +
          '<a class="sr-card" href="' + escapeHTML(e.url) + '" role="listitem">' +
            '<div class="sr-head">' +
              '<h3 class="sr-title">' + hl(e.title, raw) + '</h3>' +
              '<span class="sr-kind">' + escapeHTML(e.kind) + '</span>' +
            '</div>' +
            '<div class="sr-meta">' + meta.join(' · ') + '</div>' +
            '<p class="sr-summary">' + hl(e.summary, raw) + '</p>' +
            (e.note ? '<p class="sr-summary">' + escapeHTML(e.note) + '</p>' : '') +
            (tags ? '<div class="sr-tags">' + tags + '</div>' : '') +
          '</a>';
      }).join('');
    }

    var t;
    function debounce() { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(function () { render(); syncUrl('replaceState'); }, 80); }
    q.addEventListener('input', debounce);
    kindFilter.addEventListener('change', function () { render(); syncUrl('pushState'); });

    document.querySelectorAll('.suggest').forEach(function (b) {
      b.addEventListener('click', function () { q.value = b.dataset.q; render(); syncUrl('pushState'); q.focus(); });
    });

    // URL ?q= prefill
    var params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
    var preset = params.get('q');
    var presetKind = params.get('kind');
    if (['cipher', 'hall', 'page'].indexOf(presetKind) >= 0) kindFilter.value = presetKind;

    window.addEventListener('popstate', function () {
      var state = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
      q.value = state.get('q') || '';
      var stateKind = state.get('kind') || '';
      kindFilter.value = ['cipher', 'hall', 'page'].indexOf(stateKind) >= 0 ? stateKind : '';
      render();
    });

    function init(entries) {
      var list = Array.isArray(entries) ? entries : [];
      // Count canonical exhibit identities, not descriptive kinds or utility pages.
      var exhibitCount = list.filter(function (e) { return Number.isInteger(e.exhibitNumber); }).length;
      window.CipherSearch._count = exhibitCount || '?';
      render();
    }

    function loadIndex() {
      indexReady = false;
      statusEl.textContent = 'Loading index…';
      emptyEl.style.display = 'none';
      window.CipherSearch.load().then(function (entries) {
        indexReady = true;
        init(entries);
      }).catch(function () {
        resultsEl.innerHTML = '';
        statusEl.textContent = 'The search index could not be loaded. ';
        var retry = document.createElement('button');
        retry.id = 'searchRetry'; retry.type = 'button'; retry.textContent = 'Retry';
        retry.addEventListener('click', loadIndex);
        statusEl.appendChild(retry);
      });
    }
    if (window.CipherSearch) {
      if (preset) q.value = preset;
      loadIndex();
    } else {
      statusEl.textContent = 'Search script failed to load.';
    }
  });
```

## P224 — Teaching Resources — The Cipher Museum

- Site path: `teaching.html`
- Public page: https://ciphermuseum.com/teaching.html
- Snapshot source SHA-256: `f3ba7309b58d8cbc461548c0feeefaa852f769e20f4f52f2bf1d508a3943cca8`
- Source identities in the prior evidence ledger: LASRY-2018

### Metadata and search/social descriptions

- description: Beginner codebreaking lessons, printable activities and separate answers, plus Cipher Corpus resources for teachers and tool builders.
- keywords: cipher corpus, teaching, cryptanalysis, classical ciphers, education, benchmark, reproducibility, open data, schema

### Complete static body text and inline diagrams

Hidden/reveal panels and option labels are included. Script-generated text is supplied below and in the JavaScript/data appendices. Table cells are separated by vertical bars; superscripts/subscripts retain their HTML meaning. This is a text representation, not a screenshot.

[Skip to main content](<https://ciphermuseum.com/teaching.html#main-content>)

[The Cipher Museum](<https://ciphermuseum.com/index.html>)

- [Cipher Corpus](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-corpus.html>)

Cipher Corpus

### Teaching & Overview

Resources for educators, students, and tool builders using the classical cryptanalysis benchmark dataset.

#### A first codebreaking session

[Solve an original library notice](<https://ciphermuseum.com/first-codebreak.html>) in about 15 minutes, then extend the session with Vigenère, language samples and homophonic substitution. Work in pairs and ask each learner to defend a guess with evidence.

- [Print the student activities (no answers)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-worksheet.html>)

- [Open the separate facilitator’s answers](<https://ciphermuseum.com/codebreak-answers.html>)

- [Match classical topics to museum exhibits](<https://ciphermuseum.com/classical-guide.html>)

Print either sheet with your browser’s Print command, or save it as PDF. No account is required.

#### What is the Cipher Corpus?

- A curated library of classical ciphertext challenges with known plaintexts and metadata

- Includes synthetic examples and records labeled historical, plus multilingual and noisy records; see the source and errata for the limits of each label

- Designed for learning, teaching, and benchmarking cryptanalysis tools

#### How to Use the Corpus

- Practice codebreaking in Challenge Mode (solution hidden)

- Study metadata and solutions in Known Answers mode

- Download the dataset for research or tool development

- Contribute new records following the [contribution guide](<https://ciphermuseum.com/CONTRIBUTING.md>)

#### For Educators

[Reading the Evidence](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/reading-the-evidence.html>) offers six short, paper-informed investigations with original examples: key matching, mixed cleartext, transcription errors, recurring symbols, controlled token transformations and concealed-message reliability. Each includes feedback, a source credit and a stated limit.

[Reading the Radio Log](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/traffic-analysis.html>) is a traffic-analysis exercise on an invented two-day radio log. Learners map a network without decrypting anything, match changing callsigns, and keep a headquarters hypothesis apart from what the log shows. Missing intercepts stay visible, and a tempting wrong match has consequences they can see.

For a history-led reading group, [the Cipher Museum book companion](<https://ciphermuseum.com/the-book.html#reading-groups>) offers an opening excerpt, discussion questions and a free fictional evidence investigation. The activity needs no account or previous codebreaking experience.

- Use synthetic exercises and source-reviewed historical examples to teach cryptanalysis concepts

- Assign challenges by difficulty, cipher type, or language

- Demonstrate solver benchmarking and reproducibility

#### A small repeatable columnar experiment

Compare direct scoring and staged initialization with the [existing columnar search](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html#advanced-search>). The classroom runner uses four synthetic known-answer messages, three fixed seeds and two variants: 24 runs, including failures. It records exact plaintext and exact key recovery separately, preprocessing and total evaluations, elapsed time, settings and source-file hashes.

In a repository checkout with Node.js, run:

```text
node scripts/columnar-classroom.js > columnar-classroom-results.json
node scripts/columnar-classroom.js --check
```

[Open the classroom worksheet](<https://ciphermuseum.com/public/teaching/columnar-classroom.md>) · [Inspect the fixed fixtures](<https://ciphermuseum.com/public/teaching/columnar-classroom-fixtures.json>) · [Inspect the runner](<https://ciphermuseum.com/scripts/columnar-classroom.js>)

Keep unsuccessful and preprocessing-exhausted runs in the denominator. Repeated seeds on one message are dependent; these tiny-sample counts are not general recovery probabilities. Equal score-evaluation budgets are not equal CPU time. Exact replay excludes elapsed milliseconds.

Reading: George Lasry, *A Methodology for the Cryptanalysis of Classical Ciphers with Search Metaheuristics* (2018 published thesis), §4.7, printed pp. 59–60 / PDF pp. 80–81, and §5.3, printed pp. 67–75 and 79–80 / PDF pp. 88–96 and 100–101. This exercise adopts the comparison method, not the thesis’s recovery rates.

#### For Tool Builders

- Test solvers on a reproducible, versioned benchmark

- Use the schema for integration and validation

- Publish measured results with reproducibility receipts; the [statistics report](<https://ciphermuseum.com/public/reports/benchmark-baselines.html>) contains no measured solver-accuracy claims

#### Engine Accuracy & Provenance

Verification evidence differs by engine. The test suite combines independently published known-answer examples, pinned outputs for explicitly educational models, roundtrip and invalid-input checks, and corpus replay. Passing a model test does not establish historical authenticity.

- Independent examples include Schneier’s Solitaire vectors, historical manual examples for RS44 and German Double Playfair, and ACA examples for AMSCO.

- Some machine and codebook demonstrations are simplified models. Their limits and source editions must be read with the exhibit.

- The v0.6 replay baseline has 99,800 exact matches and 526 documented noisy or historical-variant exceptions among 100,326 records.

- Roundtrips establish consistency, not independent correctness. The public tests distinguish their evidence types.

Where an engine follows a specific historical convention (for example, the Four-square exhibit uses the ACA 25-letter I/J-merged alphabet rather than Wikipedia's Q-omitted example), the exhibit page documents that choice. The test suites are public in the [GitHub repository](<https://github.com/systemslibrarian/cipher-museum/tree/main/tests>) if you want to inspect or re-run them.

#### Resources

- [Corpus Browser](<https://ciphermuseum.com/cipher-corpus.html>)

- [Corrected v0.8 schema](<https://ciphermuseum.com/public/corpus/v0.8/cipher-corpus.schema.json>)

- [v0.8 scope and verification notes](<https://ciphermuseum.com/public/corpus/v0.8/README.md>)

#### Contact & Feedback

Open an issue on [GitHub](<https://github.com/systemslibrarian/cipher-museum>) with questions, suggestions, or contributions.

You can also email [systemslibrarian@gmail.com](<mailto:systemslibrarian@gmail.com>) — corrections are especially welcome. If you can point to a source, that is ideal; if something simply looks wrong, say so anyway and it will be checked against the sources.

History you can enter

### Secrets of the
Cipher Museum

Stories of Hidden Messages
and the People Behind Them

Paul “The Cipher Librarian” Clark

Discover how people learned to read other people’s secrets—and what happened when they did. Then enter Cipher Museum and try the ideas yourself.

[Read the opening](<https://ciphermuseum.com/the-book.html#sample>)[Find your chapter’s exhibit ↓](<https://ciphermuseum.com/the-book.html#chapter-visits>)[Try the reader’s mystery →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html>)

Book preview · Publication details to follow

[Image: Cover of Secrets of the Cipher Museum by Paul “The Cipher Librarian” Clark: gold lettering, a cipher wheel, torn parchment and a red wax seal.; source: https://ciphermuseum.com/images/cipher-museum-book-cover.png]

Twenty true investigations

#### A secret becomes readable.
What happens next?

*Secrets of the Cipher Museum* follows hidden messages and the people who tried to read them. Mary, Queen of Scots’ correspondence frames a journey through intercepted dispatches, wartime intelligence, disputed identities and the modern recoveries of Copiale, the Zodiac 340 cipher and Mary’s lost letters.

Decipherment opens another question: what do the recovered words actually establish? A message may expose a conspiracy, guide an operation or restore a voice to history. Acting on it may require corroboration, careful timing or a way to protect the source that made it readable. Some questions remain unresolved even after the words are clear.

No mathematical background is needed. Eight original diagrams and six documentary images help where the method matters. Each chapter offers an optional visit to the free Cipher Museum, through a link or QR code, to compare versions of a message, test an assumption or examine the evidence behind a published solution. The historical narrative stands on its own; the museum gives curious readers a place to continue investigating.

Before you begin

#### A few questions about the book

How does it sit alongside The Code Book and The Codebreakers?

David Kahn’s [*The Codebreakers*](<https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Codebreakers/David-Kahn/9781439103555>) and Simon Singh’s [*The Code Book*](<https://simonsingh.net/books/the-code-book/the-book/>) both explore what cryptography has meant for people and history. Singh also invited readers to take part through a [Cipher Challenge](<https://simonsingh.net/cryptography/cipher-challenge/>) and an [interactive CD-ROM](<https://simonsingh.net/cryptography/crypto-cd-rom/>).

This book’s focus is the passage from recovered words to a justified conclusion: what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain and which decisions become possible. Mary Stuart’s correspondence frames the selected investigations, and each chapter offers a specific, optional museum activity in reading, testing or judging evidence. Kahn and Singh are acknowledged predecessors in the notes.

Am I reading history or solving a mystery?

The prologue and twenty historical chapters are nonfiction, with sources and uncertainties identified. Four optional invented slips lead to The Curator’s Sealed Letter, a separate fictional case. You can enjoy the whole historical narrative without solving a puzzle.

What can I try before the book is published?

[Trace the route of Mary’s intercepted correspondence](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/babington.html#delivery-route>), [follow the two coded versions of the Zimmermann Telegram](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zimmermann.html#message-routes>), or [replay part of the published Z340 solution](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/decipherment-cases.html#z340>). The replay checks an existing solution; it does not identify the murderer. These exhibits are free, and teaching models are labelled.

Keep exploring as you read

CM

An envelope is waiting for you

#### The Curator’s Sealed Letter

Four optional slips run through the book. Solve them to open a fictional document investigation in the museum, or start the case directly online. The challenge is not just finding readable words. It is deciding what those words justify.

[Open the reader’s mystery →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html>)

Try it free, with hints. No purchase or account required.

From the prologue · Opening excerpt

#### The letters without a name

The letters were in the catalog. Their author was missing.

Pages of cipher lay among manuscripts in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, near material concerning Italian affairs in the early sixteenth century. A catalog could bring a researcher to those pages. It could not tell the researcher whose words were hidden there.

George Lasry, Norbert Biermann and Satoshi Tomokiyo were looking for historical ciphers they might decipher—a computer scientist in Israel, a pianist and music professor in Berlin, and a patent specialist in Japan, hunting in their spare hours. The unfamiliar signs were enough to interest them. They began without a famous name to guide the search.

Italian seemed a reasonable language to try. It failed. French offered a better prospect, but the manuscript resisted the simplest approach. A mark might stand for a letter, a syllable, or a whole word. Some marks contributed nothing to the reading. The team had to decide which handwriting differences mattered before a computer could count the signs reliably.

Gradually, fragments of language emerged. They carried the grammar of a woman writing about confinement and negotiation. Names began to suggest a particular household, a particular ambassador, a particular prisoner. The collection had been placed in the wrong historical neighborhood.

The researchers now had two problems. They needed to extend their key until they could read the letters. They also needed to establish that the person appearing through those readings was really the person who had sent them. A recognizable name could guide the work; it could also make a mistaken reading dangerously persuasive.

Somewhere else in the archives, earlier readers had left evidence that could test the answer. Those readers had entered the correspondence while its author was alive. They worked for her enemies.

The modern recovery would become public in 2023. To understand what it returned to history, we must first visit a different interception, in 1586, when the delivery of a queen’s letter could help determine whether she lived.

Excerpt © 2026 Paul “The Cipher Librarian” Clark. The prologue draws on George Lasry, Norbert Biermann and Satoshi Tomokiyo’s [2023 study of Mary Stuart’s recovered letters](<https://doi.org/10.1080/01611194.2022.2160677>). It follows their published account; no scene or dialogue has been invented. This is an excerpt from the prologue. Chapter 20 follows the full recovery and what the letters reveal. Biographical details follow the [publisher’s research announcement](<https://newsroom.taylorandfrancisgroup.com/codebreakers-crack-secrets-of-mary-queen-of-scots-lost-letters/>) and [NPR’s interview reporting](<https://www.wgbh.org/news/2023-02-10/3-amateur-codebreakers-set-out-to-decrypt-old-letters-they-uncovered-royal-history>); Biermann’s [university biography](<https://www.udk-berlin.de/person/norbert-biermann/>) identifies his Berlin teaching role.

[Explore the recovered letters →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/mary-stuart-castelnau-letters.html>)

A companion for further investigation

#### From chapter to experiment

Keep a short record of what you predicted, observed and still cannot establish. The narrative stands alone; these activities are optional.

- **Chapter 10:** compare [Bombe constraints](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bombe.html>) with [intercept-to-intelligence work](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/intercept-to-intelligence.html>). A candidate stop is not a checked plaintext or a finished assessment.

- **Chapter 12:** try [code terms and spelling alternatives](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/navajo-code-talkers.html#code-and-spelling>). What knowledge does the code require beyond fluency?

- **Chapter 13:** compare [Tunny / Lorenz](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/lorenz.html>) and [Colossus](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/colossus.html>). Separate analysis, machine construction and operations.

- **Chapter 16:** work through [the curator’s message](<https://crypto-lab.systemslibrarian.dev/learn/secure-message/>). Which observers receive a revocation, and which old copies survive?

- **Chapters 17–20:** use the [Evidence Workbench](<https://ciphermuseum.com/lab/evidence-workbench.html>) to preserve a transcription, alternatives, a candidate key and an independent check. A readable result does not identify its author.

For libraries, classrooms and curious friends

#### Read. Compare. Discuss.

A suggested 30-minute session, with an optional 15-minute puzzle warm-up. Use one shared screen or individual devices. No purchase, account or previous codebreaking experience is required.

- **Read · 5 minutes.** Read [the historical opening excerpt](<https://ciphermuseum.com/the-book.html#sample>). Which details are observations, and which questions still need an answer?

- **Investigate · 15 minutes.** Open the [fictional Sealed Letter case](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html>) and choose “Start the investigation.” Use its codebook to read the dispatch, then compare the four initial records. Keep the fictional case separate from the historical excerpt.

- **Decide · 10 minutes.** Choose one additional record before making a finding. Explain what it changes and what remains uncertain.

**Optional warm-up · 15 minutes.** Try the four slips before entering the case. Use hints or answer reveals whenever helpful; solving them is optional.

##### Questions for discussion

- What can a catalogue description tell you—and how could a reading overturn it?

- What changes when the same message survives in two versions?

- Which statement in the fictional case is an observation, and which is an inference?

- What one additional source would most improve your confidence?

Work individually or in pairs. Finish by naming one claim the documents support and one they leave unresolved.

[Start the group activity →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/sealed-letter.html>)

[Ancient (6)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-ancient>) [Medieval (2)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-medieval>) [Early Modern (19)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-renaissance>) [19th–Early 20th (14)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-19c>) [WWI–Interwar (12)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-wwi>) [World War II (6)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-wwii>) [Modern (17)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-modern>) [Quantum Era (1)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-quantum>) [Undated (7)](<https://ciphermuseum.com/timeline.html#era-undated>)

Ancient World

~1900 BC

#### Unusual Egyptian Hieroglyphs

🇪🇬 Ancient Egypt

Unusual signs in Khnumhotep II’s tomb illustrate deliberate variation in writing. Their purpose should not be equated automatically with secret encryption.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/egyptian-substitution.html>)

~600 BC

##### Atbash

 🇮🇱 Ancient Israel

Atbash — the ancient Hebrew reflection cipher (A<->Z, B<->Y, C<->X), self-inverse and used in the Book of Jeremiah (25:26, 51:41) for SHESHACH.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/atbash.html>)

~500 BC

##### Scytale

 🇬🇷 Sparta

The traditional scytale reconstruction illustrates transposition, but the dates and cryptographic interpretation of ancient evidence are disputed.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/scytale.html>)

c. 350 BCE

##### Aeneas Tacticus — Water-Clock Signals

🇬🇷 Greece

Aeneas’s water-clock signaling, preserved in Polybius: synchronized vessels selected preset military messages, not letters of an alphabet.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/aeneas-tacticus.html>)

c. 150 BCE

##### Polybius Square

 🇬🇷 Greece

Polybius describes coordinate signaling with the Greek alphabet arranged on five tablets. The familiar Latin I/J square is a later adaptation.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/polybius.html>)

1st century BCE

##### Caesar Cipher

 🇮🇹 Rome

Suetonius describes Caesar’s substitution with a shift of three. A short fixed shift can be tested exhaustively; no medieval encounter between Caesar and al-Kindi is implied.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/caesar.html>)

Medieval Period

~850 AD

##### Al-Kindi's Frequency Analysis

 🇮🇶 Baghdad

Al-Kindi’s surviving treatise gives an early systematic account of frequency analysis. Symbol counts can support substitution analysis, but short samples can remain ambiguous; there is no single six-century contest outcome.

~850

##### Monoalphabetic Substitution

🌍 Arabic World

A fixed substitution preserves letter counts while changing symbols. Al-Kindi’s ninth-century account is a landmark in its analysis, not the invention date of the entire family.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/monoalphabetic.html>)

Renaissance and Early Modern

1401 Mantua example

##### Homophonic Substitution

🇮🇹 Mantua

Mantua’s surviving 1401 key illustrates multiple substitutes for plaintext letters. Such choices can flatten some counts without eliminating higher-order language patterns.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/homophonic.html>)

c. 1404–1438

##### The Voynich Manuscript

 🌍 Central Europe

The Voynich manuscript remains undeciphered. Radiocarbon dating concerns its parchment; script, language and interpretation remain unresolved.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/voynich.html>)

1467

##### Alberti Cipher Disk

 🇮🇹 Italy

Alberti’s fifteenth-century cipher disk illustrates changing substitutions using two alphabets. The exhibit distinguishes historical instructions from a regular-step teaching model.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/alberti-disk.html>)

1553 and later variants

##### Vigenère Cipher

 🇫🇷 France

Bellaso’s 1553 work belongs to the history of polyalphabetic substitution. The familiar repeating-key shift model and its later attribution to Vigenère need to be distinguished from individual historical systems.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vigenere.html>)

1563

##### Porta's Polyalphabetic

🇮🇹 Naples

Porta’s work belongs to the history of reciprocal polyalphabetic tables. Repeating-key variants can expose periodic statistical patterns; the museum specifies its own table convention.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/porta.html>)

1586

##### The Babington Plot Cipher

 🇬🇧 England

The 1586 Babington Plot: intercepted nomenclator letters, a forged postscript, and the difference between compromised keys and an insecure transport channel.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/babington.html>)

1591 succession

##### The Argenti Cipher

🇮🇹 Papal States

Matteo succeeded his uncle Giovanni Battista Argenti in papal cryptographic work. Their documented methods include nomenclators, homophones and nulls; Marcello was Matteo’s younger brother.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/argenti.html>)

1623 full description

##### Bacon's Binary Encoding

 🇬🇧 England

Bacon’s biliteral alphabet represents letters with patterns of two forms and can hide them in a carrier. Binary representation is distinct from a direct historical origin for ASCII.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bacon.html>)

1640

##### Fermat's Little Theorem

🇫🇷 France

Fermat’s theorem gives aᵖ ≡ a (mod p) for integer a and prime p. It supports some primality tests, but passing a Fermat test does not prove a candidate is prime. Euler’s generalization and a prime-factor argument help explain RSA correctness.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/euler-fermat.html>)

1643

##### John Wallis and the Civil War Ciphers

🇬🇧 England

John Wallis served successive English governments as a cryptanalyst. The interactive illustrates a nomenclator rather than reproducing an authenticated Royalist key.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/wallis-ciphers.html>)

17th century

##### The Great Cipher of the Rossignols

 🇫🇷 France

The Rossignols’ syllabic nomenclator was deciphered by Bazeries in the 1890s. His proposed Man in the Iron Mask identification remains disputed.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/great-cipher.html>)

17th century tradition

##### Gronsfeld Cipher

🇩🇪 Germany

Numeric-key shifts are traditionally associated with Gronsfeld. The attribution and precise invention date are not established by the museum’s modern 0–9 model.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/gronsfeld.html>)

c. 1760–1780 manuscript

##### Copiale Cipher

🇩🇪 Wolfenbüttel

Knight, Megyesi and Schaefer deciphered the Copiale manuscript in 2011 using transcription, statistics and manual analysis. The exhibit separates that result from its invented demonstration alphabet.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/copiale.html>)

1763

##### Euler's Theorem & the Totient

🇷🇺 St. Petersburg

For a coprime to n, Euler’s theorem states aᵠ⁽ⁿ⁾ ≡ 1 (mod n). It helps explain RSA correctness; treating all message residues also requires the prime-factor or Chinese-remainder argument. The totient theorem alone is not a security proof.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/euler-fermat.html>)

1779–1783

##### Culper Ring — Washington’s Spy Network

🇺🇸 New York / Long Island

Major Benjamin Tallmadge’s 1779 codebook for George Washington’s Culper Spy Ring. Roughly 760 numbered entries covering people, places, military terms, and common words — used by Abraham Woodhull and Robert Townsend on British-occupied Long Island and Manhattan.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/culper-ring.html>)

1779–1780

##### Benedict Arnold & Major André

🇺🇸 West Point

Arnold and André used successive book references, including Blackstone and dictionary schemes. Kahn distinguishes the changing reference texts and letter-level fallback from a single fixed word-code procedure.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/arnold-andre.html>)

1786

##### Gripenstierna’s Cipher Machine

Sweden

A documented 57-disk device separates the authorized plaintext reader from the assistant copying ciphertext. The lost original was later reconstructed from documents.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/gripenstierna.html>)

1790s proposal

##### Jefferson Disk

 🇺🇸 United States

Jefferson proposed an unpublished 36-disk device. The later 25-disk M-94 illustrates a similar mechanism, but direct adoption of Jefferson’s proposal is not established.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/jefferson-disk.html>)

1794 documented example

##### Pigpen Cipher

🌍 Europe

Leeson’s 1794 Masonic inscription is a documented geometric-substitution example discussed by Kahn. It does not establish when every pigpen variant originated.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/pigpen.html>)

19th and Early 20th Centuries

1817

##### Wadsworth Cipher Device

🇺🇸 United States

Wadsworth’s 1817 device uses geared disks with 33 and 26 positions. A published 2020 ciphertext-only search studied key recovery for this historical design.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/wadsworth-cipher.html>)

1854

##### Playfair Cipher

 🇬🇧 England

Playfair cipher (1854) — Charles Wheatstone's keyed 5x5 digram cipher promoted by Lord Playfair. Used by the British in WWI; broken by digram analysis.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/playfair.html>)

1857

##### Beaufort Cipher

🇬🇧 United Kingdom

Beaufort cipher (1857) — Sir Francis Beaufort's reciprocal Vigenère variant where encrypt and decrypt are the same operation. Broken by Kasiski examination.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/beaufort.html>)

~1860

##### Civil-War Dictionary Code

🇺🇸 United States · Civil War

Dictionary codes replace words with references in an agreed book. Repeated references and language patterns can still leak information; this widget is a simplified model.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/dictionary-code.html>)

1861

##### Stager Route Cipher

🇺🇸 Union Army

The Union’s Stager system combined word transposition, code words and operational procedures. Wartime success is a historical claim, not a proof of mathematical security.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/stager.html>)

1861–1865 use

##### Confederate Vigenère

🇺🇸 Confederate States

Confederate repeating-key traffic included the Manchester Bluff key documented in an 1863 dispatch. Union success against particular messages does not prove that three keys exposed every Confederate communication.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/confederate-vigenere.html>)

1863

##### Kasiski Examination

 🇩🇪 Prussia

Kasiski published a repeating-key analysis method in 1863. Repeated-fragment distances suggest candidate periods, which require further checking. Babbage had investigated related attacks earlier.

1873 published scheme

##### Chinese Telegraph Code

🇨🇳 China

Viguier’s code and subsequent telegraph books represented Chinese characters numerically. A historical additive example uses digitwise modulo-ten arithmetic; the browser’s modulo-10,000 model is different.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/chinese-telegraph.html>)

1880s attribution

##### Nihilist Cipher

🇷🇺 Imperial Russia

The additive coordinate construction is associated with Russian revolutionary cryptography. Kahn qualifies its possible inventorship; other systems also bear the Nihilist name.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/nihilist.html>)

1885

##### The Beale Ciphers

 🇺🇸 Bedford County, Virginia

Beale ciphers — three numerical ciphers published in an 1885 Lynchburg pamphlet, said to have been written in the 1820s and to point to a Virginia treasure. The pamphlet supplies a reading for #2 using a version of the Declaration of Independence. #1 and #3 remain unresolved; the readable construction does not authenticate a treasure.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/beale.html>)

1890s methods

##### Bazeries: Cylinder and Hand Procedures

🇫🇷 France

Bazeries worked with both a cylinder and hand methods. The linked browser exhibit uses a labelled substitution-and-reversal model, not a cylinder simulation.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bazeries.html>)

~1902

##### Four-Square Cipher

🇫🇷 France

Four-Square cipher (1902) — Delastelle's digram cipher using two keyed and two standard 5x5 squares. Disrupts Playfair frequencies but breaks to digrams.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/four-square.html>)

1902 treatise

##### Bifid Cipher

🇫🇷 France

Delastelle’s posthumous 1902 treatise describes fractionation methods. Bifid separates and recombines two-dimensional coordinates over a selected period.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/bifid.html>)

1902 treatise

##### Trifid Cipher

🇫🇷 France

Trifid extends coordinate fractionation to three dimensions. The extra coordinate does not by itself establish greater security than every two-dimensional construction.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/trifid.html>)

World War I and Interwar

1914

##### German Double Transposition

🇩🇪 Germany · WWI

Two successive columnar transpositions: historical military use, attack conditions, and modern computerized cryptanalysis; not an unbroken cipher until 2013.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/double-transposition.html>)

1917 precursor

##### One-Time Pad

 🇺🇸 United States

A one-time pad offers perfect secrecy with a secret, uniform, independent message-length key used once. Try ciphertext tampering to see why secrecy is not authentication.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/one-time-pad.html>)

1917

##### Vernam Tape Cipher

🇺🇸 AT&T

Vernam’s teleprinter system combines text with a key stream. XOR supplies perfect secrecy only when the pad is uniformly random, independent, secret, long enough and never reused.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vernam.html>)

1917

##### Zimmermann Telegram

🇩🇪 Germany → 🇲🇽 Mexico

The January 1917 Zimmermann Telegram: code 0075 to Washington, then re-encoded in 13040 for Mexico. Room 40’s reading helped draw the United States into WWI.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zimmermann.html>)

1918

##### ADFGVX Cipher

 🇩🇪 Germany · WWI

ADFGVX combined a 6×6 substitution square with columnar transposition. Painvin’s June 1918 solutions exploited particular traffic and keys, not every later message automatically.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/adfgvx.html>)

March 1918

##### ADFGX Cipher

🇩🇪 Germany · WWI

Germany’s ADFGX field cipher appeared in March 1918; Painvin obtained solutions in April. Its square-plus-transposition construction required continuing key recovery.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/adfgx.html>)

1918

##### Chaocipher

🇺🇸 United States

Chaocipher (1918) — John F. Byrne's two-disk dynamic cipher. Disclosed in 2010; published known-plaintext and in-depth ciphertext-only attacks recover its keys.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/chaocipher.html>)

1920s–1945

##### Enigma Machine

 🇩🇪 Germany

Enigma developed from commercial machines into several military systems. Marian Rejewski reconstructed the German military machine in 1932; Polish, British and Allied teams continued the work against changing procedures and keys.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/enigma.html>)

1922

##### M-94 Cylinder Cipher Device

🇺🇸 US Army

The M-94, adopted by the US Army in 1922, used 25 alphabet disks. It resembles Jefferson’s earlier unpublished wheel but was independently developed.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/m-94.html>)

1926

##### KRYHA Machine

🇩🇪🇺🇸 Germany / US commercial

Kryha’s clockwork cipher devices used irregularly moving alphabets. Friedman and colleagues attacked a published challenge in 1933; this widget uses generated settings.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kryha.html>)

1929

##### Hill Cipher

🇺🇸 United States

Hill’s 1929 cipher mixes groups of letters using an invertible matrix modulo 26. Suitable matched plaintext blocks can expose the key by linear algebra.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/hill.html>)

Early 1930s

##### Japanese Navy IKA

Japan

A naval cipher studied through intercepted traffic. Its reconstructed behaviour, an American analog and its unresolved physical design are distinct kinds of evidence.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/ika.html>)

World War II

1940

##### Siemens Geheimschreiber T52

🇩🇪 Germany

Beurling’s 1940 analysis of intercepted Siemens traffic preceded the establishment of FRA. T52 variants differ in stepping and circuitry; irregular stepping should not be assigned to every version.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/geheimschreiber.html>)

1940s

##### Lorenz Cipher & Colossus

 🇩🇪🇬🇧 Germany / UK

Lorenz SZ40/42: Tiltman recovered messages and key from a 1941 depth; Tutte and the Research Section inferred the structure by early 1942; Colossus accelerated wheel-setting from February 1944.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/lorenz.html>)

1940 reconstruction

##### Grotjan’s Purple Breakthrough

 🇺🇸 Washington · Signal Intelligence Service

Genevieve Grotjan’s September 1940 insight contributed to the US Army SIS team’s reconstruction of PURPLE. Its six/twenty switching groups were not simply vowels versus consonants.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/purple.html>)

1942

##### Hagelin M-209

🇺🇸 US Army

M-209 US production begins in 1942, following 1940 trials — the US Army's portable Hagelin C-38 with six co-prime pin-wheels and a 27-bar lug cage. Broken in the field in WWII.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/m209.html>)

1942–1945

##### Navajo Code Talkers

 🇺🇸 Pacific Theater

Navajo code talkers used a specialized military vocabulary and spelling alphabet during World War II. Their language and the constructed code were distinct layers.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/navajo-code-talkers.html>)

1943–1980

##### VENONA Project

🇺🇸 Arlington Hall / NSA

VENONA analysed intercepted Soviet messages, chiefly from the 1940s, by exploiting duplicated pad material. The project ran from 1943 to 1980.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/venona.html>)

Modern Cryptography

1949

##### Shannon's Secrecy Theory

 🇺🇸 United States

Claude Shannon publishes *"Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems"* (classified 1945, published 1949) — the mathematical foundation of modern cryptography. He formalizes perfect secrecy, including the correctly used one-time pad, and describes confusion and diffusion as cipher-design principles.

1952

##### KL-7 ADONIS

🇺🇸 NSA / NATO

KL-7: an American eight-rotor cipher machine with irregular stepping and re-entry. Stolen key material compromised traffic during the Walker espionage case.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kl-7.html>)

1953 message / 1957 recovery

##### VIC Cipher

🇷🇺 Soviet Union

Information from Häyhänen’s defection enabled the Hollow Nickel message recovery in 1957. The linked exhibit separates historical VIC procedures from a simplified browser model.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/vic.html>)

1956

##### Fialka M-125

🇷🇺 Soviet Union / Warsaw Pact

Fialka was a Soviet ten-rotor machine with variant-specific alphabets, stepping and a punched-card permutation. The browser uses a simplified Latin-alphabet model.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/fialka.html>)

Historical letter-pad system · dates unverified

##### Diana Cryptosystem

Trigraph lookup convention

A public trigraph table can be used with private, one-use pad letters. The table itself is not the secret pad; the exhibit demonstrates the modulo-26 relation without establishing deployment dates.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/diana-cryptosystem.html>)

1965 POW use

##### Tap Code

🇺🇸 Adopted by POWs in Korea, Vietnam

US prisoners in Vietnam used a 5×5 tap-code convention, communicating row and column counts through knocks. This documented use does not date the origin of every coordinate tapping system.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/tap-code.html>)

1969 / Solved 2020

##### Zodiac Z-340 Cipher

 🇺🇸 San Francisco

Z408 was solved by the Hardens in 1969. Z340 combines homophonic substitution with transposition and exceptions; Oranchak, Blake and Van Eycke announced its solution in 2020.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/zodiac.html>)

1976

##### Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange

 🇺🇸 United States

Diffie and Hellman published New Directions in Cryptography in 1976. Their key-agreement construction and public-key vision transformed public research. GCHQ’s earlier classified work had distinct contributions by Ellis, Cocks and Williamson; authentication remains a separate protocol requirement.

1977

##### RSA & DES

 🇺🇸 United States

RSA was publicly introduced in 1977, and NBS standardised DES that year. Public-key encryption, signatures and symmetric block encryption serve different purposes. Cocks’s related classified proposal at GCHQ preceded public RSA research.

1980s popularisation

##### ROT13 on Usenet

🌐 Usenet

ROT13 became popular on Usenet as a spoiler obscurer in the 1980s. It is the self-inverse Caesar shift of 13. One operation toggles text in and out.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rot13.html>)

1990

##### Kryptos at CIA Headquarters

 🇺🇸 Langley, Virginia

Kryptos: K1–K3 publicly solved; K4 plaintext recovered from an archive in 2025, without a publicly demonstrated cryptanalytic solution.

 [View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/kryptos.html>)

1994

##### Shor's Algorithm

🇺🇸 Bell Labs

Peter Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms. A sufficiently large, fault-tolerant quantum computer could defeat RSA and conventional Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve systems. Post-quantum alternatives include lattice-based ML-KEM and ML-DSA and hash-based SLH-DSA, standardized in 2024.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/lattices-svp.html>)

1999

##### Solitaire / Pontifex

🇺🇸 Schneier

Solitaire / Pontifex (1999) — Bruce Schneier's hand cipher driven by a 54-card deck (written for Cryptonomicon). Crowley reported adjacent repeated output letters at about 1/22.5 rather than the 1/26 uniform expectation.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/solitaire.html>)

2001

##### AES Standardized

 🇧🇪 Belgium / 🇺🇸 NIST

NIST began the AES selection process in 1997, selected Rijndael in October 2000 and published FIPS 197 in November 2001. The standard and the selection announcement are distinct milestones.

2005

##### SHA-1 Collision Attack

 🇨🇳 China

Xiaoyun Wang and team demonstrate theoretical collision attacks against SHA-1, beginning the transition to SHA-256 and SHA-3. A practical collision was demonstrated by the CWI and Google SHAttered team in 2017.

2005

##### Learning With Errors

🇮🇱 Tel Aviv University

Oded Regev introduces Learning With Errors: noisy modular equations hide a secret vector. His result connects suitable LWE parameters to worst-case lattice problems through a quantum reduction. Hardness depends on parameters; noise is not sufficient by itself. The later ML-KEM and ML-DSA standards use structured module problems, with additional assumptions for signatures.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/hall-of-foundations/learning-with-errors.html>)

2013

##### Snowden Revelations

 🌍 Global

The 2013 disclosures intensified public debate about surveillance and communications security. HTTPS protects a connection to its TLS endpoint; it is not the same as end-to-end encryption between messaging users.

Post-Quantum Standardisation

2016–2024

##### Post-Quantum Cryptography

 🌍 Global · NIST

NIST launches the Post-Quantum Cryptography project in 2016. In 2024, ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) are standardized — intended to resist known classical and quantum attacks, under their respective assumptions.

Undated Origins and Teaching Models

Date undocumented

##### Rail Fence Cipher

🌍 Origins undocumented

Rail Fence transposes a message along a zigzag route. Rail count, offset conventions and message length define the search; there is no universal ten-rail maximum.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/rail-fence.html>)

Historical attribution unverified

##### Geʿez Context and a Teaching Model

🇪🇹 Ethiopian Highlands

The interactive uses a modern Latin-letter substitution. No identified manuscript authenticates it as a particular Geʿez monastic cipher.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/amharic-ge-ez-ciphers.html>)

Date undocumented

##### Running-Key Cipher

🌍 Europe

A running-key construction uses a passage of text as key material. Natural-language keys have statistical structure and are not uniformly random one-time pads.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/running-key.html>)

Date undocumented

##### Columnar Transposition

🌍 Military Use

Explore columnar transposition and multiple anagramming: rearrange column strips across three synthetic same-key intercepts and compare a different-key control.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/columnar.html>)

Origin not established

##### Straddling Checkerboard

🇷🇺 Russia

A keyed variable-length digit substitution gives selected letters one digit and others two. It is a component of historical hand systems, including VIC, rather than a complete secure cipher by itself.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/straddling-checkerboard.html>)

Date undocumented

##### Fractionated Morse

🌍 Telegraph Era

Fractionated Morse — converts text to Morse, regroups dots, dashes, and separators in trigrams, then substitutes via a keyed alphabet. Broken by trigram stats.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/fractionated-morse.html>)

Origin not established

##### Two-Square Cipher

🇫🇷 France

Two-square uses two keyed 5×5 squares to encipher letter pairs. This demo follows the ACA horizontal rectangle rule and discloses its extra filler-escape convention.

[View exhibit →](<https://ciphermuseum.com/ciphers/two-square.html>)

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

```javascript

(function() {
  // Card click navigation
  document.querySelectorAll('.tl-card[data-href]').forEach(function(card) {
    card.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
      if (e.target.closest('a')) return;
      window.location.href = card.dataset.href;
    });
  });

  var legend = document.querySelector('.tl-legend');
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.tl-legend-item[data-filter]');
  var events = document.querySelectorAll('.tl-event[data-era]');
  var headers = document.querySelectorAll('.tl-era-header');

  // Era legend — click scrolls to era section (navigation, not toggle)
  items.forEach(function(item) {
    item.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
      e.preventDefault();
      var era = item.dataset.filter;
      var target = document.getElementById('era-' + era);
      if (target) {
        target.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'start' });
      }
    });
  });

  // Scroll-spy — highlight current era in legend
  var eraHeaders = Array.from(headers);
  function updateScrollSpy() {
    var scrollY = window.scrollY + 180;
    var currentEra = null;
    for (var i = eraHeaders.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
      if (eraHeaders[i].offsetTop <= scrollY) {
        currentEra = eraHeaders[i].id.replace('era-', '');
        break;
      }
    }
    items.forEach(function(item) {
      item.classList.toggle('active', item.dataset.filter === currentEra);
    });
  }

  // Sticky shadow on legend
  var legendTop = legend.offsetTop;
  function updateSticky() {
    legend.classList.toggle('stuck', window.scrollY > legendTop - 62);
  }

  var ticking = false;
  window.addEventListener('scroll', function() {
    if (!ticking) {
      requestAnimationFrame(function() {
        updateScrollSpy();
        updateSticky();
        ticking = false;
      });
      ticking = true;
    }
  }, { passive: true });

  updateScrollSpy();
})();
```

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

'use strict';
(function(){
  var TOURS = [
    {id:'mathematics', file:'mathematics.json'},
    {id:'foundations', file:'foundations.json'},
    {id:'wartime',     file:'wartime.json'},
    {id:'hacker',      file:'hacker.json'},
    {id:'unsolved-culture', file:'unsolved-culture.json'},
    {id:'writing-systems', file:'writing-systems.json'},
    {id:'working-not-secure', file:'working-not-secure.json'}
  ];

  var LS_PREFIX = 'ciphermuseum.tours.';
  var grid = document.getElementById('tourGrid');

  function getVisitedCount(id, total){
    try{
      var arr = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(LS_PREFIX + id + '.visited')) || [];
      if(!Array.isArray(arr)) return 0;
      return arr.filter(function(idx, i){
        return Number.isInteger(idx) && idx >= 0 && idx < total && arr.indexOf(idx) === i;
      }).length;
    } catch(e){ return 0; }
  }

  function escapeHTML(s){
    var d = document.createElement('div');
    d.appendChild(document.createTextNode(s));
    return d.innerHTML;
  }

  TOURS.forEach(function(t){
    if (typeof fetch !== 'function') return;
    fetch(t.file)
      .then(function(r){ if(!r.ok) throw new Error('HTTP '+r.status); return r.json(); })
      .then(function(data){
        var visited = getVisitedCount(t.id, data.stops.length);
        var pct = Math.round((visited / data.stops.length)*100);
        var tile = document.createElement('a');
        tile.href = 'tour.html?tour=' + encodeURIComponent(t.id);
        tile.className = 'tour-tile';
        tile.innerHTML =
          '<span class="tour-icon">' + escapeHTML(data.icon) + '</span>' +
          '<h2 class="tour-name">' + escapeHTML(data.title) + '</h2>' +
          '<p class="tour-blurb">' + escapeHTML(data.description) + '</p>' +
          '<div class="tour-meta">' + data.stops.length + ' stops · ' + visited + ' visited</div>' +
          '<div class="tour-progress-bar"><div class="tour-progress-fill" style="width:' + pct + '%"></div></div>';
        grid.appendChild(tile);
      })
      .catch(function(){ /* skip tours that fail to load rather than break the grid */ });
  });
})();
```

#### Embedded script 1 (JavaScript)

Source text, not a record of every rendered state. Any ebook URL is replaced by a stable omission ID; redacted code is for inspection, not execution.

```javascript

'use strict';
(function(){
  var LS_PREFIX = 'ciphermuseum.tours.';

  /* Parse ?tour=mathematics from URL */
  var params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
  var tourId = params.get('tour') || 'mathematics';
  /* Whitelist valid tour IDs */
  var VALID_TOURS = ['mathematics','wartime','hacker','unsolved-culture','foundations','writing-systems','working-not-secure'];
  if(VALID_TOURS.indexOf(tourId) === -1) tourId = 'mathematics';

  var currentStop = 0;
  var tourData = null;
  var sessionVisited = null;

  function getVisited(){
    if(sessionVisited !== null) return sessionVisited.slice();
    try{
      var saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(LS_PREFIX + tourId + '.visited'));
      if(!Array.isArray(saved)) return [];
      return saved.filter(function(idx, i){
        return Number.isInteger(idx) && idx >= 0 && idx < tourData.stops.length && saved.indexOf(idx) === i;
      });
    } catch(e){ return []; }
  }
  function markVisited(idx){
    var arr = getVisited();
    if(arr.indexOf(idx)===-1) arr.push(idx);
    sessionVisited = arr;
    try{ localStorage.setItem(LS_PREFIX+tourId+'.visited', JSON.stringify(arr)); }
    catch(e){ /* Continue the tour with progress held for this page. */ }
  }

  function render(){
    if(!tourData) return;
    var stops = tourData.stops;
    var visited = getVisited();

    /* Header */
    document.getElementById('tourSub').textContent = 'Guided Tour · ' + tourData.icon;
    document.getElementById('tourTitle').textContent = tourData.title;
    document.getElementById('tourIntro').textContent = tourData.description;
    document.title = tourData.title + ' — The Cipher Museum';

    /* Sidebar list */
    var list = document.getElementById('stopList');
    list.innerHTML = '';
    stops.forEach(function(s, i){
      var li = document.createElement('li');
      li.textContent = s.label;
      if(i === currentStop) li.className = 'active';
      else if(visited.indexOf(i) !== -1) li.className = 'visited';
      li.addEventListener('click', function(){ currentStop = i; render(); });
      list.appendChild(li);
    });

    /* Main card */
    var stop = stops[currentStop];
    markVisited(currentStop);
    document.getElementById('tourCard').innerHTML =
      '<div class="tour-stop-num">Stop ' + (currentStop+1) + ' of ' + stops.length + '</div>' +
      '<h2 class="tour-stop-title">' + escapeHTML(stop.label) + '</h2>' +
      '<p class="tour-stop-note">' + escapeHTML(stop.note) + '</p>' +
      '<a class="tour-visit-link" href="' + escapeAttr(stop.href) + '">Visit Exhibit →</a>';

    /* Nav */
    document.getElementById('prevBtn').disabled = (currentStop === 0);
    document.getElementById('nextBtn').disabled = (currentStop === stops.length - 1);
    document.getElementById('tourProg').textContent = (currentStop+1) + ' / ' + stops.length;
  }

  document.getElementById('prevBtn').addEventListener('click', function(){
    if(currentStop > 0){ currentStop--; render(); }
  });
  document.getElementById('nextBtn').addEventListener('click', function(){
    if(tourData && currentStop < tourData.stops.length - 1){ currentStop++; render(); }
  });

  function escapeHTML(s){
    var d = document.createElement('div');
    d.appendChild(document.createTextNode(s));
    return d.innerHTML;
  }
  function escapeAttr(s){
    return s.replace(/&/g,'&amp;').replace(/"/g,'&quot;').replace(/</g,'&lt;').replace(/>/g,'&gt;');
  }

  /* Load tour JSON */
  if (typeof fetch !== 'function') {
    document.getElementById('tourTitle').textContent = 'Tour Unavailable';
    document.getElementById('tourCard').innerHTML = '<p style="color:var(--tx3)">Your browser does not support modern features required for tours. <a href="index.html" style="color:var(--gold)">View all tours →</a></p>';
  } else {
  fetch(tourId + '.json')
    .then(function(r){ if(!r.ok) throw new Error('Tour not found'); return r.json(); })
    .then(function(data){ tourData = data; render(); })
    .catch(function(err){
      document.getElementById('tourTitle').textContent = 'Tour Not Found';
      document.getElementById('tourCard').innerHTML = '<p style="color:var(--tx3)">Could not load tour data. <a href="index.html" style="color:var(--gold)">View all tours →</a></p>';
    });
  }
})();
```

```json
    "Abstract and §§1–4 summary, SAC 2019: an active man-in-the-middle during pairing modifies the y coordinate, which the user-checked numeric comparison does not cover; setting y = 0 gives a point of order 2 and two possible shared secrets, both known to the attacker; the encryption keys of about 50% of pairing attempts are compromised while the other 50% fail to pair; both devices must be vulnerable; vendors patched and the specification now requires public-key validation."
  ],
  "scope": "Abstract and summary verified. This deduces the session shared secret; unlike the classical invalid-curve attack it does NOT recover a long-term private key. Historical: treat as a worked example of unvalidated input, not a current advisory."
}
```

```javascript
/* ==========================================================================
   crypto-algebra.js — pure logic for Exhibits 153-156, no DOM.
   Polynomial rings (ML-KEM/ML-DSA structure), Lagrange interpolation
   (Shamir), and the bilinearity identity for pairings.
   Exposed on window.CryptoAlgebra (browser) and module.exports (Node/CI).
   ========================================================================== */
(function (root) {
  "use strict";

  function mod(n, q) { return ((n % q) + q) % q; }

  // Modular inverse of a mod p (p prime), by extended search. Small p only.
  function modInv(a, p) {
    a = mod(a, p);
    for (let t = 1; t < p; t++) if (mod(a * t, p) === 1) return t;
    return null;
  }

  // ---- Multiplicative order & primitive roots (Exhibit 143) ----
  // The successive powers g^1..g^(p-1) mod p; g is a primitive root when
  // they visit every nonzero residue.
  function powersOf(g, p) {
    const out = []; let x = 1;
    for (let i = 1; i < p; i++) { x = mod(x * g, p); out.push(x); }
    return out;
  }
  function isPrimitiveRoot(g, p) {
    return new Set(powersOf(g, p)).size === p - 1;
  }

  // ---- Polynomial ring R_q = Z_q[X] / (X^n + 1) ----
  // Negacyclic convolution: X^n = -1, so a term of degree k >= n wraps to
  // degree k-n with a sign flip. Coefficients reduced mod q.
  function ringMul(a, b, n, q) {
    const c = new Array(n).fill(0);
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        let k = i + j, sign = 1;
        if (k >= n) { k -= n; sign = -1; }
        c[k] = mod(c[k] + sign * a[i] * b[j], q);
      }
    }
    return c;
  }

  function ringAdd(a, b, n, q) {
    const c = new Array(n).fill(0);
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) c[i] = mod((a[i] || 0) + (b[i] || 0), q);
    return c;
  }

  // ---- Lagrange interpolation (Shamir's Secret Sharing) ----
  // Evaluate the unique polynomial through the given points at x = 0,
  // all arithmetic mod p. points: [[x,y], ...]. Returns the secret f(0), or null when a denominator has no inverse.
  function lagrangeAtZero(points, p) {
    let secret = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < points.length; i++) {
      let num = 1, den = 1;
      for (let j = 0; j < points.length; j++) {
        if (i === j) continue;
        num = mod(num * (-points[j][0]), p);
        den = mod(den * (points[i][0] - points[j][0]), p);
      }
      const inv = modInv(den, p);
      if (inv === null) return null;
      secret = mod(secret + points[i][1] * mod(num * inv, p), p);
    }
    return secret;
  }

  // Evaluate a polynomial (coeffs low->high) at x, mod p.
  function polyEval(coeffs, x, p) {
    let acc = 0;
    for (let i = coeffs.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) acc = mod(acc * x + coeffs[i], p);
    return acc;
  }

  // ---- Pairing bilinearity (multiplicative model) ----
  function powmod(g, e, m) {
    let r = 1; g = mod(g, m);
    while (e > 0) { if (e & 1) r = mod(r * g, m); g = mod(g * g, m); e = Math.floor(e / 2); }
    return r;
  }
  // Verify e(aP, bQ) = e(P, Q)^(ab) in a toy multiplicative target group.
  // base plays the role of e(P,Q). Returns { viaProduct, viaChain, equal }.
  function pairingCheck(a, b, base, m) {
    const viaProduct = powmod(base, a * b, m);          // e(P,Q)^(ab)
    const viaChain = powmod(powmod(base, a, m), b, m);   // (e(P,Q)^a)^b
    return { viaProduct, viaChain, equal: viaProduct === viaChain };
  }

  const api = {
    mod, modInv,
    powersOf, isPrimitiveRoot,
    ringMul, ringAdd,
    lagrangeAtZero, polyEval,
    powmod, pairingCheck
  };

  if (typeof module !== "undefined" && module.exports) module.exports = api;
  else root.CryptoAlgebra = api;

})(typeof self !== "undefined" ? self : this);
```

```javascript
/* ==========================================================================
   ec-math.js — pure elliptic-curve logic for Exhibits 142 & 150, no DOM.
   Curve arithmetic over F_p (point enumeration, chord-and-tangent group
   law) and over the reals (the hand-drawn construction in Exhibit 150).
   Exposed on window.ECMath (browser) and module.exports (Node/CI).
   ========================================================================== */
(function (root) {
  "use strict";

  function mod(n, p) { return ((n % p) + p) % p; }

  // Modular inverse of k mod p (p prime), by extended search. Small p only.
  function modInv(k, p) {
    k = mod(k, p);
    for (let t = 1; t < p; t++) if (mod(k * t, p) === 1) return t;
    return null;
  }

  // ---- The curve over F_p: y^2 = x^3 + ax + b ----
  function ecRhs(x, a, b, p) { return mod(x * x * x + a * x + b, p); }

  // All affine points (the point at infinity is represented as null).
  function ecPoints(a, b, p) {
    const pts = [];
    for (let x = 0; x < p; x++) {
      const r = ecRhs(x, a, b, p);
      for (let y = 0; y < p; y++) if (mod(y * y, p) === r) pts.push([x, y]);
    }
    return pts;
  }

  // Chord-and-tangent addition over F_p. null is the point at infinity.
  function ecAdd(P, Q, a, p) {
    if (P === null) return Q;
    if (Q === null) return P;
    if (P[0] === Q[0] && mod(P[1] + Q[1], p) === 0) return null;
    let m;
    if (P[0] === Q[0] && P[1] === Q[1]) {
      m = mod(mod(3 * P[0] * P[0] + a, p) * modInv(mod(2 * P[1], p), p), p);
    } else {
      m = mod(mod(Q[1] - P[1], p) * modInv(mod(Q[0] - P[0], p), p), p);
    }
    const x3 = mod(m * m - P[0] - Q[0], p);
    const y3 = mod(m * (P[0] - x3) - P[1], p);
    return [x3, y3];
  }

  function ecIsOnCurve(P, a, b, p) {
    return P === null || mod(P[1] * P[1], p) === ecRhs(P[0], a, b, p);
  }

  // ---- The curve over the reals (Exhibit 150) ----
  function curveY2(x, a, b) { return x * x * x + a * x + b; }

  // The group law drawn by hand: line through P and Q, third intersection,
  // reflect across the x-axis. Returns { third, sum, slope }.
  function ecAddReal(P, Q, a) {
    // A vertical chord (including a vertical tangent at y=0) reaches O.
    if (Math.abs(P[0] - Q[0]) < 1e-9 && Math.abs(P[1] + Q[1]) < 1e-9) {
      return { third: null, sum: null, slope: null };
    }
    let m;
    if (Math.abs(P[0] - Q[0]) < 1e-9 && Math.abs(P[1] - Q[1]) < 1e-9) {
      m = (3 * P[0] * P[0] + a) / (2 * P[1]);
    } else {
      m = (Q[1] - P[1]) / (Q[0] - P[0]);
    }
    const x3 = m * m - P[0] - Q[0];
    const y3 = m * (P[0] - x3) - P[1];
    return { third: [x3, -y3], sum: [x3, y3], slope: m };
  }

  // Smoothness: the discriminant -16(4a^3 + 27b^2) must be nonzero,
  // or the curve has a cusp/node and the group law breaks down.
  function ecIsSmooth(a, b) { return 4 * a * a * a + 27 * b * b !== 0; }

  const api = {
    mod, modInv,
    ecRhs, ecPoints, ecAdd, ecIsOnCurve,
    curveY2, ecAddReal, ecIsSmooth
  };

  if (typeof module !== "undefined" && module.exports) module.exports = api;
  else root.ECMath = api;

})(typeof self !== "undefined" ? self : this);
```

```javascript
/* ==========================================================================
   lattice-math.js — pure cryptographic-foundations logic, no DOM
   Shared by lattices-svp.html and closest-vector.html.
   Every function here is deterministic and unit-testable in isolation:
   feed it numbers, get numbers back. UI/SVG code lives in the pages.
   Exposed on window.LatticeMath (browser) and module.exports (Node/CI).
   ========================================================================== */
(function (root) {
  "use strict";

  // Determinant of the 2x2 basis [b1 b2] (columns). |det| = covolume = points per unit area^-1.
  function det2(b1, b2) {
    return b1[0] * b2[1] - b1[1] * b2[0];
  }

  // Shortest nonzero lattice vector by exhaustive search over |i|,|j| <= R.
  // Returns { x, y, i, j, len } or null if the lattice is degenerate.
  function shortestVector(b1, b2, R) {
    if (det2(b1, b2) === 0) return null;
    R = R || 7;
    var best = Infinity, bv = null;
    for (var i = -R; i <= R; i++) {
      for (var j = -R; j <= R; j++) {
        if (i === 0 && j === 0) continue;
        var x = i * b1[0] + j * b2[0];
        var y = i * b1[1] + j * b2[1];
        var n = x * x + y * y;
        if (n < best) { best = n; bv = { x: x, y: y, i: i, j: j, len: Math.sqrt(n) }; }
      }
    }
    return bv;
  }

  // True closest lattice point to target t={x,y}, exhaustive over the STANDARD
  // integer lattice (the canonical lattice both bases describe). Returns {x,y,dist}.
  function closestPoint(t, R) {
    R = R || 8;
    var best = Infinity, bv = null;
    for (var i = -R; i <= R; i++) {
      for (var j = -R; j <= R; j++) {
        var d = (i - t.x) * (i - t.x) + (j - t.y) * (j - t.y);
        if (d < best) { best = d; bv = { x: i, y: j, dist: Math.sqrt(d) }; }
      }
    }
    return bv;
  }

  // Babai's rounding: express t in the given basis, round each coordinate.
  // Returns the lattice point { x, y, i, j } the rounding lands on.
  // Correct when the basis is short & near-orthogonal; misfires when skewed.
  function babaiRound(t, b1, b2) {
    var det = det2(b1, b2);
    if (det === 0) return null;
    var a = (t.x * b2[1] - t.y * b2[0]) / det;
    var b = (b1[0] * t.y - b1[1] * t.x) / det;
    var ai = Math.round(a), bi = Math.round(b);
    return { x: ai * b1[0] + bi * b2[0], y: ai * b1[1] + bi * b2[1], i: ai, j: bi };
  }

  // LWE round-trip: hide lattice point v={x,y} under noise vector e={x,y},
  // then try to recover v by Babai-rounding (v+e) in the given basis.
  // Returns { recovered:{x,y,i,j}, ok:boolean, noisyTarget:{x,y} }.
  function lweRecover(v, e, b1, b2) {
    var t = { x: v.x + e.x, y: v.y + e.y };
    var r = babaiRound(t, b1, b2);
    return { recovered: r, ok: (r !== null && r.x === v.x && r.y === v.y), noisyTarget: t };
  }

  // Whether Babai in this basis returns the TRUE closest point for target t.
  function babaiIsCorrect(t, b1, b2) {
    var r = babaiRound(t, b1, b2);
    var c = closestPoint(t);
    return r !== null && r.x === c.x && r.y === c.y;
  }

  var api = {
    det2: det2,
    shortestVector: shortestVector,
    closestPoint: closestPoint,
    babaiRound: babaiRound,
    lweRecover: lweRecover,
    babaiIsCorrect: babaiIsCorrect
  };

  if (typeof module !== "undefined" && module.exports) module.exports = api;
  else root.LatticeMath = api;

})(typeof self !== "undefined" ? self : this);
```

```javascript
/* ==========================================================================
   lwe-math.js — Learning With Errors: pure logic, no DOM.
   Backs learning-with-errors.html (§157).

   Implements the Regev-style construction that ML-KEM descends from:
     public key : (A, t) with t = A·s + e   (mod q)
     secret key : the short vector s
   Encryption hides a bit behind a large shared term that only s can cancel.

   Every function is deterministic — randomness is injected by the caller as
   explicit vectors, so the CI tests can replay exact cases.
   Exposed on window.LWEMath (browser) and module.exports (Node/CI).
   ========================================================================== */
(function (root) {
  "use strict";

  // Least non-negative residue. JS % is a remainder, not a modulus.
  function mod(a, q) {
    return ((a % q) + q) % q;
  }

  // Centered representative in (-q/2, q/2]. This is the value that matters for
  // noise: 96 mod 97 is "-1 of noise", not "96 of noise".
  function center(a, q) {
    var r = mod(a, q);
    return r > q / 2 ? r - q : r;
  }

  // Modular inverse via extended Euclid. Returns null when gcd(a,q) != 1.
  function modInv(a, q) {
    var t = 0, newT = 1, r = q, newR = mod(a, q);
    while (newR !== 0) {
      var quot = Math.floor(r / newR);
      var tmp = t - quot * newT; t = newT; newT = tmp;
      tmp = r - quot * newR; r = newR; newR = tmp;
    }
    if (r > 1) return null;
    return mod(t, q);
  }

  function dot(a, b, q) {
    var s = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < a.length; i++) s += a[i] * b[i];
    return mod(s, q);
  }

  function matVec(A, v, q) {
    var out = [];
    for (var i = 0; i < A.length; i++) out.push(dot(A[i], v, q));
    return out;
  }

  function transpose(A) {
    var out = [];
    for (var j = 0; j < A[0].length; j++) {
      var row = [];
      for (var i = 0; i < A.length; i++) row.push(A[i][j]);
      out.push(row);
    }
    return out;
  }

  function addVec(a, b, q) {
    var out = [];
    for (var i = 0; i < a.length; i++) out.push(mod(a[i] + b[i], q));
    return out;
  }

  // ---- the LWE sample ------------------------------------------------------
  // t = A·s + e (mod q). With e = 0 this is an ordinary linear system and
  // Gaussian elimination reads s straight off. The error is the whole defence.
  function lweSample(A, s, e, q) {
    return addVec(matVec(A, s, q), e, q);
  }

  // ---- solving -------------------------------------------------------------
  // Exact Gaussian elimination mod prime q. Returns the unique solution to
  // A·x = b, or null if A is singular. Never sees the error term — that is
  // precisely the point: fed a noisy t it returns a confident, wrong answer.
  function gaussianSolve(A, b, q) {
    var n = A.length, i, j, k;
    var M = [];
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      var row = [];
      for (j = 0; j < n; j++) row.push(mod(A[i][j], q));
      row.push(mod(b[i], q));
      M.push(row);
    }
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      var piv = -1;
      for (k = i; k < n; k++) if (M[k][i] !== 0) { piv = k; break; }
      if (piv < 0) return null;
      var tmp = M[i]; M[i] = M[piv]; M[piv] = tmp;
      var inv = modInv(M[i][i], q);
      if (inv === null) return null;
      for (j = i; j <= n; j++) M[i][j] = mod(M[i][j] * inv, q);
      for (k = 0; k < n; k++) {
        if (k === i || M[k][i] === 0) continue;
        var f = M[k][i];
        for (j = i; j <= n; j++) M[k][j] = mod(M[k][j] - f * M[i][j], q);
      }
    }
    var x = [];
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) x.push(M[i][n]);
    return x;
  }

  // ---- encryption ----------------------------------------------------------
  // Encrypt one bit under (A, t). The caller supplies the ephemeral randomness
  // r and the two error terms, so tests can pin down exact ciphertexts.
  //   u = Aᵀ·r + e1
  //   v = t·r  + e2 + m·floor(q/2)
  function encryptBit(A, t, m, r, e1, e2, q) {
    var u = addVec(matVec(transpose(A), r, q), e1, q);
    var v = mod(dot(t, r, q) + e2 + m * Math.floor(q / 2), q);
    return { u: u, v: v };
  }

  // Decrypt with the short secret s. The large term sᵀAᵀr appears in both v
  // and sᵀu and cancels, leaving m·floor(q/2) plus accumulated noise.
  // Returns the centered residual, the recovered bit, and the noise that
  // survived — so a page can show how much of the budget was spent.
  // Distance between two residues measured around the ring, not along the line:
  // 1 and q-1 are two apart, not q-2 apart.
  function ringDist(a, b, q) {
    var d = mod(a - b, q);
    return Math.min(d, q - d);
  }

  function decryptBit(u, v, s, q) {
    var raw = mod(v - dot(s, u, q), q);
    var half = Math.floor(q / 2);
    // Round to whichever ideal — 0 or floor(q/2) — is actually nearer in the
    // ring. A fixed |centered| > q/4 threshold is the usual shorthand, but with
    // an odd q the two ideals are not symmetrically spaced and the shorthand
    // misdecodes at the boundary. Measuring both distances is exact.
    var d0 = ringDist(raw, 0, q), d1 = ringDist(raw, half, q);
    var bit = d1 < d0 ? 1 : 0;
    var noise = center(raw - bit * half, q);
    return { raw: raw, centered: center(raw, q), bit: bit, noise: noise, d0: d0, d1: d1 };
  }

  // The safe bound: while the accumulated error stays STRICTLY below this,
  // decryption is guaranteed correct. At or above it, correctness depends on
  // which side of the ring the error fell — see the tests for the exact claim.
  function noiseBudget(q) {
    return Math.floor(q / 4);
  }

  // The error that actually accumulated, measured against the bit that was
  // SENT. decryptBit's own `noise` is measured against the bit it decoded, so
  // on a failure it reports a small number — correct for what it means, and
  // misleading if you read it as "how much noise was there". Callers that know
  // the true message should use this instead. For odd q, exact boundary
  // behavior also depends on the sent bit, noise direction and tie rule.
  function residualNoise(raw, m, q) {
    return center(raw - m * Math.floor(q / 2), q);
  }

  var api = {
    mod: mod,
    center: center,
    modInv: modInv,
    dot: dot,
    matVec: matVec,
    transpose: transpose,
    addVec: addVec,
    lweSample: lweSample,
    gaussianSolve: gaussianSolve,
    encryptBit: encryptBit,
    decryptBit: decryptBit,
    noiseBudget: noiseBudget,
    residualNoise: residualNoise,
    ringDist: ringDist
  };

  if (typeof module !== "undefined" && module.exports) module.exports = api;
  else root.LWEMath = api;

})(typeof self !== "undefined" ? self : this);
```

- Served SHA-256: `5ffdc2e0aeae9d3c95e393b7bc9f277eaddb7f5e87117cde3f21f6e51cc83a92`
- Readable-source SHA-256: `5ffdc2e0aeae9d3c95e393b7bc9f277eaddb7f5e87117cde3f21f6e51cc83a92`


```javascript
/* THE CIPHER MUSEUM — Artifact Card Renderer */
'use strict';

(function () {
  var path = (location.pathname || '').toLowerCase();
  if (path.indexOf('/ciphers/') === -1) return;

  var file = path.split('/').pop() || '';
  var slug = file.replace(/\.html$/, '');
  if (!slug) return;

  function render() {
    var data = (window.__ARTIFACT_CARDS__ && window.__ARTIFACT_CARDS__.cards) || {};
    var card = data[slug];
    if (!card) return;

    var main = document.getElementById('main-content') || document.querySelector('main');
    if (!main) return;
    if (main.querySelector('.artifact-card')) return;

    var anchor = main.querySelector('.page-hero') || main.firstElementChild;
    if (!anchor) return;

    var section = document.createElement('section');
    section.className = 'artifact-card';
    section.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Artifact card metadata');
    section.setAttribute('data-artifact-slug', slug);

    var title = document.createElement('h2');
    title.className = 'artifact-card-title';
    title.textContent = 'Artifact Card';

    var grid = document.createElement('dl');
    grid.className = 'artifact-card-grid';

    function addField(label, value, trust) {
      var dt = document.createElement('dt');
      dt.className = 'artifact-card-label';
      dt.textContent = label;

      var dd = document.createElement('dd');
      dd.className = 'artifact-card-value';
      if (trust) dd.innerHTML = window.TrustLabels.badge(trust);
      else dd.textContent = value || 'Not specified';

      grid.appendChild(dt);
      grid.appendChild(dd);
    }

    if (card.hall) addField('Hall', card.hall);
    addField('Era', card.era);
    addField('Family', card.family);
    addField('Region', card.region);
    addField('Used By', card.usedBy);
    addField('Key Type', card.keyType);
    addField('Key Idea', card.keyIdea);
    if (card.trust) {
      addField('Trust', card.trust.text, card.trust);
      addField('Security History / Limits', card.securityFailure);
    }
    addField('Modern Lesson', card.modernLesson);

    section.appendChild(title);
    section.appendChild(grid);

    if (anchor.nextSibling) {
      main.insertBefore(section, anchor.nextSibling);
    } else {
      main.appendChild(section);
    }
  }

  // Companion scripts can execute in either order. The generated data bundle
  // announces readiness; a delayed document can also retry the same renderer.
  window.addEventListener('artifact-cards-ready', render);
  document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', render, { once: true });
  render();
})();
```
